INTRODUCTION 
I. the Chairman of the Committee on Home Affairs having .been authorised by the 
Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Thirtieth Report on 
the Action Taken by Government on the recommendations / observations of the Committee , 
contained in its Sixteenth Report on the Demands for Grants (1995-96) of the Ministry of 
Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions, presented to Rajya Sabha on the 8th May, 1996. 
2. The Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions was requested to furnish 
a note on the Action Taken by them in respect of The Committee's recommendations 
contained in paras 9, 11. 12, 14, 15, 18, 19, 21, 22, 24, 26, 27, 28, 32 and 36 of its Sixteenth 
Report : 
3. An Action Taken Note was received from the Ministry in respect of all the 15 
recommendations contained in the Report, on the 30th November, 1995. 
4. The Committee in its meeting held on the 16th January, 1996, had decided to 
consider the said Action Taken Note and to seek clarifications thereon from the Secretary of 
the Ministry. In pursuance of this decision a meeting of the Committee was held on the 
6th March, 1996. 
5. The recommendations/observations contained in this Report are based on the Action 
Taken Note furnished by the Ministry and the presentation made by the Secretary of the 
Ministry before the Committee. 
6. The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its meeting held on 
the 29th March, 1996.

REPORT 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS 
Public EnterpriseS Selection Board 
Vacancies of Chairman and Members In PESB 
1. Recommendation : The Committee, in para 9 of the Sixteenth Report had expressed 
concern that the post of the Chairman PESB has been lying vacant since 1.11.1993. Out of 
the three members , there was only one member and the second member ha~ been appointed 
only recently. This , in the view of the COmmittee, meant, that only one member held :(61 
meetings and made recommendations for 49 Chief Executives and 93 full time Functiomd 
Directors and part time Chairman. This in view of the Committee, assumed significance in 
view of the fact that a total of Rs. 164332 crores (1993-94 figures) of the public money is 
invested in as many as 246 Central Public Enterprises. The Committee had been informed 
that efforts were being made to locute silitable persons to fill up vacancies of the Chairman 
and the member of PESB . The Committee felt that necessary action to fill 'up the vacancies 
had not been taken with due seriousness and recommended that such important posts l{e 
filled up without further delay. 
2. The Ministry, in its Action Taken Note, had reported that out of the 3 posts of 
members, two members were in position now; the second member having joined on 2.2.95. 
The Observations of the Committee regarding the filling up of posts have been brought to 
the notice of the Cabinet Secretary und thqt the matter has also been taken up by him at the 
appropriate level. The Action Taken Note also mentioned that the Members PESB generally 
does not act alone in making recommendation for appointments in Public Enterprises . 
Besides, the Members in the PESB, the Secretary of the Administrative Ministry concerned 
with the public enterprise is also associated. The Secretary of the Ministry, in his deposition 
before the Committee informed that Mr. N. Vittal has been appointed the Chairman, PESB 
with effect from 4th January, 1996. As on 6.3.96 there were two vacant posts of members in 
the PESB and that those might be filled up in about two months' time . He also submitted 
that non-availability of suitable persons was the reason for delay in filling up of vacant posts 
in PESB. 
3. The Committee in its 16th Report had noted with concern that the post of Chairman 
of the PESB had been lying vacant since November 1, 1993. Similarly, full complement of 
members were not in position. The Committee . had, therefore, recommended that such 
important posts should be filled up without further delay. 
4. The Department of Personnd in its Action Taken Note, submitted in November , 
1995, had stated that Committee's observations regarding filling-up of the posts had been 
brought to the notice of the Cabiuct Secretary and the matter had also been taken up by 
him at the appropriate level. 
5. The Secretary , Department of Personnel who deposed before the Committee on 
March 6, 1996, stated that it was difficult to get qualified ·persons for the appointment us 
Chairman and members of the PESD. He udded that the Chairrhan and members , as per the 
resolution for appointments to these posts, should be a distinguished former chief executive 
of a public sector enterprise. There were 246 central public sector enterprises in the country 
and normally chief executives of Schedule 'A' PSUs only were considered for appointment 
to these posts . Therefore , Government had to wait till a suitable person was available from 
amongst the Chairmen of the Central PSUs of Schedule 'A' category. He informed the 
Committee that the post of Chairman had, however, been filled-up on January 4, 1996. The 
incumbent was the Secretary, Department of Electronics , who was due to retire towards the 
end of the month . 
6. During the discussions that followed it emerged that the entire action to .fill-up the

2 
top level of posts in the PESB, namely, Chairman and the members rests with the Cabinet 
Secretary and the Department of Personnel had practically no role to play. The Secretary, 
Personnel, in his deposition had stated that they only intimate to the Cabinet Secretary. 
7. In order to examine the matter in· the correct perspective, the Committee had 
requested the department of Personnel to furnish certain data such as details of qualifica­
tions for appointment to these posts and list of Chairmen and members of PESB during the 
past few years. Unfortunately, till the finalization of the Report, the Committee had not 
received the requisite information from Government. 
8. The Committee notes with deep concern the manner in which the Chairman and 
members of the PESB are appointed by Government. The PESB is charged with the 
responsibility of recommending Board level appointments for the Central Public Sector 
Undertakings, which number 246. Some of the PSUs are in the Core sector of the economy 
and thus occupy a very strategic and cruclal place in the country's economy. Therefore, the 
Committee emphasises the importance and the need of selecting qualified and suitable persons 
to man the top level posts in the PSUs. This would be possible only if PESB itself bas full 
complement of its· members. However, the Committee notes with deep regret that Government 
has handled the matter of manning the PESB with rather cavalier fashion. Over the years 
only lAS officers have been selected as Chairma&inembers of the Board and these too who 
are either retired or were due to J."ftire In the near future. Therefore, it is no w~nder thqt 
performance of the majority of PSUs h~d not been satisfactory. The Committee would, 
therefore, reiterate that timely action should be taken to fdl-up the posts in the PESB, which 
should not necessarily be from the lAS alone. 
Monitoring mechanism in PESB 
9. Recommendation: The Committee, in. para11 of the Sixteenth Report had observed 
that there was no mechanism of monitoring in the PESB regarding implementation of its 
recommendations by the Administrative Ministries. In the absence of such a mechanism, it is 
not understood as to how the PESD can monitor whether or not its recommendations are 
being implemented by the concerned Ministries expeditiously. The Committee was of the 
view that the recommendations of the PESB need to be closely monitored at the level of 
PESB. 
10. In its Action Taken Note the Ministry had stated that, the PESB has since set up a 
mechanism for monitoring the implementation of its recommendations by the Administrative 
Ministries-Departments concerned. lt has formulated a proforma to be filled in and 
furnished by the Administrative Ministries/Departments concerned by the 7th of every 
mo~th, giving details of the action taken by them on its recommendations. This would 
enable the PESB to regularly monitor the progress made by the various Administrative 
Ministries/Departments in implementing the recommendation made by it. 
11. ·The Committee is pleased to note that a monitoring mechanism at the level of PESB 
has been instituted as per its recommendation. The Committee hopes that the PESB will be 
able to monitor effectively whether-. or not. its recommendations are being implemented by the 
concerned Ministries/Departments expedi.tiously. 
Public Grievances 
12. Recommendation (Para 12): Acw-rding to the Ministry's Annual Report (1994-95), 
the Department of Public Grievancc.~s had received a total of 8152 complaints from January­
December 1994, a bulk of which were referred to the concerned Ministries/Departments/ 
State Governments, leaving merely 61 grievances for intensive monitoring and follow-up by 
the Department. The Committee is not uware whether any monitoring was done in respect 
of the referred grievances/complaints. As the nodal Department for public grievances, th~ 
Committee · expects a little more exercise by the Department in this regard. 

3 
13. The Ministry in its Action Taken Note had mentioned that efforts were being made 
for improving the monitoring of the taken up cases from amongst the referred cases. It also 
mentioned that considerable progrct~s hus already· been made in this regard and it will be 
ensured that by the end of the yenr (1995) further substantial number of grievances are 
taken up for active monitoring, with a view to positive redressal of public grievances. The 
Secretary of the Ministry informed the Committee on 6th March , 1996 that as per the 
directions of the Committee, the Department of Public Grievances had taken up 208 
grievances, plus the backlog for intensive monitoring and follow up. 
14. The Committee is of the opinion that the reply of the Ministry is too general. It does 
not indicate specifically the efforts beln& made to improve monitoring of the cases, as well as 
the progress made in cases which have been taken up by the Department of Public 
Grievances. The Committee feels that its direction for taking up a larger number ot 
grievances for intensive monitoring bas not been taken in the right earnest. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry may look into the matter and report back to the 
Committee on the Action Taken in implementing the recommendation. 
Surrender of Posts 
15. Recommendations (Paras 13 & 14): The Ministry had stated that as per instructions 
issued by the Ministry of Finance, the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions

remaining 38 posts identified for surrender, another 14 posts have since been surrendered.

time limit fixed by the Ministry for surrender of the remaining p~sts will be adhered to. 
ExpmdiJure of UPSC 
18. Recomm endation (Para 15): The Committee found that the Demands of the UPSC, 
a 'charged' expenditure, is not included in the detailed Demands for Grants (1995-96) of the 
Ministry. The Committee felt that as the UPSC is under the administrative control of the 
Ministry, the Demands of the UPSC be included, alorigwith the detailed Demands of the 
Ministry, even though the expenditure of the UPSC is 'charged'. Accordingly, the 
Committee recommended that the Demands of the UPSC may be included alongwith the 
detailed Demands of the Ministry- from the next financial year. 
19. The Ministry in its Action Tuken Note submitted that the matter has been 
considered in consultation with the Ministry of Finance and it has been decided to include 
the Demands relating to UPSC, alongwith the Demands of the Ministry of Personnel, from 
the next financial year. 
20. The Committee is pleased to note that its recommendation has been accepted In 
principle and hopes that it will be implemented from the financial year 1996-97. 
Kendriya Bhandar 
Functio11i11g of KeiUiriya Bhandar 
21. Recommendation (Para 18): Notwithstanding the performance and achievements of 
the Kendriya Bhandar, the Committee felt that there is a lot of scope for improvement in its 

4 
functioning. The Committee felt that the J(endriya Bhandar is not being run on professional 
lines and suggested some specific steps to improve their functioning. In the Committee's 
view, issues like proper maintenance of notice boards, upkeep of stores, especially display of 
goods, cleanliness, maintenance of stores, availability of goods, quality of goods, behaviour 
of sales staff and the issue of having uniform timings and weekly off in all the stores need to 
be seriously looked into, to make such stores consumer friendly and run on professional 
lines. 
22. The Ministry in its Action Taken Note outlined the following steps, taken to 
implement the items of improvement suggested by the Committee:-
(a) Special training courses are belf1g arranged for the staff to inculcate professional 
attitudes and impart professional skills to them; 
(b) Face lifting of stores is being done and 24 stores were earmarked for this purpose 
in 1995; 
(c) A food testing laboratory has been opened in Kendriya Bhandar HQs to provide 
for large scale pre-testing of samples. Samples lifted from stores are also tested in 
the laboratory. 788 such ~ samples were tested from 1.4.95 to 31.7.95 and only 12 
did not come up to the prescribed specifications; 
{d) Digital weighing and packing machine has been installed to ensure quality by 
packing goods hygienically; 
(e) As regards limited choice of goods in most of the stores, the Ministry submitted 
that Kendriya Bhandar wus selling more than 2000 consumer, and grocery items 
through its stores. As fair price shops are attached to these stores and as most of 
the stores are situated in Type I and Type Ii staff quarters, the accommodation 
available does not permit the range of goods made available, being expanded; 
{f) The Ministry felt that having uniform timings and weekly off for all the stores was 
not feasible and it will not suit the customers as timings and weekly off are decided 
by stores' location and sales activities. 
23. The Committee has taken note of the steps initiated by the Ministry to implement Us 
recommendations. It feels that constant efforts should be made to improve functioning of the 
Kendriya Bhandar and that they should be run along professional lines. 
Installation of Alpha Numeric Machines in Kendriya Bhandars 
24. Recommendation (Para 19): The Committee had recommended that Alpha Numeric 
Machines, which also print the name of the items purchased and their prices on the cash 
memos, should be installed in all the 84 stores of Kendriya Bhandar within the financial year 
(1995-96). In view of the Committee, it should not be difficult to achieve as the financial 
position of Kendriya Bhandar was sound. 
25. The Ministry in its Action Taken No~e reported that it has been decided in principle 
to provide Alpha Numeric machines in ull the 84 ~tores in a phased manner in the financial 
year 1995-96. The Ministry also reported that this would involve a capital expenditure of 
Rs. 27 lakhs, apart from maintenance expenditure of Rs. 4 lakhs per annum. 
26. The Committee would like to know the progress made so far in regard to installation 
of Alpha Numeric machines in all ·the 84 stores.

Vice Chairman and members of Tribunal are filled up expeditiously and that action be

the delay in setting up additional courts in the Principal Bench and in the AUahabad Bench of

REPORT 
COMMITTEE FOR IMPLEMENTING LEGAL AID SCHEME (CILAS) 
Recommendation: 
From the information furnished by the Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs 
and deposition made by its representatives, the Committee notes that the Minimum income 
ceiling prescribed by CILAS for providing free legal aid to the poor and needy has been 
revised by some States viz. Assam (Rs 10000), Jammu and Kashmir (Rs. 7200), Karnataka 
(Rs. 8000), Punjab (Rs. 18000), Sikkim (Rs. 78CX>) and West Bengal (Rs. 7000), 
Maharashtra and l laryana had already revised the income ceiling for the purpose. The 
Committee has abo been apprised that the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 contains a 
provision for enhancement of income ceiling from Rs. fiOOO to Rs. 9000 or such higher 
amount as the State Governments may prescribed if the case is before a court other than the 
Supreme Court and from R'>. 9000 to 12000 or '>Uch higher amount as the Central 
Government may prescribe if the case IS before the Supreme Court. The Committee is of the 
view that if benefits are to reach to a larger number of people across the country, examples 
set by the above States should be followed by the remaining States. 
2. The Committee has been informed that the Partial Legal Aid Scheme for middle 
income group is optional and is on self-financing basis with no additional cost to the public 
exchequer. It is Imtwlly applicable for cases pending or intended to be filed in the High 
Courts and Supn.:m2 Court. In the beginning, the scheme was adopted by Delhi, 1 iaryana 
and Punjab. Later, Maharashtra also adopted the scheme on 5.1.1995. The maximum 
income ceiling prescribed for eligibility under the scheme by these States is Rs. 75,00<Y-, 
Rs. l.OO,{)()(Y-, Rs. 75,0()(Y- and Rs. 1.20,(}()(Y- respectively. The Supreme Court Legal Aid 
(middle income group) Committee has also adopted the scheme and the maximum income 
ceiling prescribed by it is Rs. 1.20,(X)(Y-. 
3. The Committee has, in its 11th Report on the Demands for Grants (1994-95) of the 
Ministry of Law, Just ace and Company Affairs recommended that the Partial Legal Aid 
Scheme should be adopted by more and more States and extended to the subordinate courts 
also as done in the case of Haryana. The Committee, in this context, finds that the response 
is not very encouraging as only one State i.e. Maharashtra has so far. come forward to adopt 
the scheme. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its earlier recommendation that the 
scheme should be implemented by more and more States and extended to subordinate courts 
also. 
4. The Ministrv Ill tts Actton Taken Note has stated:-
"The State Legal Aid and Advtce Boards have been requested to mJtaate action for 
giving effect to the recommendations of the Parliamentary Committee." 
1 • 

2 
5. The Additional Secretary, Department of Legal Affairs, while appearing before the 
Committee and clarifying the queries relating to this issue, stated:-
"The State of Andhra Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh, Rajasthan and Sikkim have fixed a 
limit of Rs. 15,000 on the basis of the recommendations of this Committee. The State 
of Punjab has fixed Rs. 18,000 as the minimum income ceiling for providing free legal 
aid to the poor and needy." 
6. The Committee notes that overall position with regard to fixing minimum income 
ceiling by the States for providing free legal aid to the poor and needy is still not encouraging 
as only a few states have come forward to adopt the scheme. This is primarily because of the 
reason that the Ministry bas not taken any concrete steps except requesting the State Legal 
Aid and Advice Boards. The Committee, therefore, desires that the Ministry should evolve 
suitable mechanism for effective coordination between the Centre and the States so that the 
progress made by the State Legal Aid and Advice Boards may be monitored continuously. 
ENFORCEMENT OF LEGAL SERVICES AUTHORITIES ACT 
Recommendation: 
7. On a query raised regarding the present status of the enforcement of the Legal 
Services Authorities Act, the Committee has been apprised that the Act is yet to come into 
force. The Committee has also been apprised that the Draft Model Rules for the State Legal 
Services Authorities Act drafted by the CILAS have been forwarded to the State Legal Aid 
and Advice Boards and the Legislative Department for finalisation/vetting. The Act will be 
brought into force only after the rules have been framed and approved by the competent 
authorities. The Committee feels that the Legal Services Authorities Act, if brought into 
force, will assume special significance as it is intended to provide statutory basis to the 
CILAS. The Committee therefore, strongly urges upon the Government to expedite its 
enforcement. 
8. In its Action Taken Note, the Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs has 
stated:-
"The proposal to enforce the Act is under process in consultation with the Legislative 
Department." 
9. The Additional Secretary, Department of Legal Affairs, in his deposition clarified as 
under:-
"The Legal Service Authorities Act has now been brought into force on 
9th November, 1995 except Chapter 3. Chapter 3 deals with the constitution of the 
Legal Services Authority for the States. The States are being requested to frame the 
rules as early as possible." 
10. From the explanation of the representative of the Ministry, the Committee notes 
that notwithstanding the Legal Services Authorities Act assuming special significance, the 
Ministry has not made serious efforts to enforce it in letter and spirit. As of now, the Act 
has been brought into force partially with the Chapter 3 yet remaining to be enforced subject 
to framing or fules by the States. The Committee, therefore, stresses the need for early 
enforcement of the Act and calls upon the Ministry to take necessary steps in this direction. 
INCOME TAX APPELLATE TRIBUNAL (ITAT) 
Recommendation: 
The Law Secretary in his deposition informed the Committee that the total number of 
pending cases before the ITAT as on 1.2.1995 was, 2,79,722. One of the reasons for 
accumulation of the cases is the number of vacancies of the members in the !TAT. Out of 
the total sanctioned strength of 76 members (38 Judicial and 38 Accountant members), 

3 
18 posts (9 posts of Judicial and 9 posts of Accountant members) are vacant at present. The 
Committee has also been apprised that presently there are 38 benches of the IT AT spread 
over 19 cities . The Ministry has accepted that the present strength of 38 benches was fixed in 
the year 1972 when the pendency of the cases before the Tribunal was less than one lakh . 
Over the years, there has been increasing gap ~tween the rate of institution and the rate of 
disposal of such cases. Now there is a (>roposal for constituting 20 additional benches to cope 
with the increasing number of cases. The Committee expresses its deer> concern over the fact 
that even though the number of cases pending before the ITA T has increased rapidly over 
the years, the Ministry has not been able to assess the dimension of the problem with the 
result that number of benches of ITAT created in 1972 has remained static till now. 
12. The Law Secretary further explained that a selection committee headed by a Judge 
of the Supreme Court is in the midst of the process of selecting candidates to fill up the 
vacant posts in the Tribunal. The Committee feels that the procedure for selecting 
candidates takes considerable time as the selection committee has to visit various areas! 
places for the purpose. The Committee is of the opinion that the procedure for selection 
should be less time consuming and suitable steps be taken to make proper assessment of the 
vacancies well in advance. 
13. The Committee emphasises upon the Ministry that the vacant posts of the member 
in the IT AT should be filled up with utmost expedition and adequate financial support be 
given for early creation of additional benches of the ITA T. 
14. In reply, the Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs has s tated:-
"The proce ss of Selection of Candidates for filling up vacant posts of Members in 
Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (IT AT) is now complete. The Selection Board headed 
by a Judge of the Supreme Court has recommended a panel of candidates suitable for 
appointment to the posts of Judicial and Accountant Member s in the Tribunal. These 
names have subseque ntly been approved by the Appointments Committee of the 
Cabinet. Offers of appointment have already been sent to 18 selected candidates. All 
necessary formalities such as medical examination, etc. are being completed in respect 
of the se candidates. The new Members are expected to join the Tribunal very shortly. 
As regards the creation of additional benches of the Tribunal, the President of the 
Income Tax Appellate Tribunal has been requested to furnish concrete proposals to the 
Department indicating the number of additional benches required in the light of the 
latest pendency position, the number of posts required to be created for these Benches , 
the financial implications in terms of both recurring and non-recurring expenditure, 
etc." 
15. Further, the Secretary, Department of Legal Affairs in his deposition before the 
Committee apprised that as on 7 .3.1996, out of the sanctioned strength of 38 Judicial 
Members, 34 members are in position and there are four vacancies. Now appointments to 
these four vacancies have also been processed and they are likely to be filled up very 
shortly. Similarly, in relation to Accountant Members, 30. Members are in position. There 
are eight vacancies. Action has been taken to fill up five vacancies and the selected 
candidates are likely to join shortly. 
16. As regards creat ion of 20 additional benches of ITAT , the Secretary stated:-
"We have taken up the matter with the President of the !TAT and have sought his 
recommendation. He gave us the justification for creation of 15 additional benches. We 
still have sought certa in clarification from him which are awaited. We shall be 
processing this proposal with the Ministry of Finance very shortly." 

4 
17. The Committee notes that though the Ministry has initiated action to fill up vacancies 
in the ITAT in pursuance of the Committee's recommendation, yet the time taken in the 
procesS has been unreasonably long. More so, 7 posts of members are yet to be filled up. The 
committee hopes that the remaining vacancies will be filled up shortly and reiterates its earlier 
recommendation that the procedure for selection should be less time-consuming and suitable 
steps be taken to make proper assessment of the vacancies well in advance. 
18. As regards creation of 20 additional benches of ITA T to cope with the rapidly 
increasing pendency of cases before its benches, the Committee finds that the Ministry bas 
taken up the matter with the President, ITAT and he has given justification for creation of 15 
additional benches instead of 20 as proposed earlier. The Committee, expresses its concern 
over this State of affairs as in its view, the proposal for creation of additional benches has 
been pending since long and the Ministry is still in the process of finalising the proposal either 
with the President, ITA T or with the Ministry of Finance. The Committee, therefore , 
recommends that the Ministry should make all out efforts to ensure that the additional 
bench~&. of IT AT are created without any further delay. 
RECOMMENDATIONS MADE BY THE CHIEF MINISTERS AND THE CHIEF 
JUSTICES. 
Recommendation: 
The Committee notes that the recommendation s made in the Conference of the Chief 
Ministers and Chief Justices , suggesting ways and means to solve the problem of 
accumulating arrears of cases, were forwarded to all the State Governments /UT Administ­
rations , High Courts/Tribunals by the Department of Legal Affairs in December, 1993. 
Subsequently, the Department of Justice was made nodal Department for the implement a­
tion of the recommendations which fell within its purview ; The Department of Justice has 
since also written to all the State Governments / UT Administrations and High Courts, in 
May , 1994 for taking necessary action on the recommendations. 
20. The implementation of December, 1993 resolution adopted in the Chief Mini sters I 
Chief Justices Conference was reviewed by the Law Ministers at their Plenary meeting held 
in Calcutta in November, 1994. In that meeting, the Law Ministers noted that the progress 
made in the implementation of the recommendations made by the Chief Ministers and Chief 
Justice was not completely satisfactory. Some notable observations made by the Law 
Ministers included, inter-alia, a fresh comprehensive legislation or arbitration and concilia­
tion in place of the existing one, adoption of 'Pilot Project Scheme" evolved by the High 
Court of Karnataka by other States and immediate steps for bringing into force the Legal 
Services Authorities Act, 1987, etc. The observations of Law Ministers were also forwarded 
to all State Governments and to the High Courts on 2.1.1995. 
21. The Committee is pained to note that notwithstanding reminders to the State · 
Governments I UT Administrations and High Courts to take speedy follow-up action on the 
recommendations I observations made in the Conference of the Chief Justices I Chief 
Ministers and Law Ministers response has been lukewarm . The Committee endorses the 
observations made by the Law Ministers that financial and other constraints should not be 
allowed to stand in the way of implementation of the recommendations within a reasonable 
time and full cooperation in the matter should be extended by all concerned. 
22. The Ministry in its Action Taken Note has furnished the following position:-
"Copies of the Resolution adopted by the Chief Ministers and Chief Justices and 
the Resolution adopted by the Law Ministers at their Calcutta Meeting have been 
forwarded to all Ministries/Departments of the Government of Indi a, all State 
Governments, all High Courts etc. with a request that the recommendations contained 

5 
therein be implemented speedily. Specific recommendations contained in the Resolution 
adopt ed by the Chief Ministers and Chief Justices on which action is to be taken by 
various organisations have also been identified and detailed statements have also been 
forwarded to the Stat e Governments, High Courts , etc. reque sting them to take action 
for implementing such recommendations as are relevant to them. The matter regarding 
review of the implementation of these recommendations will be placed before the Law 
Ministers at their next plenary meeting which will be held in Hyderabad during 24-26 
Novemb er. 1995." 
23. Ft~ >m the deposition of the Law Secretary, the Committee notes that Government 
has taken certain measures/steps to implement the recommendations of the Chief Ministers 
and the Chief Justices. Some of the notable achievements are enforcement of the Legal 
Services Authoriti es Act , 1987, review of the strength of Judge s in different High Courts , 
Comprehen sive revision of the IPC , Cr. P.C. and the Indian Evidence Act , establishments 
of courts at Tehsil level to assist rural litigation, computerisation of courts etc. 
24. The Committee while expressing its satisfaction over the steps initiated by the 
Government in pursuance of the recommendations of the Chief Ministers and Chief Justices 
feels that pace of implementation is still tardy. The Ministry has coordinating role and it 
should ensure that concerted efforts are made by all the States, High Courts in this direction. 
The Committee, therefore, impresses upon the Ministry to effectively oversee the implementa­
tion and review the progress made in this regard from time to time. 
ELECTION PETITIONS 
Recommendations: 
25. The Committee understands that a large number of election petitions are pending , 
in some cases , for considerably long time. The pendency of such cases for long period is not 
in the interest of justice and acts as a deterrent to filing of election petitions. In this 
connection , the Committee notes that as per sub-section (7) of section 86 of the 
Representation of the People Act, 1951 'every election petition shall be tried as expediti­
ously as possible and endeavour shall be made to conclude the trial within six months from 
the date on which the election petition is presented to the High Court for trial'. However, 
the fact is that the time limit of six months, although desirable, is not adhered to. 
26. Public accountability in all spheres of life is the essence of parliamentary democracy. 
The Committee , therefore , while expressing its deep concern in the matter, recommends 
that Government should come forward with concrete proposals for speedy disposal of 
election petitions . In this context, the Government may also consider referring the matter to 
the Law Commission for comprehensive study. The Committee suggests that the Ministry 
may include this subject for discussion at the next Conference of the Chief Justices with a 
view to evolving suitable guidelines for speedy disposal of election petitions. 
27. The Law Secretary . in his deposition informed the Committee that the matter 
relating to election petitio11s has been referred to the Law Commission of India for 
examination. On the question of giving this issue proper attention, the Secretary assured the 
Committee that the matter would be placed before the Chief Justice requesting him to 
consider it in the next Chief Justices ' Conference. 

6 
28. The Committee rmds that there has not been any significant progress in t~e matter 
relating to election petitions. The Committee, therefore, desires that the Ministry should ask 
the Election Commission of India to expedite the examination of the issue and reiterates its 
earlier recommendations to include the subject for discussion at the next Conference of the 
Chief Justices with a view to evolving suitable guidelines for speedy disposal of election 
petitions. 
DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE - RATIONALE BEIDND ITS BEING UNDER ADMINIS­
TRATIVE CONTROL OF MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
Recommendation: 
29. The Committee notes that the Department of Justice is a part of the Ministry of 
Law, Justice and Company Affairs and Demands for Grants of the Department are also 
accounted for on behalf of the Ministry. However, its administrative control lies with the 
Ministry of Home Affairs. On the question of rationale behind keeping the Department 
under the administrative control of the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Justice 
has explained that the Department was brought under the administrative control of the 
Ministry of Home Affairs in the year 1971 following a Presidential Order. Initially, seven 
items of work being handled by the Ministry of Home Affairs were transferred and the staff 
was also provided by the Ministry to the Department of Justice. Subsequently, ten items of 
work were transferred to the Department. At present, the Home Secretary and one 
Additional Secretary in the Home Ministry function concurrently as Secretary and 
Additional Secretary in the Department of Justice. 
30. All work of the Department of Justice relating to the administration, cash and 
accounts and other general housekeeping functions like stationery, furniture, typewriters, 
accommodation, receipt and issue etc. continue to be handled by the Ministry of Home 
Affairs. The parliamentary work of the Department is handled by the Parliament Section of 
the Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs. 
31. The Department of Justice has also stated that the inter-linkage of the Department 
with the Ministry of Home Affairs ensures close coordination between the Ministry and the 
Department in the matter of appointment of Judges of High Courts and the Supreme Court. 
It also ensures better coordination for the administration of criminal justice with the States. 
Any change in the existing arrangements with a view to making the Department of Justice 
entirely self-contained would entail the creation of large number of additional posts involving 
financial implications. It would also upset the close coordination that exists now between the 
Department of Justice and the Ministry of Home Affairs. 
32. The Committee is not convinced with the arguments advanced by the Ministry. The 
Committee feels that the existing set-up of the Department wherein some of the its functions 
are being handled by the Ministry of Law and some others by the Ministry of Home Affairs, 
gives an anomalous picture which needs to be set right. In this context, the Committee finds 
that the apprehension of the Department of Justice is misplaced as the idea of the 
Committee is not to create an independent Department but to place it under the Ministry of 
Law for all purposes, thereby dispensing with the administrative control of the Ministry of 
Home Affairs. This can be done by transferring back the items of work relating to the 
Ministry of Home Affairs to the Ministry of Law which· are presently being handled by the 
Department of Justice. 

7 
33. The Action Taken Note furnished by the Department of Justice stated:-
"ln this context it may again be pointed out that a considerable part of the work of the 
Department of Justice deals with appointments, transfers of Judges for which close 
cOordination with \'arious agencies under the Ministry of Home Affairs is very essential. 
Further, the Judicial administration of the UTs is also with the Department of Justice 
which requires close coordination with the various Divisions of the Ministry of Home 
Affairs. Further in most of the States, the administration of Justice Department is- with 
the Home Department of the State Government!UT administration. In view of this, it 
is felt that there are some advantages in the present stipulation that the Department of 
Justice would be under the administrative control of Ministry of Home Affairs. In view 
of this position, the Government has re-considered the question of the administrative 
control of the Department of Justice and has with the approval of Minister of State for 
Law, Justice and Company Affairs decided to continue with the present arrangement." 
34. The Committee is not convinced with the reply given by the Ministry as it appears to 
be a mere repetition of what the Ministry had stated earlier at the stage of consider~tion of 
the issue by the Committee. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its earlier recommendation 
that the Department of Justice should appropriately be placed under the Ministry of Law for 
aiJ purposes, thereby dispensing with the administrative control of the Ministry of Home 
Affairs. Alternatively, in case it is deemed convenient from coordination point of view, the 
Department of Justice can be merged with the Ministry of Home Affairs for all purposes. 
COMPANY LAW BOARD (CLB) 
Recommendation: 
35. The Committee notes that the total number of petitions and applications pending 
before the CLB was 2377 as on 31.12.94. The Department has informed the Committee that 
as per the Companies Act , 1956, the Company Law Board comprises Chairman, Vice­
Chairman and seven Members. It has only three members at present, one out of which is· 
officiating as Chairman of the Board. Since there are no members in the Eastern and 
Southern benches, the regular permanent members at the headquarters have to visit these 
stations to hear and dispose of the cases before those benches. The Committee finds that the 
pendency of the petitions/applications before the CLB could broadly be attributed to the 
vacancies of members at different benches as a consequence of which the members at 
headquarters have to bear extra burden of the work and they have to divert their attention 
to hear the cases at other benches. This certainly hampers the process of expeditious 
disposal of cases. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the vacant posts of the 
members be filled up within the shortest time frame. 
36. The Department of Company Affairs, in its Action Taken Note has stated:-
"5 posts of members (4 Judicial and 1 Technical) are vacant in the Cop1pany Law 
Board. The posts have been advertised. The last date for receiving the applications was 
20.9.95. The applications have been received and the Department has initiated action 
for making the selection for these posts which are expected to be filled up shortly." 
37. The Secretary, Department of Company Affairs , on being asked about the reason 
for delay in filling up the vacancies of members of Company Law Board, explained that the 
number of applications for these posts were received under pre-revised rules. Subsequently 

8 
the rules were requ ired to be amended and fresh applicat ions were invited to be processed 
under the rev ised rules. Further under the rules, the appo intment were to be made by the 
Govern ment in consultation with the Chief Justice of India or his nominee . As a result 
thereof, the vacancies of membe rs could not be filled up within a reasonable time . 
38. From the reply o f the Department of Company Affairs a nd the deposition of the 
Secretar y, the Committee finds that action has been initiated t o fill up 5 vacant posts of 
members of CLB. T he Committ ee while expressing its d ispleasure is of the v iew, that in 
futu re, the Ministry should evolve a m echanism so that the vacancies could be filled up well in 
advance of their actual o'ccurence. The Committee also impr esses upon the M inistry to take 
immediat e action to fill up all the vacancies in CLB. 
DEPARTMENT OF COMPANY AFFAIRS- RATIONALE BEHIND ITS BEING PART OF 
LAW MINISTRY 
Recommendation: 
39. On a pointed query as to why t he Department of Company Affairs is part of the 
Ministry of Law, Jus tice and Company Affa irs and why it should not be the part of the 
Ministry of Industry, the .Ministry stated as under: -
"The Department of Company Affairs is primari ly concerned with orderly growth and 
functioning of Joint Stock Companies. It seeks to prov ide appropriate basis for their_ 
working without unnecessary restr ictions and irritants. The Department also seeb to 
provide adequate protection to shareholders, creditors and members of public through 
adm inistration of Company Law. Through, operation of the Monopolies and Restrictive 
Trade Practices, it is responsible for ensuring competition in the domestic market by 
control of monopolies restrictive and unfair trade practices. The Monopolies and 
Restrictive Trade Practi ces Commission, an organ of the Department, enquires into and 
takes appropriate actions in respect of these trade practices. The work of the 
Department , therefore. mainly relates to administration of Corporate Laws." 
40. The Committee is of the view that the matters handled by the Ministry of Industry 
and the Department of Company Affairs are related to each other. Moreso, both the 
Ministry of Industry and the Department of Company Affairs seek to achieve similar 
objectives. lt will, therefore, be appropriate if the Department of Company Affairs is made 
a part of the Ministry of Industry. The Committee, therefore, recommends that this issue be 
examined by the Government. . 
41. In its Action Taken Note, the Department of Company Affairs has stated the 
following position: -
"The Department of Company Affairs has at times been part of Ministry of Finance, 
Ministry of Industry and Ministry of Law, Justice & Company Affairs. At present, 
though it is under the Ministry of Law, Justice & Company Affairs, the Secretary, 
Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion , is also the Secretary, Department of 
Company Affairs and thus close coordination is achieved between the two Depart­
ment s." 
42. The Committee notes that the repl y of the Department is too general and doe~ not 
satisfactorily explain the position as to why the Department of Company Affairs should 
continue to be part of the Ministry of Law, Ju~tice & Company Affair s. The Committee is of 
the view that the function s of the Department of Company Affair s, as enumerated above , 
can be discharged in a better way, if it forms part of the Ministry of Industry. The 
Committee, therefore, reiterates its earlier recommendation that it will be appropriate if the 
Department of Company Affairs is made part of the Ministry of Industry

The Ministry of Home Affairs has been entrusted broadly with the following functions: 
(a) To deal with all matters relating to internal security; 
(b) To deal with all matters relating to Centre-State relations and Inter-State relations; 
(c) Implementation of the provisions of the Constitution relating to Official Language 
and the provisions of the Official Language Act, 1963; 
(d) To discharge certain basic functions like notification of assumption of office by the 
President and the Vice-President; notification of appointment of the Prime Minister 
and other Ministers; notification of appointment, resignation and removal of 
Governors and Lt. Governors, appointment of Lt. Governors, Chief Commissioners 
and Administrative Officers in Union Territories; and 
(e) To deal with matters like citizenship and naturalisation census of Population, 
National Anthem, National Flag of India, etc. 
To discharge the above fuRctions, the Ministry has been divided into four Depart­
ments:-
(i) Department -of Internal Security - to deal with Police, Law and Order and 
rehabilitation; 
(ii) Department of States - to deal with Centre-State relations, inter.-State relations, 
Union Territories and Freedom Fighters' Pension; 
(iii) Department of Official Language - to deal with the implementation of the 
provisions of the Constitution relating to Official Language and the provisions of 
the Official Language Act, 1963;

President and Vice-President, notification of appointment of the Prime Minister 
and other Ministers, etc.

INTERNAL SECURITY 
8. The Secretary of the Ministry in his presentation gave a broad overview of the 
internal security scenario of the country and submitted that various factors such as 
demolition of the disputed Ram Janam Bhoomi-Babri Masjid structure at Ayodhya, the riots 
and a series of bomb blasts thereafter in Mumbai, activities of certain insurgent groups with 
aid from certain external forces, proxy war by Pakistan in Jammu and Kashmir abetted by 
infiltration by Afghan and other foreign mercenaries (as per some American agencies' 
reports there are about three million pieces of AK-46 rifles lying in an unopened condition 
in Pakistan), have had some negative impact on the security environment in the country and 
the security forces have come under severe strain. In this context, he referred to the 
malfunctioning of police system in some of the States where transfers of police officials 
particularly at the senior level are effected in haste for reasons unrelated to their efficiency 
so much so that even in a few months 5-6 persons change places. This has a debilatating 
effect on the functioning of the police force and tends to demoralise it. He underlined the 
need to do something in this regard. 
9. On the basis of the evidence tendered by the Secretary of the Ministry, the 
Committee has come to the conclusion that the law and order situation in the country as a 
whole is not a happy one. The budgetary outlays which run into thousands. of crores of 
rupees for Central Para Military Forces to maintain tranquillity within the country as also 
across its borders seem to be a substantial drain on our resources. There is no denying the 
fact that maintenance of law and order is the responsibility of the State Governments 
concerned but the Ministry of Home Affairs has to play nodal role in this regard by 
coordinating activities of intelligence agencies and having necessary liaison with the Home 
Departments of the States concerned. The Committee is given to understand that some 
thinking in the Government is going on to bring law and order on the Concurrent List and 
that would perhaps help deal with the matters concerning law and order in a better and 
integrated way. The Committee feels that before any exercise to include the subject of law and 
order in the Concurrent List is undertaken, necessary consultations be had with the State 
Governments concerned at the appropriate level and their views be ascertained in the -matter. 
10. The CommiUee expresses its concern that the infiltration of people from the 
neighbouring countries particularly Bangladesh is continuing unabated and our Security 
Forces have perhaps not been that much successful in checking this influx. The migration of 
people from other countries on this scale tends to not only disturb the cultural ethos of the 
country but also creates law and order problem and acts as a severe strain on the economy of 
the country. The Committee in this context feels that the intelligence agencies of the 
Government have failed together necessary intelligence about the infiltration of secessionist 
elements and once they have entered the country the efforts to nab them have either been half 
hearted or have not met with the desired results. The recent incident of arms dropping in 

4 
Purulia has exposed the inherent flaws in our security network. Special emphasis has to be 
laid on our air surveillance. Our Coastal security set up also needs to be suitably geared up to 
prevent smuggling of huge consignments of arms and ammunitions through our vast coastline 
which has assumed menacing proportions. 
11. The Committee n;commends to the Government to take urgent steps to ensure that 
the networking of Central and State Intelligence Agencies is institutionalised and their 
strength and capabilities are raised to an appropriate level so that they act in a well 
coordinated and integrated manner and share information with their State counterparts so 
that the phenomenon of illegal migration is brought to an end. Suitable mechanism may also 
be evolved ~o lay down certain norms of accountability in case there are cases of intelligence 
failure and with that end in view a nodal officer be appointed for each State to coordinate 
activities of the Intelligence Agencies-whether they be Central or State-in that area. 
Something also needs to be done to mount special surveillance on our porous international 
borders. 
12. The Committee has also noted that of late there has been a spurt in the violent 
activities in different parts of the country and some anti-national organisations particularly in 
North-East and extremist groups in Andhra Pradesh have become active. The Committee feefs 
that the discontentment, which· may be brewing among the people in these regions because of 
socio-economic factors or underdevelopment, is exploited by the extremist elements to rope 
them in violent and seccessionist activities. What is, therefore, needed most is to have a 
dialogue with them; motivate them to come in the national mainstream, identify the causes of 
their unrest and to undertake speedy development of their areas. Special emphasis in that 
context is required to hasten up the process of land reforms which seems to have somewhat 
got bogged down. The Committee also expresses its displeasure over the tardy pace of 
implementation of various Accords entered into by the Government with different organisa­
tions such as Assam Accord, T.N.V. Accord, Bodo Accord and MOU involving representative 
organisations of Karbi, Anglong and North Cachar Hills Districts and. urges upon Govern­
ment to speed up their implementation. 
13. In the course of the evidence of the Secretary it came to the notice of the 
Committee that the practice of issuing Photo Identity Cards to the people in the border 
areas was prevalent in some cases but after the Election Commission decided to issue Photo 
Identity Cards to the voters all over country it was thought that they would be of better use 
even in border areas and the earlier exercise of issuing Identity Cards to the border people 
was somewhat slowed down and neither could make any headway, Government has now 
decided to resume the exercise of issuing Photo Identity Cards to the people in border areas 
as it was being done earlier, and to begin with, border areas in Rajasthan and certain areas 
in the North-East are proposed to be taken as a pilot scheme. 
14. Tht! Committee feels that expenditure of enormous proportions has already been 
incurred on the Photo Identity Cards for voters but we still are at a dead end. The Photo 
Identity cal'ds, as a matter of fact, issued on a national plan will be of immense use to the 
citizens in many ways particularly from the point of view of internal security. They will also 
help identify the illegal foreign migrants who could be deported back to the countries of their 
origin. A look in its entirety has, therefore, to be had on this issue and since the Photo 
Identity Cards are of prime importance in a national perspective it may be ensured that they 
are issued lo all the people within a definite tirite frame. 
15. The Committee is of the view that the functioning of Police system in our country 
leaves much to be desired and periodically it has come in for severe criticism from different 
quarters. To reform this system a National Police Commission headed by Dr. Dharma Vira. 

5 
was set up long back and the vital recommendations which it had made in its report have got 
bogged down awaiting their implementation. The Committee strongly feels that implementa· 
tion of recommendations of this nature needs to be accorded top priority. The Committee does 
not know what factors are delaying their implementation. It, therefore, urges upon the 
Government to submit a status paper to it on the recommendations which have found 
acceptance and which have not and whether the ones which have been accepted could be 
implemented in a time bound manner. 
16. The Committee views very seriously the growing phenomenon of frequent transfers of 
senior police and civil officials in some of the States which has a demoralising effect on the 
administration and a serious bearing on the law and order situation. The Committee feels that 
this tendency has to be curbed in the interest of generating an efficient and vibrant law 
enforcement machinery. It is quite imperative that this matter may be taken up by all States 
concerned at the highest level, if possible, through a conference of Chief Ministers and an 
objective transfer policy in the matter of high police and civil officials be worked out and 
effectively implemented. The officers concerned should have a fixity of tenure particularly in 
the districts, where they can grapple with the problems of the area seriously and purposefully. 
TRAINING OF INSURGENT GROUPS 
17. In reply to a point regarding insurgent activities in the North-Eastern region the 
Ministry has informed that there exists a number of camps of various insurgent groups 
including United Liberation Front of Assam (ULFA), National Socialist Council of 
Nagaland (Issao Swu/Muivah), All Tripura Tiger Force (ATTF), Tripura Revolutionary 
Army (TRA), National Liberation Front of Tripura (NLFT), People's Liberation Army 
(PLA), etc. in Bangladesh across the Indian border. The training includes training in use of 
arms, information about Indian Security Forces, etc. Similarly camps of Bodo Security 
Force, ULFA and NSCN exist in Bhutan across Indian border. Joint training camps are also 
being organised by these militant groups. 
18. The Ministry has stated that to prevent the activities of the insurgent groups from 
across the border an Institutional mechanism for ongoing cooperation with neighbouring 
countries has been evolved. This has been very successful in restricting the activities and 
bases of insurgent elements from Myanmar. While this mechanism is also in place with 
Bangladesh, though not very effectively, it has so far not been possible with Bhutan. Since 
dealings with other countries are being conducted in coordination with Ministry of External 
Affairs, a proposal for starting, such institutional mechanism for on going cooperation with 
Bhutan is under discussion with Ministry of External Affairs. 
19. The Committee feels that establishment of bases and running of training Centres by 
the insurgent groups in Bangladesh, Bhutan and Myanmar is a matter of serious concern 
much as they encourage them to pursue their hostile activities in our country. A viable 
strategy has to be devised to strengthen the borders with these countries on priority basis, seal 
the escape routes of the insurgents and if necessary, as a last resort, if. the diplomatic efforts 
do not yield results, doctrine of hot pursuit which is internationally accepted, be adopted to 
foil their designs. 
20. The Committee has also noted that of late all groups involved in anti-India activities 
are having an easy passage through our border with Nepal and either no institutional 
mechanism for cooperation with that country to check activities of such elements is currently 
in place or it is· not working effectively. India has had traditionally ;good relations with Nepal 
and cooperation of the _two countries is manifest in different areas. The Committee sees no 
reason why we should not have necessary cooperation from that country to prevent the entry 

6 
of terrorists and secessionist elements into our country. The Committee recommends that an 
all out diplomatic initiative be undertaken at the appropriate level with Nepal to work out a 
satisfactory solution of the problem.

49. The Committee drew the attention of the Commissioner to the existing set up of 
Delhi Police which seems to give an impression as if its administrative structure is highly 
centralised with all powers concentrated in one man and whether in the interest of increased 
level of efficiency and quick decision making, it would not be appropriate to appoint three 
officers of I.G. rank as Special Commissioners who could hold independent position~ in the 

14 
set up and deal with the matters accordingly. The Committee also wanted to know whether 
in view of the heavy responsibilities cast on the Force, it was not imperative to effect certain 
structural changes in the set up such as separating the security and Traffic Departments and 
removing Vigilance from the purview of the Administrative Branch and bringing it under an 
independent branch headed by a Senior Additional Commissioner or an I.G. 
50. It was submitted to the Committee that any disciplined organisation, particularly a 
Police Force, is supposed ·to have a well defined hierarchical structure with a functionary at 
the apex level to provide ieadership, direction and guidance to the Force , and unity of 
Command .is an a~cepted and time tested principle . Each member in the hierarchy has been 
assigned a specific task to perform and contributes in the decision making process. Regular 
meetings are held by the Commissioner with the officers at various levels which enable Delhi 
Police to function as a cohesive and close knit team. 
51. The Committee does not feel convinced that the Delhi Police is presently working as a 
cohesive and close knit teain. The Committee feels that the command structure of the Force 
needs to be reviewed and decentralisation by creating separate Wings such as Traffic, Security

incharge of these wings. The Committee was informed that the proposals for posting an 
officer of the rank of I.G . of Police to supervise Security and Training Wings and assigning

Committee feels the implementation of these proposals will definitely bring about some 
improvement from functional and administrative point of view, but it would be better if 
Security, Training and Vigilance Branches are made three separate and distinct Wings/

Armed Forces have three separate organs namely Army, ·Navy and Air Force-each headed 
by a separate Chief-and they have worked quite successfully showing high standards of 
discipline and in the view of the Committee there is no reason why a similar set up on these 
lines as suggested by the Committee for carving out separate wings of Training, Security and 
Vigilance etc. can not be brought about.

56. To check smuggling of contraband, arms, narcotics and prevent infiltration of 
terrorists and saboteurs our International borders have to be made secure by effective 
policing and sealing porcus stretches. In order to achieve this twin objective, the fencing! 
flood lighting of 180 Kms./195.8 Kms of International Border in Jammu Sector was approved by 
the Cabinet in March, 1995 at an estimated cost of Rs. 71.76 crores. The work was started 

16 
but it had to be :-.uspenclcd due to firing from Pakistan side. In an lnter-Ministrial meeting 
held in August. 1995. a decision was taken to resume the work with the help of bullet proof 
screens. Preparations for this purpose were made, but due to Parliamentary elections, a 
decision wa:-. taken to go slow with the work. 
57. As submitted to the Committee by the Ministry , Pakistan appears determined not to 
allow the fencing and flood lighting works to go on as they do not accept the Jammu borders 
as an Int ernational Border and call it is a working boundry. In this situat ion restarting of 
fencing work in this sector may lead to escalation of tension on the Internat ional Border. 
58. The Committee feels that strengthening of country's border with Pakistan, 
particulary in context of the proxy war it is waging in Jammu & Kashmir , is of paramount 
importan ce. It is every country's rights to make its border secure . The firing from Pak side is 
a provocative gesture and a message has, therefore, to go that such brazen interference in the 
affairs of the country must cease. Managing our borders is our sovereign right. The 
Committee is of the view that the issue may be dealt with utmost priority either bilaterally by 
flag meetings of Commanders or diplomatically or else other avenues be explored to complete 
fencing/flood lighting work in Jammu Sector in our larger National interest.

98. The Freedom Fighters' Pension Scheme has been in operation since 15th August , 
1972 when it was introduced on the occasion of the Silver Jubliee of our Independence. The 
Scheme provides for grant of pension to those who had suffered at least six months of 
imprisonment/detention/externmentlinternment/abscondence etc., while participating in the 
National freedom struggle. The scheme was renamed as "Swatantrata Sainik Samman 
Pension Scheme" in 1980 after liberalisation of certain provisions. The amount of Samman 
Pension hus been increased from time to time. 
99. Issues like delay in· processing the cases for grant of Samman Pension to genuine 
freedom fighters and their widows, bribes to expedite sanction of pension and rejection by 
the Ministry of Home Affairs of a number of cases forwarded by State Governments with 
favourable recommendations have come to the notice of the Comm ittee. 
100. It was submitted before the Committee that claims for grant of freedom fighters 
pension are being processed strictly in accordance with the procedure laid down in the 
Swatantrata Sainik Samman Pension Scheme, 1980 and the policy guidelines issued there­
under from time to time. The pension is granted only in those cases which are covered by 
the provisions of the said Scheme and the policy decisions taken thereunder. The applicants 
are never ·required to pay anything to get their work done. However, if any complaint is 
received against the staff members, it is examined thoroughly and appropriate action is taken 
against the concerned person if found guilty. The Secretary of the Ministry stated that many 
cases received from State Governments are rejected by the Ministry because they lack the 
necessary s upporti ng documents. He expressed his readine ss to set up a Com mittee of non­
officials to review as a one time measure, all the cases, which have been rejected by the 
Ministry for want of supporting documents . 
101. The Committee feels that the Pension Scheme which was launched as a noble 
gesture to the freedom fighters who suffered immensely to liberate the country from foreign 
rule is not allowed to get bogged down in red tapism and bureaucratic delays. The State 
Governments concerned should also ensure that the cases of freedom fighters recommended 
for grant of pension are supported lzy ·necessary documents and delays in decisions do not 
occur on this account. 
102. The Committee appreciates the proposal of the Ministry to reconsider applications 
for Samman Pension rejected earlier on account of their not being supported by documents 
and trusts that the outcome thereof will be placed before it soon. The Committee would also 
like to emphasise that personnel with proven integrity and excellent behaviour are given the 
task of dealing with pension cases with utmost care, caution, swiftness, sympathy and respect.

responsibilities of the Ministries of the Central Government for scrutinising and sanctioning 
the scheme s under their purview. The factual position regarding budgetary procedure in this 
regard is that the entire budget requirement for Plan and Non-plan revised estimates for 
current year and Non-Plan budget estimates for the ensuing year is discussed by the Ministry 
of Finance in the pre-budget meetings with the representatives of the concerned Union 
Territorie s and Ministry of Home Affairs. An overall ceiling is fixed in respect of each 
Union Territor y. Annual Plan allocations for the ensuing year and decided by the Planning 
Commission. Based on the ceiling fixed by the Ministry of Finance and the Planning 
Commission , the Union Territory Administrations prepare budgetary break-up showing 
budget provisions according to their respective budgetary heads and also showing the 
allocations against Ministries/Departments of the Central Government administratively 
concerned. This budgetary break-up is included in the Demands for Grants of the Ministry 
of Home Affair s. 
HOME MINISTER'S ADVISORY. COMMITTEES (HMACs) 
105. In the course of the consideration of Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Home 
Affairs a point was raised about the institution of the Home Minister's Advisory 
Committees(HMACs) for the Union Territories without Legislature/Metropolitan Council 
virtually becoming defunct. It was emphasised that the HMACs were entrusted with the task 

26 
of rendering advice on important matters relating to UTs and they were understood to be 
performing very useful functions. It was submitted to the Committee by the Ministry of 
Home Affairs that the HMCAs are no longer in existence and no demand for constituting 
them has either been received in the recent past. The matter, nevertheless, is being 
examined. 
106. The Committee falls to understand why an instrument like HMACs which was 
devised to serve public interest has become inoperational. The Committee does not feel 
convinced with the answer given by the Ministry that there has been no demand from any 
quarter for their revival. They should have as a matter of fact, been continued, unless there 
were reasons strong enough to do away with them. The Committee recommends to the 
Government to take appropriate action in the matter to ensure that HMACs become 
functional and in case the Government feels that they need to be restructured action may be 
taken accordingly.

REPORT 
The Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions was created as a separate 
Ministry from 1970 onwards in pursuance of the recommendations of the Administrative 
Reforms Commission (ARC). The ARC felt that the size of the Civil Services in the country 
warranted that a separate Ministry be created to deal with manifold problems which had 
emerged. However, the ARC recommended that this Ministry should always be under the 
charge of the Prime Minister. It was earlier created as a Department and in March, 1985 was 
constituted as a full-fledged Ministry. It is under the overall charge of the Prime Minister 
assisted by a Minister of State. The Ministry comprises the following three departments:-
(i) Department of Personnel and Training; 
(ii) Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances; 
(iii) Department of Pensions and Pensioners' Welfare. 
The three Departments function under Secretary (Personnel), assisted at present by 
three Additional Secretaries, four Joint Secretaries and other supporting officers and staff. 
2. The Department of Personnel and Training .also functions as the Administrative 
Ministry for the following agencies:-
(i) Central Bureau of Investigation· (CBI). (It is a premier investigative agency of the 
Government with Police powers, especially created to deal with corruptions related 
matters). 
(ii) Central Vigilance Commission (CVC). (Central agency to advise on all vigilance 
matters). 
(iii) Union Public Service Commission (UPSC). (A statutory body al}d recruitment 
Agency for Group 'A' and 'B' services/posts). 
(iv) Staff Selection Commission (SSC). (A recruitment agency for Group 'C' posts and 
also a few selected Group 'B' posts in the Central Secretariat). 
(v) Central Administrative Tribunals (CAl'). (A judicial body to provide justice to the 
Central Government employees in their service matters). 
(vi) Institute of Secretariat Training and Management (ISTM). (A training Institute for 
Secretariat Officers and Staff). 
3. Functionally, the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions is divided 
into following seven divisions:­
- Establishment Officers. 
- All India Services and Administrative Vigilance. 
- Establishment. 
-Administrative Tribunal, Administration and Staff Welfare. 
-Training. 
- Central Services and Pension and Pensioners' Welfare. 
- Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances.

Civil Services. 
(ii) Deputation of officers I experts to other countries and United Nations and its

(iii) Redeployment of staff rendered surplus in Central Government Offices. 
(iv) Formulation and coordination of training policies for All India Services and 
Central Services.
