11. The Committee having considered all aspects makes recommendations/observations 
in respect of the following:-
Public Grievances 
12. Cognizance· and redressal of Public Grievances are an integral part of a responsible 
administrative set up. According to the Annual Report (1995-96) of the Ministry, Internal 
Grievance Redressal Machinery (IGRM) is functioning in Ministries/Departments of the 
Central Government. Grievance redressal units are also functioning in subordinate offices/ 
public sector undertakings which. have public dealings. Instructions have been issued to the 
Ministries/Departments to take note of and attend to grievances appearing in .the 
newspaper columns. The Department of Administrative Reforms & Public Grievances 
(DAR & PG) receives statistical report about receipts and disposal of grievances. According 

5 
to the information furnished by the Ministry, there are about 45000 such grievances pending 
disposal and; the disposal of such grievances is the responsibility of concerned Ministry I 
Department and that DAR & PG receives regular feedback from them on the receipt and 
disposal of public grievances. 
13. The DAR & PG takes up about 3-5% of the grievances it receives directly and 
pursues their final disposal by the concerned Ministry /Department. All other cases are 
transferred or referred to the Ministries I Departments for final disposal under intimation to 
the DAR & PG. In response to a query regarding the action taken by Ministries/ 
Departments on Grievances appearing in newspaper columns, the Ministry stated that there 
role is limited to issuing policy guidelines and monitoring of implementation of these 
guidelines is not done. The Committee was also informed that the Directorate of Public 
Grievances (DPG) under Cabinet Secretariat is an independent grievance redressal agency 
for notified Departments I Agencies and that it has the authority to call for and examine 
officials and files of the Ministries/ Departments concerned. Further the recommendations 
of the DPG are almost invariably to be acted upon by the concerned Ministry or 
Department. 
14. The Committee feels that the whole approach towards ~edressal of public Grievances 
lacks coherence and that clear guidelines, explicitly fixing the responsibility for time bound 
redressal of grievances is a must. Provisions for punitive action in case of non-redressal of 
grievances within the stipulated time, without any valid reason be made. The Committee feels 
that the working procedure as obtaining in the DPG should be adopted and improved upon by 
DAR & PG to make the grievance redressal machinery more effective. The Committee would 
also impress upon the Ministry, the need for widely advertising the existence of Public 
Grievances cells in .Ministries/Departments, specifying the mechanism for seeking redress 
and mentioning the time frame for such redressal. The DAR & PG would do well to institute 
an effective mechanism for monitoring of implementation I non-implementation or the policy 
guidelines issued by it and take requisite corrective steps on a regular basis. The Committee 
desires that the Department should come out with specific suggestions and stipulations to 
improve Public Grievance redressal. 
ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS 
15. Administrative Reforms are important inasmuch as they help the Administration to 
re-orient and reinvent itself to be in step with ground-realities. The DAR & PG conducts 
research on general issues of Administrative Reforms, sponsors management studies to 
identify Grievance prone-areas and studies them for remedial action. As the nodal agency, it 
offers help and advice to the Ministries/Departments in performance of 0 & M activities. 
16. On being queried about the follow up done by it on the management studies done 
by the Department , the Ministry replied that the recommendations are only advisory in 
nature and that the organizations concerned are expected to implement the suggestions. In 
response to a query whether there existed any mechanism to ensure quick follow up action 
to such studies , the Department has replied that it undertakes impact analysis in respect of a 
few selected studies which assess the extent of implementation made in the study reports. 
The depar tme nt had also undertaken a study on the working of the Emergency Departme nt 
of Dr. Ram Manoh ar Lohia Hospital, New Delhi. The Committee would be interested in 
knowing as to when the study was undertaken, the findings thereof and what follow up 
action has been taken. 
17. The Committee would like to express its dissatisfaction with the state or things. In the 
wake or liberalization there is an urgent need for change in administrative ethos as also in the 

6 
organization and functioning of the administrative set up. The expense and effort involved in 
conducting studies for identifying problem areas and initiating changes in the administration 
is not justified, if the same is not complemented by a rigorous implementation mechanism. 
Bureaucratic inertia is legendary and has given birth to organized interests. These are proving 
to be a big drain on national resources. It is the considered view of the Committee that the 
emphasis on reduction of staff through retrenchment and various voluntary retirement 
schemes is not a solution to the problem of overstaffing referred to by the Secretary. The 
Government should instead focus on streamlining and reducing the multiplicity of unnecessary 
procedures and rules etc. There is an urgent need for reduction of a number of functions the 
Government is called upon to perform. 
18. The Committee would also like to impress upon the Ministry the need for developing 
a rich corpus of case studies on real life working of administration, through the management 
studies sponsored by it. lhis can be used as a very important training tool for new recruits. 
MODERNIZATION OF OFFICES 
19. Modernization of Offices is imperative for improving their administrative efficiency 
and productivity as well as for facilitating access of the public to organisations I units of 
Government. A plan scheme for the purpose was introduced in 1987-88. The Committee had 
queried the Ministry about efficacy and impact of the said scheme. In its reply the Ministry 
had detailed the functional changes resulting from the drive to modernize the offices. 
Specifically, the reply states that functional layout of offices has improved, facilitating better 
supervision and coordination; efficient management and processing of information and 
records has been achieved. The Secretary of the Ministry in the deposition before the 
Committee mentioned that modernization of offices has increased the scope for reducing the 
office staff, especially in Group 'C' & 'D' posts. 
20. The point about improvement in administrative efficiency and better public service as 
a result of modernization of offices is well taken. But the Committee would like to know, 
whether Government has taken any long term view of the changes being introduced in form of 
mechanization of work. Apart from having a bearing on employment generation in future, 
this shift wiU also considerably restrict the pool from which people are selected against future 
vacancies. The Committee would ~ke to know whether Government have devised any long 
term plan to create an adequate training base to cater to skill imparting and upgradation 
needs in view of increasing mechanization of Government work. The Committee emphasizes 
the need for evolving a transparent and time-hound procedure for facilitating improvement in 
the interface between the Government and public at large. 
21. In light of the new Economic- Policies, the Government sought to suitably modify, 
C.C.S. (Conduct) Rules; Fundamental Rules (FRs); Supplementary Rules (SRs); and All 
India Service (Conduct) Rules,' 1968. A Special Review Group was set up for the purpose. 
According to the Ministry, necessary action to amend the relevant rules in most cases has 
been taken. The Committee has taken note of the action in initiating the move to effect 
suitable relevant changes in Rules and expects that such a proactive approach will continue in 
future also. · 
PROGRESSIVE USE OF HINDI IN OFFICIAL WORK 
22. Hindi is the official language of India. Due to a variety of reasons it has not been 
able to gain country wide acceptance as the official language. As a corollary the efforts to 
develop it as the national link language have also not borne fruit. On being queried about 
the steps being taken to facilitate wider acceptance of Hindi, the Ministry replied that 

7 
the subject matter concerns the Department of Official Language under the Ministry of 
IHome Affairs. 
23. The Committee takes strong exception to this reply. In its view this reply aptly sums 
up the official attitude wherein promotion of Hindi is treated as a ml:ltter of official routine. 
Technically the onus of initiating the policy may be the responsibility of Ministry of Home 
AtTairs, but that in no way prevents the Ministry of Personnel from taking a proactive 
approach in the matter. In view of the Committee an efforts could be made to simplify the 
language as it ls used for official purposes, thereby making it intelligi~le to a larger number of 
people and helping it gain wider acceptance. 
ADMINISTRATIVE VIGILANCE 
24. Administrative Vigilance is important for the maintenance of integrity in the public 
services. The Department of Personnel and Training (DoP&T) determines policy on the 
subject and coordinates the work of ·various Ministries/Departments for maintenance of 
discipline and eradication of corruption. The DoP&T also handles all policy and administra­
tive matters pertaining to the Central Bureau of Investigation and Central Vigilance 
Commission. It also deals with the complaints of corruption against the Chief Ministers of 
States and the Union Ministers. The DoP&T is also responsible for appointment of Chief 
Vigilance Officers in the Central Public Sector Undertakings, autonomous bodies and other 
Government offices. 
25. The Committee had asked the Ministry of furnish details about the vacancy position 
of Chief Vigilance Officers in Central Public Undertakings, aut~nomous bodies and other 
Government offices, indicating the period since they have been vacant and the reasons why 
they have been vacant so. In its reply the Ministry stated that out of 145 such full-time posts 
of Chief Vigilance Officers 76 posts are already filled up and that efforts were underway to 
fill up remaining 69 posts. The Ministry also submitted that such a large number of posts of 
CVOs, were vacant because of the unwillingness of the selected candidates to accept the 
offer of joining. This, in view of the Ministry was due to the lack of comparable facilities 
and administrative and financial powers, which the selected officers enjoy in their parent 
cadre. In order to make the posts of CVOs more attractive, Government has notified 
recently some measures, so as to enthuse more officers to join willingly as CVOs. Among 
them are enhancing the administrative/financial powers of the CVOs and making the post of 
CVOs a tenure post, with a tenure of five years. The Ministry did not have any information 
about the period for which the posts of CVOs have been vacant. 
26. The Committee express its displeasure at the reply furnished by the Ministry, and 
desires that the information about period-wise pendency of the posts of C~ntral Vigilance 
Offi('ers in Central PSUs be furnished at the earliest. The Committee recommends that time 
bound action should be taken to fill up the posts of CVOs and in any case they should be 
filled up within a year of their falling vacant. The Committee feels that hitherto the 
appointment of CVOs in different central PSUs is by and large restricted to the officers of 
lAS and IPS. The Committee understands that there are some instructions/guidelines of the 
Central Vigilance Commission regarding extension of zone of consideration for appointment as 
CVOs to the Officers belonging to other Group 'A' Services. The Committee would, 
therefore, recommend that such instructions/guidelines of the eve in this regard should be 
implemented. 
27. The Committee feels that it is evident from the reply furnished by the Ministry · that 
over the years the profile of the post of CVOs has developed into that of a 'punishment 
posting'. This is an unfortunate development especially when we see that Rs. 1,60,000 crores 

8 
of public money is invested in the Central Public Undertakings. It stands to reason here that 
the less than adequate efficiency and return these Public Sector Enterprises provide is partly 
due to the weak vigilance structure. This Committee would like to impress upon Government 
the need for instituting and maintaining a strong and impartial Vigilance structure. The 
Committee recommends that Government should consider giving additional career points to 
the officers who are posted as CVOs thereby making the incentive package for them more 
attractive. Further, the Government should come out with a concrete proposal to implement 
the above rtcommendations within a period not exceeding a year. 
CENTRAL BUREAU OF INVESTIGATION 
28. The CHI is a premier investigating agency of the Government, with police powers, 
especially created to deal with corruption related matters. Presently CBI is functioning as 
per provisions of Delhi Police Establishment (DSPE) Act, 1946 and enjoys full functional 
autonomy · in investigations. Under the DSPE Act CBI requires the consent of State 
Governments before investigating crimes in the State. This is so because "Police" is a state 
subject in List - II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution and the CBI needs to the 
invested with such powers by the State Government . 
29. The workload of the CBI is increasing tremendously. What is more the nature of 
cases, it is being asked to investigate are getting increasingly complex. A fair number of 
these cases pertain to white collar crimes. It is absolutely necessary that reorganization/ 
IT'Odemization of the CBI is· done on a regular basis to enable it to keep in step (if not 
ahead), with the challenges, it is called upon to tackle. The ministry in reply to the queries 
to this effect has detailed the steps being taken to reorganize/modernize the Bureau. The 
reply also mentions that a housing proposal including proposal for owned office space for 
various branches of CBI throughout the country is being mooted. On the question of 
granting absolute autonomy to the CBI, the Ministry replied that the CBI has full functional 
autonomy in investigations. Further in view of the Ministry the question of making CBI an 
absolutely autonomous organization requires an in-depth study. 
30. The Committee has taken note of the reorganization/modernization drive being 
effected in the CBI. The measures being taken and the results thereof to fill up the vacant 
posts in CBI have also been noted and Committee is satisfied on this account. In this regard, 
the Committee would like to know whether there are any provisions for pre-entry and/or 
post-entry training of the CBI personnel to enable them to deal with increasing number and 
complexity of white collar crimes. In view of the Committee, it would be better if the 
investigative teams of CBI coordinate with other such teams of different Ministeries/ 
Departments, while working on cases of similar nature. This will make the investigation more 
effective. It will also prevent the working of different investigative team at cross purposes, 
thereby help in optimizing time, effort and resources. The Committee is not aware, whether 
the CBI has a countrywide dedicated communication network at its disposal. Such a network 
will facilitate speedy disposal of information among various centres of CBI , as well as help 
maintain confidentiality of the same. In raising the question of autonomy for CBI the 
Committee in no way wishes to take it outside the purview of Parliament. Such investigative 
organizations need to be accountable. The idea behind, raising the question of autonomy is to 
ensure that executive arbitrariness does not impinge upon impartial functioning of the CBI. 
The contention of Government that the matter requires careful and in-depth study does not 
appear to be convincing. The Committee understands that several reports to this effect have 
been prepared and that no action has been taken on them. The L. P. Singh Committee 
appointed to review the functioning of CBI bad inter-alia recommended reconstitution of 
CBI; derming its power and charter of work; defining the method of selection of 

9 
Director, CBI, the terms and conditions of appointment and the manner of his removal. 
Similarly the Estimates Committee (1991·92) under the Chairmanship of Jaswant Singh, had 
made some major recommendations in its 13th Report, which included giving status and well 
defined legal powers to CBI. The Committee would like to know how many such reports exist 
and what are their recommendations~ and impresses upon Government, the nee~ for taking 
steps to study them and implement those which are found desirable and feasible. 
CADRE MANAGEMENT 
31. The Department of Personnel & Training (DoP&T). deals with the senior 
appointment and personnel policies in the Government of India. This is done primarily 
through the Establishment Officer and the Additional Secretary in the DoP&T who is also 
the Secretary to the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (ACC). The Establishment 
Officer is also the ex-officio Member-Secretary of the Civil Services Board (CSB), which is 
chaired by the Cabinet Secretary. The Board makes recommendations for appointment and 
extension of tenure to the posts of Deputy Secretary, Director and Joint Secretary under the 
Central Staffing Scheme. The CSB makes recommendations to the ACC for inclusion of 
officers in Joint Secretary suitability list and also recommends cases for premature retirement 
of senior officers. The Central Establishment Board, chaired by Secretary (Personnel) inter­
alia also recommends cases of premature retirement for officers below the rank of Joint 
Secretary. 
32. In this connection the Committee had asked the Ministry to furnish details of senior 
officers who have been retired prematurely during last three years alongwith criteria and 
guidelines for the same. The same were furnished by the Ministry. The Committee also 
desired to know the objectives of monitoring the career pattern of officers which come under 
the purview of the Department of Personnel. In its reply the Ministry has stated that this 
exercise is regularly carried out to enable the DoP&T to make recommendations for all 
senior appointments under the Government of India. The same is done under the provisions 
of the Central Staffing Scheme. A total of 460 such postings (350 at the level of Deputy 
Secretary/Director/equivalent and 110 at the level of Joint Secretary/equivalent) were 
effected in the year 1995-96. The Committee had also enquired about the number of All 
India Services (AIS) officers who have never come on Central deputation under provisions 
of the Central Deputation Reserve (CDR), or who had stayed on deputation.over and above 
the prescribed tenure. The Committee had sought to know, whether such a practice was 
violative of rules and regulations governing the AIS officers. In its reply the Ministry had 
merely stated the provisions regarding deputation as they exist and mentioned that there are 
2900 lAS officers who have never come on Central deputation. The Ministry offered no 
comment, whether such a practice was violative of rules and regulations governing AIS 
officials. 
33. The Committee would like to impress upon Government the need to dispose off the 
requirement of taking permission from cadre controlling authorities for proceeding against 
senior officers in cases involving gross impropriety on their part. It is understood that many 
such cases are not proceeded with, because such a permission is not fortbcof!.1ing. The 
Committee recommends that such a permission be made a part of the mandate given to the 
investigative bodies. The report(s) thus received should be an important criteria for making 
recommendations about pre-mature retirement and shortlisting of officers for senior level 
appointments. 
34. The Committee understands that, over the years the Civil administration has become 

10 
top heavy. The Committee in this regard would like to know, as to what is the span-of-control 
obtaining in the Ministries/Departments/Subordinate offices of the Government of India. The 
Committee notes with concern the tendency to create new departments and accommodate 
senior officers against vacancies thus created. This in view of the Committee is creating a 
considerable drag on resources without giving commensurate results. In this regard the 
Committee would like to be apprised of the details of new departments/posts created since 
1980 with rationale thereof and to what extent the objectives for which these were created 
have been achieved. 
35. As is evident from the reply furnished by the Ministry there are 2900 lAS officers 
who have never come on Central deputation. This is a staggering 57.23% of the authorised 
cadre strength of the lAS. Viewed against this backdrop the rationale of lAS as a national 
integrating service, by virtue of which the service lays claim to and appropriates a significant 
proportion of functionally and administratively important posts, is seriously undermined. The 
whole objective of cross-fertilisation of experience in matters of planning and policy 
formulation comes to nought. Moreover these lAS officers block the promotional avenues for 
Provincial Civil Services {PCS) officers. The Committee bas strong reservations on this 
account and recommends that Ministry look into this and formulate a long term policy 
encompassing all the issues regarding cadre management of Group 'A' officers, keeping in 
view the changing dynamics of Centre-State rel~tions. 
36. The Committee had desired that Ministry provide infonnation about consultants and 
advisors engaged by the Government of India, indicating the number of retired government 
servants beyond the age of 62 years, so engaged. The Ministry in its reply stated that there 
were a total of 30 consultants engaged by the Government of India of which 21 were retir~d 
government servants, four of them being over the age of 62 years. The Ministry explaining 
the rationale of engagement of consultants had put forth the view that consultancy is being 
used to restrict the size of regular Civil Service by hiring experts to undertake assignments of 
a short term nature. 
37. The point is well taken, but the Committee finds that 21 out of a total of 30 
consultants engaged are retired government servants. It stands to reason that they have 
obtained the requisite expertise by serving in their official capacity and as such their 
replacements in the regular bureaucracy should logically be competent enough to handle 
whatever is being attended to, by the consultants. The Committee recommends that 
government look afresh into the policy, especially as hiring of retired government servants 
opens up avenues for playing favourities. Further, the engagement of consultants should be 
resorted to only in very exceptional circumstances. The assignment of consultants thus 
engaged should be time-bound and no extensions should be granted in any case whatsoever. 
The assignments should be wound up if they are not completed within the prescribed time. 
38. The Committee had asked the Ministry to set up a time frame for finalization of 
panels of Group-1 of CSS Officers on the basis of common seniority list as per the Central 
Administrative Tribunal's Order of March 22, 1995. The Ministry in its reply has given 
elaborate explanation detailing various steps that are involved in finalising the panels. It is 
stated that the number of officers to be considered are very large. Moreover, the procedure 
involved for making such recommendations is lengthy. The Committee appreciates the 
quantum of work involved in finalizing the panels. Be that as it may, it also has a human 
angle. CSS Grade-l panel has not been brought out for the last 9 years due to no fault of the 
Ministry. Nevertheless, in the absence of panel not only promotions have been delayed, a 
large number of officers would have retired without getting their promotions. Therefore, any 

11 
further delay would cause avoidable hardships. The Committee is therefore of the view .that 
this is a subject-matter which requires special action. This matter should not be dealt with in 
the routine bureaucratic manner. It should be possible for the Ministry to set up a special 
task force to complete the various steps that are being required le\lding upto the constitution 
of DPC and finalization of panel. The Ministry sbo~Jd assess bow much time it would require 
and a tim'-! frame should be drawn up to complete this exercise. The Committee feels that it 
should be possible, given the necessary will to complete the job within 6 to 9 months. 
PUBLIC ENTERPRISES SELECTION BOARD (PESB) 
39. The PESB is entrusted with the responsibility of making recommendations for 
appointment to the full-time board level posts of Chief Executives and functional Directors 
and P.art-time Chairman in the Central Public Sector Undertakings. According to the Annual 
Report {1995-96) of the Ministry. PESB makes such recommendations well in advance 
except in cases where the vacancies are not foreseeable due to death/resignation of the 
existing incumbents. Yet, when asked about the vacancy position, the Ministry replied that 
as on May 31, 1996 there were 105 vacancies of Chief Executives/full-time Directors lying 
vacant in different Central Public Sector Undertakings. This is quite contrary to the assertion 
made by the Ministry that prompt action is taken to fill the vacancies in the Central PSUs. 
The Committee is, therefore, not convinced about the use of the data bank of the PESB 
Secretariat which stores the Bio-data received from various sources-Public, Government 
and the Private Sectors and that the data base has been computerised to facilitate easy 
storage and retrieval. 
40. The Committee had also inquired about the vacancy position within the Board and 
sought the information regarding requisite qualifications, experience and tenure for the posts 
of Chairman and Members of PESB. The Committee had specifically inquired about the 
appointment of Sh. A.C. Wadhawan as Member, PESB w.e.f 23.07.1996 despite his 
indictment by an enquiry Committee of the Union Ministry of Mines. 
41. Additionally the Committee had inquired about the procedure adopted by PESB, 
while recommending the candidates for appointment to Central PSUs, and wanted to know 
from the Ministry whether PESB ensures that the incumbent recommended is clear from 
vigilance angle? It is apparent from the reply furnished by the Ministry, that the PESB does 
not insist on vigilance clearance of the candidates before making its recommendations. 
42. The Committee is not too pleased with the reply furnished by the Ministry. Excepting 
questions of factuai nature the replies furnished are very vague and do not address the issues 
raised by the Committee. Regarding the delay in filling up the vacant posts in Central PSUs 
nothing by way of explanation has been offered. The PESB now has full complement of its 
members, according to the Ministry. But the specific question regarding reasons for 
appointment of Shri A.C. Wadhawan as member PESB, despite his indictment, bas not been 
answered. Merely stating that the appointment has been effected following the prescribed 
procedure is in fact no answer, because no appointments are possible without following the 
procedure as prescribed by law. The Committee regrets that Government bas given an evasive 
reply in an important issue like this. It would, therefore, like to have full details of this case. 
According to the Committee the PESB must streamline further the mechanism to monitor the 
implementation of its recommendations. The PESB should look into the feasibility of making 
it statutorily binding on the Ministries/Departments to provide information alongwitb reasons 
for implementation/non-implementation of its recommendations within a stipulated time­
frame. The Committee does not concur with the opinion forwarded by the Ministry that 
insistence on vigilance clearance by the PESB will lead to delays in finalization of the 

12 
recommendations, especially in view of the fact that vacancies are anticipated well in advance 
and there exists a Data Bank on the prospective candidates. It is the considered view of the 
Committee that vigilance clearance be made mandatory for the candidates recommended for 
appointment by PESB. 
BACKLOG OF RESERVATIONS FOR SCsiSTs 
43. Regarding the filling up of backlog vacancies for SCs/STs, the Ministry informed the 
Committee that the Fifth Special Recruitment Drive (SRD) was completed on 31.03.1996 
and after its completion 12,815 vacancies for SCsiSTs are yet to be filled up. The reasons 
advanced by the Ministry for non-filling of such vacancies is that these have been classified 
as 'hard-core' vacancies and includes posts such as nurses, technicians, pathologists, scientists 
etc. These require candidates with specialized skilVtechnical qualifications, and that non­
availability of such candidates has resulted in persistence of vacancies. The Ministry further 
states in its note that every effort is being made to fill up the vacancies meant for SCs/STs. 
In this regard the Sixth SRD has been started from 9.07.1996 and it would continue till 
31.03.1997. 
44. The Committee feels that the reply furnished by the Ministry is inadequate. Merely 
stating that 'suitable candidates' are not available does not adequately addres:; the issues 
raised by the Committee. The Ministry in this regard may provide the details of the steps 
taken to recruit the SCIST candidates through the SRDs indicating whether the information 
about such vacancies was suitably disseminated to prospective candidates. The Ministry may 
also provide the total number of posts which have been dereserved if any, since the launch of 
Special Recruitment Drives (SRDs). The Ministry should seriously look into the possibility of 
recruiting such candidates who are marginally below the prescribed criterion for recruitment 
and then providing them adequate training to help them acquire the necessary proficiency. 
The Committee understands that the details of the vacancy position, Ministry/Department­
wise, are available before the SRDs are launched. In light of this fact, the Committee would 
urge the Ministry to seek report from the concerned Ministries/Departments regarding their 
experience from SRDs. The information so gathered should be used to make subsequent SRDs 
more effective. 
CENTRAL ADMINISTRATIVE TRmUNAL 
45. The Central Administrative Tribunal was set up on 01.11.1985 under the 
Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985. As on 01.01.1996 it has 17 regular benches operating at 
the principal seats of High Courts in different parts of the country. The sanctioned strength 
of Chairman, Vice-Chairmen and Members of CAT as on 01.01.1996 is as follows:-
Chairman 
Vice-Chairmen 
Members 
1 
16 
49 
The jurisdiction of CAT extends to all the civilian employees of Central Government . 
Organizations like Council for Scientific and Industrial Research, National Labour Institute , 
the Central Social Welfare Board, the Council for Agriculture Research, the Employee s 
State Insurance Corporation and Sports Authority of India have also been brought within 
the jurisdiction of the CAT. 
46. The Ministry in its note has submitted that there were 8 vacancies of Vice-Chairmen 
and 11 Members as on 31st July, 1996, and that selections have been made for all the 
vacancies, except one vacancy of an Administrative member which arose on 22.06.1996 due 

13 
to demise of the incumbent. Regarding the proposal to set up additional courts in the 
Principal Bench and in the Allahabad Bench, the Ministry, states that the matter is under 
consideration in consultation with the Chairman CAT. Further the Committee has been 
informed by the Ministry that there are a total of 42,878 cases pending in CAT. 
47. The Committee is concerned at the pendency of large number of cases in the CAT 
and its benches. According to the information furnished by the Ministry to the Committee, 
as on March 31, 1996, a total number of 42,878 cases were pending .d,isposal before the CAT 
and its different benches, the details of which are as under:-
(i) Less than 1 year 14735 
(ii) Between 1-2 years 11710 
(iii) Between 2-3 years 7407 
(iv) Between 3-5 years 6511 
(v) Over 5 years 2515 
TOTAL: 42878 
It is somewhat surprising that such a large number of cases are pending disposal 
despite the fact that the Administrative Tribunals are not bound by the technicalities 
of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. The objective of Tribunal is to provide speedy 
and inexpensive justice and, in the opinion of the Committee this is being undermined 
due to the pendency of such a large number of cases. As the saying goes "Justice 
delayed is justice denied." The Committee feels that the full complement of Vice­
Chairmen and Members of CAT should be in place to ensure expeditious disposal of 
cases. In this connection, the Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation as 
contained in its 16th Report wherein it bad recommended that in view of the large 
number of cases pending before the Principal Bench and AUababad Bench, the number 
of courts in those Benches needs to be increased for speeding up the disposal of 
pending cases. Further, the Committee recommends that a time frame instituted to 
expedite the clearance of each stage of a case. Concerned Government offices should 
be asked to provide required information at the earliest and strlngent provisions 
should be made to cbargesbeet the departments/officials not doing so within the 
stipulated time. 
KENDRIYA BHANDAR 
48. The Kendriya Bhandar (Central Government Employees Consumer 
Cooperative Society) , a Welfare Cooperative Society was set up in 1963 to provide 
essential commodities to the consumers at reasonable prices. This it endeavours to 
do by operating at a marginal rate of gross profit . It receives no subsidy from the 
Central Government except Government accommodation allotted to it at a 
nominal rent of Rs. 11-per month, per premises. Kendriya Bhandar seeks to 
constantly improve upon the services and range of goods provided by it to the 
customers. 
49. The Committee appreciates the operation of Kendriya Bhandar, and is 
pleased about the fact that it receives no subsidy from the government , save on 
accommodation, and yet it has been running on profit since 1982-83. In this regard 
the Committee recommends that a study be carried out, wherein the impact of 

14 
operations of the Kendriya Bhandar on the price and quality of goods in the open market be 
studied. The insights gained from such a study will help the Kendriya Bhandar to make 
suitable changes in its operational strategy to improve upon its achievements. 
50. The Kendriya Bhandar has its branches located in various parts of Delhi which 
include areas where Officers belonging to higher income group also reside . With the 
liberalization of the economy and other fast changing developments, possession of credit cards 
is a fairly common phenomenon. Therefore, the Committee would suggest that to enhance its 
sales turnover the management of Kendriya Bhandar may consider accepting payment s 
through credit cards. This facility may be introduced on trial basis in few selected bran ches to 
begin with. 
UNION PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION 
51. The Committee was informed that UPSC conducts 17 examinations in all and that the 
candidates have the option to write the answers in all the papers, including optional subjects, 
in any of the languages included in the VIIIth Schedule to the Constitution apart from English 
in the Civil Services Examination only. The Committee wanted to know as to why regional 
languages are not being used in all the examinations conducted by the UPSC. In reply the 
Ministry submitted that on an average about 88% candidates giving the Civil Services 
Examination opted to take it in the English medium. Whereas the corresponding figure for 
Hindi and regional languages was 9% and 3% respectively. The Secretary informed the 
C...ommittee that most probable explanation for these figures was that good quality literatur e 
was not available in Hindi/regional languages and thus the case for use of Hindi/region al 
languages was not very strong. Continuing further, the Secretary submitted that the propo sal 
for introduction of such option in all the examinations being conducted by the UPSC was 
under active consideration. 
52. In this regard the Committee is of the view that low percentage of candidate s o pting 
for regional languages and non-availbility of good quality literatu re in the same is a historical 
build up and that this can not be a excuse for not allowing use of regional languages. It must be 
recognized that support systems only come up in response to felt needs. The question papers of 
the examinations can continue to be in English and Hindi but the candidates should be given the 
option of replying in any of the languages specified in the Vlllth Schedule of the Constituti on, 
in all the examinations being conducted by the UPSC. The Ministry bas argued that sufficient 
number of candidates do not offer regional languages as the medium of writing the 
examinations and that the pass percentage of such candidates who do opt for regional languages 
as the medium of examination is very poor. This argument is not tenable. The Committee would 
like to point out that the right of use of regional languages is enshrined in the Constitution and 
that this Constitutional obligation should be honoured. Also, there are two unanimous 
resolutions of Parliamen t and directions of the Hon'ble President of India that the use of 
regional languages as recognised by our Constitution be permitted by UPSC in all the 
examinations conducted by it, just as use of regional languages is permitted for the All India 
Civil Services Examinations. The importance of local languages is evident from the fact that the 
AIS officials have to Pcquire functional proficiency in the language of the States to which they 
are assigned. 
53. The fact that sufficient number of books and other relevant material are not available , 
also is not relevant . If sufficient number of books/other literat ure is not available the reason is 
that there is not adequate demand for t he same. If examinees are a llowed the use of regional 
languages, the Committee is of the view that other things will follow. The Committee, ther efore, 
recommends that use of regional languages as listed in the Vllltb Schedule to the Constitut ion, 
be permitted in all the examinations conducted by UPSC and SSC without any further delay.

OVERVIEW 
The Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs comprises the following 
Departments:-
(i) Department of Legal Affairs, 
(ii) Legislative Department, 
(iii) Department of Justice , and 
(iv) Department of Company Affairs. 
2. The main functions of the Department of Legal Affairs are:-
(i) To render advice to the various Ministries/Departments of the Government of 
India on legal mat ters; 
(ii) To carry out the conveyancing work of the Central Government; 
(iii) To attend the litigation work in the Supreme Court, High Courts and some of 
the subordina_te courts; 
(iv) To handle the treaties and agreements with foreign countries in matters of Civil 
Law; 
(v) To authorise officers to execute contracts and assurances of property on behalf 
of the President under Article 299 (1) of the Constitution. 
(vi) To sanction grants-in-aids to certain institutions engaged in research in the field 
of law. 
3. The Department of Legal Affairs is further concerned with appointment of the Law 
Officers, namely the Attorney-General of India, the Solicitor-General of India and the 
Additional Solicitors-General of India, etc. It is also administratively incharge of the Foreign 
Exchange Regulation Appellate Board. 
4. The Legal Affairs Department has a two-tier organisational set-up, namely, the main 
Secretariat at New Delhi and the Branch Secretariats at Mumbai, Calcutta, Madras and 
Bangalore. 
5. The Legislative Department is concerned mainly with the following matters:-
(i) Scrutiny of Notes for the Cabinet in relation to all legislative proposals from 
drafting and constitutional points of view; 
(ii) Drafting of all Government Bills including Constitution (Amendment) Bills 
before introduction in Parliament; translation of all such Bills into Hindi and 
forwarding both English and Hindi versions of the Bills· to the Parliament 
Secretariat; drafting of non-official amendments and rendering of assistance to 
Administrative Ministries to decide on the acceptability or otherwise of non­
official amendments; 
(iii) Rendering assistance to Parliament and Joint, Select or Standing Committees of 
Parliament at all stages through which a Bill passes before enactment. This 
includes scrutiny of and/or preparation of reports of such Committees, and 
Hindi Translations of such reports and minutes of dissent; 
(iv) Drafting of Ordinances to be promulgated by the President;

(v) Drafting of legislations to be enacted as President's Acts in respect of States 
under President's rule; 
(vi) Drafting of Regulations to be made by the President; 
(vii) Drafting of Constitution Orders, i.e., Orders required to be issued under the 
Constitution; 
(viii) Scrutiny of all statutory rules, orders and notifications and their translation into 
Hindi; 
(ix) Scrutiny of State Legislation in the Concurrent field which requires assent of the 
President under article 254 of the Constitution; 
(x) Scrutiny of legislations to be enacted by Union Territory Legislatures; 
(xi) Election of Parliament, Legislatures of States and Union Territories and Offices 
of the President and Vice-President; 
(xii) Election Commission; Electroral Reforms; 
(xiii) Apportionment of expenditure on Election between the Centre and the States! 
UTs with Legislatures; 
(xiv) Bringing out three Journals and reporting the cases of Supreme Court and 
selected cases of the High Courts in Hindi; 
(xv) Translation of Central Acts in the regional languages enumerated in the Eighth 
Schedule of the Constitution of India and publication of Authoritative Texts 
thereof. 
6. The Department of Justice deals with the constitutional organisation of the Supreme 
Co urt and the High Courts and the appointment of Judges thereto, conditions of their 
service and with the administration of judicial services in the Union Territories. Besides , it is 
the nodal Department in so far as the administration of Justice in States is concerned , 
although the Actual responsibility of judicial administration below the High Court level rests 
with the concerned State Government and High Court. Though this department forms a part 
of Ministry of Law, Justice & Company Affairs, it is under the administrative control of 
Ministry of Home Affairs. The Committee in its Seventeenth Report had observed that this 
state of affairs gives an anomalous picture which needs to be set right. The Committee in the 
said Report had recommended that the Department of Justice should be placed under the 
Ministry of Law for all purposes thereby dispensing with the administrative control of the 
Ministry of Home Affairs. But so far no change has been made in this set-up. 
7. Till 1992-93, the budget of the Department of Justice was salary oriented. From 
1993-94, the Demands of the Department of Justice also include provision for the Centrally 
Sponsored Scherhe relating to infrastructural facilities for the judiciary and National Judicial 
Academy. From this financial year i.e., 1996-97 provision has also been made for the 
National Judicial Pay Commission. 
8. The Department of Company Affairs is the primary agency responsible for the 
development and efficient functioning of the corporate sector comprising the joint stock 
companies. The objectives in this regard are sought to be achieved by the Department 
mainly through administration of the Companies Act, 1956 and the Monopolies and 
Restrictive Trade Practices Act, 1969. Further, it is also concerned with the Chartered 
Accountants Act, 1949, the Cost and Works Accountants Act, 1959 and the Company 
Secretaries Act, 1980. Apart from the aforesaid Acts, the responsibility of discharging the 
functions of the Central Government relating to the Administration of the Partnership Act, 
1932, the Companies(Donations to National Funds) Act, 1951 and Societies Registration 
Act, 1860 also rests with the Department. This Department first came into existence on the 
first August, 1955.

DEPARTMENT OF LEGAL AFFAIRS 
National Legal Services Authority 
15. From the information provided by the Legal Affairs Department, the Committee 
notes that now with the enforcement of National Legal ·Services Authority Act, 1987, w .e.f. 
9.11.1995, the Committee for Implementing Legal Aid Scheme has been replaced with the 
Legal Services Authority. As stated in the Annual Report of the Ministry, the Supreme 
Court Legal Services Committee has also been constituted under the Act for rendering 
competent legal services to the weaker sections of the society whose cases are before the 
Supreme Court. The Act also provides for constitution of the State Legal Services 
Authorities, High Court Legal Services Committees, District Legal Services Authorities and 
Taluk Legal Services Committees. The main object of the Act is to provide free and 
competent legal services to the weaker sections of the society on a uniform basis throughout 
the country. Under the Legal Services Authorities Act, free legal aid is admissible to every 
citizen whose income is less than Rs. 9,000 per annum in cases before subordinate Courts 
and High Courts and Rs. 12,000 in cases before the Supreme Court. The limitation as to 
income is, however, not applicable in case of persons belonging to the Scheduled Castes, the 
S,eheduled Tribes, women, children, handicapped persons etc. A budgetary provision of Rs. 
80 lakh~. has been made for grants under this Act in the Budget. Estimates for the year 1996-
97. A question was posed to the Department as to whether the estimated amount will be 
sufficient to fulfil the Government's commitment to give free legal aid to poor people. In 
reply to it, Committee was informed that with the enforcement of the Legal Services 
Authorities Act, 1987, the legal aid movement has been placed on a statutory base. For 
holding Lok Adalats, Legal Literacy Camps, 'Training of Para-Legals' etc., more funds are 
likely to be requisitioned by the. State Legal Aid & Advice Boards/State Legal Services 
Authorities etc. It is estimated that during the year 1996-97, about Rs. 1.00 crore will be 
needed for these programmes. The Department was informed that the Committee was 
prepared to extend help and to impress upon the Government to make provisions, but the 
Department should come out with some concrete proposals. 
16. In the written reply to the point raised by the Committee regarding progress made 
in implementing the legal aid scheme, the Department has informed that as on 1.8.1996 

5 
about 23,23,910 people have been benefited through Legal aid. As regards Lok Adalats, the 
Committee notes that 13,802 Lok Adalats were organised in the count ry where 60,87,467 
cases were settled. Compensation of Rs. 975,70,474 was awarded in about 3,06,086 Motor 
Accident Claims cases. 
17. The Comm itt ee has been informed by the Department that to reduce the number of 
the pending cases, special initiatives are being taken as regards Lok Adalats. In the first 
phase S-6 States are being selected whe re Lok Adalats at all the levels will be held every 15 
days. The Committee recommends that more categories of cases, i.e. cases pert aining to 
matrimony, election and education matters should also be covered und er Lok Adalats. The 
Committee feels that judgements of Lok Adalats should have legal sanction so as to serve the 
purpose of reducing the work load of courts. The Department informed the Committee that in 
the Budget propo sals for the year 1996-97, Rs. 50 lakhs have been allocated for holding Lok 
Adalats. but the Secretary, Legal Affairs in his presentation requested the Committee to 
recommend that this amount needs to be rai sed suitably to a level of Rs. 2 crores. The 
Commi ttee feels that the propo sed Budget allocation be suitably increased. The Committee 
furth er recommends that instead of deputing sitting judges of courts, retired judge s of courts 
should hold Lok Adalats so that the sitting judg es can devote their time in disposing of the 
cases listed in regular courts. 
18. While appr eciating the steps being taken by the Departm ent to enforce the National 
Legal Services Authority Act in letter and spirit , the Committee expresses its concern that the 
fee being paid to the Advocates taking up the cases under Free Legal Aid Scheme is very less. 
As a result of this good Advocates do not want to take up cases and the cases are not being 
handled prop erly. The Committee also feels that the Government lawyers either do not appear 
in time or do not file the papers properly as a result of which the cases are unn ecessarily 
delayed. The Committee , therefore, recommend s that the fees to be paid to the Advocates 
handling cases under Free Legal Aid Scheme should be suitably r aised so that proper talent is 
available. The Commi ttee also recommends that the process of appointing Govcrnm l·nt 
law)·ers and Government Standing Counsels at all the levels should be s treamlined . Some joint 
process should be evolved. The Go\'ernm ent lawyers should also be made accountable 
regarding handling the case entrus ted to them. 
19. The Committ ee expresses its concern over the complete lack of awareness among the 
common people with regard to their right s and obligations and emphasises the importa nce of 
para-legal training programme for creat ing legal awareness among the common people. The 
Committee expresses its serious doubts about the sufficiency of allocation of fund s proposed in 
the Budget Estimate for this purpose. The Committee is of the view that more alloction is 
req uired to be made for para-legal training progr amme, ::\S extensive work is to be done on 
this score . 
20. On a point raised regarding the jury system the Committee was inform ed th at on 
lower levels there is no jury system. Only in High Courts and Supreme Court Benches of 
more than one judge are constituted according to the requirem ent of the case. The Com mittee 
stresses the need for instituting jury system to make judicial system more credible and 
transparent. 
21. The Committee notes with concern that many grantee institutions could not fully 
utilise the grants-in-aid sanc tioned to them. The Department was pointedly asked as to what 
steps the Department is cotemplating to ensure that such grants-in-aid are fully utilised. 
1. Thl! Department has informed the Committee that-they have tentatively 
earmarke d the amount of the grunt-in-aid to be released to each State.

2. The grant-in-aid shall be released periodically so as to afford sufficient time to the 
grantee institution for utilisation of the grant-in-aid. 
3. The quantum of fresh grant-in-aid is determined on the basis of the trend of the 
expenditure by a grantee institution of the earlier grant-in-aid sanctioned to it. 
22. The Committee is constrained to note that most of the schemes launched by the 
Government were not upto the mark. The Committee feels that all these schemes must have 
been vetted by the Department of Legal Affairs. The Committee stresses that the Department 
of Legal Affairs should take special care to ensure that they don't approve the schemes/ 
policies which are not implementable. The Committee also observed that the Government is 
the biggest litigant in most of the cases. Hence the Committee recommends that while 
rendering legal advice, proper care must be taken so that unnecessary litigations can be 
avoided. Concerned officials must be made accountable for the advice renderd.

LAW COMMISSION 
26. The Law Commission of India is a non-statutory body constituted by the 
Government from time to time. The Commission was originally constituted in 1955 and is 
reconstituted every three years. The administrative control of the Law Commission vests 
with the Department of Legal Affairs. The terms of reference of ·the Law Commission are 
also determined by the Department of Legal Affairs. The Law Commission presents its 
reports on various subjects to the Government which are then processed by the Department 
of legal Affairs for placing them on the Tables of Parliament. These reports are thereafter 
forwarded to the various Ministries/Departments of the Government of India who are 
administratively concerned with their implementation. A total of Rs. 78 lakhs Budgetary 
provision has been made for the expenses of Law Commission for the year 1996-97. 
27. The Committee had stressed the need for amending the Indian Penal Code, Code of 
Criminal Procedure and Evidence Act so that speedy justice can be provided to poor people. 
In reply to this the Department has informed the Committee that Government has requested 
the Law Commission of India to undertake comprehensive revision of these enactments. 
The Committee recommends that besides the above mentioned enactments, the revision of 
Code of Civil Procedure should also be undertaken. The Committee further recommends that 
while amending the C.P.C., provisions relating to service of process should · be 
comprehensively modified and streamlined. The Committee feels that there are certain 
procedural lacunae in the existing Code which prolongs the case. Hence Committee 
recommends that provision should be made to ensure quickers service of summons/process, 
all the steps of service i.e., sending through a process server, through registered post, etc. 
should be taken simultaneously. The Committee is of the view that in this modern age of 
communication and transport the Courts should not stick to the ancient system of sending a 
person with summons . The Committee also notes that as regards C.P.C. and Cr. P.C. at 
present there are different provision in different parts of the country whicb creates lots of 
problems. Hence the Committee also recommends that whUe modifying these enactments, 
efforts should be made to ensure that similar provisions are applied in the whole nation. The 
Committee further recommends that efforts should also be made to study the different 
customary laws prevalent in different parts of the country specially in North-Eastern parts. 
These customary laws give cheaper ~nd quicker justice. The Department should take steps to 
codify these laws. The Law Commission should be requested to expedite the Reports on the 
amendments of these Acts and some time frame should be fixed for it. The Committee also 
feels the Reports of the Law Commission should have some sanctity and the Department 
should ensure that these Reports are acted upon.

in turn impart similar training to ADR practitioners in workshops to be organised all over 
the country. The Asian Development Bank has urged to provide small scale technical 
assistance not exceeding U.S.$ 100,00<Y- for these workshops. This Departments will be the 
execut ing agency for these training programmes and the International Centre for Alternative 
Dispute Resolution (l_CADR) will be the implementing agency for these training 
programmes.

LEGISLATIVE DEPARTMENT 
29. The Committee point ed out that even after the Legislative Department vest the 
administrative proposal drafts a Bill, so many lacunae and anon talies are found which give 
way to avoidable disputes in the Courts. The Committee suggested to the Legislative 
Department that some loud thinking should be done and they should take steps to 
modern ise thei r Department by making use of Internet system and should have its own 
Research Wing to go into this aspect. The y should re-orient and sensitise the Department. 
They should take initiatives to rectify the mistakes, lacunae and anomalies at the initial stage 
so that the Act s a re in good form and they are not challenged in the Courts. The Committee 
further expressed its view that basic objective of the law should be to resolve a dispute rather 
than create bitterness. The Committee also suggested that there should be a separat e cell in 
the Department which should undertake an intergrated, holistic and a comprehensive 
research, not with an academic object ive but with a practical objective to make more 
practical Jaws which are less time-consuming, and less expensive. The Committee is of th.e 
view that necessary Budgetary provision should be made in this regard. 
30. The Committee also stressed the need for bringing out comprehensive Bill on electoral 
reforms. The representatives of the Legislative Department inform ed the Committ ee that a 
proposal has been submitted to Ministry of Parliament ary Affairs to convene an all-Party 
meeting to finalise the draft of comprehen sive electoral reforms Bill. 
31. The Committee also pointed out that since Manipuri, Nepali and Konkani 
Languages have been included in the 8th Schedule of the Constitution, appropriate 
provisions whould be made for the translation of Central Acts into these langu ages. The 
Department was also asked to give detailed information regarding publication of Central 
Acts in other regional languages. The Committee had pointedly asked the Department to send 
details, in the context of Budget proposals, as to under what Head the Department would like 
to have more money. But the Committee is pained to note that not such details could be 
furnished' by the Department. The Committee would like the Department to submit a 
comprehensive note covering all the points raised by the Committee. 
DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE 
32. The Committee expressed it concern over the pendency of cases in the courts. The 
Committee stressed that some time frame should be prescribed for the disposal of cases. While 
expressing concern over the pendency of cases, the Committee feels that mere filling up all the 
vacancies of judges in Supreme Courts and different High Courts will not solve the problem. 
Number of benches sMuld be increased. The Committee suggests that the Benches of High 
Courts could be set up according to the distance or the areas of the population they cover. 
The Committee specifically referred to the State of Uttar Pradesh and stated that Seventy-five 
percent of the cases in the Allahabad High Court pertain to the Western part of Uttar 
Pradesh which accounts for one third of the State , population-wise and one fourth area-wise. 
The Committee stressed that there is a long standing demand for setting up a Bench of 
Allahabad High Court in Western Uttar Pradesh. The Committee also recomm ends that 
posibility of decentralisation of Supreme Court, with Benches in different parts of the 
Country, may be considered. 
33. On the concern expressed by the Committee regarding pendency of cases, the 
Department of justice in its written reply informed the Committ ee that steps have been 
taken to fill up the vacancies of the Judges in the High Courts at the earliest possible. The 
Department informed that the memorandum of procedure for appointm ent of Judges of the. 

9 
High Courts prescribing a time schedule has been revised in consultation with the Chief 
Justice of India. Now, the pr( :'osal for appointment of a Judge of a High Court shall be 
ini~iated by the Chief Justice of that High Court as early as possible but at least six months 
before the date of occurrence of the vacancy. The Committee was not fully satisfied with the 
explanation given by the Department of Justice with regard to filling the vacant posts of 
Judges. On the query made by the Committee regarding transfer of Judges of High Court, 
the Department informed the Committee that the Government has accepted as a policy that 
one-third of Judges in each High Court should be from any other State. 
34. The Committee stressed that the Department should undertake study and research to 
evolve an alternative disputes resolution. The Committee also suggested that there should be 
some provision to specify time limit for the completion of each stage of the case. The 
Committee also suggested that stringent rules should be framed in the exercise of 
discretionary powers by the presi ding officers specially with regard to grant of adjournments. 
On the above mentioned points, the Committee was informed that the institution of Lok 
Adalats has been made functional and the Legal Services Authorities Act has been brought 
into force. The Arbitration and Conciliation Bill to encourage an alternate mode of dispute 
resolution has also been enacted. 
35. On a query made by the Committee as to whether ~llocation of adequate funds 
through the auspices of this Committee can help reduce the pendency of cases, the 
Department in its written reply informed the Committee that the reasons for accumulation 
of arrears are very complex and the provision of funds alone cannot be the solution. 
36. On a suggestion made by the Committee that as regards implementation of the 
Centra lly Sponsored Scheme for the development of infrastructural facilities grant to the

Committee to consider recommending to the Planning Commission that the Scheme be 
continued beyond the 8th Plan as the Planning Commiss ion had approved this scheme for 
the Eighth Five Year Plan only. 
37. The Committee takes note of the efforts being made by the Government with rega rd 
to the developmen t of infrastructur al facilities for the judiciary and urg es upon the 
Governm ent to take up the matter with the Plannin g Commission for its continu ance b eyond 
the E ighth Five Year Plan. The Committee also recommends that the Centr al Government 
share s hould be 75% under this head and for the rest 25% may be provided by th e State 
Govern ments. 
38. As regards the National Judicial Academy , the Committee expressed its concern that 
though the Academ y was r egistered in 1993, it could not start full-fledged f!-)nctioning till now. 
The C ommittee suggests that f or the time being , the training a ctivities of Judicial officers can 
commence in the rented building rath er than waiting for the completion of Academy' s own 
building. 
39. The Committee notes that the Central Government has set up the Judici al Pay 
Commission for judicial officers of all States . The report of this Pay Commi ssion w ould be 
advisory in nature an d it, is for the Stat e Govern ments to ta ke a final view with regar d to its 
acceptance/i mplementat ion. O n a point raised by the Committe e r egard ing the Budgeta ry 
prov ision unde r this heaa, the Department has inform ed the Committee that an advance of 
Rs. 15 lak hs has been obtained from the Contingency Fund of I ndia to mee t the immediate 

10 
requirement of the Commission. This amount would be recouped to the Fund out of the 
provision of Rs. 17 lakhs which has been provided for the Commission (Major h ead '2014' in 
the regular Budget for the year 1996-97). It is expected that the Commission may incur 
expenditure of about Rs. 100 lakbs during the current financial year. The additional 
requirement would be met through advance from the Contingency Fund of India and suitable 
provision will be requested for in the supplementary Budget. 
40. The Committee recommends that the Government should evolve a mechanism to 
assess the situation in the State Governments where the pay and other facilities of the Judicial 
Officers ,are not at par with the executive thereof of that level. 
41. The Committee pointed out that though decision of separating Judiciary from 
Executive bas been taken way back, this separation has still not been effected in whole of 
Nagaland State and some parts of Andbra Pradesh, Assam and Megbalaya. The Committee 
pointedly enquired whether any decision has been taken in this regard and whether any 
provision has been made in the proposed Budget Estimates for establishing Courts in those 
areas. The Department of Justice in its written reply has informed that the Code of Criminal 
Procedure, 1973 sought to ensure the separation of Judiciary from the Executive on all India 
basis by providing for a new set-up of Criminal Courts. Though provisions regarding setting 
up of Criminal Courts do not apply to State of Nagaland and tribal areas, these States may 
by notification apply such provisions to the concerned States with such supplemental, 
incidental or consequential modifications as may be specified in the notification. The 
Committee has been informed that the State of Nagaland decided on 5th July, 1994 to 
separate the Judiciary from Executive and steps are being taken to implement the decision. 
The Committee further notes from the written reply of the Department of Justice that in 
Meghalaya, separat ion of Judiciary from the Executive .extends o nly to the cantonm ent and 
the normal areas of Shillong town. In Mizoram, phased separation of J udiciary has already 
been taken up by constituting separate Judicial Service and separate court buildings . T he 
Committee urges u pon the Government to take all possible steps to ensure that Judiciary is 
separated from the Executive. T he States where such separation has not been effected, 
should be impressed upon to take steps for the complete separation of Judiciary from 
Executive. 
42. Regarding use of Hindi in courts, the Committee notes that Article 348(1) of the 
Constitution provides that all proceedings in the Supreme Court and in every High Cour t 
shall be in English until Parliament by Law otherwise provides. No law has been made by 
the Parliament so far. The Chief Justice of India had reported in October, 1991 that 
replacement of English at lower levels of the judiciary by the State Language had already 
been implemented throughout India. 
43 •. The Committee was informed that with a steep increase in number of advocates, the 
existing Supreme Court building complex having about 135 chambers for the lawyers of the 
Supreme Court, has been proved insufficient. The Government had approved the 
construction of 136 additional chambers and on that account administrative approval and 
expenditure sanction of Rs. 5.76 crores was issued. The CPWD had reported in June, 1996 
that the main building work was already under progress and also had sent a proposal for a 
revised estimate of Rs. 7.46 crores owing to the increased expenditure in respect of certain 
civil and electrical work. The Committee ur;es upon the Government to take suitable steps 
for completion of the work so that the lawyers could be allotted the chambers. 
44. The Committee recommends that a cell may be set up to go into the Judicial reforms 
which would monitor the recommendations/observations made in various conventions, 
conferences, seminars, symposia, parliamentary debates etc. and the Government, based upon 
this research work should come forward with concrete suggestions in this regard. 

11 
45. The plenary meeting of Law Secretaries and Law Ministers was held in Hyderabad 
during 23·25 November, 1995 to consider inter·alia, reforms in legal education and entry into 
legal profession. During the meeting the Law Ministers expressed their concern at the 
standards in legal education and also observed that the Supreme Court of India had also 
reacted to the fall in the standard of legal advocates. The Committee recommends that there 
is an urgent need of establishing a National Law School and funds must be provided therefor 
in the Budget. 
DEMAND NO. 59-ELECTION COMMISSION OF INDIA 
46. The Election Commission of India and Electoral Reforms come under the purview 
of the Legislative Department of the Ministry. The Demands for Grants of the Election 
Commission do not form part of the composite Demand No. 58. Demand No. 59 has 
separa.tely been assigned to Election Commission. The Expenditure of the Election 
Commission is 'Voted'. Budgetary allocation of a total of 547 crore rupees has been made 
for the year 1996·97 as against 355 crores allocated under the Revi sed Estimates for the year 
1995·96. The Committee appreciates that with a view to achieve the aim and objel.:tive of the 
Voters' awareness, the Commission has launched a 'National Voters' Awareness Campaign' 
and has allocated a sum of Rs. 30 crores for this purpose. The Committee stressed that since 
a huge amount has already been spent on the issuance of Voters Identity Cards, final decision 
must be taken on the issue of use of Identity Cards at the time of conduct of Assembly/ 
Parliament Elections/by-elections. The Committee has directed the Department to furnish 
the Committee a Detailed Note in this respect. 
DEMAND NO. 60-SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
47. Demand No. 60 in the detailed Demands of Grants of the Ministry has been 
assigned ·to the Supreme Court of India. The expenditure to be incurred on tl.e Supreme 
Court of India is 'Cha rged' . As regards the Committee's concern regarding pendency of 
cases, the Committee has been informed that at present there is only one vacancy in the 
Supreme Court and the pendency position has improved to a great extent during the last 18 
months. The number of pending cases which was over one lakh on 1st December, 1995, has 
come down to 37,000. It is expected that during the current financial year there will be lesser 
expenses on the Foreign Travel Head (Rs. 20 crores as against Rs. 55 crores granted for the 
year 1995·96) Salaries Head (Rs. 1079.60 crores as against Rs. 1330.19 crores for the year 
1995·96) and Office Expenses Head (Rs. 225 crores as against Rs. 340 crores allocated for 
the year 1995·96). Hence the total Budget Estit:pates of the Supreme Court of India under 
the Revenue are Rs. 14.07 crores as against Rs. 18.08 crores of Revised Estimates for the 
year 1995·96. 
DEMAND NO. 61-DEPARTMENT OF COMPANY AFFAIRS 
48. The total budgetary allocation (BE) made for the Department of Company Affairs 
for 1996·97 is Rs. 17.5 crores. The Department has no plan expenditure. The entire budget 
of the Department is non·plan and establishment·oriented. In his presentation, the 
representative of the Department informed the Committee that out of Rs. 17,50 crores 
which is projected for this year, 69.5 per cent goes for salaries and rent; 22 per cent for 
office expenses; a sum of Rs. 1.38 crores has been provided for computerication in the ROC 
offices. 
49. The Committee expressed its view that in the wake of liberalisation, the task which 
the Department of Company Affairs is facing is a very challenging one. So many companies 

12 
are being registered, so many multinational companies are coming in, so many 
amalgamations are taking place. The whole concept of a company has undergone a sea­
change. The role of companies has acquired a new dimension in an increasingly competitive 
market. There is, therefore, all the more need for greater supervision over them lest they 
may indulge in unfair and unhealthy trade practices. Most of the companies float public 
issues and debentures and collect huge amount from the public. Many companies again 
collect huge sums of money from the public through their Fixed Deposit Schemes. The 
Committee asked the Department to lay particular emphasis on the key areas and to explain 
difficulties which the Department is facing. In reply to this the representative of the 
Department informed the Committee that though there has been a steep increase and 
phenomenal growth in the number of companies registered during the last decade, the 
strength of the Registrars of Companies has almost stagnated. The Department informed the 
Committee that it had collected revenue by way of fees from companies of Rs. 240.60 crores 
during 1995-96 whereas in 1989-90 it was Rs. 29 crores only. 
50. The Committee is happy to note that to protect the interest of investors and to cope 
up with the increasing work load of investors' complaints, the Department has set-up an 
Investors' Pro tection Cell which is functioning satisfactorily. 
51. The Committee stressed that in view of the changing scenario in the field of 
Industry, the Companies Act, 1956 needs exhaustive amendments. The Depar~ment 
informed that the Government is aware of the fact that the Companies Act needs to be re­
written comprehensively. The Committee appreciates that a working group has been set up 
to prepare a new draft of the Company Bill and make it ready for public debate by January 
1997. 
COMPANY LAW BOARD 
52. As regards the Company Law Board, the Committee in its Seventeenth Report had 
observed that the pendency of the petitions/applications before the CLB could broadly be 
attributed to the vacant position of members at different benches as a consequence of which 
the members at headquarters have to bear extra burden of the work and they have to divert 
their attention to hear the cases at other benches. This certainly hampers the process of 
expeditious disposal of the cases. The Committee had recommended that the vacant posts of 
the members be filled up within the shor test time-frame. The Department has made an 
allocation of Rs. 81 lakhs to meet the expense s of the Board. In the context of the above 
mention ed recommendation the Committee asked the Department categorically if it could 
allocate some more amount for spending on the administrative machinery available to 
Company Law Board. The Department informed the Committee that the Company Law 
Board has indicated that the budgetary Outlay of Rs. 81.00 lakhs for 1996-97 is adequate. 
53. The Committee notes that the total number of petitions and appl ications pending 
before the CLB was 2579 as on 31.3.96. The Department has inform ed the Committee that 
as per the Companies Act , 1956, the Company Law Board is to consist of Chairman, Vice­
Chairm an and seven Memb ers. It has only three members at present, one out of whom is 
officiating as Chairman of the Board. The Committee was inform ed that the Selection 
Committe e und er the Chairmanship of Hon'ble Justice Shri J.S. Verma, Judge of the 
Supreme Court recomm ended 3 candidates for appointment as members of the Company 
Law Board and after approval by the competent authority, offers had been sent on the 18th 
July, 1996. The Department expressed the hope that the rate of disposal is likely to go up 
after these memb ers join Company Law Board. 

13 
54. The Additional Secretary, on a pointed query regarding the exemption to be sought 
by the multinational companies coming into our land, informed the Committee that no 
exemption would be extended. If it was a Branch Office of a foreign company, it must file 
with the Registrar of Companies its Balance sheets and other things. If it was purely a 
Liaison Officer then the Central Government would consider and give an exemption but 
there also it would have to file certain returns like its assests, liabilities etc. The Committee 
expressed satisfact ion over this.
