REPORT 
I, the Chairman of the Committee on Home Affairs, having been authorised by the 
Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this Thirty-fifth Report of the 
Committee, relating to the Companies (Amendment) Bill, 1996•. 
2. In pursuance of the Rules relating to Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha referred*" the Companies (Amendment) Bill, 1996, 
as introduced in the Rajya Sabha on the lOth September, 1996 and pending therein. to the 
Committee for examination and report. 
3. The statement of objects and reasons of the Bill states that following suggestions from 
different fora and to take care of the changes which have taken place in the Capital market, 
operation of corporate sector and liberalisation policies. a need has been felt to undertake a 
comprehensive revision of the Companies Act. 1956 and accordingly Government has set up 
a Working Group to rewrite the Act. Since the whole exercise will take a considerable time 
to complete, some changes in the Act were felt imminent and therefore , this Bill. The Bill 
mainly seeks (i) to provide protection to the depositors; (ii) to provide protection to 
employees' interest in case of winding up of a Company; and (iii) to simplify some 
procedural and legal requirements in the interest of corporate sector. 
4. In its meeting held on the 8th October. 1996 the Committee heard the Secretary, 
Legislative· Department on various aspects of the Bill, but deferred his further evidence till 
the representative of the Department of Company Affairs which was the administrative 
Ministry concerned with the Bill appeared before it and explained the nature of the 
proposed amendments and their broad thrust. 
5. In its meeting held on the 9th October, 1996 the Committee heard the representative 
of the Department of Company Affairs on the salient features of the Bill and the urgency of 
the Bill pending the comprehensive redrafting of the entire Companies Act currently in 
progress. In the course of his presentation, the Committee was informed about the 
composition of the Working Group which has been assigned with the task of redrafting the 
Companies Act. The Committee expressed its displeasure over the composition of the 
working group as it was not broad ba~ed and representative in character in that the investors 
and the representatives of Industry and institutions like Institute of Chartered Accountants 
of India, Institute of Cost and Works. Accountants of India , institute of Company Secretaries 
of India etc. had not been given adequate representation . The Committee strongly feels that 
the Working Group be expanded so as to include official representatives of the said 
organisations/institutions formally sponsored by them and well known experts in. the related 
fields so that it inspires greater confidence in the minds of the public. 
6. In its sitting held on the 23rd October, 1996. the Committee took up clause-by-clause 
consideration of the Bill. 
7. The Committee also invited suggestions/views of the different repre sentative 
organisations of industry such as Confederation of Indian Industry (Cil); Associated 
• Publi~hed in the Gazette of India Extraordinary Part-11. Section 2. dated the lOth September. 1996. 
••Rajya Sabha Parliamentary Bulletin Part II. dated the 12th September. 1990. 
1 

2 
Chambers of Cpmmerce and Industry of India (ASSOCHAM); Punjab, Haryana and Delhi 
Chamber of Commerce and Industry (PHD) and Federation of Indian Chambers of 
Commerce and Industry (FICCI) on the amendments sought to be effe.cted in the 
Companies Act through this Bill. The Committee, however, got response only from the CII 
by the due date in the form of an exhaustive paper covering entire gamut of framework of 
the Companies Act, 1956 submitted by them earlier to the Government as also to the 
Working Group engaged in revising Company Law. The Committee noted that the proposed 
amendments in the Bill before it were limited in scope and already cover some suggestions 
advanced by the CII in their note under reference. The Committee feels that their 
suggestions which are exhaustive in nature and touch upon various aspects of Companies Act 
as a whole will be taken note of by the Working Group on redrafting of Companies Act, 
1956. 
8. The Committee considered and adopted this Report in its sitting held on the 1st 
November, 1996. 
9. The principal changes suggested by the Committee in the Bill and the reasons 
therefor are set out hereinafter: -
Ciause 4 
The Committee welcomes the amendment proposed to be made through this clause in 
Section 58 (A) of the Companies Act , 1956 to debar such companies as default in making 
timely repayment of deposits to the public from accepting further deposits till the default in 
this behalf is made good by them. The Committee, however , feels that the penal provision s 
which presently exist in the Act'to bring to book the Companies Which harass the depositors 
are seldom invoked or even if they are invoked , the necessary will to pursue them to their 
logical end is lacking on the part of official enforcement machinery. The Committee is, 
accordingly, of the view that the enforcement machinery be geared up to ensure more 
vigorous implementation of these penal provisions so that the depositors, particularly the 
small investors who cannot afford to wage protracted legal battles with the defaulting 
companies, do not continuously suffer in getting their hard earned money back. The 
Committee also recommends that strict norms of accountability be laid down in this regard 
and such of the officials as show laxity in dealing firmly with the companies fiddling with 
public money are held liable and proceeded against under the rules. 
Clause 5 
This clause seeks to amend Section 80 (SA) of the Companies Act, 1956 to enhance the 
issue period of redeemable preference shares from ten years to twenty years so as to enable 
the companies to mop up finance for capital intensive projects, particularly in the 
infrastructure sector. The Committee , while agreeing with the general principal of this 
clause , recommends that a provision should also be made in this clause whereby investors 
can exercise the option of redeeming the shares at the end of ten years' period, unless they 
opt to keep them with the companies for a full period of twenty years. 
Clause 6 
This clause seeks to amend Section 86 of the principal Act which presently permit s 
companies to issue only two kinds of shares viz.(i) equity shares and (ii) preference shares , 
by making an additional provision for issue of Non-Voting Shares (NVS) by companies upto 
25% of their equity capital with voting rights , subject to their making some basic disclosures 
while obtaining approval of their existing shareholders for issue of such shares. The intention 
is to enable the corporate sector to tap a pool of investors who may be interested in trading 

3 
off higher dividend yield against absence of voting rights and thus mobilize funds for their 
expansion and growth without running the risk of hostile take-overs. 
The Committee is not convinced with this line of argument as in its view the objectives 
contemplated may perhaps not be achieved and foreign investors who may only be interested 
in making big investments in the companies will hardly be forthcoming to invest their money 
in Non-Voting Shares unless they acquire a substantial say in the companies' affairs. In any 
case, when the entire Companies Act is proposed to be rewritten, the Committee fails to 
understand the logic or urgency behind introducing the concept of NVS by amending Section 
86 of the Act. The Committee is, therefore, of the view that there should be informed public 
debate and extensive inter-action with the experts in the field over this issue before NVS is 
made a part of corporate practices and incorporated in the corpus of company law. The 
Committee accordingly recommends that Clause 6 be dropped from the Bill. 
Clause 10 
This clause seeks to amend Section 530(2) of the principal Act, thereby providing an 
enabling provision and conferring powers on Central Government to prescribe such an 
amount from time to time as may be considered appropriate. by way of payment of salary 
and wages to its employees by a company. instead of rupees one thousand as stipulated 
under the Act at present, in the event of its being wound up. The Committee recommends 
that there should be a mandatory provision for review of the amount payable to its 
employees by a company, at specified regular intervals and the amount which is notified by 
the Government should be kept within the realm of realities and linked to the cost of living 
index. 
10. Clauses 2 to 4. 7 to 9 and 11 were adopted by the Committee without any change. 
11. Clause 1, the Enacting Formula and the Title were adopted. 
12. The Committee recommends that the Bill as reported by it , be passed.

Clauses 2 and 3 
The Clauses were adopted without any change. 
Clause 4 
The Committee welcomed the proposed amendment as the bar on the Companies to 
raise fresh deposits unless thev repay in full the deposits along with the interest accruing

thereon to the depositors would deter the Companies in some measure from defaulting on 
this account and unnecessarily withholding public money. The Committee, however, felt that 
the penal provisions existing in the Companies Act, 1956 to deal with the Companies which 
do not care to repay the deposits to the depositors on their maturity have hitherto had no 
salutary effect and the depositors have to wage protracted legal battles against such 
Companies. The Committee, therefore, took a view that the Government should take 
necessary steps to strengthen the enforcement machinery vested with the task of 
implementing these penal provisions and if necessary, incorporate more stringent provisions 
in the new legislation currently under way to replace the existing Act so as to ensure that the 
companies which fiddle with public money do not go scot free. With these observations

ClaUJe 5 
The Committee did not feel convinced with the reasons advanced for enhancing the 
issue period of redeemable preference shares by the Companies from the existing 10 years to 
20 years. The Committee expressed the apprehension that the locking period for such shares 
would be doubled and the money of holders of such shares will remain locked substantially 
for a long period without their exactly knowing the state of affairs of such companies, which 
may jeopardize the interest of shareholders. The Committee, however , keeping in view the 
explanation given by the Government that the proposed amendment is basically intended to 
meet the requirement of the Companies which might like to raise the capital in the form of 
preference shares for a longer period and accepting the concept as such, felt that a proviso 
could be added in Clause 5 of the Bill to the effect that the holders of such redeemable 
preference shares, will have an option to take their share money back after expiry of a 
period of 10 years. The Committee accordingly decided to recommend that clause 5 of the 
Bill may be amended accordingly. 
Clause 6 
The Committee felt that it failed to understand the urgency behind introducing a 
provision for issuance of Non-Voting Shares by the Companies when the exercise for 
redrafting of the Companies Act, 1956 in its entirety is currently stated to be in progress.

Shares will somewhat reduce the risk of hostile take overs of companies. The Committee 
rather expressed the apprehension that if in a case where an Indian Company has Non­
Voting Shares and a foreign Company has voting shares , the proposed amendment may turn 
out counter productive. The Committee opined that the concept of Non- Voting Shares even 
though in vogue in some countries is somewhat new to the corporate sector in our country 
and before it is brought into the corpus of legislation there should be informed public debate 
over this issue. The Committee accordingly decided to recommend that Clause 6 may be 
dropped from the Bill.

INTRODUCfiON 
I, the Chairman of the Committee on Home Affairs, having been authorised by the 
Committee, to present this Thirty-sixth Report of the Committee . The Report is on the 
'Insurgency situation in the North-Eastern Region'. 
2. The Committee, in its meeting held on the 25th November , 1993, briefly discussed 
insurgency situation in the North -Eastern region, as a part of consideration of the Annual 
Report of the Ministry of Home Affairs for' the Year 1992-93 and decided to take up the 
subject for detailed examination. 
3. The Committee heard the Home Secretary on the subject in its meetings held on the 
7th, 27th and 28th June , 1994. 
4. The Committee further considered the matter in its meetings held on the 20th 
September and 18th October, 1995. In its meeting held on the 20th September, 1995, the 
Committee decided that a Study-Group of the Committee may visit Assam, Meghalaya, 
Manipur and Nagaland for an on-the-spot assessment of the insurgency situation in those 
States. In pursuance of this decision, a Study Group of the Committee (Annexure- !) was 
constituted to undertake the visit. Accordingly, the Study Group visited lmphal, Kohima 
and' Guwahati from the 28th October to 3rd November, 1995 and had an interaction with 
representatives cJf various political parties, persons from cross section of society and, the 
concerned State Government's officials to obtain the ground realities. A list of persons with 
whom the Study-Group interacted is placed at Annexure-H. 
5. In its meeting held on the 19th February, 1996, the Committee further discussed the 
subject. It was of the view that its study only partially reflected the insurgency situation in 
the North-Eastern region as its Study-Group had visited only three States, out of the seven 
States of the region. The Committee also felt that besides the insurgency problem, the States 
like Arunachal Pradesh and Tripura were facing the pere·nnial. problem of influx of Chakma 
refugees from Bangladesh and of their rehabilitation. It was of the opinion that another 
Study-Group of the Committee may visit the Meghalaya, Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram and 
Tripura. Accordingly, a Study-Group of the Committee (Annexure-III) visited Shillong, 
ltanagar, Aizwal and Agartala from 16th to 21st March, 1996 and held discussions with 
representatives of various political parties, State Government's officials and persons from 
cross section of society to. find out the ground realities. A list of persons with whom the 
Study-Group interacted is placed at Annexure-IY. 
6. The term of the Committee came to an end on April 8, 1996 and the Committee 
which was reconstituted on 1st August , 1996, took up the ~atter afresh. In its meeting held 
on the 23rd September, 1996, the Committee considered the draft Report and felt that in 
view of the long time elapsed since the visits of the Study Groups on the basis of which the 
draft Report has been prepared and its consideration the points covered in the Report need 
to be updated in the context of latest developments in the North-Eastern region. The 
Committee elicited the suggestions/views of the Members on various aspects of the 
insurgency problem for making necessary changes/modifications in the draft Report.

REPORT 
BACKGROUND 
Some parts in the North-Eastern region, comprising the States of Assam, Arunachal 
Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland and Tripura, have been afflicted with 
insurgency due to different factors which include ethnic, linguistic, historical, economic and 
geographical factors. Aid and support to the insurgent groups from across the borders have 
also contributed considerably to the insurgency in the region. Of these States, Nagaland, 
Manipur and Assam, and to some extent Tripura, are the most seriously affected. 
2. The North-Eastern region has 1126 Km. long international border with China, 
489 Km. with Bhutan, 1643 Km. with Myanmar and 1187 Km. with Bangladesh. The hills 
and basins of the region are a mixture of high mountain ranges, plateaus and low hills, 
covering an area of 90,160 sq. kms. i.e. roughly 60% of the whole region. 
3. There are wide ethnic, religious and cultural diversities in the region, which is 
reflected in the fact that over 200 tribes inhabit this region and speak as many as 192 
languages/dialects. Numerous tribes and sub-tribes living in the region perceive their status 
to be in danger in remaining with the major groups/tribes in a district or state. 
4. The States of Nagaland, Manipur, Assam and Tripura have long and porous 
international borders with Bangladesh, Bhutan and Myanmar. The population on either side 
of the borders with Bangladesh and Myanmar is ethnically similar. The populated areas 
along the Indo-Bangladesh borders, in particular, extend upto the zero line in many sectors. 
This has resulted in infiltration on the one hand and cross-border movements of negative 
elements on the other. 
5. The region abounds in natural resources. However, there are locational disadvantages 
and absence of proper and adequate infrastructure. There has been substantial inflow of plan 
and non-plan assistance from the Centre. But its benefits have not fully reached the people 
due to various reasons. The growth in employment opportunities has not kept pace with the 
number of entrants to the job market. 
6. The problem of threat to life and extortions have assumed considerable proportions, 
particularly in the States of Nagaland and Manipur. The State of Assam, besides extortions, 
is also witnessing the problem of kidnappings, etc. 
7. The phenomenon of insurgency, which was earlier rural-based , has, over the years, 
got transformed into an urbanised one. 
MANIPUR 
8. The State, with its Capital at lmphal has an area of 22,326, sq. Kms., and a 
population of 18,26,714 (1991 census). The major communities are the Meiteis, inhabiting 
the Valley areas and the Nagas and Kukis, inhabiting the hill areas. The rate of literacy is 
60.96%. Manipuri (Meiteilon) is the State's official language and is spoken by a majority of 
the population. The State has witnessed violent Kuki-Naga ethnic conflicts, which sparked 
off in mid 1992 and took a violent form in 1993, during which year there were as many as 
192 violent incidents. In 1994 and 1995 (upto 18.10.95) the number of such incidents was 74 
1 

2 
and 90, respectively. Apart from destruction of a large number of houses by the rival 
communities , nearly 600 persons were reported killed in such clashe s during 1993-95. 
9. The State 's hill areas are afflicted with violent activities of the National Socialist Council 
of Nagaland (I) and the Kuki extremist groups . The Meitei extremist organisations, viz., 
People's Liberation Army (PLA), People 's Revolutionary Party of Kangleipak (PREPAK), 
United National Liberation Front (UNLF) and the Kangleipak Communist Party (KCP) are 
active in the Valley areas. 
10. The main concentration of major insurgent gro1:1ps active in the .State and the area of 
their known operations are set out below:-
A. Insurgent groups active in hill areas: 
(J) National Socialist Councn of Nags/and (NSCN): 
It was formed in the year 1980, with the following main objectives:-
(a) to liberate the State of Nagaland from the Indian Union; 
(b) to declare Nagaland as an independent sovereign State of the Nagas; 
(c) to maintain a separate identity of the Nagas . 
To fulfil these objectives , the NSCN activists have been continuously indulging in violent 
and subversive activities since inception of the NSCN. In the year 1988, the Council got divided 
into two factions, namely, NSCN (Khaplang) and NSCN (Muivah) . 
(Ji) Kuki National Army (KNA): 
It was formed in May, 1988 in Myanmar. Its main objective is to form an independent 
sovereign Kuki State, by carving out the Kuki populated areas of Myanmar and incorporating in 
them some parts of Thoubal, Ukhrul and Chandel districts of Manipur. 
The Organisation has two wings (i) Kuki National Organisation (KNO)-the political wing 
of KNA; and (ii) the Kuki Defence Force-the defence .wing of KNA , to protect the Kuki 
people against attacks by the Nagas. The KNA is mainly a Myanmar based organisation, but it is 
also active in Manipur, especially in· Chan del and Tamenglong district~. 
B. Main Insurgent groups active in the Valley: 
(J) People's Liberation Army (PLA): 
It was formed in 1978. Its main objectives are:-
(a) to secede from India and form a sovereign State; 
(b) to regain the lost territories of Manipur, viz. Kabow Valley , which is now in 
Myanmar. 
(ii) People's Revolutionary Party of Kangleipak (PREPAK): 
It was formed in the year 1977. Its objectives are :-
(a) to free Manipur from India and establish an independent common State; 
(b) to abolish capitalism; 
(c) to intro9uce land ceiling, Panchayati Raj System and Jo"'-"'"'""'t"" 
education. 
The organisation has since got divided into two factions, namely-(i) PREP AK (Khomba); 
and (ii) PREPAK (Selungba). 

3 
(iii) The United National Liberation Front (UNLF): 
It was' formed in the year 1964. Its object ives are:-
( a) to libetate Manipur and some of its neighbouring areas from India ; 
(b) to restore the lost political sovereignty of Manipur and its neighbouring 
areas; 
(c) to establish and independent Sovereign Republi c compris ing Manipur and its 
neighbourin g areas; and 
(d) to regain the lost territories of Manipur from Myanmar. The Organisation 
has since been split into two factions: (i) UNLF (Meghen); and (ii) UNLF 
(Oken). 
(iv) Kangleipak Comm unist Party (KCP): 
The organisation was formed in the year 1980, with the· following objectives: 
(a) to win freedom for Kangleipak (Manipur); 
(b) to preserve the ethn ic identity of the peop le of Kangleipak; 
(c) to liquidate the political parties which are against them; 
(d) to defertd the liberty of the: proletariat class and farmers. 
The organisation has also got divided into two factions, namely - (i) KCP (Ibohanbi); 
and (ii) KCP (Ibopishak). 
11. At lmphal, the members Qf the Study Group held wide ranging discussions with 
officers of the State Government , Chief Minister Shri Rishang Keishing and representatives 
of various political groups in the State. 
12. The Director-General of Police , Manipur, in his presentation , gave an overv iew of 
the law and order situation in the State. He stated that although the State was heavily 
infested with the armed extre mists, their activities had been checked to a considerable 
extent. Joint combing operations had been carried out by the Army, CRPF and Manipur 
Police, due to which the extremists were now on the run. He was of the view that a sense of 
security could be gradually infused in the minds of genera l pub lic by conti nuing such heavy 
deployments and joint operations. He stressed the need for strengthening and revamping of 
the State Police by providing more manpower and vehicles to make the police stat ions in the 
hills and the Valley areas as viable functional units. To effectively counter the activities of 
armed extremists, he desired one full battalion of well-trained commandos in lmphal and 
one company for all the remaining seven districts, with adequate number of vehicles and 
communication system. He felt that the State Police should be reorganised by providing 
adequate number of armed battalions for residential guard s, escort, security of vital 
installations and other static duties, crowd/ mob • dispersal duties , counter-insurgency 
operations and assisting the civil police in maintenance of law and order. To help the 
District Superintendent of Police in admin istering his district properl y and more efficiently, 
he emphasised the need for posting of officers with legal background in each district , to co­
ordinate with the Public Prosecutors and the investigating officers. He expressed his anxiety 
over the failure of the State Police in the investigat ion of important crimes , as a result of 
which, appropri ate proceedings/action could not be taken against the accused persons. In 
order to take effective steps in this regard, he felt the necessity of spec ialised teams of 
investigating officers to investigate into extremist-related and other cases, like 
misappropriation of Government money, embezzlement, forgery , etc. For a better

coordination between the prosecuting and investigating agencies, the Director-General 
favoured the idea of the Directorate of Prosecution to be shifted from the administrative 
control of Law Department and placed under the administrative control of Police 
Department. Further, drug trafficking in the State is quite a serious menace and has caused 
severe damage to the society. The police have geared themselves up in their fight against 
illegal drug trafficking, by using the Preventive Detention Laws i.e. Prevention of Illicit 
Trafficking in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1988, and have achieved 
encouraging results. The Naga-Kuki ethnic problem has also compounded the strife-torn law 
and order scenario in the State. Housing for the police is quite inadequate and is affecting 
their- morale. The arms and ammunition with the State Police do not match with those of the 
extremists. He informed the Study-Group that the State Police had submitted a proposal to 
the Government for revamping of police mobility, weaponry, communications, 
accommodation, etc. The State Government has sanctioned about Rs. 11 crores to meet 
some of the emergent requirements of the State Police. 
13. The Chief Secretary, in his presentation, stated that insurgency in the State was 
qualitatively different as compared to other North-Eastern States. The entire State is 
afflicted with two or three-layer insurgency. Mizoram and Nagaland have only one tribe/ 
group but in Manipur they have three tribes/groups- the Meiteis, the Nagas and the Kukis. 
Insurgency in Manipur also differs from 'the other States because of the ethnic clashes. The 
Nagas inhabit most of the parts of the northern hill districts, Kukis are inhabiting in the 
southern parts of the State, but are dominant in Churacharedpur District. The most 
unfortunate part . is that they kill each other mercilessly and try to drive each other out. 
Burning of houses is also very common. The N~CN (IM), which is the most organised 
group, has a strength of about 3000. This group is organised on army lines and has its own 
battalion command~rs. The other group is NSCN (K). Both these factions try to dominate 
each other and are fighting for control in Manipur and in some parts of Nagaland. They 
have their sources of arms supply from outside. Their arms are brought from Thailand, 
Singapore and Bangladesh as the route is very safe and convenient. They can enter from 
Moreh on the Myanmar border and from th~re go into Thailand or Bangladesh. They can 
move freely all along the Myanmar border. The insurgent groups purchase arms with the 
money they extort from the shop-owners business communities, small industrialists and local 
Government Officers working in various departments. 
14. The valley of Manipur is very fertile. The consumption of fertilizers here is more 
than that in other developed States. The State is self-sufficient in food. If the situation 
improves, the State can export many items to Myanmar. He· mentioned that there is a 
large unemployment problem. A target of 1600 under the Prime Minister's Rozgar 
was fixed last year, which has been increased to 2200 this year. He was of the view that 
the State could have railway line. The trade and commerce would improve, as the 
agricultural products can be marketed to other parts of the country. The sma 
industries can also thrive well. Manipuris are very fond of sports. They are well-talented 
sports and have been champions at junior level and have participated in many national 
international competitions. They bring lot of laurels for the country. If we can make 
develop, 'it will really help, in bringing the youths in the mainstream of national life. 
can also be developed as an industry. The Chief Secretary mentioned that · 
problem in the State has thwarted its economic progress. He opined that military 
does not promise much and a political solution to the problem has to be found. 
15. The Chief Minister, Shri Rishang Keishing apprised the Study Group 
insurgency in the States of Manipur and Nagaland was the oldest in the North-

5 
region. He felt that political instability in the State had also helped in the deterioration of 
the situation. To fight insurgency, he sought full cooperation of the Centre. He mentioned 
that with the deployment of Para-Military forces, the situation has improved and these forces 
should not be withdrawn from the State at this juncture as this would jeopardize all the 
success achieved by these forces so far. He stressed that lack of development and 
unemployment are the root causes of insurgency in the State. Hence, developmental 
activities should go on unabated. He also emphasized the need for laying of railway lines in 
the State and informed that the matter had been taken up with the Ministry of Railways but 
nothing has been done , on the plea that it was not economically viable. 
16. In the meeting of the Study Group with representatives of various political groups in 
the State, the Deputy Chief Minister expressed his concern over the problem of extprtions 
prevailing in the State. He stated that a number of insurgent groups had come up and are 
indulging in violent and subversive activities. They are getting training and. other facilities in 
Bangladesh and Myanmar. He drew attention of the Study Group towards violent Naga­
Kuki ethnic clashes and the poor condition of National Highway Nos. 39 and 53, connecting

Shi1long Accord, was signed in 1975' by various Naga underground leaders and they

been indulging in violent activities and targetting the Security Forces. It has also established 
trans-border linkages.

38. The State of Meghalaya, which was created as a full-fledged State in 1972, has an 
area of 22,429 ·sq. kms. and a population of 760,626 (1991 Census). The State is 
predominantly inhabited by Khasi, Jaintiya and Garo tribes. The State has not witnessed any 
insurgency. However, there have been ethnic conflicts between the tribals and non-tribals. 
the presence of non-tribal traders and businessmen is resented to by the tribal people who 
fear that they will be swamped by the non tribal people. 
3~. The Khasi Students' Union (KSU), Garo Students' Union (GSU), the ' Federation of

assault and intimidation, the non-tribal traders/businessmen being main targets. Recently, 
the Hynniewtrep Achik Liberation Council (HALC) is reported to be indulging in 
extortions, kidnappings and jail-breaks. Some other North-Eastern insurgent groups like

parade on the day of retirement or immediately after retirement of the ~olice personnel have 
been undertaken, to boost the morale of the police force. The wives of the senior police 
officers have also formed an Association, called the Police Officers Wives Association for 
Care (PSWAC). There has been a remarkable improvement in the disposal of cases at the 
investigation stage. The introduction of the City Patrol Scheme in Shillong has widely 
improved the response time of the poiice to .attend to any situation. One India Reserve 
Battalion has been sanctioned to Meghalaya in February 1986 by the Ministry of Home 
Affairs to cope up with the incidence of robbery/dacoity on the national highway. To 
effectively deal with infiltration of foreign nationals , some proposals, like creation of posts of

Const itution of India.

118. Government have taken the following steps to control insurgency in the North­
Eastern States:-
A. Insurgency and other law and order problems: 
(a) With a view to meeting the genuine demands and redressal of grievances of 
the tribal people, agreements/accords were signed with the Nagas in 1975, 
Mizo National Front (MNF) in 1986, Tripura National Volunteers (TNV) in 
1988 and Assam Accord in 1985. 
(b) The NSCN, Meitei Extremist Groups (PLA, PREPAK, KCP and UNLF), 
BDSF, and ULFA have been banned under the Unlawful Activities 
(Prevention) Act, 1967. 
(c) Insurgency-affected areas/States, viz. the whole of Manipur, Nagaland, Assam 
and Tirap and Changlang Districts of Arunachal Pradesh and a 20 km. belt 
from Assam in the neighbouring States have been declared as "disturbed 
areas" under the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act, 1958, as amended in 
1972. 
(d) The North-Eastern State Governments have been provided units of CPMFs 
and Army units, inducted from time to time for the aid of civil authorities. 
(e) In addition to the normal Central grants under the Scheme for Modernisation 
of State Police Forces, speciai Central assistance amounting to Rs. 14.70 crores 
to Assam,· Rs. 10.50 crores to Manipur and Rs. 7.40 crores to Nagaland was 
provided in the year 1993-94. Government of Manipur was also sanctioned Rs. 
00.50 crores in February, 1995 for repair/maintenance of State Police vehicles. 
During 1994-95, allocation under the Modernisation Scheme was doubled to all 
the seven North-Eastern States. 
(f) Collection and sharing of intelligence/information with the States/Security 
Forces have been improved. 
(g) Two India Reserve Battalions for Assam and one Battalion each for Manipur 
and Mizoram were sanctioned in 1993. 
(h) To facilitate co-ordination between the State administration/Police, Central 
Para-Military Forces and the Army, mechanism for co-ordination has been 
established, both for co-ordination within a State as also for ·the inter-state co­
ordination. 
(i) The situation in the North-Eastern States is also· reviewed at various levels 
from time to time. The Union Home Minister met the Chief Ministers of 
North-Eastern States on the 22nd January and 19th July, 1994. The Minister of 
State (IS) also reviewed the situation with North-Eastern Chief Ministers on 
the 29th April, 1995. The situation is also reviewed periodically in the meetings 
of North-East Regional Security Co-ordination Conference with Chief 
Secretaries/DGPs and senior officers of, Central Agencies. The last such review 
was held on the 28th April, 1995 at Shillong. Decisions taken in these meetings 
are followed up. Some of the major decisions taken/followed up are ots 
under:-
(i) Need for optimum co-ordination between States and Ce.ntral Security 
Agencies; 
(ii) Optimum use of units of Central Para-Military Forces for effective counter­
insurgency duties; 
(iii) Strengthening of jail security; 

28 
(iv) Effective implementation of legal provisions, particularly the Unlawful Activities 
(Prevention) Act, 1967; 
(v) Effe.ctive prosecutions/transfer of hardcore detenues outside the North-Eastern 
States; 
(vi) Sharing of actionable intelligence; and 
(vii) Constituting Special Squads to prevent extortions etc. 
B. Economic Development: 
In view of weak fin~ncial resource base of the States of North-Eastern region, in 
addition to the Plan expenditure, assistance to meet the non-Plan expenditure has also been 
provided. All the seven States have been declared special category States for Central 
assistance. For speedier economic development of whole of the region, the North-Eastern 
Council had also invested an amount of Rs. 2474 crores till March, 1995. It may be noted 
that 87% of this amount has been spent on the development of two major infrastructure 
sectors viz. power, transport and communications. 
C. Initiatives with neighbouring countries: 
With a view to take up matters of mutual concern at various levels with the 
Governments of Bangladesh and Myanmar, an Indo-Bangladesh Joint Working Group was 
set-up in 1994 and an Agreement for maintenance of peace and tranquility on the lndo­
Myanmar border was signed in January, 1994 with the Government of Myanmar. Two 
national level meetings at the level of Home Secretary and five sectoral level meetings have 
been held with Myanmar. This initiative has been very successful. The Myanmar authorities 
and army have, in recent months, been providing good co-operation. With Bangladesh, one 
meeting at the level of Home Secretary and two meetings at the Joint Working Group level 
have been held. There has been partial success only in the initiative so far. Initiatives have 
also been taken with Thailand,' as some insurgent groups have been procur ing arms from 
that country. 
RECOMMENDATIONS AND CONCLUSIONS 
119. The Committee is of the view that despite a number of measures taken by 
Government to control insurgency and to improve the law and order situation in the North­
Eastern region, the situation demands a Jot more to be done. Government is duty-bound to 
guarantee a secured life to its people. The Committee notes with serious concern that a 
number of Ministers in Manipur are under threat to life and are not feeling secure despite 
tight security. The Committee, therefore, feels that first and foremost. the local police, 
which is a demoralised Jot today, has to be given a morale boosting. They must be well­
equipped with matching arms and training. They need adequate number uf vehicles. The 
intelligence network needs urgent improvement for effective collection. collation and 
dissemination of intelligence information. The affected States must be provided with 
adequate police force, Central Para-Military forces and other security forces and there 
should be harmonious co-ordination between them. The kith and kin of the local policemen 
require adequate security so that they can work fearlessly in discharging their d~ties. It is 
suggested that a separate police housing colony may be set-up for the families o_f the police 
personnel in each of the insurgency-affected States. All the necessary funds should be made 
available for this purpose. 
120. The problem of insurgency cannot be solved by force alone. ll must be combined 

29 
with dialogue and negotlatton with various insurgent groups, in an atmosphere of mutual 
trust and understanding. The Committee is fully convinced that a permanent solution to the 
insurgency problem in the region can be found only through political negotiations. The 
Committee, theref ore, takes this opportunity to call upon the Government to try to create a 
conduc ive atmosphere for bringing all toe insurgent groups across the table for a dialogue, 
without any precondition. The insurgent groups must also understand that violence is no 
solution to any problem and it is only through dialogue that they can put forth their 
demands before Government and evolve an amicable solution. 
121. The existence of basic transport infrastructure such as rail, road and air link is the 
pre-requisite for economic and industrial development of the region. There is no denying the 
fact that most of the North-Eastern region is underdeveloped due to lack of proper air, rail 
and road network. Most of the places are not easily accessible. Even within the same State, 
it is extreme ly difficult to reach from one point to another. Transportation of goods is 
equally difficult. Communication network is in a bad shape. Power is also in short supply. 
Unless these difficulties are removed , all efforts for bringing about development of the 
region would be retarded. It is in this context that the Comm ittee feels that constr uction of 
roads, laying of new rail lines and adequate air service in the region need highest priority. 
The Committee is of the view that laying of a rail line from Danshree to Imphal shou ld be 
considered on a priority basis to improve the trade and commerce in the region. The North­
Eastern States have to be placed on a different footing in this regard. Action in these areas 
need to be taken in a time bound programme. 
122. The Committee also notes that the newly introdu ced Pawan Hans helicopter service 
with subsidy from Central Government in the States of Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland has 
not been fully operational. The Committee feels that frequency of these services should be 
enhanced and larg er helicopters (24 seater) instead of the present one (8 seater) be 
introduced immediately not only in the existing routes but also in other States/areas of the 
North-Eastern region, having regard to the needs of the people. 
123. The North-Eastern States are faced with the problem of large scale unemployment , 
especially amongst the youth. These yout hs, who are without jobs, fall an easy prey to 
insurgent activities. It is very essential that these youths are used for constructive work and 
brought in the mainstream of national life. If we are able to properly channelise their 
services in productive work, it will be, on the one hand, a serious blow to the insurgent 
activities, and on the other, it will lead to the economic development of the region. lt is, 
therefore , an immense need of the hour that these youths ttrc provided with gainful 
employment under various employment/self employment schtmes/program mes of the 
Government. Further, these programmes/schemes require periodic review and the follow -up 
action of their outcome is also essentially required. The small scale industries would also 
have to be developed in a big way to utilise the manpower potehtial. Government should 
establish recruitment Centres and launch recruitment drive in the region for Government 
undertakings such a~ Civil Aviation, Railways and Post & Telegraph etc., so that the 
unemployed youth ge~ an opportun ity of employment. It will be better if recruitment boards 
of these undertaking!- have representation from the North-East also . Government must 
explore all the possibilities in this regard. 
124. The Committee feels that financial construints should not come in the wa~ of 
fighting insurgency and undertaking speedy economic development of the North-Eastern 
region . insurgency i~ a nat ional problem and everyone will be required to make sacrif ice to 
solve this problem . The Committee has been apprised that there has been no proper 
utilisation of funds, with the result that the benefits intended- (or the common peop1e have 

30 
not reached them. The Committee, therefore, opines that there should be regular and close 
monitoring of funds to ensure their proper utilisation. 
125. There are reports that the NSCN (I) and other insurgent groups like ULFA , PLA , 
UNLF, ATTF, NLFT, TRA etc. have been enjoying training and other facilities in 
Bangladesh. The NSCN (Khaplang) is having its training camps on the Burmese side. There 
are reports of smuggling of arms by insurgent groups from Thailand via Bangladesh and then 
through the Indo-Myanmar borders in Mizoram and Manipur. Besides, the insurgents of 
insurgency affected States are setting up their training camps and sanctuaries in the 
comparatively peaceful neighbouring States. The Committee is seriously perturbed over this 
and urges upon Government to take urgent effective steps to tackle the situation. The 
Committee feels that efforts of Government in this regard have not yielded the desired 
results as the movement of illicit arms, narcotics and the insurgent outfits from across the 
borders is going on unabated. To combat the problem it is essential to take immediate steps 
for sealing of the border totally by providing fencing and increasing vigil by security force. 
The Committee is also of the view that to mitigate the discontentment among the inhabitants 
of these insurgency afflicted States, various accords signed by the Central Government with 
various insurgent groups like the Shillong Accord, MNF Accord, TNV Accord, A TTF 
Accord and Assam Accord etc., need to be implemented in true spirit. 
126. There are wide ethnic, religious and cultural diversities in the entire Region. 
Numerous tribes, sub-tribes in the region perceive their status in danger in remaining with 
other groups/tribes in that district/State. The problem has been aggravated due to poor vigil 
on our borders, resulting in illegal infiltrations and demographic changes. This situation has 
led to frustration, discontentment and insecurity among the original inhabitants of that State. 
This is why, a demand is now being raised for an ethnographic survey of the North-Eastern 
Region. The Committee, therefore, feels that · this problem needs immediate attention with 
due care for Constitutional safeguards.

129. The Chakmas and Hajong refugees problem is a burning problem in Arunachal

130. The Members of the Study Group were informed that a number of . proposals 
submitted by the Governments of North-Eastern States including· rai.s(ng. of strength of

131. Government should provide adequate protection and security to the business and 

31 
trading community from other States carrying on thier business activities in the North­
Eastern States. Government should take steps for protection of life and property and also 
ensure immediate compensation and return of business premises of the traders whose 
premises were ransacked and destroyed. 
132. Government should ensure proper allocation of funds for enabling the Autonomous 
District Councils entrusted with the development of the Scheduled Tribes and preserving

134. To strengthen National Integration and to boost economic development, the

Ministers of all the North-Eastern States. The Council should hold regular meetings. These 
meetings should be held in each State Capital by rotation. 
135. At the end, the Committee feels that the problem of insurgency in the North­
Eastern Region has become a national problem with multifaced dimensions. The problem 
needs to be viewed as the problem of the entire region, not confined to one State and 
should be tackled accordingly. This requires a concerted and sincere effort on the part of all 
concerned, rising above narrow considerations and without making any prestige issue , in the 
intere st of the country.

REPORT 
The Ministry of Home Affairs has been entrusted broadly with the following functions: 
(a) To deal with all matters relating to internal security; 
(b) To deal with all matters relating to Centre-State relations and Inter-State 
relations; 
(c) Implementation of the provisions of the Constitution relating to Official 
Language and the provisions of the Official Language Act, 1963; 
(d) To discharge certain basiC'-functions like notification of assumption of office by 
the President and the Vice-PreSident; notification of appointment of the Prime 
Minister and other Ministers; notification of appointment, resignation and 
removal of Governors and Lt. Governors, appointment of Lt. Governors, Chief 
Commissioners and Administrative Officers in Union Territories; and 
(e) To deal with matters like citizenship and naturalisation, census of population·, 
National Anthem, National Flag of India, etc. 
2. To discharge the above functions,. the Ministry has been divided into four 
Departments:-
(i) Department of Internal Security-to deal with Police, Law and Order and 
rehabilitation; 
(ii) Department of States-to deal with Centre-State relations, inter-State relations, 
Union Territories and Freedom Fighters' Pension; 
(iii) Department of Official Language-to deal with the implementation of the 
provisions of the Constitution relating to Official Language and the provisions 
of the Official Language Act, 1963; and 
(iv) Department of Home-to deal with the notification of assumption of office by 
the President and Vice-President, notification of appointment of the Prime 
Minister and other Ministers, etc.

12. The Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs made a detailed presentation before the 
o1 Committee on 26th March, 1997 in the cours~ of which he explained the broad thrust of the 
demands relating to his Ministry, the reasons for variation in these demands as compared to 
the Revised Estimates of the previous year (1996-97), the nature of allocation for important 
sector such as housing needs of CPMF personnel, modernisation of police forces and dwelt 
at some length on the general internal security situation obtaining in the country. The 
Committee brought to his notice that as against total outlay of Rs. 7547.36 crores provided 
for the Ministry at the RE stage during the year 1996-97, budgetary provision of 
Rs. 7440.72 crores had been made for the Ministry for the year 1997-98 which was 
comparatively Rs. 107 crores lesser than the Revised Estimates of 1996-97. Similarly 
Demand Nos. 45 and 46 reflected allocations as proposed for 1997-98 on a considerably 
lower side. On the contrary, the budgetary outlay as proposed for the year 1997-98 for the· 
Union Territories (without Legislature) namely Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Dadra & 
Nagar Haveli, Daman & Diu and Lakshadweep showed an upward trend. The Secretary was 
asked to clarify this phenomenon underlying the Demands of this Ministry. The Secretary 
pointed out that the reasons for lesser allocations as proposed for 1997-98 vis-o-vis the 
Revised Estimates of 1996-97 were manifold in that parliamentary elections coupled with 
assembly elections in some States necessitated movement of para military personnel from 
one State to another involving additional cost; two additional battalions-one each in BSF 
and CRPF-had to be raised specially for recruitment of surrendered militants in Jammu & 
Kashmir a sum of Rs. 85 crores was earmarked, pursuant to Delhi High Court decision, to 
pay compensation to the victims of 1984 anti-Sikh riots; and additional provision to meet the 
expenditure on providing relief/succour to the victims of riots between the Bodos and 
Santhals had also to be made. This was one time expenditure involving substantial amount 
of additionality at the RE stage in 1996-97 and if this is excluded, then the outlay for 
1997-98, is higher by Rs. 355.35 crores (5%) over the Budget Estimates of 1996-97. 
Responding to a query from the Committee about the higher allocations for most of the 
Union Territories (without Legislature), it was explained by the Secretary that more 
attention was being given to Andaman & Nicobar Islands and enhanced allocat~ons were 
also made to take care of the normal growth. 
13. The attention of the Secretary was also drawn to the lesser allocations to the tune of 
Rs. 463.30 crores proposed for the UT of Chandigarh for the year 1997-98 as compared to 
Rs. 471.12 crores (RE) during 1996-97. The Revised Estimates of 1996-97 included a non­
plan component of Rs. 368.66 crores (as against projected demand of Ministry of Home 
Affairs of Rs. 370.90 crores) whereas the non-plan outlay for 1997-98 was pegged at Rs. 
353.30 crores as against the demand of Rs. 400.80 crores made by the Ministry. No 
satisfactory reply was, however, given by the Ministry about slashing down of outlay of 
Chandigarh for 1997-98 except saying that the Ministry of Finance finally accepted a ceiling 
of Rs. 353.30 crores for non-plan sector in 1997-98 as against RE of Rs. 368.66 crores for 
1996-97. The Committee does not find any convincing reason for effecting a reduction in the 
budgetary outlay of UT of Clrandigarh for 1997-98 when for all the other UTs without 

6 
legislature the allocations have been prop osed on the higher side. The Committee trusts that 
the outlay in respect of Chandigarh will be suitably enhanced at RE stage and adequate 
provision particularly for the propos ed settin g up of a Medical College there as also to meet 
the requirements of providing authori sed electricity connections to the residents of 
unauthorised colonies so as to enabl e the UT Administration to implement the order of 
Punjab and Haryana High Court in Civil Writ Petition No. 7740 of 1995 will be made. 
14. Commenting on the gener al l aw and order situation in the country, the Secretary 
stated that there has been a sea change in Jammu & Kashmtr after the installation of a 
popular Government and there is much more rapport now between the Government of India 
and 'the State Government though there h ave been some incidents of killings by the 
militants; the situation in the North -Eas tern region has been somewhat volatile because of 
persistent external support by Pakistan . T he efforts are nonethe less under way to improve 
relations with the neighbouring countries and persuade them not to allow insurgent groups 
to operate from their land significant progress in t his regard has been made with Banglades h 
which has assured that it will not allow the insurgents to operate from its land. The relations 
with Myanmar have also been fairly good . The area pf concern is, however, Bhutan where a 
number of insurgents have gone . There is a need to have some understanding with the King 
of Bhutan to keep constant watch on these insurgents and the Ministry of External Affairs, 
being quite aware of this problem, is takin g up this matter with the Government there. The 
Secretary of the Ministry also submitt ed b efore the Committee that as a result of the recent 
offer made by the Prime Minister for unconditional talks with the underground militants in 
tl\.e North-East , the situation is some what improving in Nagaland. The developments in 
Triputa a{e, however, a matter of concern as ethnic riots between tribals and non-tribals 
have been erupting time and again . There is some amount of peace obtaining there but the 
situation needs to be watched constan tly and some sort of measures are necessary to build 
confidence among the tribals without sacrificing the interests of the non-tribals. 
15. According to the Secretar y, the law and order problem in UP and Bihar has been a 
matter of concern. In Bihar, in par ticular, even though the incidents of killings betwee n 
Naxalite groups have somewhat been brought under control, a number of "Senas" such as 
"Ranvir Sena" etc. have taken root s which are having a bearing on the law and o~der 
situation there. Even though these "Senas" have been banned, they continue to ope rate and 
there is no effective monitoring of their activit ies. Carnage of Bath ani Tola in Bhojpur 
District of Bihar on July 11, 1996, and the massacre of ten Dal its at hawaspur under 
Ranitalab Police Station on March 23, 1997 show that the "Senas" continue to strike and kill 
innocent people. The Secretary informed the Committee that afte r the Bathani Tola incident 
a Central Task .Force comprising of representatives of CRPF, Intelligence Bureau, local 
police and the State CID had been constitute d to look into the activities of various Senas

MODERNISATION OF POLICE FORCE 
22. There is a scheme of the Ministry of Home Affairs for modernisation of police 
forces under which financial assistance is provided to the State Governments in th~ form of 
50% grants-in-aid and 50% loan to be utilised for expenditure of non-recurring nature qn 
purchase of vehicles, wireless equipments, computers and other sophisticated equipments. 
This scheme has been in operation since 1969-70. During 1996-97, an allocation of Rs. 55 
crores was made at the RE stage under this scheme and an outlay of Rs. 50 crores has been 
provided for during 1997-98. The Secretary, in the course of his submissions before the 
Committee, conceded that while modernisation of police force is very important, it has been 
neglected over the years. In this context, he cited the example of Nagaland which is in the 
throes of insurgency, where during the last 15 years not a single additional constable has 
been recruited and even police stations are put up in rented houses or thatched houses. 
Being deprived of the faciiity of accommodation, the police personnel have per force to live 
with . the villagers or urban population as the case may be, as a result of which they are 
exposed to all kinds of threats from militant groups. The police there does not have proper 
arms, proper shoes, proper communication system and proper vehicles and the whole thing 
appears to be in a mess. The. feeling there is perhaps that with the army being called upon to 
tackle insurgency, there is not much of a role for policemen. But, the matter cannot be set 
right alone by the army unless there is increased role for police which can provide vital input 
in terms of intelligence. In any case in a democratic . set-up it is the duty of civil 
administration to maintain law and order and provide security to the citizens. Army has only 
a limited role and that too in emergencies. Army can not be and should not be deployed on 
long term basis. At a time when Naxalite problem is spreading its tentacles to the States like 
Andhra Pradesh, Bihar and parts of Madhya Pradesh and Orissa and the various 
organisations involved in these activities are networking with other militant groups in other 
States, the issue of modernisation of police forces is to be attached highest priority, 
23. The Committee feels that in the present context when the terrorist and extremist 
activities are on the increase and sophisticated weapons and explosive devices are reaching 
their hands, there is all the more greater need for modernisation of our police forces so that 
they can effectively deal with such elements. The Committee is aware that Government is not 
oblivious of this problem and at various stages, steps have been taken to equip police forces 
with latest weaponry and production of arms in our ordnance factories for police forces has 
also been upgraded, but the progress in this regard is not altogether satisfactory. Our police

administration rests with the State Governments' concerned and onus is primarily on them to 
keep them well equipped, but as pointed out by the Secretary of the Ministry, it is a national 
problem and has to be dealt with utmost priority. The Committee had earlier also dealt with 
this issue in its lStb and 32nd Reports and emphasised the need to suitably enhance the

demanding nature of their duties for which higher allocations have to be provided for

24. Traffic management is one of the assigned tasks of Delhi Police and the Committee 
drew the attention of the Secretary of the Ministry to the chaotic conditions on Delhi roads,

sitution. The Committee was informed that there has been a phenomenal growth in the 
vehicular traffic in Delhi over the past two decades and the number of vehicles has increased 
from 3.12 lakhs in 1976 to 26.82 lakhs in 1996. As per a study conducted by the Indian Road 
Congress, the optimum capacity o·f a three lane road is 4500 vehicles per hour. However in 
Delhi the figure goes upto 15,680 at places like ITO bridge. The number of vehicles on 
Delhi roads is in fact greater than the combined strength of vehicles in Madras, Calcutta and 
Bombay. 
25. This volume of traffic on Delhi roads and unruly driving have resulted in road 
accidents more than in any of the remaining metropolitan cities. The number of road 
accidents which occurred in Delhi during 1995 and 1996 were of the order of 10,141 and 
11,310 respectively, which include 1,981 and 1,953 fatal road accidents during the respective 
years. 
26. The Ministry also submitted that though the number of vehicles in Delhi outnumber 
the vehicles in the three other major metros taken together, yet the number of traffic 
policemen to handle this mammoth number is less than that in any of them. A significant 
number of road accidents involve red and blue line buses and a special drive to rein in these 
buses . has been continuing in coordination with the State Transport Authority since 13th 
October, 1995. During the period 1.1.1996 to 28.2.1997, 343 permits of these buses were 
suspended. Besides during the year 1996, 1363 red and blue line bus drivers were tested, out 
of which 391 were found not upto the mark. Further , about 30,000 vehicles were checked for 
pollution, out of which 20,795 were found not having the "pollution under control" 
certificate and were prosecuted. 
27. As intimated to the committee, Delhi Tra.ffic Police has taken a number of 
measures to improve the traffic situation in Delhi which include:-

(ii) Parking discipline 
(iii) Roundabout discipline 
(iv) Lane discipline 
(v) Surveillance of vehicles 
(vi) Mobile patrolling 
(vii) Installation of latest road traffic signal techniques

examine traffic related problems and to evolve solutions thereto. Further, in an effort to

29. The Committee feels concerned that with all types of vehicles operating on Delhi 
roads and adherence to the traffic rules thrown to the winds, sane driving on the roads is a 
nightmarish experience. As a matter 1of fact the volume of traffic is so much that the roads are 
unable to bear the burden and skeleton traffic staff find it unmanageble to cope with the 
magnitude of the problem. The problem becomes aggravated particularly at important 
trijunctions in the event of traffic light going out of order, which now a days is a common 
sight. The measures which have been initiated by traffic police do not appear to go far beyond 
and strike at the root cause of the problem. What is needed most is an integrated . and 
coordinated approach to the problem and need for a perspective long term plan aimed 
particularly at finding other modes of transport and planning futuristic roads as m.ay 
withstand the volume of traffic which is bound to increase manifold in coming years. 
Construction of Oyovers at important trijunctions should be undertaken in a time·bound 
programme to ensure smooth and uninterrupted Oow of traffic. In the view of the Committee 
it would be quite useful to undertake a study in respect of Oow and behaviour of traffic in 
Delhi so that the points of obstructions could be identified and coorective measures taken. For· 
this the Delhi Police should closely inter-act with the Delhi Administration and necessary 
action taken within this year. The problem of managing traffic on Delhi roads is quite a 
serious one requiring a gigantic effort and the requirements of manpower to augment the Oeet 
of traffic police be seriously examined to ensure that earnest efforts in this direction are not 
hampered on account of shortage of manpower. The Committee has noted that the incidence 
of accidents on Delhi roads is particularly of staggering proportion and most of the time it is 
the blue line or red line buses involved in such accidents. It appears to the committee that the 
primary reason for this increasing phenomenon of accidents is the highly untrained drivers of 
such vehicles who manage to procure driving licences without having proper skills/training. 
The Committee feels that this menace can be suitably dealt with if the licencing regime is 
made more strict and accountable and a premier driving school is established in Delhi 
particularly to teach driving techniques to drivers of commercial vehicles. It could perhaps be 
more advantageous if similar driving schools are established in other States as well for 
highway driving. The Committee also feels that the policemen manning traffic should be given 
better training.

allocations are suitably increased, bottle-necks, if any, in the execution of the projects are 
expeditiously removed and other agencies with proven record are involved in construction 
activities. As an alternative the feasibility of buying ready built dwelling units from agencies 
like HUDCO or State Housing Boards can also be examined to avoid the phenomenon of cost

of NCf of Delhi has taken necessary follow up action in the implementation of the direction 
and a provision of Rs. 85 crores was kept for the purpo se in the RE-1996-97 of the Ministry. 
43. The Committee notes the submission of the Ministry in providing compensation to the

REHABILITATION OF 1947 REFUGEES IN J&K 
61. In the course of the meeting of the Committee on March, 26 and April 9, 1997 
points were raised to the effect that in the wake of Pakistani aggression in J&K in the year 
1947, thousands of families from former West Pakistan and areas now under the illegal 
occupation of Pakistan migrated to J&K, but they have yet not be properly rehabilitated. 
People who came from Sialkot have no right to vote for the State Legislature and are not 
even considered as citizens of the State. 
62. The Ministry has clarified that displaced persons from the Pak Occupied Kashmir 
have not been given any compensation under the Displaced Persons (Compensation & 
Rehabilitation) Act, as the whole of Jammu and Kashmir has always been considered an 
integral part of India and the areas presently under the occupation of Pakistan are 
considered to be under illegal occupation. The claims in respect of the properties left behind 
by these displaced persons could not be verified. Pak occupied areas are part of India and 
the 'Evacuee Property Law' as such does not apply to that State. In view of this, 
Government decided that these families may be given ex-gratia payment which had nothing 

23 
to do with the value/quantum of properties )eft by these displaced persons in PAK. 
Accordingly; · Ex-gratia payment was made as per the following scale:-
(i) Urban families · Rs. 3,5(}()1- per family 
(ii) Agricultural families Rs. 1 ,000'- plus 2 to 3 acres of irrigated or 4 to 6 
acres of unirrigated land, depending upon the 
strength of each family. 
63. However, these displaced persons have been making representations from time to 
time ..regarding: · 
(i) Compensation for properties left behind in PoK; 
(ii) Removal of deficiency in their land allotments; and 
(iii) Improvement in living conditions in their colonies. 
· 64. These demands have been examined by the Government from time to time. 
However, it has not been found feasible to accede to these demands on the grounds that 
(i) the amount of Rs. 350(¥- paid to these families in 1960 would compare favounibly with 
what they have been demanding ' subsequently, (ii) these families were provided such 
assistance long back and they now ought to be treated to have been absorbed in the national 
mainstream, and (iii) any reconsideration of their demands may trigger similar demands 
from o~her quarters. However, the Government of India has agreed, on the recommenda­
tions of 1he National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) to consider payment of cash 
compensation to 8409 families in lieu of deficiency in their allottable units of land in 
consultation with the State Government of Jammu and Kashmir. The matter is being 
processed in consultation with the State Government. 
65. With regard to the displaced persons from former West Pakistan, who had been 
settled in Jammu and Kashmir State, the Ministry has stated that they were paid 
compensation under the Displac~d Persons (Compensation & Rehabilitation) Act/Rules 
1954/1955 for the properties left behind by them in West Pakistan. These displaced persons 
were also allotted land by the State Government of Jammu and Kashmir and were also 
allotted house, shops etc. like displaced families from PoK. However, these persons are not 
treated as permanent residents of the State of Jammu and Kashmir in terms of the 
Constitution of Jammu and Kashmir and, therefore, are not citizens of the State, although 
they are citizens of India and can a.Iso vote in the Lok Sabha elections. A writ petition was 
filed by the West Pak displaced persons in the Hon'ble Supreme Court in this regard. The 
Hon'ble Supreme Court observed that it is for the State Legislature to make suitable 
amendment in the State Laws to provide relief to these persons without amending the 
Constitution of J&K. The Government of India is of the view that it would be most 
appropriate if the , amendment to the State Laws is left to the Jammu and Kashmir State 
Assembly. 
66. The Committee feels that the matter of settlement of migrapts from Pakistan has 
lingered on far too long and they continue to be in lurch being deprived of their rights. It is 
really very strange that they are staying in the State of J&K, owing land, are treated as 
citizens of India and c_an vote in Parliamentary elections but cannot participate in the elections 
to the State Assembly. The Committee strongly feels that this state of affairs must come to an 
end and all the rights due to the citizens in J & K should be made available to them including 
the right to vote· in Assembly/Municipal elections. The dividing line which has been drawn 
between the displaced persons from Pakistan and /the displaced persons from Pak occupied, 
Kashmir may, though, for technical reasons hold good but in the view of the Committee the 
persons from Pak occupied Kashmir had perforce to leave their ancestral homes and 
properties behind and they are being deprived of their legitimate -claims for so long which 
tantamounts to heaping further misery on them. What is needed most is to adopt a 
•

humanitarian approach to the entire issue. The Committee, thercefore, recommends that the

with the IPS quota in its entirety and instead fill up such posts at the level of DIGs and IGs 
from within the cadres of CPMFs . The Committee appreciates that the Ministry of Home 
Affairs has already taken note of this aspect .and taken steps to divert IPS quota vacancies to 
cadre Officers in BSF and CRPF keeping in view the operational requirements and 
streamlining of procedure for selection of IPS Officers for deputation to CPMFs is also being 
undertaken. 
INTELLIGENCE BUREAU 
71. Intelligence Bureau is a premier intelligence organisation of the Government. It has 
however, come to the notice of the Committee that most of the appointments at the senior 
level in the Bureau are ·made on deputation by drawing people from other police 
organisations . The Committee feels that in the interest of continuity the Intelligence Bureau 
should . have its own cadre and the. practice of inducting officers on deputation be kept to the 
barest minimum . The Committee would also like to be apprised of the number of vacancies 
existing at different levels in the Bureau .
