Clause 12 
The Committee felt that in view of the change proposed by it in sub-clause {3) of clau<>e 
10 for raising the period of limitation for complaints from 5 years to 10 _years, consequential 
change should be made in clause 12{l){a) and the period of 5 years mentioned therein be 
substituted to read as 10 years. Likewise, in view of the proposed deletion of sub-clause (2) 
of clause 10, consequential change in clause 12 {1) {b) should also be effected. 
The Committee also noted that the wording of sub-clauses (c) and {d) of clause 12 {11 
confers unguided and arbitrary powers of in-limine rejection of complaints on the Lokpal. 
The Committee felt that it would be in the public interest to ensure proper investigation of 
complaints and accordingly it was necessary that the language of sub-clause {1) (c) of clause 
12 should be reworded to read 'that the complaint is manifestly false and vexatious' and sub­
clause {l){d) should llltogether be deleted. 
Clause 13 
The Committee expressed the view that the provision of in camera proceedings by the 
Lokpal as provided vide sub-clause (2) of clause 13 was not in consonance with the system 
128 

129 
of open court hearings currently prevalent in our country. Besides, it created unnecessary 
apprehensions in the minds of the people about the fairness of inquiry. The Committee, 
accordingly, felt that sub-clause (2) of clause 13 should be amended and the words in 
camera occurring therein should be substituted by the words in open and a proviso be 
added thereto as follows: 
'Provided that the Chairman and the Members of the Lokpal may conduct an 
inquiry in camera in exceptional circumstances for reasons to be recor<ted in 
writing.' 
Clause 14 
The Committee felt that as under Clause 14 the Lokpal could scuttle investigations 
being pursued by the Police officials under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, it 
should be deleted. 
Clause 15 
The Committee noted that under sub-clause (4) of clause 15 information as may be 
relevant or useful to the conduct of inquiry by the Lokpal can be withheld on various 
grounds as mentioned thereunder so much so that the Secretary to the Government of 
India or the Chief Secretary of the State Government have been given extensive powers 
to prevent disclosure of information to the Lokpal. The Committee felt that as sub-clause 
( 4) was inconsistent with the nature of proceedings before the Lokpal and denial of 
information would reduce the institution of Lokpal to a mockery, sub-clause (4) of clause 
15 should be deleted. The Committee also felt that in view of the deletion of sub-clause 
(4), consequential amendment in sub-clause (3) of clause 15 would become necessary. 
Clause 16 
The Committee was in broad agreement with the prov1s1ons of this clause. It was, 
however, of the view that the proviso to sub-clause (2) of clause 16 may be modified to 
provide that in cases where the documents seized by the Lokpal are required t.o be 
returned, the Lokpal shall return the same after retaining the copies thereof with due 
authentication. The Committee also felt that the explanation added to sub-clause (2) of 
clause 16 should be dropped. 
Clause 17 
The Committee considered the provisions of this clause in detail. It was of the view 
that after inquiry, the Lokpal should make a Report of its findings to the competent 
authority whether the offences alleged in the complaint have been found to be 
substantiated or not either wholly or partly and under no circumSlances it should be 
empowered to close the case. The complainant and the public functionary concerned 
should also be informed by the Lokpal about its having made such a Report. The 
Committee also felt that the Lokpal should, while communicating its findings and 
recommendations to the competent authority, clearly specify the action to be taken 
against the pubhc functionary against whom the offence alleged in the complaint has been 
found to be substantiated. either wholly or partly. The Committee was also of the 
opinion that as in substance sub-clauses (u) and (b) of clause 17 (1) related to findings of 
the Lokpal on the conclusion of inquiry, they could be combined together and brought 
under claw:e 17(1). 
The Committee was also of the opinion that sub-clause (3) may also be amended to 
provide for laying of the Report received from the Lokpal before the House of the 
People or the Council of States. as the cuse may be. within thr first week (instead of 

130 
within a period of 90 days as presently stipulated in the Act) on their assembling for a 
Session and for chronological reasons, the Committee suggested renumbering of sub­
clause (3) as amended, as sub-clause (2) and sub-clause {2), as sub-clause {3). 
Clause 18 
The Committee noted that clause 18 is too general in nature and accordingly felt 
that it should be amended to provide for -
(i) Furnishing of return of assets by the members within a period of 90 days on 
their becoming members and annually thereafter, within 90 days of 
commencement of each Financial Year; 
(ii) addition of an Explanation to- the clause to define the family as including both 
the spouse and dependent children; 
(iii) Reporting by the Lokpal of the details of the returns filed by the Members of 
Parliament to the Chairpersons of the House of the People and the Council of 
States; and 
(iv) a deterrent clause to deal with cases of non-filing or delayed filing of returns 
by the Members of Parliament or their filing them in an incomplete or falsified 
manner. 
Clause 19 
The Committee felt that the language of clause 19 should be slightly modified in 
the interest of clarity and the words 'the Members' occurring therein should be 
substituted with the words 'the Chairman and the Members of the Lokpal'. 
Clause 20 
The Committee was of the view that the bar placed on the courts to use evidence 
collected by the Lokpal under this clause was not justified and hence this clause should 
be deleted. 
Clause 21 
The Committee was in broad agreement with the provisions of clause 21 as it was 
necessary to respect and protect the dignity of the office of the Lokpal. The 
Committee, however, expressed the view that the sweep of sub-clause (2) of clause 21 
is too wide and tantamounts to an unreasonable restriction on free speech. The 
Committee felt that even otherwise the purpose contemplated under sub-clause (2) is by 
and large achieved by sub-clauses {1) and (3) and hence sub-clause (2) should be 
deleted. Reference to sub-clause (2) in sub-clause (3) consequentially would also have to 
go. 
Clause 22 
The Committee was of the view that sub-clause (1) of clause 22 should be deleted 
as provisions for summary trials for offences of the nature sought to be covered 
thereunder already exist in the Code of Criminal Procedure 1973. Accordingly, reference 
to Sections 175, 178, 179 and 180 of the Indian Penal Code in sub-clause (2) of clause 
22 becomes unnecessary and the words from 'in Section 175... to the Indian Penal 
Code' occurring therein be substituted by the words 'in clause 21{1) of this Act'. 
The Committee also felt that having regard to the status of the Chairman and 
Members of the Lokpal which is akin to the Chief Justice and Judges of the Supreme 
Courts, sub-clause (4) of clause 22 should be amended to provide for appeals against 
the convictions pronounced by the Lokpal to the Supreme Court (and not to the High 

131 
Court). The Explanation to sub-clause (4) would consequently become redundant and hence 
it should be deleted. 
Clauses 23, 24 & 25 
The Committee noted that Clauses 23 and 24 confer powers on the Lokpal to try 
offences arising out of printing or publication of any information in relation to any complaint 
or making of such complaints as are held by it to be false. Clause 25 has been provided for 
modified application of the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure for the trial of 
offences under clauses 22, 23 and 24. 
The Committee felt that there has to be transparency in the functioning of the Lokpal 
and it should not convert itself into a criminal court except for the purpose of punishing ex­
facie cases of contempt under clause 21(1). Clause 23 tends to make the proceedings of the 
Lokpal too confidential and clause 24 confers penal jurisdiction on the Lokpal to punish 
complainant whose complaints are held to be false. The Committee observed that on the 
analogy of the Lokpal having no powers to prosecute or punish guilty public functionary, no 
powers should be vested in it to prosecute or punish the complainant or any witness who 
could at best be left to be prosecuted under the Indian Penal Code in the normal course. 
The Committee, accordingly felt that clauses 23 and 24 should be dropped and clause 25 
which would consequentially become redundant should also be deleted. 
Clause 26 
The Committee noted that the bar placed on prosecution under this clause in respect of 
allegations not proved or .substantiated before the Lokpal and the courts being barred from 
taking cognizance of such allegations was contrary to the spirit of the ordinary law of the 
land which provided for appeals at various stages in the courts. The Committee, accordingly, 
felt that the complainants should have a right to go to the courts to seek appropriate 
remedies in case they are not satisfied with the decision of the LokpaVcompetent authority 
and clause 26 should, therefore, be dropped. 
Clause 27 
The Committee was of the view that for the words 'notwithstanding anything contained 
in this Act' occurring in clause 27 (1) the words 'subject to the provisions of clause 12' 
should be substituted to set at rest any apprehensions arising from the orders issued by the 
President requiring the Lokpal to inquire into any allegation subject to the conditions or 
limitations specified therein. 
Clauses 28 & 29 
The Committee was of the view that the areas covered by clauses 28 and 29 were 
somewhat similar in nature and inter-linked and hence it would be more appropriate if both 
these cluuses were combined into one and provision was made for the amount of 
compensation/reward or punishment to be decided by the Lokpal while concluding its 
findings. The Committee also felt that the words 'and the Central Government shall pay, the 
amount or amounts so determined, to the complainant' occuning at the end of clause 29 
should be substituted by the words and the Lokpal shall determine the person by whom the 
said compensation or award shall be paid after giving that person a reasonable opportunity 
of being heard'. 
Clause 30 
The Committee noted that it has already favoured deletion oi clause 26 and accordingly 
felt that sub-clause (2) of clause 30 which bars Courts jurisdiction on the proceedings or 
decision of the Lokpal should also be dropped.

Clause 31 
The Committee was of the view that in view of the deletion of sub-clause {1) of clause 
22 and clauses 23 and 24 proposed by it, consequential changes will become necessary in

Clause 33 
The Committee was of the view that the basic objective behind the setting up of an 
institution of Lokpal is to cleanse public life from the scourge of corruption and it w~s, 
therefore, paramount to ensure that the Lokpal was not fettered in any way from conducting 
any inquiries upon its own knowledge and information. The Committee, accordingly, 
suggested deletion of sub-clause (b) of clause 33 which tends to bar any inquiry suo motu by 
the, Lokpal into cases of corruption against public functionaries. 
Clause 35 
The Committee felt that clause 35 should be amended to take care of the amendments 
proposed by it in sub-clause (3) of clause 9.

The Committee was of the view that the consequential changes in respect of Clause (1),

REPORT

1, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Home Affairs, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its
behalf, present this Forty-first Report of the Committee, relating to the High Court and
Supreme Court Judges (Conditions of Service) Amendment Bill, 1998.*

2. In pursuance of the Rules relating to Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha in consultation with the Speaker, Lok Sabha
referred** the High Court and Supreme Court Judges (Conditions of Service) Amendment
Bill, 1998 as introduced in the Lok Sabha on the 28th May, 1998 and pending therein, to the
Committee for examination and report by the 3rd July, 1998.

3. The Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Bill states that the salaries of the
Judges of the Supreme Court and the Judges of the High Courts were last revised with effect
from 1५ April, 1986 under the Constitution (Fifty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1986 as
indicated below:—

Chief Justice of India Rs. 10,000 per month
Judges of the Supreme Court Rs. 9,000 per month
Chief Justice of a High Court Rs. 9,000 per month
Judges of High Courts Rs. 8,000 per month

3.1 The Statement further states that the Fifth Central Pay Commission had recom-
mended the revision in the salaries and allowances of the Central Government employees
including the members of All India Services and the Government accepted the majority of
the recommendations. The notification dated the 30th September, 1997 amending the
existing pay rules, namely, the Central Civil Services (Revised Pay), Rules, 1997 had also
been issued and the revised pay rules deemed to have come into force on the Ist day of
January, 1996, The Statement further adds that having considered all aspects of the matter,
a necessity was felt to increase the salaries of the Judges with effect from
Ist January 1996 as detailed below:—

Chief Justice of India Rs. 33,000 per month
Judges of the Supreme Court Rs. 30,000 per month
Chief Justice of a High Court Rs. 30,000 per month
Judges of High Courts Rs. 26,000 per month

3.2. The Statement also states that since the Parliament was not in session, the
President promulgated the High Court and Supreme Court Judges (Conditions of Service)
Amendment Ordinance, 1998 on the 24th April, 1998 to give effect to the increase in the
salaries of the Judges. The Bill seeks to replace the said Ordinance.

* Published in the Gazette of India Extraordinary Part I, Section 2, dated the 28th May, 1998.
** Rajya Sabha Parliamentary Bulletin, Part 1, dated the 10॥ June, 1998,


2

4. The financial Memorandum of the Bill states that the additional expenditure on
account of revision in salaries in case of Judges of the Supreme Court, Delhi High Court and
6% (approximately) for Punjab and Haryana High Court will be charged on the
Consolidated Fund of India. The additional expenditure in respect of the Judges of other
High Courts will be charged on the Consolidated Fund of respective States. The sanctioned
strength of Judges of the Supreme Court, the Delhi High Court and the Punjab and Haryana
High Court is at present 26 and 31 (including 6 additional Judges) and 37 (including 7
additional Judges), respectively. On an average there will be an increase of Rs. 10,000 per
month per Judge. Thus, additional expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India on
account of revision of salaries would be about Rs. 71 lakhs per annum. No other
expenditure, either recurring or non-recurring, is likely to be incurred.

5. In its meeting held on the 25th June, 1998, the Committee heard the Additional
Secretary, Department of Justice, Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs on various
aspects of the Bill. ‘fhe Committee was informed that the Bill seeks to replace the
Ordinance promulgated on the 24th April, 1998 which is to expire after six weeks of
reassembly of the Parliament session. The Parliament's session commenced on the 27th May,
1998 and the six week period would be over on 8th July, 1998 and as such the Bill is to be
passed by both the Houses of Parliament before that date.

5.1 The Committee noted that the recommendations of the Fifth Central Pay
Commission were accepted by the Government in September, 1997 and it failed to
understand why the Government could not bring a Bill to amend the relevant Acts to effect
the enhancement in the salaries of the Judges of the Supreme Court and the High Courts.
The Committee did not appreciate the recourse taken by the Department in promulgating an
Ordinance which if not converted into an Act by 8th July, 1998, would result in an
anamolous situation in asmuchas the salaries of the Judges would revert back to the pre-
revised scales until the current session of Parliament was prorogued cn or after August 14,
1998 and another Ordinance promulgated on the subject. Such a situation could be very
awkward and embarassing for Parliament in view of the provisions of Articles 125 and 221
of the Constitution in terms of which the allowances etc. of the Judges of the Supreme Court
and High Courts shall not be varied to their disadvantage after their appointment.

5.2 Members sought clarifications from the representatives of the Department of Justice
on the various provisions of the Bill which were replied to.

5.3 The Chairman of the Committee informed that he had received a copy of a
representation dated 3rd June, 1998 from the All India Judges Association regarding the
revision of salaries of the Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts. The Committee
was apprised of the issues raised therein. The said representation has been forwarded to the
Department of Justice for their consideration. In this connection the Committee urges upon
the Government to seriously consider the suggestions made in the representation expediti-
ously. The Committee recommends that the Government should have a second look at the
salaries and allowances of the Judges of the Supreme Court and the High Courts and take
decisions in that regard at the eartiest.

6. The Committee considered and adopted this Report in its sitting held on the 30th
June, 1998.

7. The Committee agreed to the amendments proposed to be effected by Clauses 2, 3
and 4 of the Bill in the High Court Judges (Conditions of Service) Act, 1954 and adopted
them without any change.


3

8. The Committee also agreed to the amendments proposed to be effected in the
Supreme Court Judges (Conditions of Service) Act, 1958 by Clauses 5, 6 and 7 of the Bill
and adopted them without any change.

9. Clauses 8 and 9 of the Bill were adopted without any amendment.
10. Clause 1, the Enacting Formula and the Title were adopted.
11. The Committee recommends that the Bill as reported by it, be passed.

approach Hon'ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha for grant of extension of time. 
9. The Committee further considered the Bill in its silting held on the 2nd July, 1998 
and sought clarifications on the various provisions of the Bill from the Secretaries in the 
Ministry of Home Affairs, Department or Legal Artairs and Legislative Department. The 
Commillee thereafter took up clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill. 
10. The Commillee considered and adopted this Report in its silting held on the Jrd 
July, 1998. 
II. The Commillee notes with serious concern the adverse effec ts cast by the lottery 
trade on the public in general and persons belonging to the economically weaker sections of 
our society in particular. It observes that persons from middle income group, low income 
group and a large number of daily wage earners are lured most by the idea of making quick 
buck without sweating. The Committee notes that draws of lotteries are held every half an 
hour or 45 minutes and the lottery buye~ sit for the whole day purchasing tickets and 
waiting with a hope for a prize . This has the effect of turning people away from productive 
and purposeful avenues of employment. A large number of persons have been ruined on 
accou'nt of this trade. Cases of suicides by persons who lost everythin in hope of good 
fortune through purchase of lottery tickets are also coming to light at regular intervals. 
12. The Committee does not feel conv inced about the arguments advanced in favour of 
lollery trade which inter alia include providing employment to unemployed, being a source 
of revenue for the States organising them and investment of the profits earned through this 
trade on development and social welfare activities. The Committee disapproves 
development/welfare activities of this n:Hure which in turn does more harm to the society 
than good. The Committee is of the considered view that instead of providing employment 
through lottery trade Government should endeavour to find alternative productive 
employment for the unemployed persons. 
13. The ComrRittee notes the frequent incidents of irregularities and malpractices 
·wolved in the lottery trade and how unsuspecting buyer of lottery ticket is duped and 
cheated by the lottery mafia. 
' 
" . . 

3 
14. The Committee note that the Government has been seized of the question of lottery 
trade since 1960s, if not earlier . The Committee suo moto took up consideration of the 
subject and it heard the Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs in its meeting held on the 11th 
July, 1997. II also invited public opinion and views/comments from State Governments and 
Union Territory AdminislTations. Public notices to this effect were also published. Whilst the 
subject was still under consideration of the Committee and the Ministry of Home Affairs was 
aware of the exercise undertaken by it, the first Ordinance on lotteries was promulgated on 
October 1, 1997. This was followed by two successive Ordinances. The Committee strongly 
disapproves this course of action and considers it as an act of impropriety inasmuch as the 
Government did not wait for the recommendations of the Committee. When the evil was 
already prevalent in the society for quite some time~ what was the rationality of 
promulgating the Ordinance in haste when the subject was pending with the Parliamentary 
Standing Committee? 
15. Having considered the maner in all its aspects the Commiltee recommends thot as a 
first step the pre.sent Bill may be passed with some amendments as suggested in the 
succeeding paras. At the same time, in the light of the overwhelming view in the Committee 
for across the board ban on all kinds of lonerics, it strongly recommends to Government to 
come forward with a comprehensive Bill at the earliest in consultation with all the State 
Governments and the Union Territory administrations imposing complete ban on the lottery 
trade in the country having regard to the feasibility of effective implementation of the 
recommended legislation. 
16. The principal changes suggested by the Commiltee in the Bill and the reasons 
therefor are set out hereinafter:-
CLAUSE 4 
The Cause enumerates tbe conditions subject to which a lollery may be organised, 
conducted or promoted by a State Government. 
Sub-clause (e) of the clause provides that the prize money unclaimed within ~uch a time 
as may be prescribed by the State Government or not otherwise distributed, shall become 
the property of that Government. 
One of the conditions laid down by Supreme Court in the case of State of Haryana v/s. 
Suman Enterprises [1994 {4~ SSC 217) was that the sale proceed of the tickets either sold in 
retail or wholesale should be credited to the funds of the Government, however, the clause 
does not contain any such provisions. The Ministry of Home Atrnirs has stated that since the 
Bill relates to organisation, conduct and promotion of lolleries by the State Governments it 
is implied that the sale proceed of the louery tickets will get credited to the funds of the 
State Government concerned. The Commillee is not satisfied with the explanation and 
rec<>mmends that explicit provision in this regard may be incorporated in the Clause. 
Sub-clause (i) of the Cause provides that the number of bumper draws of a lottery shall 
not be more than six in a calender year. The Committee observes that the term "bumper 
draw" has not been defined in the Bill, as a result of which it can be interpreted differently 
by different organisers of the louery trade to escape from the effect of this provision. The 
Commillee understands that the intentio n of this provision is to limit the frequency of 
lotteries offering big prizes and thereby luring the common man for a quick buck. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the term "bumper draw" should be defined suitably 
to achieve the desired objective. 

4 
CLAUSES 
It empowen a State Government to prohibit within its territorial jurisdiction the sale of 
tickets of a lottery organised, conducted or promoted by another State. As this appears to 
be an enabling provision , one State Government may show favour towards the lottery 
orpniled by a particular State by not prohibiting it in its territory while banning the lotto·ry 
of another State Government. The Committee notes that as per proviso to Article 298 of lhe 
Constitution, the executive power of each State shall, in so far as a trade or business or such 
purpose is oot one wilh respect to which the State Legislature may make laws, be subject to 
legislation by Parliament. The Committee notes that as per Article 301, trade , commerce 
and intercoune throughout the territory of India shall be free, subject however , to other 
provisious of Part XD1 of the Constitution. The Committee fu~er notes that under Article 
302, Parliament may by law impose such restrictions on the freedom of trade , commerce or 
intercourse between one State and another or within any part of the to:rritory of India as 
may be required in the public interest . Notwithstanding the provisions of Article 302, Article 
303 imposes restrictions on the legislative powen of the Union and of lhe States with regard 
to trade and commerce on grounds of giving preferential treatment to one State over 
another or discriminating between one State and another, by virtue of any entry relating to 
trade and commerce in any of the Lists in the Seventh Schedule. 
The Clause appean to be violative ul Arti _cle 303. It is prr st discrirninawry . The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that this clause may be suitably modified with a view to 
ensuring its uniform application by all the States . 
CLAUSE 7 
The Qause provides for penal provisions for any person who acts as an agent, promoter 
or trader in any lottery organised, conducted or promoted in contravention of the provisions 
of this Act or sells, distributes or purchases the ticket of such lottery . Primary entity in the 
legislation is 'State'. U the State decides to itself organise lotteries then the violation of the 
provisions of the Bill by the concerned Government o£ficen is not punishable. The Clause 
may be suitably modified so as to include State authorities in addition to othen. 
17. The Committee agrees with the provisions contained in the remaining clauses of the 
Bill. 
18. Clause 1, the Enacting Formula and the Title wae adopted. 
19. The Committee recommends that the Bill, as reported by it, be passed.

INTERNAL SECURITY-AN OVERVIEW 
13. The Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs made a detailed presentution before the 
Committee on June 22, 1998 in the course of which he explained the broad thrust of the 
Demands relating to his Ministry. A major portion of his presentation was devoted to the 
internal security scenario, left wing extremism, insurgency , ethnic conflicts in the North · 
East, communal violence, caste clashes and other extremisvterrorist activities in the country. 
The Home Secretary apprised the Committee that out of the 535 districts in the country, 210 
districts are affected by one crisis or the other. Out of the 14 districts in Jammu and 
Kashmir, 10 are affected by militancy. Out of 69 districts in the North-Eastern region, as 
many as 48 are affected by insurgency or ethnic violence. The situation in Assam is worse 
because 23 of its districts are badly affected by violer.ce, the Home Secretary stated. He 
further stated that in Jammu and Kashmir during the period 1990-1998. Indian Security 
Forces arrested 4397 Pak trained militants and intercepted 711 gangs of Pak trained militants 
from the border. The Security Forces killed 1501 terrorists and arrested 1031. Besides, 2820 
militants of various outfits , including 1003 Pak trained , surr endered to the authorities, the 
Home Secretary informed the Committee. He went on to apprise the Committee that 
Pakistan has shifted its focus towards Nepal which is a porous border. lSI agents in 
Kathnwndu and Dhaka have been imparting training to youth in border areas, particularly 
on Indo-Nepal border and the interceptions have revealed that not only funds flow from that 
route, but unwanted el~ments also are intruding through that route. In the North-East, while 
the situation in Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh and Mcghalaya is comparatively peaceful as 
compared to other States, the situation in Assam is pretty bad. The situation in Nagaland is 
somewhat uneasy, the Home Secretary briefed the Committee. According to the Home 
Secretary, Jaw and order situation in Tripura is a matter of deep concern and if a good offer 
is made to the Tribal leadership in Tripura, the situation could improve. With regard to 
Manipur, the Home Secretary mentioned about the unrest in the State due to the extremist/ 
insurgent activities of the Naga, Kuki and Meitei outfits particularly the Nagas and Kukis. 
14. The Home Secretary went on to inform the Committee that the situation in Punjab 
has considerably improved. As per his submissions before the Committee, the overall law 
and order situation in Bihar is characterised by increasing crime growth and increasing 
activity of organised criminal groups as also left-wing extremists. The Home Secret ary 
further stated that the situation in Uttar Pradesh is marked by Communal incidents. ln 
Tamil Nadu, three factors have adversely affected the internal security situation . These are 
the intluence of the LTTE, growth of~ Muslim fundamental organisations and caste clashes. 
The Secretary made a reference to the series of bomb blasts in Delhi and apprised the 
Committee of reports of intensification of movement of anti-social elem e nts in Delhi. 
15. The Committee devoted considerable time in discussing the internal security situation, 
the problem of insurgency, left wing extremism especially naxalitc activities, ethnic clashes, 
the operation of private senas, etc. In this context the Committee noted that the States have 
been demanding the assistance of CPMFs from the Centre to deal with internal disturbances. 
The Committee noted that the supply of CJ>MFs to the States has not been commensurate 
with the demands of the States. The Committee also noted that a fresh look on BSF 
deployment is necessary. The existing BSF deployment has left large gaps, as a result of which 
the movement of extremists across the border is taking place very easily. This movement is 
not specific to any State but is regional in character. Unless additional BSF posts are created 
and deployment is increased, the border will remain porous particularly in the North-Eastern 
region as a result of which it will be difficult to contain the activities of the extremists. 
16. Article 355 of the Constitution enjoins upop the Centre to protect every State

of the Union to protect every State ugainst externa l agg ress ion and internal dist urbance and

of the Constitution ." The Committee feels if Central assistance could not be provided due to -... 
inadequacy of the forces, then the Centre shou ld raise more fo rces on urgent basis so that 
the requ irem ents o f the States may be adequately met. In this regard, the Ministry should 
formul ate their additional budgetary requirements and present them for approval. The 
Ministry should also ensu re that the existing vacancies in different CPMFs including the 
backlog vacancies of SCs!STs/013Cs should be filled in a time boun d manner . 
17. The Committee in this regard also takes note that a proposal for a special schem~ for 
modernisation of the Police Forces of insurgency affiicted States of the North-Eastern region is 
under active consideration of the Government and the Ministry is currently running this 
scheme on an adhoc basis out of the savings from the budget ullocated to it. The Committee 
strongly recommends that while there is a general necessity to substantially enhance the level 
of allocation under the ongoing scheme of modernisation of police forces, a similar proposal 
should also come from the Ministry for the States affected by the menace of a naxalism, left-
··• wing extremism etc. with a view to equipping their police forces · with latest arms and 
ammunitions, vehicles and sophisticated gadgets. 
18. The Committee also notes from the evidence tcnrkred before it by the Home 
Secretary that in recent times Pak has shifted its focus towurd s Indo-Nepal border and that 
I.S.I. agents in Kathmandu and Dhaka are imparting training to youth in border areas, 
particularly on Indo -Nepal border. It also notes that not only fund s flow through this.route 
but also unwanted elements are intruding through this route. The Committee takes a serious 
view of the situation in our neighbourhood. The Committee strongly urges upon the 
Government to take up the issue with Governments of Nepal and Bangladesh so that the 
ongoing I.S.I. activities could be curbed. The Committee also recommends that patrolling on 
borders with these countries may also be intensified . 
19. To deal with the terrorist/insurgency situation in various parts of the country, the 
Committee feels that there is a greater need for co-ordination amongst va~ious security and 
intelligence agencies at the Central Government level and their co-ordination with agencies of 
the State Governments. It is also required that all States suffering from terrorist/insurgency/ 
left-wing extremism activities should have a joint command under the control of Civil 
Administration with participation of security agencies of the Central Government as well as 
the State Governments. There is also a necessity for construction of roads and upgrading the 
communication facilities in the extremist affected and extremist prone areas . It has also been 
brought to the notice of the Committee that there is a lack of co-ordination between the Coast 
Guard and BSF in the border areas of Gujarat. The Committee therefore, recommends to the 
Government to examine these issues and apprise it of the outcome thereof.

DELHI POLICE 
29. During consideration of the Demands for Grants (1997-~8) of the Ministry, it was 
submitted to the Committee that in order to manage the 1450 beats in the Capital round-the­
clock to keep a tab on criminals, 4350 Head Constables against the existing strength of 1180 
and 8700 Constables against the present complement of 2472, were required. The Committee 
in its 37th Report had recommended that constraints of manpower should not be allowed to 
hamper the task of preserving law & order in the Capital and the requirement of additional 
manpower be considered favourably. 
30. The Ministry has informed that in order to strengthen and augment the available 
police force in Delhi, a proposal to establish in the first phase 17 police stations involving 
creation of 3100 posts in various categories is under active consideration including 1125 posts 
of Head Constables/Constables for manning the beats under the proposed Police Stations. 
31. In reply to a point raised in the meeting of the Committee held on June 30, 1998 the 
Delhi Police has replied that as per criteria fixed by the S.D. Srivastava Committee which 
was set up to assess the resource requirement of Delhi Police, there is a need of 59 new 
police stations in Delhi. Many new localities like Rohini, Dwarka etc. do not have adequate 
police presence. Due to shortage of manpower, police personnel are forced to work for 
more than 12 hours a day without a weekly off. This has :.~fleeted the quality of performance 
of police personnel and resulted in distortion in their behavioural pattern. 
32. The Committee notes that the present strength of pc•·sonnel in Delhi Police is not

adequate to cater to the need of effectively and efficiently managing the law and order and 
security duties in the Capital. It notes that there is a proposal for creation of 17 new Police

from satisfactory proposition. The Committee notes with concern that due to shortage of 
manpower some new localities do not have adequate police presence and due to this shortage 
police personnel are required to work more than 12 hours a day without getting a weekly orr

37 new police stat ions were added to the then existing strength bringing the total to 100. 
Though the police stations strength had been increa sed, the sanction was actually given in 
1987 on the basis of the data submitted in. 1985. And since 1987 till date no increase has

was around 80 lacs. Now, <,tccording to ration card figures, it has risen to 1.63 crores and 
according to census figures it is 1.30 crores. This does not take into account the floating 
population. Delhi has three important railway stations, one domestic and an international 
airport and a number of inter-state bus terminals. On an average, more than three to four

people are coming from adjoining areas in search of jobs. Out of all four metropolitan cities, 
Delhi has the highest slum population. According to official figures, 40% people are living in 
slums. Delhi Police is entrusted with the task of maintaining Jaw and orde r with limited 
resources in the fastest growing metropolis which has a large share of young people prone to

. Legislature, Chief Minister, President, Supreme Court, High Court, diplomatic zones,

34. The Committee reviewed the subject at length in the background of the scenar !o 
drawn above. It is of the considered view that there is an imperative need to augment in fuU

recommends to the Ministry to take a ho)istic view and initiate immediate action for rais ing

other important personalities. Any untoward incident s in the National Capital will have a 
chain react ion within the country and outside. In view of the unique position of Delhi a 
special dispensation is needed. There is, therefore , an urgent nee d to not only raise the 
strength of Delhi Police personnel to the desired level but also to equ ip them suitably with 
latest equipments, arms and ammunitions to effectively deal with all types of situations

39. The Committee understands that the task of managing traffic on Delhi roads is truly 
herculean. The Committee, however, does not understand why the strength of traffic police is 
not maintained upto the required level. The Committee notes with concern the bureaucratic 
delay h1 sanctioning of the proposals for creation of posts. It feels that in view of the volume 
of traffic and different modes of vehicles, it is, therefore, not wise to manage it through Home 
Guards who are not qualified to regulate the traffic in an efficient manner. The Committee 
expresses its dissatisfaction with this kind of adhoc arrangements and feels that there is a need 
to look into the matter seriously . The Committee recommends the Government to undertake 
an exercise to assess the requirement of mlditionnl manpower for traffic police as on date and

three months. The Committee furOter notes that the casually rate in road accidents in Delhi 
as illustrated in the Table (Annexure) is very high and thousands of persons die every year in 
such a~cidents. In many cases accident victims die due to non-availability of immediate 
medical first aid. The Committee feels that if a rudimentary knowledge of first aid is made 
mandatory for acquiring driving licences then in the event of road accidents the driver/owner 
of the vehicle can render valuable aid, to the victim and many lives can be save~. The 
Committee, therefore, urges upon the Ministry to take necessary action in the matter and 
make knowledge of medical first aid compulsory for all persons holding driving licenses. The 
Committee also feels that if police personnel possess medical first aid knowledge then in the 
case of accidents, they can also render valuable service to the victim. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that emergency first aid should be an integral part of the training 
courses of police personnel. The NGOs and the Automobiles Associations should also be 
involved in the exercise.

44. The Committee in its Thirty-second Report while reviewing the law and order 
situation in the country also deliberated on the functioning of police system. It observed that 
"the functioning of Police System in our country leaves much to be desired and periodically 
it has come in for severe criticism from different quarters. To reform this system a National 
Police Commission headed by Dr. Dharma Yira was st:t up long back and the vital 
recommendations which it had made in its report have got bogged down awaiting their 
implementation. The Committee strongly feels that implementation of recommendations of 
this nature needs to be accorded top priority. The Committee does not know what factors 
.are delaying their implementation. It, therefore urges upon the Government to submit a 
status paper to it on the recommendations which have found acceptance and which have not 
and whether the ones which have been accepted could be implemented in a time bound 
manner." 
45. The Ministry in their Action Taken note furnished on the subject has stated that 
'police' being a state subject, it was Primarily for the State Governments to implement the

have been requesting them to ensure expeditious action on the implementation of these 
recommendation. Responses received from the states indicate that the report have been 
considered by them and action has been taken to implement many of the recommendations.

Central Government, have been identified. Action has already been taken on the 
recommendations accepted by the Government. Some points, especially those where 
amendments to existing laws are required, are at various stages of implementation.

action taken thereon. He had also addressed the Chief Minister and the Administrators of 
Union Territories in April, 1997 for expeditious action on some of the vital recommendation

the Union Territories and centrally administered areas.

PRISON REFORMS 
93. In the meeting of the Committee held on Jun~ 22, 1998 a point was raised regarding 
the problems of prisons in the country and the reforms undertaking by the Gov~ ~rnment. In 
this respect, the Committee was informed that a 'Prisons' is a State subject the Central 
Government h·ave been interacting with the State Governments on the various issues relating 
to prisons and prisoners. As a result of reviews being conduct.ed by the Government and the 
periodical interactions with repersenatives of the State Governments the following problem 
have come to ! tne fore:- · · 
(i) The State Governments are according very low priority to the prison administration 
and there is no systematic monitoring of prison conditions in the States due to frequent 
transfers of officers at the senior level. Even the funds being released by the Central 
Government under the scheme of modernisation of prison administration are not being 
utilised; 
(ii) The high percentage of under-trials also affects the living conditions of prisoners. In 
most of the States, the under-trials population in the prisons nmges from 80% to 90%. The 
wider use of alter~atives to imprisonment and the reduction of under-trials in the prison 

23 
population are the two main areas that assume high priority in any action meant to ·reduce 
overcrowding in prisons; · 
(iii) Even though some of the State Government have·upgraded the basic amenities and · 
facilities in recent years with regard to food, clothing, medical care etc. the requirement~ ~(' ·· 
sanitation, water supply-, electrification etc . are yet to be adequately met; · 
(iv) There is also need for bringing improvement in the service conditions of prison 
personnel. The recruitment policy, recruitment procedures and promotional prospects are 
not properly orierited to attract the requisite talent. There is also problem of residential 
accommodation and schools for the children of prison personnel in most of the States; ·and 
I 
(v) The criminals who are lodged in jails for petty crimes come out as hardened 
criminals. 
94 .. The Committee was informed that in order to address . the aforesaid problems and 
keeping the importance of correctional administration in mind the Central Government have· 
been sending senior officers of the Ministry of Home Affairs frequently to States in order to 
assess the conditions of prisoners. In order to tackle the problem of und~r-trials, the Central 
Government has been stressing the need for devising effective procedures so that the 
periodical meetings of the representatives of the judiciary, district administration, poliqe 
department and prison authorities are conducted. A qu:uterly statement of under-trials is 
submitted to the High courts which in turn issues necessary instructions to the Courts for 
speedy disposal of cases and initiate suitable steps for setting up of special courts. The State 
Governments from time to time have also been advised to resort to the use of alternative 
measures to imprisonment such a the grant of bail, release of prisoners on probation, parole, 
grant of remission etc. and also to encourage the setting up of open prisons where the work 
release programmes help the prisoners to earn money to be used for their accommodation in 
the prisons and for the suppor~ of their family. 
95. The Committee was also informed that the Central Government had constituted a 
high pgwet committee known as AIJ India Jail Reforms Committee in 1980 under the 
Chairmanship of Justice A.N. Mullah (Retd.) to study various aspects of prison 
administra tion in the country and to suggest ·remedial measures to improve living conditions 
in prisons. The Mullah Committee made ·650 recommendation in 1983 majority of which 
pertained to the State Governments. Only 10% of the recommendations concerned the 
Central~ Government. The recommendation on which action was to be taken by the State 
Governments were forwar ded for their necessary action. The recommendations for which the 
Central Government had to take action mainly rehited to providing a financial assistance for 
strengthening of security , training of the prison staff, vocational training and rehabilitation, 
provision of medical and psychiatric services' etc. The Mullah Committee in its report, inter 
alia also recommended that all 'the Acts per.taining to prison administration should be 
consolidated and a new uniform and comprehensive legislation be enacted by Parliament for 
the entire coun try. In 1986 the Government of India also set up a Special Group with Shri 
R.K. Kapoor, former Director , IB, as Chairman to examine and review various aspects of 
administration and management of prisons. The group recommended better communication 
system, watch towers, wire fencing etc. In pursuance of recommendations of Mullah 
Committee and the Kapoor Group a scheme for modernisation of prison administration vras1 
introduced in 1987. Under this scheme an amount of about 100 crores have been rele~sed · to 
the various St(lte Governments. Besides, this the lOth Finance Commission have also 
recomr11ended ~n amount of Rs. 66.31 crore~ covering the period 1996-2000 for upgradation 
of.Jail Administration : The Ministry has also been interacting with National Human Rights 

24 
Commissi_on and the National Commission for Women. A proposal for enactment of 
legislation for transfer of foreign convicted nationals has also been under consideration so 
that they could be transferred to their Home Countries to serve the remaining period of jail 
terms. 
96. As far as the aspect of overcrowding in Central jail, Tihar, was concerned, the 
Committee was informed that Tihar had an authorised capacity of 3237 prisoners, while as 
on 19.6.98, there were 8767 prisoners in the jail. The Government of National Capital 
Territory of Delhi, in order to overcome the problem of overcrowding have taken steps to 
construct six new jails. These include four jails with a capacity of 1800 prisoners in the Tihar 
Jail Comp -lex, another jail with a capacity of 2000 prisoners at Mandoli and a jail at Rohini 
for lodging 950 prisoners. These jails are at present in various stages of construction and it is 
expected that one jail will be ready every year from 1998 onwards. The prisoners are 
provided round the clock medical services and separate medical faci 'ity also exists for women 
prisoners. Over 100 NGOs are engaged in providing vocational training to the prisoners. The 
prisoners are also encouraged to take parts in the games, sports and cultural activities 
organised for their benefit. A Committee in this respect appointed under the Chairmanship 
of Justice Santosh Duggal had since presented its Report. The recommendation made by this 
Committee have been accepted and implemented by the Government of Delhi. 
97. The Committee is dismayed over the sluggish pace of reforms in the Prison 
administration. It feels that the prevailing reforms are inadequate to meet the basic amenities 
of the swelling population of the prison inmates. The Committee notes with distress that the 
undertrials who are lodged in the prisons on charge of petty crimes, come out as hardened 
criminals. The Committee is shocked at the overcrowding in most of the prisons and expects 
that the Government will come out with well defined policies to decongest the prison premises 
and give a humane face to the prisons.

REPORT 
The management of personnel policies in Government of India, to begin with, was the 
joint responsibility of the Ministries of Home Affairs (Services and Establishment Wing) and 
Finance (Establishment Division) with· Union Public Service Commission playintz an 
important advisory role. The Establishment Officer to the Government of India, functioning 
under the Cabinet Secretary had an important role to play in the senior appointments under 
the Government of India. All this made for improper division of responsibility and lack of a 
unified central direction. 
2. To plug this organisational loophole, the Estimates Committee of the Third Lok 
Sabba in its 93rd Report (April 1966) observed that "the ever expanding role of the 
Government in a welfare state with its natural concomitant of a large civil service calls for 
effective personnel control through a singJ.e agency". • The Administrative Reforms Commi­
ssion too urged upon the Government to set up a separate Department of Personnel, to be 
placed directly under the Prime Minister to serve as a nodal agency for the personnel 
functions of the Government. 
3. The Union Government accepted this recommendation and. as a consequence the 
'Department of Personnel' was set up in August, 1970 and placed within the Cabinet 
Secretariat. In February 1973, the Department of Administrative Reforms, tilr then with the 
Ministry of Home Affairs, was amalgamated with the Department of Personnel and the 
newly created department was christened, the 'Department of Personnel and Administrative 
Reforms'. In 1977, this department was transferred to the Ministry of Home affairs. In 
March, 1985 a full fledged 'Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions' was 
created. The Ministry comprises three departments, namely:-
1. Department of Personnel and Training. 
2. Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances. 
3. Department of Pensions and Pensioners' Welfare. 
4. The Ministry is under the overall charge of the Prime Minister~ assisted by a Minister 
of State. All th~ three departments are functioning under the charge of Secretary 
(Personnel) assisted. by four additional Secretaries, three Joint Secretaries and other officers 
and staff. 
5. Functionally, the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions is divided 
into the following seven divisions:-
- Establishment officer 
- Establishment 
- Administrative Tribunal and Administration 
-Training 
- Pension and Central Services 
- Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances 
6. DEPARTMENT OF PERSONNEL AND TRAINING AND THE VARIOUS AGEN.CIES 
UNDER ITS ADMINISTRATIVE CONTROL 
6.1 The role of the Department of Personnel and Training can be conceptually divided 
into two paos. In its larger nodal role, it acts as the formulator of policy and the watch dog 
*Ninety-third Report of the Estimates Committee (Third Lok Sabha), New Delhi, Lok Sabha Secretariat, 1966, 
pp 18-19. 
1 

2 
or tlie Government ensuring that certain accepted standards and norms, as laid down by it, 
are followed by all Ministries/Departments in the recruitment, regulation of service 
conditions and deputation of personnel as well as other related issues. Towards this end, 
guidelines are issued by it for the benefit of all Ministries/Departments and it monitors the 
implementation of these guidelines. It also advises all organisations of the Central 
Government on issues of personnel management. At a more immediate level, the 
Department has the direct responsibility of being the cadre controlling authority for the 
Indian Administrative Service (lAS) and the Central Secretariat Service (CSS). The 
Department also operates the Central Staffing Scheme under which suitable officers from All 
India Services and Group 'A' Central Services are selected and then placed in posts at the 
level of Deputy Secretary/Director and Joint Secretary, on the basis of tenure deputation. 
The Department also deals with cases of appointment to posts of Chairman, Managing 
Director, full-time functional Director/Member of the Board of Management of various 
public sector undertakings/enterprises, corporations, banks and financial institutions. It also 
deals with the assignment of Indian experts to various developing countries. 
Recruitment Agencies 
6.2 The two organisations through which the Department ensures recruitment of 
personnel for the Government are the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) and the' 
Staff Selection Commission (SSC). The former is constituted under a provision of the 
Constitution and is responsible for conducting examinations for appointment to the higher 
civil services and civil posts under the Union Government, including recruitment to the All 
India Services. There is a mandatory provision for consulting the Commission on all matters 
relating to methods of recruitment, principles to be followed in making promotions and 
transfers from one service to another and all the disciplinary matters. The sse is responsible 
for making recruitment to subordinate staff such as Assistants, Stenographers etc. 
Training Institutions 
6.3 Two major training institutions directly under the administrative control of the 
Department are the Lal Bahadur Shastri Nlltional Academy of Administration (LBSNAA), 
Mussoorie and the Institute of Secretariat Training and Management (ISTM), New Delhi. 
The former is mainly responsible for providing induction training to recruits to the Indian 
Administrative 'Service and other All India Services and Central Services. The Institute of 
Secretariat Training and Management provides induction as well as in-service training to 
members of the Central Secretariat Service. 
Senior Appointments under the Government of India 
6.4 All proposals for senior appointments under the Government of India, which 
require the approval of the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (ACC) are processed 
through the Establishment Officer as Secretary of the ACC. These include board level 
appointments to Central Public Sector Undertakings and appointments of Joint Secretaries, 
Directors and Deputy Secretaries in the Ministries/Departments. In addition, all 
appointments by promotion, which require the approval of the ACC are also processed 
through the Establishment Officer. 
Public Enterprises Selection Board 
6.5 The Public Enterprises Selection Board (PESB) is entrusted with the responsibility 
of making recommendations for appointment to the full-time Board level posts· of Chief 
Executive and functional Directors and part-time Chairman in the Central Public Under­
takings. 

3 
Administrative Vigilance 
6.6 The Department of Personnel and Training determines Government policy for the 
maintenance of integrity of the public services and eradication of corruption and CC?Ordinates 
the activities of various Ministries/Departments in that area. 
Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) 
6.7 Advice on all vigilance matters is provided by the Central Vigilance Commissbn. It 
has jurisdiction and power in respect of all matters to which the executive power of the 
Union Government extends. The Commission enjoys the same measure of independence and 
autonomy as the Union P"!blic Service Commission. 
Central Bureau of Investigation 
6.8 The CBI is the premier investigating agency of the country. Originally set up as an 
anti-corruption agency of the Government of India, the role of CBI has undergone a sea 
change. It is now dealing with a variety of offences which include anti-corruption, special 
crimes, economic offences, major financial frauds, terrorist crimes and other serious crimes 
having inter-state and international ramifications. A large number of such cases are now 
referred to the CBI by High Courts and the Supreme Court. 
Joint Consultative Machinery 
6.9 There is a well-structured machinery for joint consultation between the Central 
Government and its employees on a wide variety of service matters having a bearing on the 
administration and the general interests of the Government employees. It is a three-tier 
machinery consisting of the National Council, the Departmental Council and the Regional! 
Office Council. Service matters pertaining to the interests of the generality of employees or 
specific groups of them are dealt with by this machinery. 
Central Administrative Tribunal 
6.10 In order to provide speedy and inexpensive justice to employees aggrieved by 
Government decisions, the Government set up the Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) 
in 1985, which now deals with all cases relating to service matters which were previously 
dealt with by Courts upto and including the High Courts. There are now 17 regular Benches 
of the CAT functioning in various parts of the country, including its Principal Bench in 
Delhi. 
Staff Welfare 
6.11 The Department supports various staff welfare programmes, which are provided _in 
various Ministries/Departments, Central Government Employees Welfare Coordination 
Committees in Central Government Offices located outside Delhi, Residents' Welfare 
Associations! Area Welfare Officers; Benevolent Fund and Departmental Canteens. 
Department of Personnel and Training is the nodal agency for three registered societies set 
up for the welfare of the Government employees and their families. These societies are the 
Central Civil Services Cultural and Sports Board, Grih Kalyan Kendra and Kendriya 
Bhandar. As a welfare measure, the Government had also decided, during the course of the 
year, to have a Civil Services Officers Institute in Delhi which has been set up as a 
registered society. 
DEPARTMENT OF PENSION AND PENSIONERS' WELFARE 
7. The Department of Pension & Pensioners' Welfare is the nodal agency of the 
Government of India for formulation of general policy on pension and other retirement 
benefits, as also for redressal of grievances on retirement benefits. The Department was set 

4 
up in 1985 as a part of Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions and has been 
rendering service for the benefit of pensioners since then. Department has taken a number 
of steps over the years for streamlining the pension administration system, for greater 
convenience and welfare of the pensioners. 
DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS AND PUBLIC GRIEVANCES

agencies in particular . The Department disseminates information on important activities of

Management Publications and Documentation. It also undertakes activities in the field of

concerned areas for the purposes of investigation including the powers of officer incharge of 
police station by the officers in the rank of sub-inspectors and above. At present CBI has 
three investigation divisions viz. Anti. Corruption Division; Special Crimes Division; and 
Economic Offences Division.

PUBLIC GRIEVANCE REDRESSAL 
33. Public grievance redressal remains an area of concern. It is a major cause of 
public dissatisfaction and the subject of criticism by elected representatives. Inaccessibility of 
officials, failure to acknowledge applications, unwarranted delays and non-enforcement of 
time limits, ignorance of procedures and forms and the unsympathetic attitude of officials at 
all levels only serve to further accentuate the problem of public grievances and their non­
redressal. The Committee understands that the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and 
Pensions had issued an office memorandum on 31st October, 1996 to all Ministries! 
Departments asking them to fix time limits for dispos:tl of grievances and endorsing a copy 
of the instructions issued in this regard to the Ministry. The Committee would like to be 
apprised of the action taken in the matter. 
34 .. The Committee has been taking up the issue of inadequate redressal of public 
grievances repeatedly. In response, the Ministry had been taking the plea that the process of 
public grievance redressal has necessarily to be decentralised for making it more effective. 
The argument of the Ministry is well taken but the Committee feels that the Department of 
Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances (DAR&PG) in its nodal role, should ascertain 
whether the policy of decentralisation of public grievance redressal is yielding desirable 
results. The fact that Directorate of Public Grievances in the Cabinet Secretariat and the 
Prime Minister's Office also have to take up the issue of public grievance redressal indicates 
some inadequacy in the existing mechanism. The Committee expects that the DAR&PG would 
take up a pro-active approach in the matter and induce the introduction of necessary 
corrective steps. 
CITIZEN'S CHARTER 
35. The Citizen's Charter concept was adopted as a pro-active instrument to achieve 
responsive administration. It indicates the commitments for improved service and grievance 
redress machinery of the organisation. The Ministry informed the Committer that these 
charters are indicative and that they are non-justiciable in nature. The Committee welcomes 
the concept of Citizen's Charters but it is of the view that their non-justiciable nature and 
lack of accountability for specific matters is hardly an improvement over the state of affairs. 
The Committee feels that a system of Administrative Courts should be set up to look into and 
adjudicate upon that acts of omission and commission of the administrative officials. These 
courts should have on their bench eminent citizens and Government officials of proven 
integrity and merit. The Citizen's Charters' should be made a justiciable document so as to 
empower the citizens with a view to introduce efficiency and transparency in administration 
by ensuring accountability. 
FREEDOM OF INFORMATION 
)6. In January 1997, Government had constituted a "Working Group on Right to 
Information and Promotion of Open and Transparent Government" under the Chairmanship 
of Shri H.D. Shourie. The Working Group submitted its Report to the Government on the 
21st May, 1997, which contained a draft "Freedom of Information Bill". The Group has 
recommended amendments to Section 5 of the Offical Secrets Act, 1923, Section 123 and 
124 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 together with consequential amendments in the Code 
of Civil Procedure, 1908 and in the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973, Rule 11 of the CCS 
(Conduct) Rules, 1964 and the Manual of Departmental Security Instructions relating to 
classification of information. The draft Bill, thus submitted has been circulated to all State 
Governments/Union Territory Administration and the Ministries/Departments of the Union 
Government for their views/comments. 
37. The Committee had inquired of the Ministry the reasons for bringing forth a 
'Freedom of Information Bill' and not a 'Right to Information Bill'. The Ministry contends 
that t,he u~e of the word "Right" in a "Right to Information Bill", has connotations which 
may ·make the legislation susceptible to avoidable litigation. The Working Group has 
explained that "the right to inf~rm~\ion has already received judicial recognition as a part of 

12 
the fundamental right to free speech and expression and the purpose in enacting the 
freedom of Information Act is mainly to provide a statutory framework for this right". 
38. Be that as it may, the Committee feels that explicitly providing for a 'Right to 
Information" will enable the citizenry to ensure accountability in administration. Moreover, 
the draft Bill on 'Freedom of Information Bill' as proposed by the Working Group bas a 
provision for "an internal review of decisions to refuse access to information taken by Public 
Information Officers (Clause 14)" The Working Group bas also proposed that the most 
suitable institution for discharging the appellate f':.lnction u.nder the Act would be the 
machinery Created under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986. The Committee feels that a 
more appropriate appellate body would be the 'Administrative Courts' as proposed by it 
elsewhere in this report. The Committee understands that a number of States have enacted 
the Right to Information Act. The Committee would like to be apprised of the applicability of 
the Union Legislation to such States and situation arising therefrom. It would be necessary to 
reorient the training schedule of Government employees to enab:e them to acquire special 
skills and aptitudes in tune with the proposed enactment.

SENIOR APPOINTMENTS AND PERSONNEL POLICY 
43. The Department of Personnel and Training deals with the senior appointments and 
personnel policies in the Government of India, DoPT is also charged with the responsibility 
of Cadre Management in respect of certain services namely, the lAS, the Central Secretariat 
Service (CSS) etc. The Establishment Officer and the Additional Secretary in the 
department is nodal officer who oversees the senior appointments, personnel policies and 
cadre management and he also serves as Secretary to the Appointments Committee of the 
Cabinet (ACC). All proposals for senior appointment under the Government of India which 
require approval of the ACC under the Government of India (Transaction of Business) 
Rules, 1961, are processed through the Secretary of the ACC. The appointments inter-alia : 
include Joint Secretaries, Directors and Deputy Secretaries in the Ministries and Department 
of the Government of India. 
44. The Committee was informed that in order to regulate the posting of officers of 
various cadres at different levels-Deputy Secretary, Director, Joint Secretary, Addtional 
Secretary, Secretary-the Union Government has administratively devised a procedure 
known as the 'Central Staffing Scheme', which has been in operation' for over three decades 
now. Under this scheme, a modality has been laid down by which the officers on offer, at 
different levels from different cadres, are systematically considered for appointment to 
Secretariat and non-Secretariat posts governed by the Central Staffing Scheme. The 
significant features of the procedure so prescribed are, as under:-
(a) Keeping in view the academic background, work experience, seniority, 
representation of different cadres at a particular level in the Central Secretariat, a 
panel of three names is offered to the Ministry /Department for consideration; 
(b) These three names are discussed and considered by the Civil Services Board at its 
next Meeting, and a choice in order of preference is made of the candidates; 

14 
(c) Thereafter, the Ministry concerned obtains the formal approval of the Minister-in­
Charge to the officer placed first in the order of preference. In case the Minister does 
not approve the officer placed first in the order of preference, the Ministry has to 
furnish detailed reasons for choosing the second or the third officer in order of 
preference; and 
(d) After the selection by the Ministry..f)epartment is received, a suitable note is 
submitted through the Cabinet Secretary, to the ACC comprising, the Home Minister 
and the Prime Minister. 
45. The Ministry also submitted that only the All India Services, viz. Indian 
Administrative Service, Indian Police Service and Indian Forest Service, provide for Central 
Deputation Reserve (CDR), in each State Cadre of these services. Further, that there is no 
rationale for having Central deputation quota in Central Services Group 'A' as they have been 
constituted to cater to needs of the Central Government only. The Ministry had also informed 
the Committee that there are thirty-four services participating under the Central Staffing 
Scheme. 
46. The Committee has gone into the reply given by the DoPT to paras 42 and 43 of its 
Thirty-eighth Report. In regard to the reply submitted to para 42, the Committee has noted 
that the eligibility criteria for promotion as VAder Secretary from the level of Section Officer is 
8 years of service. The comparison of such Officers with AIS Officers or Central Service Group 
'A' Officers is neither fair nor feasible. In the case of AIS and Central Service Group 'A' 
Officers they come on deputation to the Government of India on a tenure basis after completing 
5 years ofservice in Group 'A' whereas CSS Officers do not have any tenure. It has to be noted 
that the CSS is a participating service in the Central StafTmg Scheme. The Committee do not 
agree with the contention of the DoPT that a CSS OfTacer with 8 years in Group 'B' and 13 
years in Group 'A' becomes eligible for being on the Joint Secretary panel while an Officer of 
the AISCentral Services Group 'A' directly joining in Group- 'A' service becomes eligible for 
being on Joint Secretary panel after 17 years of service. According to a provision of the Central 
Staffing Scheme the eligibility is counted from the service rendered in Group 'A'. Therefore, 
the counting of service rendered in Group 'B' is not at all relevant nor logical. 
47. Similary the Committee do not agree with the rationale given by the DoPT regarding 
eligibility for empanelment as Additional Secretary. The Committee, Therefore, reiterate its 
views that no comparison can be drawn in the matter of number of years of Group 'A' service 
between CSS and other Central Group 'A' services. From the reply furnished by the PoPT, the 
Committee has observed that out of 106 posts of Additional Secretary in the Government of 
India as on 1.6.98 only 3 posts were being handled by Officers of the CSS. The Committee has 
also observed that out of the 273 posts of Joint Secretaries, 33 posts were held by CSS Officers. 
This shows that the representation of CSS Officers in the post of Additional Secretar)V,Joint 
Secretary in Government of India is quite low as compared to the lAS and the various other 
Central Services Group 'A'. 
48. In this connection the Committee would emphasize that DoPT has not appreciated the 
fact that how much time is taken by that department in empanelling the Officers of the CSS and 
their actual appointment at the level of Joint Secretary and Additional Secretary in the 
Government of India. This intervening period of time between the delay in the empanelment 
and their actual appointment at these levels is counted nowhere. Besides, there have been 
occasions in the recent past where some of the Officers who otherwise fulfllled all requirements 
for consideration for promotion to higher level but were left out on account of the 
Establishment Officer not forwarding names to the concerned Division (CS Division) of the 
Ministry for necessary processing. This is causing considerable and accumulated loss to the 
Officers of CSS for promotion to the higher posts. The Committee, therefore, is of the view that 
the DoPT should have a re-look at promotiopal avenues of the CSS Officers particularly at the 
level of Director, Joint Secretary and Additidnal Secretary so that these Officers are empanelled 
and appointed within a time-frame to be specified by them. 

15 
4?. In regard to reply given by the DoJYf to para 43 of its Thirty-eighth Report the 
Committee deeply regret to observe that its vie\vs-tecommendations have not been considered 
in its true perspective. The DoPT have wrongly interpreted the recommendations made by the 
Committee in this para that the amendments of CSS Rules, 1962 to bring the post of Director 
and above within its purview would tantamount to earmarking of post for CSS in the Central 
Secretariat. The CSS Rules were framed in the year 1962 i.e. about 36 years ago. The DoJYf 
have not bother ed to have a fresh look on the various provisions of these Rules keeping in 
view the past experience and operation of these Rules during the last 36 years. In this 
connection, the Committee has noted that the AIS and even the various Central Group 'A' 
services have their own set of service rules. And whenever any need has arisen in the past 
necessary amendments are being'had been made in the rules applicable to these services. the 
amendment to the service rules and earmarking of posts are two distinct issues. Whenever any 
amendment is carried out in the rules it does not necessarily mean that such an amendment 
would amount to earmarking of post for a particular service. 
50. The basic objective of the Central Staffing Scheme is to provide a systematic 
arrangement for selection and appointment of officers to senior administrative posts at the 
Centre, excluding posts which are specifically encadred within the organised Group 'A' 
Services or filled by recruitment through the UPSC. Under the Central Staffing Scheme 
officers from the AIS and participating Group 'A' Services, which are havig their own service 
rules, are borrowed for manning posts for a specified tenure and the cardinal principle being 
that all such officers who are so borrowed will serve the government of India for a stipulated 
tenure on deputation and, thereafter, return to their parent cadre. 
51. It is a well recognized fact that officers of the CSS have always been and or been 
manning the posts at the level of Director, Joint Secretary and Additional Secretary in the 
Government of India and acquitted themselves with distinction . When such officers can be 
appointed to these posts the Committee fails to understand why such posts could not be 
brought within the purview of the CSS Rules, 1962 by making suitable amendments to these 
rules. The Committee do not agree with the conclusion reached by the DOPT that if 
earmarking of posts is to be done in favour of a particular service, AIS might also demand 
earmarkign of posts to the extent of Central Deputation Reserve. The Central Staffing Scheme 
does not prescrib e earmarking of any post for any particular service including the AIS. The 
Central Deputation Reserve of AIS Officers of various State cadres varies from State to State . 
In Certain States the Central Deputation Reserve is over-utilised whereas in other States the 
Central Deputation Reserve is extremely under-utilised. Moreover, over-utilisation or under­
utilisation of quota of Central Deputation Reserve of a particular State cadre depends upon 
the number of names of officers sponsored by the respective State Governments for Central 
Deputation . It is, therefore, wrong to say that if the necessary amendments to the CSS Rules 
is carried out this will amount to earmarking of posts for this service, giving rise to demands 
for such earmarking by various other services. It is relevant to note here that Central Staffing 
Scheme provides that the growth , development and career prospects of the officers brought on 
deputation to the Centre, will be mainly in their own service. 
52. The Central Secretariat Service Rules, 1962 have become quite old .and the 
Committee is of the strong view that there is an urgent need to review these rules and carry 
out necessar,Y amendments in these rules in light of their operation during the last 36 years 
and to include the post of Director, Joint Secretary and Additional Secretary within the 
purview of these rules as the officers of this service have been holding these posts during the 
last so many years. The Committee, therefore, recommends accordingly. 
53. Keeping in view the above mentioned facts the Committee is of the view that the

structure and operation of the Central Staffmg Scheme is heavily biased towards the AIS 
and especially towards the lAS. The O>mmittee in its 38th Report had noted that 
appointments to the level of Joint Secretary and above in Government of India is marked by

information (Service-wise, for all the services participating in the Central Stamag Scheme)

The Ministry bas not furnished the information on the ground that there is no correlation

of a particular service in senior level post vis-a-vis other services. The Committee expects the

inter-aHa provided that single women officers would not be sent to 'disturbed areas' owing to

'law of administration with specific responsibilities enforced in specific manner' and for fixing

57. The Committee is unable to understand the re~sons for reluctance of Ministry in 
enacting a law on administration. In emphasizing the formulation of law on administration the 
Committee is not refe~g merely to regulation of service conditions of the civil service. Such 
laws should confer rightS and immunities in matters of administrative decisions on ofracers of

59. The Committee in its Thirty-eighth Report had recommended that the officials

I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Home Affairs, having been authorised by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, 
do hereby present this Forty-fifth Report on the Demands for Grants (1998-99) relating to 
the Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs.

relevant documents placed before it at its meeting held on 24th and 20th June, 1998. 
3. The Committee while its observations I recommendations has mainly relied upon the

OVERVIEW 
1. The Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs comprises the following 
Departments:-
(i) Department of Legal Affairs, 
(ii) Legislative Department, 
(iii) Department of Justice, and 
(iv) Department of Company Affairs. 
2. The main functions of the Department of Legal Affairs are:-
(i) To render advice to the various Ministnes!Departments of the 
Government of India on legal matters; 
(ii) To carry out the conveyancing work of the Central Government; 
(iii) To attend the litigation work in the Supreme Court, High Courts and 
some of the subordinate courts; 
(iv) To handle the treaties and agreements with foreign countries in matters 
of Civil Law; 
(v) To authorise officers to execute contracts and assurances of property on 
behalf of the President under Article 299 (1) of the Constitution; 
(vi) To sanction grants-in-aids to certain institutions engaged in research in the 
field of law. 
3. The Department of Legal Affairs in further concerned with appointment of the 
Law Officers, narr.~ly the Attorney-General of India, the Solicitor-General of India

4. The Legal Affairs Department has a two-tier organisational set-up, namely, the 
main Secretariat at New Delhi and the Branch Secretanats at Mumbai, Calcutta, 
Madras and Bangalore.

dissent;
