935 RS F-3·A 

2 
6. An All India Notaries' Conference took place at Panjim in Goa on the 16th 
February, 1997. ,The Conference was attended by the notaries from most of the States in 
india. It was .inaugurated by the then Union Minister of State for Law & Justice. The 
Conference considered the Report of the Committee. It disagreed with the recommendation 
of the Committee for the amendment of Section 5. It was stated in the Conference: 'Once a 
notary always a notary is our moto. Rigours of renewal should be dispensed with specially 
when the notaries have already put in professional experience of 10 years and are also 
eligible for Higher Judicial Service.' The Conference was also against prescribing any age 
limit or number of renewals. Similar views were also received from various State Notaries' 
Associations before and after the Conference. The then Minister had accepted the 
suggestion that renewal should be for five years; there should be no limit on renewals; and 
there sho~Ild be no age limit. However, he had also agreed with the view that the renewal 
should not be automatic. 
7. The then Minister had d~sired that the notaries may be involved in the court process 
to ease the burden of courts and tribunals throughout the country; that they could make 
useful contribution in the Alternative Dispute Redressal System by working as arbitrators, 
mediators and conciliators for settling petty cases. He was of the view that with the opening 
of the world economy increase in trade would result in a new regime of legal system and 
notaries would have grea~er role with an increasing demand for documentation. He, 
therefore, suggested that the notaries who have 10 years' experience at the Bar should be 
eligible for appointment as pro tem judges or magistrates in the absence of sitting judge or 
magistrate on being so directed. They should also be able to act as commissioners to record 
evidence in any civil and criminal trial if so directed by any court or authority. 
8. The amendments in the Notaries Act were also considered by the Law Ministers from 
various States in their Conference held on the 301h June and the P1 July, 1997. The Law 
Ministers unanimously accepted the proposed amendments. 
9. The Notaries (Amendment) Bill, 1997 seeks to amend the Notaries Act, 1952 to 
provide inter alia for:-
' 
(a) rationalisation of the procedure for renewal of certificate of practice; 
(b) the exercise of the functions of pro tem judge, magistrate, commissioner, arbitrator 
etc. by a notary when so directed; 
(c) the removal of the name of a notary on convictiOn by a court for any offence 
involving moral turpitude or for failing to get the ~ertificate renewed; 
(d) enhancing the quantum of punishment for falsely representing as a notary or doing 
any notarial act in contravention of Section 9 from three months to one year. 
10. Based on the papers supplied by the Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs 
(Department of Legal Affairs), certain questions/issues were framed and comments of the 
Ministry were sought thereon which have been summadsed as follows: 
935 RS F-3·B 

3 
Question/issue 
(I) Which are the circumstances or conditions under which the renewal of certificate 
may be refused by the Government to a notary? Will the Government have 
absolute discretion in such matters or whether it will not be desirable as 
recommended by the Committee on Notaries to provide grounds in the law itself on 
the basis of which the renewal of a certificate of practice may be refused to a 
notary? 
Government's reply 
Discretion is always exercised judiciously. If a notary files his return in time 
requesting Government to renew the certificate, deposits requisite fee for renewal in 
time, no case is pending against him, he is of sound health and is not otherwise 
unfit, normally his certificate will be renewed. For the renewal of a certificate of 
practice he has to follow the above noted procedure. 
Committee's views/observations 
The reply is not at all satisfactory. The pointed question has not been replied. 
Question/issue 
(II) Whether Government has ever conducted any survey to evaluate the performance 
of notaries? Whether it will not be desirable to have some kind of standing 
mechanism to monitor the functioning of the notaries and bring about necessary 
improvements from time to time? 
Government's reply 
The Government has standing mechanism to monitor the functions of the Notaries. 
The District Judges, being the competent authority appointed by State Government, 
have the power to check the notarial register used by a notary while discharging his 
functions . .The competent authority appointed for the purposes of the Act also 
receives the annual return from the notaries and scrutinizes it. The specimen 
signatures and rubber stamps/seals are checked from time to time. These measures . 
are ad.opted to streamline their functions. · 
Committee's views/observations 
The reply is unsatisfactory. 
Question/issue 
(III) The Committee on Notaries Act has made some observations concerning the 
Notaries Rules, 1956, particularly about fixation of upper age limit for Notaries, 
qualifications for their appointment, fees payable to a notary and enlarging , the 
source for appointing. the notaries. What is Government's views regarding these 
observations/recommendations and whether the Notaries Rules are also proposed to 
be amended accordingly? 
Government's ' reply 
The amendment of the Notaries Rules, 1956 will be taken up after the notaries Act, 
1952 is amended. 

4 
Committee's views/observations 
The reply is evasive. 
11. The previous Committee heard the then Law Secretary in its meeting held on the 
29th September, 1997. In the said meeting of the Committee , several queries were put 
relating to provisions of the Bill which were replied to by the then Secretary. The main 
thrust of the discussion in the Committee, however, revolved around clause 4 of the Bill 
proposing to empower the notaries to act as a pro tern judge or magistrate in the absence of 
a sitting judge or magistrate; to act as a commissioner to record evidence in any civil or 
criminal trial; and to act as an arbitrator, mediator or a conciliator. The Committee in 
particular wanted to know as to how and under what circumstances the notaries would be 
required to act as pro tern judge/magistrate/commissioner/conciliator; whether the 
Government would fix responsibility and accountability on them consequent upon giving 
them additional powers which would be in the nature of judicial functions; whether 
Government was contemplating to make rules and regulations more stringent to ensure their 
responsibility and accountability; what would be the additional qualifications concomitant 
with higher responsibility and corresponding accountability attached to the additional power. 
12. A view was expressed in the Committee that the proposed amen·dment would have 
far reaching cpnsequences. An apprehension was also expressed that the proposed 
amendment in Section 8 of the Principal Act ·giving powers to the Government was 
arbitrary. In the same genre a question was posed whether it was proper to give too much 
power to any entity including the Government. What would happen if that person acting as 
pro · tem judge or magistrate pronounced some judgement which was bad in law, was among 
the several other questions posed. 
13. In response to the above questions/queries and apprehensions the then Law 
Secretary inter alia stated that clause 4 of the Bill seeking to amend Section 8 of the 
Principal Act was not recommended by the Committee on Notaries. It was based on the 
suggestion by the then Law Minister in the All India Notaries Conference. It was more• in 
the nature of an enabling provision. If there was any shortage of judges/magistrates or in 
any case the courts did not find time for recording evidence, then they could call a notary 
and ask him to sit and record evidence. It was only to expedite the process. If the court 
decided, then only notaries could be permitted to discharge the functi9ns. 
14. The Secretary went on to explain that the intention behind the proposal was that if a 
judge/magistrate was on leave or unavailable and if the Government thought it proper, it 
could direct a particular notary to record evidence in a civil or criminal trial. The Secretary 
observed that even presently advocates were being given this function under the C.P.C. The 
notaries were also advocates and without this amendment they could be directed to record 
evidence. To act as arbitrators they did not need any authority under the Act. Any person 
can be appointed as an arbitrator. 
15. The Secretary went on to say that so far as the pro tern judge or magistrate was 
concerned, such a ·system was prevailing in Goa sometime back under the Portugese Law 
and this had been included in the Bill on the suggestion of Law Minister. 
16. The Secretary further, observed that the Ministry was ·considering to add a provision 
in the C.P.C. conferring power on Government to appoint a person as a pro tern judge and 
in that case a notary too would be entitled to be appointed as such. The present Bill. only 
makes a notary eligible to be appointed as a pro tern judge. 

5 
17. Thereafter, a Member of the previous Committee while stating that -the Law of 
Notaries in the country was defective in many ways, shared with the Committee at length his 
knowledge of the functioning of notaries during the French Rule in Pondicherry . He inter 
alia requested the Committee to visit Pondicherry and study the institution which was 
prevalent during the French Rule. 
18. In conclusion, the previous Committee felt the need to study in greater detail the 
various aspects related to the proposed amendments and in this context decided to examine 
the system of Notaries prevailing in the U.K., Switzerland, Sweden, France, the U.S.A. and 
Malaysia. In order to facilitate the work of the Committee, the Chairman of the Committee 
had specifically asked the then Law Secretary to furnish notes on the current status of the 
institution of the Notaries as it obtained in the aforesaid countries and how the functions of 
the Notaries were being discharged there. 
19. The pr~vious Committee also decided to visit Pondicherry at a convenient date to 
study the operation of the Law of Notaries there vis a vis the one prevalent during the 
French Rule and interact with some of the persons associated with the a4ministration of the 
Law during that period . The Committee further decided to hear the representatives of Delhi 
Notaries Association in the matter . 
19.1 In this connection , the then Chairman had also asked the then Law Secretary ·to 
study various aspects of the institution of Notary as it obtained in Pondicherry during French 
Rule and send a report thereon to the Committee. 
20. Sub~quent to the meeting of the Committee held on 29th September, 1997 the 
Department of Legal Affairs vide their O.M. dated the 17'h October, 1997 had forwarded 
copies of relevant Acts of England on Notaries. In the said communication that Department 
had stated that the Notaries Act of the various countries like France, Switzerland, Malaysia, 
Sweden, the U.S .A. had not been traced out in any Library. However, that Department had 
been searching for the relevant material. 
20.1 On the 23rd October, 199'7 a communication was sent from the Secretariat to the 
Department of Legal Affairs reminding them to take jmmediate necessary action to furnish 
detailed notes on (i) current status of the institution of Notaries obtaining in the aforesaid 
six countries and whether some of the features thereof could be adopted to suit our needs 
and (ii) Institution of Notary in Pondicherry during French Rule. 
20.2 As no reply was forthcoming, the Department of Legal Affairs was again reminded 
on the 17th November, 1997. Thereafter, there had been no response from the Department 
in the matter. Subsequently, the previous Committee got dissolved consequent upon the 
dissolution of the Eleventh Lok Sabha on the 4th December , 1997. The then Chairman of 
the Committee directed the Secretariat that since the Lok Sabha had been dissolved the 
matter may be placed before the new Committee. 
21. After constitution of the present Committee, a reference was made to the 
Department of Legal Affairs on the 4'h August, 1998 to let the Committee know the 
willingness of the Government in pursuing the Bill in its present form. The Department after 
nearly three months responded on the 29'h October, 1998 stating that the Government 
wanted to pursue the Bill in Parliament in its present form. 
22. The Committee in its sitting held on the 8'h Februar y, 1999 took up consideration of 
the Bill from w.here it was left by the previous Committee . 
23. At the outset, the Chairman apprised the Committee of the decisions taken by the 
935 RS F--4-A -

6 
predecessor Committee particularly in regard to the study of the system of Notaries 
prevailing in the U.K., Switzerland, Sweden, France, the USA and Malaysia and also with 
regard to operation of the Law of Notaries in Pondicherry vis a vis the system prevalent 
there during the French rule. In this regard the Chairman informed the Committee that

24. After some discussion the Committee deplored the indifferent attitude of the 
Government in complying with the directions of the Committee. The Committee desired 
that its displeasure in the matter may be taken note of by the Government and it strongly

25. With regard to the Committee's proposed visit to Pondicherry in order to g..:.:t a

Chairman stated that the visit did not materialise because of dissolution of the last Lok

26. Thereafter, the Committee decided that since the amendments proposed to be 
carried out in the Notaries Act, 1952 were of non-contentious nature, it may dispose of the 
Bill and report to Parliament with its observations/recommendations. 
27. In this context the Committee finds that except one provision . in the Bill, namely, 
clause 4 (a) (ha), relating to exercise of the functions of pro tem judge or magistrate by a 
Notary when so directed, all other provisions were innocuous. With regard to the aforesaid 
clause, the Committee finds it totally incongruent with the uther Jaws of the country. The 
Committee opines that the functioning of a Notary is different from that of a judge or 
magistrate. Since a notary's duty is basically to authenticate, verify, certify documents, 
promissory notes etc., it will be inadivisable and unjustified to ask him to act as a judge or 
a magistrate in the absence of a sitting judge or a magistrate on being so directed. A note of 
caution has been expressed in the Committee that such a provision may also be misused.

work of a judicial nature. However, they may act as commissioner to record evidence in any 
civil or criminal trial if so directed by any court or authority and may also act as an

CHAPTER-III 
THE NOTARIES ACT, 1952 
The present Notaries Act, 1952 (Act 53 of 1952) was passed by the Parliament on 
9th August, 1952. Before this Act came into force, the notaral functions were regulated by 
the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (Act 26 of 1881). After India, became independent , it 
was felt that these provisions were insufficient to satisfy the needs of developing India and 
there should be a separate Act comprehensively dealing with all aspects of notaries. Hence , 
iii '19521 Parliament enacted the Notaries Act, 1952. It came into force on 4th February , 
1956. No major amendment has been made in the Act since then. 
2. The Notaries Act, 1952 extends to the whole of India including the State of Jammu 
and Kashmir. It was extended to the State of Sikkim by an order of the Government of 
India No. S.0.210(E) dated 16th May; 1975. 
3. Amendment of Section 2(c) 
3.1 Section 2 of the Notaries Act, 1952 contains definitions. It does not define the word 
'Advocate'. Sub-section (c) of Section 2 defines the word 'legal practitioner'. The said 
definition is as follows: 
" 'legal practitioner' mean S" any advocate or agent of the Supreme Court or any 
ad'o(ocate, vakil or attorney of any High Court or any pleader authorised under any 
law for the time being in force to practise in any court of Jaw." 
3.2 The Committee felt that after coming into force of the Advocates Act , 1961 this 
definition is no more relevant. Various categories of legal practitioners, such as, vakil~ 
pleaders, mukhtars, attorneys do not exist any longer. Now, advocates enrolled under the 
Advocates Act, 1961 alone are entitle to practise law in any courts. In view of the above, 
the Committee is of the opinion that this definition requires to be amended in terms of the 
provisions of the Advocates Act, 1961. 
3.3 The Committee therefore, recommends that the said definition of the word 'legal 
practitioner' may be substituted by the following definition: 
" 'legal practitioner' means an advocate entere·d in any roll under the provision~ of 
the Advocates Ac.t, 1961 (Act 25 of 1961)." 
4. Amendment of. Section 5 
4.1 Section 5 of the Notaries Act, 1952 is an important provision. Sub-section (2) of 
Section 5 gives a right to a notary who wishes to continue practise, after the expiry of the 
period for which he was appointed as notary, that on payment of the prescribed fee, he shall 
be entitled to the renewal of his certificate of practice for three ye.ars at a time. It is as 
follows: 
"Every such notary who wishes to continue to practise after the expiry of the period 
for which his certificate of practise has been issued under this section shall, on 
application made to the Government appointing him and payment of the prescribed 
fee, if any, be entitled to have his certificate of practice renewed for three years at a 
time." 
4.2. The Committee noted that this· provision gives a right to a notary to get his

certificate of practice renewed for a period of three years. Once a notary submits an 
application for the renewal of his certificate of practice and pays the prescribed fee, the 
certificate of practice has to be renewed. The use of the word "shall" in section 5(2) creates 
a vested right in favour of a person once appointed as a notary. Further the said provision 
does not place any limit on the number of renewals. A certificate of practice can be renewed 
for indefinite number of times. In other words, the extension of the term of a notary is 
automatic and perpetual. The appropriate Government has no discretion in the matter. The 
said provision does not give power to the appropriate Government, even to scrutinise the 
application at the time renewal is sought, with a view to ascertaining whether the certificate 
of practice of a notary deserves to be renewed or not. 
4.3 The experience of some of the representatives of the State Governments has been 
that this provision has not worked well in the past. The Government had no choice in the 
matter of renewal of a certificate of practice even if it is of the opinion, for valid reasons, 
that the ·certificate of practice should not be renewed. 
4.4 The Committee generally agreed that it is necessary to fix a limit beyond which a 
certificate of practice must not be renewed. With this end in view, various options were 
considered. Some members of the Committee were of the view that limit should relate to the 
age of a notary. After the notary has attained a particular age, he should not be eligible for 
seeking renewal of the certificate of practice. In this context various age limits, such 13S 65 
year, 75 years, 80 years were suggested . Other members felt that the fixation of age limit for 
the purposes of renewal of the certificate of practice would not be appropriate, 'the reason 
being that an advocate is more in need of money when he is old and unable to attend the 
court work. To deprive him of the benefit of notaryship at that age will not be appropriate. 
After long deliberations, the Committee came to the conclusion that this provision which 
deals with renewal should not be linked with age. 
4.5 The Committee, therefore, feels that the limit sh9uld be linked to the renewals. A 
certifi'cate of practice should not be renewed for more than three time, each renewal being 
of 3 years. Thus, the total ·period permissible to a person, once appointed as a notary, 
should not be more than 12 years - three years being initial appointment period and nine 
years being three renewals of three years each. Further that such renewals should not be 
automatic and compulsory. The appropriate Government should have a right to. scrutinise an 
application for renewal and may renew the certificate of practice at its discretion. 
4.6 The GovemmeJ.I)t, however, should not have absolute discretion in the matter. The 
said discretion should be· guided or regula ted by law. The law should provide grounds on the 
basis of which the renewal of a certificate of practice may oe refused. Such ground may 
include public interest, medical grounds, ethical grounds, and so on. Further, the principles 
of natural justice demands that before an application for renewal of a certificate of practice 
is rejected, the notary should be given an · opportunity of being heard. · Thus, if a 
Government proposes to reject an application for the renewal of the certificate of practice, 
the notary should be given a show cause notice to reply within 15 days. 
4.7 The Committee has expressed the view that the total period during whfch a person 
can act as notary should be 12 years. The Committee does not wish to debar a person from 
becoming notary again after 12 years, if he is found fit for such an appointment by the 
Government. Hence, it should be specifically provided that after 12 years a notary may be 
eligible for re-appointment. 
4.8 The Committee is, therefore, of the opinion that the existing sub-section (2) of 
Section 5 should be repealed and substituted by the following sub-section:-

32 
"Every such notary who wishes to continue to practice after the expiry of the 
period for which his certificate of practice has been issued under this section may 
make · an , application to the Government appointing hil]l for renewal of his 
certificate of practice. On receipt of such application the Government appointing 
him may ' renew his certificate of practice for a further term of three years on 
payment of the prescribed fees, subject to a maximum of three such renewaJs. No 
application of a notary for renewal of a certificate of practice shall be rejected 
unless he has been given a notice to show cause. The notary who has ceased to be 
so may be eligible for re-appointment." 
5. Amendment of Section 10 
5.1 Section 10 of the Act prescribes grounds for removal of name of a notary from the 
Register of Notaries maintained by the Government under Section 4 of the Act. It is a& 
follows: 
"Removal of names from Register:- The Government appointing any notary may, 
by order, remove from the Register maintained by it under Section 4 of the name 
of the notary if he -
(a) makes a request to that effect; or 
(b) has not paid any prescribed fee required to be paid by him; or 
(c) is an undischarged insolvent; or 
(d) has been found , upon inquiry in the prescribed manner, to be guilty of such 
professional or other misconduct as, in the opinion of the Government , 
renders him unit to practise as a notary. " 
5.2 This section contains four grounds. If any of the ground exists, the name of a notary 
can be removed from the Register of Notaries. These grounds do not include conviction of a 
notary, by a criminal court, for an offence. Thus, the name of a notary can't be removed 
from the Register of Notaries even if he commits an offence or is sentenced by a court. The 
conviction of a notary by a court of competent jurisdiction for an offence involving moral 
turpitude is a serious matter. Such a person looses the confidence of the society and should 
not be allowed to practice -as a notary. Further, conviction for an offence involving moral 
turpitude is also a disqualification under various other laws. The Committee, therefore, is of 
the view that conviction by a court for an offence involving moral turpitude should be a 
ground for the removal of his name from the Register of Notaries. 
5.3 While recommending amendment of Section 5(2), the Committee has recommtnded 
that the Government should have a right to scrutinise an application for the renewal of the 
certificate of practice. If for valid reasons, the Government decides that a particular 
certificate of practice should not be renewed, then, it should be a ground for the removal of 
name of the notary from the Register of notaries. In fact this is a consequential amendment. 
If the certificate of practice has not been renewed, he cannot practice as a notary and his 
name has to . be removed from the Register of Notaries. 
5.4 Another ground which needs to be added in this section is a failure to renew a 
certificate of practice. If a notary does not apply for the renewal of the certificate of practice 
and the period for which it was issued or previously renewed has expired, his name has to be 
removed fro~ the Register of Notaries. Though in the normal course also when a certificate 
of notary is not validly in existence, the notary ceases to be so. Nevertheless, the Committ ee 
feels that since amendments to the Notaries Act, 1952 are being considered, it is better to 

33 
make a specific provision rather than to leave it for future dispute~ and varying court 
interpretations. 
5.5 The Committee is, therefore, of the opinion that the existing section 10 should be 
substituted by the following:-
"Removal of names from Register:-The Government appointing any notary may, 
by order, remove from the register maintained by it under section 4 of the name of 
the notary if he-
(a) Makes a request to that effect; or 
(b) has not paid any prescribed fee required to be paid by him; or 
(c) .is an undischarged insolvent; or 
(d) has been found, upon inquiry in the prescribed manner, to be guilty of such 
professional or other misconduct as, in the opinion of the Government, 
renders him ·unfit to practise as a notary; 
(e) is convicted by any court for an offence involving moral turpitude; 
(f) ·does not get his certificate of practice renewed; and 
(g) the certificate of practice is not renewed by the Government appointing him." 
On the removal of the name, the person shall cease to be a notary from the day the order 
is passed removing the name from the Register of notaries. 
6. Amendment of Section 12 
6.1 Existing Section 12 provides for punishment to a Notary who falsely represents that 
he is a notary without being appointed as such or practices as a notary or does any notarial 
act in contravention of Section 9. The punishment provided is imprisonment for a term 
which may extend to three months or with fine or with both. It is as follows: -
"12. Penalty for falsely representing to be a notary, etc. - Any person who -
(a) falsely represents that he is a notary without being appointed as such, or 
(b) practises as a notary or does any notarial act in contravention of section 9, 
shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three 
months, or with fine, or with both." 
6.2 The Committee feels that the period of imprisonment of three -months is inadequate. 
It does not have sufficient deterrent effect. In order that this provision should act as a 
deterrent for a person to commit the offence mentioned above, the quantum of punishment 
should be increased. Some Members of the Committee were of the opinion that in order 
that this provision really acts as a deterrent, a minimum punishment of six months should be 
provided. A discretion should be given to the court to provide a punishment of less than six 
months for reasons to be recorded in writing. The other Members were of the opinion that 
the ··nature of offence prescribed by Section 12 is not such as to warrant a minimum 
punishment. After a long deliberation, the Committee decided against prescribing a 
minimum punishment. On the question of maximum punishment, the views of the Members 
were unanimous. It was agreed that the punishment should be increased from three months 
to one year. " 
6.3 The Committee is, therefore, of the opinion that in Section 12, quantum of 
punishment should be increased to one year thus the words by "one year or with fine or with 

34 
both" may be substituted for the words "three months or with fine or with both. The 
amended Section 12 should read as follows: 
"12. Penalty for falsely representing to be a notary, etc. - Any person who­
(a) falsely represents that he is a notary without being appointed as such, or 
(b) practises as a notary or does any notarial act in contravention of Section 9, 
shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one 
year, or with fine, or with both." 
7. Amendment to Section 15. 
7.1 Section 15(1) of the Act enables the Central Government to make rules to carry out 
the purposes of the Act: Sub-section (2) of Section 15 enumerates matters in respect of 
which rules can be made. 
Clause (a) of Sub-section (2) of Section 15 enables the Central Government to make 
rules regarding qualification of a notary, the form and manner in which applications for 
appointment as, a notary !Jla.Y be made and the disposal of such applications. 
This sub-section does not provide for prescribing age limit' for the purposes of eligibility 
for appointment as a notary. The Committee is of the view that this sub-section .should be 
suitably amended to enable the Central Government to frame rules to prescribe the age limit 
for the purpose of eligibility for appointment as a notary. 
7.2 Clause (e) of Sub-section (2) of Section 15 enables the Central Government to make 
rules regarding fees payable by a notary to the appropriate Government for appointment as 
a notary for issue and renewal of a certificate of practice. This suh-sedion reads as follows: 
-"(c) The fees payable for appointment as a notary and for the~issue and renewal of a 
certificate of practice, and exemption, whether wholly or in part, from such fees in 
specified classes of cases." 
7.3 Sometimes, the notaries submit applications seeking extension or enlargement of the 
area of practice. There may be various reasons for a notary seeking enlargement of the areas 
of practice. In many such cases the Government also does not have any objection to such an 
enlargement of the area of practice . However, as there is no provision for levying fees for 
such services the Governments have in the past been reluctant in doing this service or 
charging fees for such service without authority of law. 
7.4 The Committee is, therefore,' of the view that Section 15(2)(a) and 15(2)(c) may he 
amended so as to read as follows: 
"(a) The qualifications of a notary, age limit for the purpose of eligibility of 
appointment as a notary, the grounds for refusal for renewal of a certificate of

(c) the fees payable for appointment as a notary for the issue and renewal of a

CHAPTER-IV 
THE NOTARIES RULES, 1956 
1.1 After having examined the provisions of the -Notaries Act, 1952, the Committee 
desires to make use of this opportunity to consider the Notaries Rules, 1956 also. In 
pursuance of the power conferred by Section 15 of the Notaries Act, 1952 (Act 53 of 1952) 
the Central Government has made the Notaries Rules, 1956. These rules were notified on 
14th February, 1956. 
1.2 Section 3 of the Act gives a power to the Central Government to prescribe 
qualifications of the persons who may be appointed as notaries. Section 15(2)(a) of the Act 
also gives a power to the Central Government to ma~e rules prescribing the qualifications of 
a notary, the form and manner in which applications for appointment as a notary may be 
made and the disposal of such applications. In pursuance of the aforesaid provision , rule 3 
has been made prescribing qualifications for appointment as a notary. It is as follows: 
"Qualifications for appointment as a notary - No person shall be eligible 
for appointment as a notary unless on the date of the application for such 
appointment - (a) he is notary to be appointed by the Master of Faculties in 
England; or (b) he has been practising as a legal practitioner for atleast 10 years." 
1.3 The Committee feels that clause (a) has become redundant and may be deleted. 
1.4 The Committee felt that one of the important objective of the Notaries Act, 1952 is 
to provide facilities to the public to get their notarial functions performed without much 
difficulty. The provision limiting the appointment of notaries from the legal practitioners of 
atleast 10 years standing has restricted the choice of the Government. Tl)ere is a need for 
enlarging the source from where the notaries can be appointed. The Committee also felt that 
officers working in the Law Ministries of the Central and the State Governments are also 
adequately qualified and should be appointed as notaries. This will help the Governments as 
well as the public in easy availability of notaries. 
1.5 The Committee observed that at present there is no age limit for the appointment of 
a person as a notary. At a very old age, a person may be unable to function as a notary. His 
faculties may not be that alert as are necessary for functioning as a notary. The Committee, 
therefore, felt that some age limit should be prescribed beyond which a person should not be 
eligible for appointment as a notary. During the discussion, various age limits were 
suggested by the members. Some members were of the view that the maximum age of 
eligibility for appointment as a notary should be 60 years. Since the Committee has 
suggested in para 5 of Chapter III that no person should be allowed to function as a notary 
for more than 12 years (three years on appointment and three renewals of three years each 
i.e. nine years making the total to twelve years), this will ultimately mean that a person can 
practise as a notary up to the age of 72 years. Other members were of the view that the age 
limit of 72 years for a man to stop practising as a notary will be too short. They were of the 
view that age at the time of appointment plus the 12 years period should be fixed in such a 
way that the person should not exceed 80 years of age. After much deliberations, the

will be reasonable. The reason being many persons at that age do not come forward for 
appointment as a notary. Generally, the appointment as a notary takes place at a young age. 
Therefore, the limitation of 75 years will be more or less observed by way of upper limit. 
1.6 The Committee, therefore, recommends that rule 3 may be substituted by the 
following: · 
"No person shall be eligible for appointment as a notary unless on the date of the 
application for such appointment:-
(a) he has been practising as a legal practitioner for atleast ten years; and 
(b) he is or has been a member of Indian Legal Service under the Central

REPORT 
1, the Chairman of the Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Home Affairs having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, 
present this Fifty-third Report of the Committe~. The Report is on the Immigration 
(Carriers' Liability) Bill, 1998. • 
2. In pursuance of the rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha in consultation with the Speaker, Lok Sabha 
referred** the Immigration (Carriers' Liability) Bill, 1998 as introduced in the Rajya Sabha 
on the 23rd December, 1998 and pending therein, to the Committee for examination and 
report. 
3. The Bill intends to make the carriers liable in respect of passengers brought by them 
into India in contrav entio n of the provisions of the Passport (Entry into India) Act , 1920, 
and the Passport (Entry into India) Rules, 1950. The said Act and the 'rules made. 
thereunder prescribe the conditions for the entry of a person' coming from any place outside 
India by water, land or air. Under these rules, foreign nationals are required to be in 
possession of a valid passport and a visa. An Indian national must be in possession of a valid 1 
passport. The Immigration authorities posted at various checkposts covering land checkposts, 
seaports and airport s are required to do a thorough checking of the persons coming by 
different mpdes of transport. 
4. The Ministry of Home Affairs in their Background Note on the Bill has stated that it 
has been observed in recent years that a large number of passengers at the four major 
Internat ional airports at Delhi, Bombay , Calcutta and Madras manage to come without any 
valid documents, creat ing problems for the immigration authorities. Airlines do not exercise 
proper check of travel documents before allowing passengers to board the plane. It has, 
therefore, become nece~sary that stat utory responsibility is cast on the airlines/ship carriers 
bringing such passengers by imposing financial liability on them, states, the Ministry in their 
Note.· 
5. International air travel is governed by the guidelines adopted at the Convention on 
Internatinal Civil Aviation signed at Chicago on December 7, 1944, known as the Chicago 
Convention. It has various annexures finalised over a period of time during the last 50 years. 
Ann exure 9 to the Convention on International Civil Aviation deals with "Fac ilitation " and 
incorpo rates recomm ended practices in this area, para 3.35 of this Ann exure, requir es the 
public author ity of a contract ing state to accept the passengers and crew for examination as 
to their admissibility in the country without unreasonably delay. The ope rator has been 
made responsible for the custody and care of the passenge rs until they are accepted after 
such examination . The operator is responsible for the custody of passengers and crew 
between aircraft and the terminal builiding and within the transit area of the terminal 
builiding . However, it has been left to the contracting authorities to relieve any operator 
from any of these responsib ilities.

copy of the Bill, plca~cs sec Annexure.

6. Para 3.36 of the aforementioned Annexure to the Chicago Convention states that a 
person found inadmissible is transferred back into the custody of the operator who will be 
responsible for his prompt removal to the point where the person commenced his journey or 
to any other place where the person is admissible. An inadmissible person is defined as a 
person who is refused admission to a State by its authorities. The public authorities are 
required to inform, without delay, the operators when a person is found inadmissible. 
7. Para 3.37 of the said Annexure casts responsibility on the operator to take 
precautions at the point of embarkation to the end that passengers are in possession of 
necessary control documents prescribed by the contracting States. It has been further stated 
that the contracting State shall not fine operators in the event that passengers are found 
inadmissible unless there is evidence to suggest that the carrier was negligent in taking 
precautions to the end that the passengers complied with the documentary requirements for 
entry into the receiving States. 
8. The Ministry has informed the Committee that India is a party to the Chicago 
Cenvention and, ordinarily, it would not have been desirable to make provision through a 
domestic enactment imposing a financial liability on the carrier/operator to pay certain 
amount for carrying a passenger who does not have a valid passport, visa or other travel 
documents. In this connection, the Ministry has informed the Committee that over the 
course of time, a number of countries have deviated from the standards laid down in the 
Annexure to the Convention and have enacted legislations by which they seek to cast 
financial liability on the carrier/operator to pay a certain amount for every passenger carried 
without a travel document. The USA, U.K., Canada, Saudi Arabia, Singapore and Australia 
are some of the couq.tries who have enacted such legislation. It has been noticed, for 
example, that the U.K. Government has enacted Immigration (Carriers' Liability) Act, 1987. 
A duty has been cast through this Act on the owners or agents of the ship or aircraft to pay 
an amount of Pounds 1,000.00 (One thousand Pound Sterling) which has been amended to 
pounds 2000.00 in 1991 for every carrier who carries a person without proper documents, the 
Ministry has stated in their Background Note .. 
9. The Ministry has further stated that the US Nationality and Immigration Act 
provides for imposition of penalty of a sum of $ 1,000.00 payable by the owner, master, 
commanding officer, agent, charterer, or consignee of any vessel or aircraft for every alien 
who is brought to the U.S.A. without a valid visa. In addition, they have to pay a sum equal 
to that paid by such alien for his transportation from the initial point of his embarkation. 
According to the information given by Directorate General of Civil Aviation, U.S.A. has 
not filed differences with respect to para 3.37.1 of Annexure to the Convention on 
International Civil Aviation (Chicago Convention). 
10. The Ministry has also inform ed the Committee that besides traffic through airlines , 
there are shipping lines also which control traffic from outside India. Some inadmissible 
foreigners enter thro4$h sea-routes also. International sea travel is governed by the 
Convention for Facilitation of International Martime Traffic, London (April, 1965) to which 
India is also a signatory. Para 3.15 of the said Convention provides that the public 
authorities shall not impose any penalty upon ship owners in the event that any control 
document in possession of a passenger is found by public authorities to be inadequate or if, 
for that reason, the passenger is found to be inadmissible. 
11. The Committee has been further informed that the Ministry of Surface Transport 
who were consulted by the Ministry of Home Affairs, have opined that the Government of 
India has to file "differences" in respect of para 3.15 of the Convention for Facilitation of 

3 
International Maritime Traffic, 1965 after the enactment of the proposed legislation. The 
Committee has been apprised that action will be taken for this purpose after the legislation 
has been enacted . 
12. The Committee has then been apprised by the Ministry that the carriers bringing 
passengers by road etc. have not been included in the proposed legislation because in case of 
passengers coming by road or other land transport, the person is physically in the territory of 
the neighbouring country until he is admitted into Indian territory through the immigration 
check-post. If found inadmissible, he is not allowed entry into India at all. Whereas in the 
case of airlines passengers or the passengers brought by ship, the carrier as well as the 
passenges have already entered Indian territory except for the ,technicality of having to pass 
through the immigration and customs barriers. If such passengers are . found to be 
inadmissible for any reason, the authorities are faced with the problem of ensuring their 
removal from Indian territory. 
12.1 The Committee has been informed that the Ministry of Home Affairs consulted the 
Ministry of External Affairs on the point dealt with in the preceeding para and the stand 
taken by the Home Ministry is in accordance with the advice tendered by the latter Ministry. 
13. The salient features of the new legislation are as follows:-
(i) Owners of any carrier would be liable to pay a monetary penalty where the 
competent authority at the point of entry finds that the carrier has brought into 
India any passenger without valid documents for entry. The valid documents 
would be: 
(a) a valid passport with photograph or some other document satisfactorily 
establishing the identity and nationality I citizenship of the passenger; and 
(b) a valid visa, where required, under the relevant immigration laws. 
(ii) The penalty will be a sum of Rs. one lakh for every passenger brought by it 
without relevant documents to be paid to an authority notified by the Central 
Government for the purpose. Provided that the order issued by the competent 
authority imposing financial liability shall be passed after giving the carrier an 
opportunity of being heard. 
(iii) bn failure to pay the penalty the amount may by recovered by seizing, 
detaining or selling:-
(a) the aircraft or the ship; or 
(b) any goods on the ship or aircraft belonging to the carrier. 
(iv) These provisions of the proposed legislation will be without prejudice to the 
liability of the carrier to take back the inadmissible passengers to the point of 
origin or to any other point. The provisions of the proposed legislation will be 
in addition to and not in derogation of the provisions of the Registration of 
Foreigners Act, 1939, the Passport (Entry into India) Act, 1920, Foreigners 
Act, 1946 and of any other enac~ment for the time being in force dealing with 
entry into India of persons without valid travel documents. 
14. The Ministry of Home Affairs has declared in their background Note that once the 
aforesaid proposal is approved and the legislation is enacted, the Ministry of Civil Aviation 
would be requested to file differences with the International Civil Aviation Organisation 
with respect to ~ant 3.37.1 of Annexure 9 to the Chicago Convention on International Civil

Aviation as required under Article 38 of the said Convention. Similarly, the Minsitry of 
Surface Transport would be requested to file differences with the International Maritime 
Organisation with respect to p~ra 3.15 of the Convention of Facilitation of International 
Maritime Traffic, 1965. 
15. The Committee considered the Bill in its sitting held on 19th February, 1999. The 
Special Secretary in the Ministry of Home Affairs made a presentation on the Bill. The 
Committee was informed that in recent years, it had come to the notice of the Central 
Government that large number of passengers had been coming to India without any valid 
travel document. It has also been observed that airlines did not exercise proper check of the 
travel documents of the foreigners coming to India at the time of commencement of the 
journey. That resulted in arrival of passengers fn contravent:on of the provisions of the 
Passport (Entry into India) Act, 1920 and the rules made thereunder. In order to tackle that 
problem, It had become necessary in the national interest to impose a statutory obligation 
on the carriers to properly scrutinise travel documents of the persons before bringing them 
to India, the Special Secretary informed the Committee. 
15.1 With that end in view the Bill was introduced in the Rajya Sabha on 23th 
December, 1998. The subject matter of the Bill falls within the purview of Entry 19 of List-! 
Union List in the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, namely, "Admission into, and 
emigration and expulsion from India; passport and visas", the Committee was informed by 
the representative of the Ministry. 
15.2 The Special Secretary then went on to state that the Passport (Entry into India) 
Act, 1920 had five sections only. Section 3 of the Act provided that the Central Government 
may make rules requiring that persons entering into India shall be in possession of passports 
and for all matters ancilliary or incidental to that purpose. Sub-section (2) of this Section 
provided inter alia that withoblt prejudice to the generality of the foregoing power such rules 
may Prohibit the entry into India or any part thereof of any person who has not in his 
possession a passport issued to him. The 'said sub-section (2) also provided for the exemption 
either absolutely or on any condition of any person or class of persons from any provision of 
such rule. The Act further provided that the rules made under Section 3 may provide that 
any contravention thereof or of any order issued under the authority of any such rule shall 
be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three months or with fine 
or with both. In this context, the representative of the Minsitry informed the Committee that 
a proposal to amend the Passport (Entry into India) Act, 1920 was under the consideration 
of the Ministry. It was proposed to make the punishment under this Act more rigorous. 
15.3 The representative of the Ministry also informed the Committee that there were 65 
immigration checkposts; 30 of them were land checkposts; 17 at the airports; and 18 
checkposts were located at seaports. 
15.4 The representative of the Ministry further informed the Committee that the 
present Bill related only to those inadmissible passengers who come by air or sea and it did 
not cover passengers coming by land i.e., by road or other modes of transport. 
15.5 The Special Secretary went on to inform the Committee that 1n the year 1997, the 
country had received as many as 24.92 lakhs foreign visitors. 82.91% of these visitors had 
come to India by air, i.e. roughly 83% ; 15.5% visitors came by land route; and only 1.5% 
visitors came by sea routes. He then apprised the Committee . of the statistics for the years 
1997 and 1998 of inadmissible passengers detected at th~ five international airports at Delhi, 
Mumbai, Calcutta, Chennai and Thiruvananthapuram: 
15.6 The Special Secretary apprised the Committee that it had been proposed .to impose 
761 RS F-3-B 

, 
5 
a penalty of Rs. one lakh per person on the carrier who failed to pedorm the statutory 
obligation imposed on it under the proposed legislation. He further informed that the power 
to impose penalty was proposed to be given to the concerned Civil Authority appointed 
under the Foreigners Order, 1948, made under the Foreigners, Act, 1946, or any other 
officer notified by the Central Government. The representative of the Ministry added that 
an appeal against the order of the Civil Authority or any other officer notified would lie to 
the Joint Secretary in the Ministry of Home Affairs responsible for dealing with the 
foreigners. The Bill further provided that in the event of failure to pay the penalty, the 
amount would be recovered by seizing, detaining or selling the aircraft or ship, or any goods 
on the ship or aircraft belonging to the carrier, the representative of the Ministry informed 
the Committee. . 
16. Members raised I made the following issues I queries to the representatives of the 
Ministry:-
(a) Figures of the last five years, year-wise, airport-wise and seaport-wise Of the 
number of inadmissible passengers who had managed to come through all the 
airports and seaports in the country having immegration counters. 
(b) Modus operandi of the persons who had entered the country without valid 
documents through the airports and seaports and their nationaJitie!t', year-wise.-
(c) Names of the airliners and sealiners involved in bringing inadmissible persons 
during the last five years. 
(d) Expenditure incurred by the Government during the last five years on account 
of such inadmissible persons who had entered the COl,lntry. 
(e) Inadequacy of the penalty proposed to be imposed on the carriers and the ne~d 
for enhancing the same. 
(f) Need for bringing the road carriers within the purview of the Bill and made 
liable like air carriers and ship carriers. 
(g) Mandatory checking of travel du-:uments by all the airliners and shipliners 
before allowing the passengers to board the aircrafts or the ships. 
(h) Need for comprehensively and explicitly defining 'Carriers' in Clause 2 so as to 
cover the chartered aircrafts I ~hips and the carriers owned by the State in 
order to determine the onus of liability in case of a dispute. 
17. The representative of the Mnistry replied ~o some of th~ issues I queries. The chair 
also clarified the position in regard to the issues/ queries. As regards the queries at (a) to 
(d) supra the Committee directed the representative oi the Ministry _ to furnish written 
responses thereto. · 
18. With regard to the issue raised about inclusion of road carriers within the ambit of 
the Bill, it was explained to the committee that in the scheme of the present Bill it would not 
be feasible to make the road carriers liable in respect of passengers brought. by them into 
India in contravention of the provisions of the relevant Jaws and · rules or orders made 
thereunder. After· some discussion, the committee decided that while the present Bill may be 
cleared, it may recommend to the Government to bring in a separate Bill to make the road 
carriers liable in respect of passengers brought by them into India in contravention of the 
relevant laws and rules or orders made thereunder, with a view to put an effective check on 
infiltration through the various land routes. 

6 
19. During the course of evidence of the Special Secretary of Ministry of liome Affairs 
before the Committee on 19th February, 1999 certain specific questions were posed to him 
for written replies. The Ministry vide their communications dated 23rd and 26th February, 
1999, has furnished the replies thereto. The questions and Ministry's replies thereto are 
reproduced below: 
Question: 
(a) figures of the last five yc;trs, year-wise, airport-wise and seaport-wise of the number

The Passport (Ent ry into India) Rules, 1950 made under the Passport (Entry into India)

valid passport confirming to the cond ition s provided in rule 5 of the said rules. In recent 
years, it has come to the notice of the Central Government that large number of p~ssengers 
come to Indi a without any valid travel document. It has also been observed that airlines do 
not exercise proper check of the travel docum ents of the foreigners coming to India at the 
time of commencement of the journey . This result in arrival of passengers in contravention 
of the provi sions of the Passport (Entry into India) Act, 1920 and the rules made thereunder 
which causes not only harassment to the passengers but also unnecessary burden on the 
Government which can be easily avoided. In order to tackle this problem, it has become 
necessary to impose a statuto ry obligation on the carriers to properly scrutinise travel 
documents of the persons before bringing them..to India. It is proposed to impose a penalty 
of Rs. 1 lttkh per person on the carrier who fails to perform the statutory obligation imposed 
on it under the proposed legislation. Further, the power to impose penalty is proposed to be 
given to the concerned Civil Authority appo inted under the Foreigners Order , 1948 made 
under the Foreigners Act, 1946 or any other officer notified by the Central Government. An 
appeal against the order of the Civil Authority or any other officer notified shall lie to the 
Joint Secretary in the Ministry of H ome Affairs responsible for dealing with the foreigners.

REPORT
 The Ministry of Home Affairs has been entrusted broadly with the following functions;
(a) To deal with all matters relating to internal security;
(b) To deal with all matters relating to Centre-State relations and Inter-State relations;
(c ) Implementation of the provisions of the Constitution relating to Official Language
and the provisions of the Official Language Act, 1963;
(d) To discharge certain basic functions like notification of assumption of office by the
President and the Vice-President; notification of appointment of the Prime Minister and
other Ministers; notification of appointment, resignation and removal of governors and
Lt. Governors, appointment of Lt. Governors, Chief Commissioners and Administrative
Officers in Union Territories;
(e) To deal with matters like citizenship and naturalisation, census of population,
National Anthem, National Flag, etc.; and
(f) To deal with all constitutional provisions with respect to the State of Jammu and
Kashmir and all other matters relating to the State of Jammu and Kashmir excluding
those with which the Ministry of External Affairs is concerned.
2. To discharge the above functions, the Ministry has been divided into five Departments:-
(i) Department of Internal Security – to deal with Police, Law and Order and
rehabilitation;
(ii) Department of States – to deal with Centre-State relations, inter-State relations,
Union Territories and Freedom Fighters’ Pension;
(iii) Department of Official Language – to deal with the implementation of the
provisions of Constitution relating to Official Language and provisions of the Official
Language Act, 1963;
(iv) Department of Home – to deal with notification of assumption of office by the
President and Vice-President, notification of appointment of the Prime Minister and
other Ministers, etc.; and
(v) Department of Jammu and Kashmir Affairs – to deal with all constitutional
provisions with respect to the State of Jammu and Kashmir and all other matters
relating to the State of Jammu and Kashmir excluding those with which the Ministry of
External Affairs is concerned.
3. On behalf of the Ministry, ten Demands have been presented to Parliament.

Home Affairs; (ii) Demand No 43 – Cabinet; (iii) Demand No. 44 – Police; (iv) Demand No. 45 – Other
Expenditure of the Ministry of Home Affairs; and (v) Demand No. 46 – Transfers to Union Territory

rd Report on the Demands for Grants (1998-99) of the Ministry.

fighting militancy which was enhanced to Rs.273 crs. in 1998-99 has further been raised to Rs.295
crores in B.E. 1999-2000; monthly allowances to the families which migrated from the State in the wake
of militancy there has been raised to Rs.2500 from Rs.1500 w.e.f. April, 1999 and a three year Action
Plan to tackle militancy in the State has been formulated. In respect of Action Plan for the State he
enumerated the various features of the Plan which included –
(i) Curbing infiltration
(ii) Countering militancy in hinterland
(iii) Protection of minorities
(iv) Greater interaction with border population
(v) Enhancing intelligence capabilities
(vi) Countering overground secessionist forces
(vii) Greater functional integration between Security Forces, Police & Intelligence
agencies.
(viii) Technology upgradation for security forces & J&K Police; and
(ix) Constitution of Operations & Intelligence Groups.

making provision for rehabilitation & maintenance of migrants in Assam, Manipur and Tripura and relaxion of

the country. He stated that during last year Ministry had taken initiatives in anticipating these problems and
preventing/containing them. These initiatives have payed positive results. The overall internal security
situation in the country has shown some improvement in the last year over the previous year, he claimed.

20. Regarding the State of Jammu & Kashmir, the Secretary apprised the Committee that there was a
sense of optimism in the State. The number of incidents in the year 1998 has declined as compared to
those in the year 1997. There had also been a decline in the number of persons killed in 1998 as
compared to those killed in 1997. The number of militants killed in the year 1998 was higher as against
those killed in the previous year. The situation in Srinagar has vastly improved. In 1998, nearly one lakh
tourists visited the State as against 7,000 the previous year. Nearly 1.5 lakh pilgrims participated in the
Amarnath Yatra in 1998. The Republic Day functions were held throughout the State with great pomp
and grandeur and these were free from violence. The local recruitment of militant outfits for exfiltration
or for sabotaging the market places or other installations within the State has sharply declined. The
local people are coming forward to support and cooperate with the security forces he added. However,
the situation is still difficult in certain other ways. The militants are attacking Hindu minorities in isolated
places and are trying to extend the garb of militancy to other areas of the State. There is nothing to
indicate that Pakistan Army or the Pak ISI have decided to follow the spirit of the Lahore Declaration or
the spirit that has been unanimously sponsored and supported by Members of Parliament in India and
Members of various sections within Pakistan itself. The Secretary further apprised the Committee that
the Government of India was extending all assistance to modernise the State Police Force. There was
better coordination between the Security Forces and the State Police. Everything was being done to
keep the morale of the State Police very high. The Secretary went on to state that 12,855 Special
Police Officers had been appointed and Village Defence Committees had been set up in the State. He
further stated that the people of the State were tired and disillusioned with militancy. It was therefore,
necessary to accelerate the pace of development process so that they may benefit from the fruits of
democracy and development in the State. The Ministry has been impressing upon the State
Government to involve local people in development programmes he stated. There was also a need to
further strengthen the forces in the State. The proposed Panchayat Elections which were going to take
place this year after a gap of more than 20 years would be a landmark, he added. They would facilitate
accelerating the pace of rural employment generation and infrastructure development work in villages
like construction of roads, construction of schools, irrigation channels, health centres, handlooms and
so on.
21. Regarding insurgency situation in North East, the Secretary submitted that the overall situation in the
North East had shown signs of improvement in certain areas. There has been a decline in the total number of
killings as also the total number of incidents in the affected States. In some of these States, the insurgency
has deteriorated in terms of ideology but it persists in some kind of a cottage industry for kidnapping and
demanding money by way of extortions purely for private gains, he added. In Nagaland, the cease-fire has by
and large helped the process of peace. Some progress has been made with regard to talks between the
Government and the NSCN(IM) leadership. The other groups are also willing to have talks with the
Government of India. However, the level of extortion by these outlawed elements has increased and has
created hardships to officials, businessmen and general public, and this has also meant the continued
diversion of development funds to the insurgent outfits. The situation in Tripura has not improved. It is mainly
directed by outlawed militant groups in the form of attacks on non-tribals, lootings, extortions, kidnappings,
ransoms, highway robberies and attacks on trucks and vehicles. The Government of India is very keen for
initiating dialogue between the insurgent tribals and the Government, the Secretary stated. But, this is
possible when the security forces are in command of the situation and the insurgent elements come to
realise that there is no other way but to go for dialogue, he stated. In Manipur, the overall violence involving
the Naga and Kuki extremists as also ethnic groups has shown a slight decline. Peace has been attained in
the State as a result of signing of an MOU between Kukis and Zomis on 26
th March, 1998. In Assam, the
ULFA menace is on the decline, but the tensions on account of the role of National Democratic Front of
Bodoland (NDFB) and Bodo Liberation Tiger (BLT) continues. There have been frequent clashes last year
between the Bodos and the Santhals which resulted in the killing of 191 persons. In Mizoram clashes have
taken placed between the Mizos and Reangs, resulting in exodus of large number of Reangs from Mizoram

Fifty Fourth Report-Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/54_rep.html[30-06-2016 17:34:25]
to Tripura and Assam. These Reangs need to be repatriated back to Mizoram, the Secretary stated.
22. With regard to the menace of Left Wing extremism in the States of Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya
Pradesh, Maharashtra and Orissa, the Secretary stated that to tackle the problem effectively a `Coordination
Centre’ had been set up which comprises Union Home Secretary as its Chairman and the Chief Secretaries
and Directors General of the concerned States as members. Under this scheme, Action Plans have been
prepared by each State and now there is greater degree of intelligence co-ordination between them. The
setting up of this `Co-ordination Centre’ has yielded positive results, he stated.
23. On the communal front, the Secretary apprised the Committee that the situation was vitiated on account
of tension between Hindus and Christians. There were incidents directed against the Christian community in
Jhabua in M.P., and Dang, Surat and Valsad in Gujarat. He stated that the Government of India had taken
measures to deal with the situation appropriately and the State Governments had been impressed upon to
make the District Magistrates and the Superintendents of Police personally responsible for any incident of
such nature. A commission of inquiry, headed by a judge of the Supreme Court had been instituted after the
grusome murder of Dr. Graham Stewart Stains and his two minor children, he stated.
24. On the caste front, the Secretary stated that three States namely, Tamil Nadu, Bihar and U.P. are facing
difficulties.
25. The Secretary also informed the Committee that the Ministry had recently initiated action for raising of 26
Bns. of B.S.F., I.T.B.P. and CRPF. He expressed his concern over persistent dependance on Army in dealing
with militancy and insurgency in some parts of the country.
26. Regarding modernisation of the Police Forces in the North Eastern region, the Secretary stated that it
had been decided by the Chief Secretaries and DGPs of the North-Eastern States to approach their
respective State Government so that they could earmark 10% of the total budget or 20% of the non-plan
budget for police every year. 25 percent of that money would be earmarked for police stations, housing and
matter related thereto. There was a need to take similar steps in Jammu and Kashmir, he stated.
27. The Secretary also informed the Committee that this year seven India Reserve Bns., two each for Bihar,
J&K and Tamil Nadu and one for Nagaland had been sanctioned. He further stated that while the ex-gratia
payment in case of death of CPMF personnel in action against enemy had been raised from Rs.2 lakh to
Rs.7.5 lakh, it had been raised from Rs.2 lakh to Rs.5 lakh in case of death in act of violence by terrorists or
anti-social elements.
28. Regarding fencing/flood lighting/construction of roads on the Indo-Pak and Indo-Bangaldesh border, the
Secretary informed that while work on the former had made good progress, it was somewhat slow in case of
the latter. He stated that the Ministry was endeavouring to ensure that the first phase of this Project be
completed by year 2001 and the second be completed by the year 2007. He stated that completion of this
project will greatly help in checking illegal influx of Bangaldesh nationals into India.
29. The Secretary, thereafter, informed the Committee about proposal of the Ministry for introduction of a
`National Identity Card’ for every Indian citizen. A `Person of Indian Origin Card’ (PIO Card) is also being
introduced by the Ministry which will give the card holder freedom from taking visa for a period of six months
at a time. It would also give them certain educational, cultural and property rights, he submitted.
Activities of Pak ISI on Indo-Nepal Border
30. The Committee in its 43rd Report on the Demands for Grants 1998-99 of the Ministry had expressed its
concern over the increasing activities of Pak ISI on the Indo-Nepal Border in recent time. It had noted that not
only funds flow through this route but also unwanted elements were intruding through this route. The

Fifty Fourth Report-Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/54_rep.html[30-06-2016 17:34:25]
Committee had urged the Government to take appropriate action so that the onging disruptive activities of ISI
could be curbed. The Committee had also recommended that patrolling on the borders also needed to be
intensified.
31. The Ministry in its Action Taken Note on the observation of the Committee has apprised that there is
excellent cooperation between various agencies in India and Nepal and the two countries have constituted a
Joint Working Group for monitoring the activities of terrorists and other undesirable elements across the Indo-
Nepal Border. Further, the Government of Uttar Pradesh has constituted a Special Task Force headed by an
Additional Director-General of Police to maintain special vigil on its border with Nepal. This Task Force has
been introduced with the objective of preventing smuggling of consumer goods, weapons, narcotic
substances, explosive substances and keeping an eye on controlling trans-border activities of anti-national
elements, illegal and anti-national organisations and institutions and also to collect operational intelligence
and launch various operations and drives in this regard. This Task Force has proved effective to some extent
in curtailing illegal and undesirable activities there. The Ministry has also submitted that our relationship with
His Majesty’s Government of Nepal was based on Treaty of Peace & Friendship which was signed on 31
st
July, 1950. The Treaty provides for free movement of citizens of both the countries through the Indo-Nepal
Border. The major portion of the border runs along the densely populated Terrai area, a region where the
trans-border population is linked with shared history, language, culture, religion and economic interest.
Keeping this in view, no Central Forces have been deployed on the Indo-Nepal border. Owing to the said
provisions in the Treaty and absence of any physical barriers, the control on Indo-Nepal border is, therefore,
exercised through the State Police.
32. In reply to a query whether the Treaty of Peace and Friendship with Nepal bars Government of India in
deploying Para Military Forces on its border with that country, the Ministry has replied that there was no bar
for such deployment under the Treaty. However, in view of India’s traditional friendly and special relationship
with Nepal, it was not considered advisable to deploy CPMFs on the borders with it. The Committee was also
apprised that the activities of certain agencies on the border, which were inimical to interests of the country
had been brought to the Notice of Government of Nepal and they had been requested to make efforts to
discourage such activities. Such diplomatic efforts would continue to be made. The Government of India has
also separately advised the State Governments of U.P., Bihar, West Bengal and Sikkim to upgrade policing
along the Indo-Nepal Border. The Government of India has assured financial assistance to these States in
this task.
33. The Committee notes the diplomatic efforts being made by the Government of India with
Government of Nepal in sensitizing that country about the evil designs of Pak ISI directed towards
India and for taking necessary action in the matter. The Committee also notes the efforts being made
by Government of U.P. in constituting a Special Task Force to curb the illegal and anti India activities
on its border with Nepal. The Committee also appreciates the stand of Government of India in
extending financial support to the States bordering Nepal in upgrading policing along the borders.
The Committee, however, does not feel convinced with the reason put forth by the Ministry in not
deploying Central Forces along the Indo-Nepal Borders. The Committee acknowledges the
importance of India’s friendly and special relationship with Nepal and feels that they need to be
strengthened further. But, it does not feel convinced that only because of this friendship we should
hesitate in deploying our Central Forces to assist the Police Forces of States bordering Nepal in their
effort to check activities of elements which are inimical to the interests of our country. It strongly
feels that our friendship with Nepal should not become our weakness in not feeling confident for
deploying our forces on the borders and thereby to be exploited by others for anti-India activities .
The Committee, therefore, urges upon the Government to examine this issue from different angles
with an objective to make the border completely sealed for those who do not want to see India strong
and united.

th Pay Commission’s report, a cadre restructuring exercise is being undertaken and

rd Report, there has been no improvement in the filling-up of

Increasing dependence of State Governments on CPMFs
46. It has been observed that of late the dependence of State Governments, all over, on the Central Para
Military Forces in dealing with difficult situations arising on the law and order front has increased significantly.
The Committee while considering Demands for Grants of the Ministry deliberated on this issue and noted that
though the subjects `Public Order’ and `Police’ falls under entry `1’ and `2’ respectively, of the `State List’ of
the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, making thereby the State Governments primarily responsible for
maintenance of the law and order in their respective States, yet, it has been experienced in recent years that
their dependence on CPMFs for maintaining general law and order in their respective States has increased
significantly. Whenever any incident of serious proportion takes place, the concerned State Government take
the stand that the incident occurred because of inadequate presence of the Para Military Forces. The CPMFs
are called by the State Governments even for holding elections to the Panchayats or local bodies.
47. This changing trend over the years has given rise to a situation of dichotomy wherein while on the one
hand the State Governments tend to demand more and more power and autonomy, on the other hand they
appear to be prepared very inadequately to perform their one of the most primary duties of maintaining law
and order and peace and normalcy in their respective State. On every incident of minor or major proportion
they tend to seek help of the central police forces, which only throw poor light on the preparedness of their
police forces in dealing with adverse situations. Maintenance of law and order being the primary
responsibility of the State Governments, every effort should have to be made by them to strengthen and
modernise their respective police force. It becomes more necessary because of the hard truth that even if
union government provide adequate number of central forces to the State having problem on the law and
order front, they can be effective only to a certain extent and can not root out the problem. This limitation of
central forces is because of the fact that they do not have policing powers and they have to perform under
civil authorities. Therefore, under the present situation only the State police, for having policing powers can
be effective if it is adequately trained and modernised.
48. In this context, the Committee has also noted that the increasing dependence of State Governments on
CPMFs has also put these forces under lot of stress and strain. Due to persistent demands of State
Governments these forces are over deployed which leave no room for the training, rest and recuperation of
their personnel. The excessive commitment of forces over a prolonged period also adversely affect the
welfare activities needed to take care of their physical and psychological needs. This extensive deployment
also affect their efficiency and operational preparedness.
49. The Committee has noted from the papers/documents submitted to it that during the years 1995, 1996,
1997, 1998 and 1999 (upto 15.3.1999), the deployment of CRPF was to the extent of 94%, 94.3%, 98.2%,
97.66% and 98% respectively. The Rapid Action Force (RAF) which was originally raised out of CRPF to
deal with the problems of communal violence, has also been over deployed. This heavy dependence of State
Governments on the central forces have also resulted in aberration of their duties. The increasing
dependence has also compelled central forces to withdraw Bns. from their primary roles and deploy them to
perform duties which are of secondary nature in its charter of duties. In this regard the Committee has noted
with concern that the Border Security Force (BSF) whose primary role is to guard our borders with the
neighbouring countries, has withdrawn its 21 Bns. from borders and has put them on internal security duty to
fulfil the requirements of State Governments. Not only this, but 19 out of 22 Reserve Bns. of BSF have also
been deployed on internal security duty. This diversion of BSF Bns. from its primary role has got telling

Fifty Fourth Report-Home Affairs

effects on the training, standard of efficiency, time for rest/relief/recupertion and availability of reserves.
50. In this context the Committee has observed that the Government of India is providing assistance to the
State Governments from quite some time in the form of cash as well as kind. Under the scheme of
modernisation of Police Forces, the Central Government is providing financial assistance to State
Governments since 1969-70 in the form of 50% grant-in-aid and 50% loan to be utilised for expenditure of
non-recurring nature on purchase of vehicles, wireless equipments, computers and other sophisticated
equipment. The Committee is pleased to note that in pursuance of the recommendation of the Committee,

increased component of allocation i.e. Rs.50 crores is proposed to be kept for release as "Special
