R E P O R T
           I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs, having been
authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this Sixty-fourth Report of the Committee,
relating to the Companies (Second Amendment) Bill, 1999¨
.
2.        In pursuance of the Rules relating to Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees, the Chairman,
Rajya Sabha  referred©
 the Companies (Second Amendment) Bill, 1999,  as introduced in the Rajya Sabha on  23
December, 1999 and pending therein, to the Committee for examination  and report.
3.0      The Statement of  Objects and Reasons of the Bill states that the Government introduced a comprehensive
Companies Bill, 1997 in Rajya Sabha on 14 August, 1997 and the same was  referred to Standing Committee of
Parliament for examination and report thereon.  As the process of  examination was not yet over and Government
considered it desirable that some more important changes in the Companies  Act, 1956 were brought about in order to
provide immediately certain measures for good corporate governance and for protection of investors,   the present Bill
was introduced.
3.1      This Bill mainly seeks to ensure better corporate governance, transparency in working of companies and also

64th report of committee on Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/64threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:35:37]
ensure more effective enforcement by enhancing the penalty/punishment for contravention so as to ensure better
compliance of the provisions of the Companies Act, 1956.
4.0      The present Committee in its first meeting held on 18 January, 2000, reviewed the status of the Bills/subjects
pending consideration of the Committee and noted that  a new Bill, namely, the Companies (Second Amendment) Bill,
1999, had been referred to it for examination and report.
4.1      The Committee, in its meeting held on 7 February, 2000, decided that it may  take up the Companies (Second
Amendment) Bill, 1999, for examination along with the Companies Bill, 1997, referred to it earlier, after the Budget
Session, as it would take considerable time to dispose them of.
5.        After the Budget Session was over, the Committee again  reviewed the position of the Bills pending before it, at
its meeting held on 17 May, 2000, and decided to give top priority to pending legislation and dispose them of in the
order of priority assigned by it. The Committee decided to take up the two Bills relating to the Company Law first
followed by other Bills, in the four rounds of sittings – 29, 30 & 31 May and 1 & 2 June,  in the first round; 12, 13 & 14
June  in the second round; 26, 27, 28, 29 & 30 June  in the third round;  and 10, 11, 12, 13 & 14 July, 2000 in the fourth
round. 
6.0      In its meeting held on 30May, 2000, the Committee heard the Secretary of the Department of Company Affairs
on the salient features of the two Bills, namely, the Companies Bill, 1997 and the Companies (Second Amendment)
Bill, 1999. 
6.1      The Secretary, Department of Company Affairs made a detailed presentation on the two Bills in the said meeting
of the Committee.  Following are the salient points of his presentation :-
º          As on 1
st January 2000 a total number of 5,32,580 companies were at work and their estimated paid up capital
was Rs. 2,72,865 crores. 
__________________________________________________________________________
2
 
º          India was in the forefront of Company Law.  The first Companies Act was enacted in 1913.  Certain amendments
were passed in 1936 and 1951.  The present Act was enacted  in 1956 as a result of Industrial Policy Resolution and
federalisation of corporate laws in different States, pursuant  to the integration of princely states in the Union of India.
º          The 1956 Act has been amended 17 times, in the years  1960, 1962, 1963, 1964 (twice), 1965, 1966 (twice),
1967, 1969, 1971, 1974, 1977, 1985, 1988, 1996 and 1999. 
º          There is an imperative need to further amend the Companies Act 1956 pursuant to the New Economic Policy
announced in 1991, rapid economic developments taking place globally, liberalisation of economies, access to world
market, WTO etc.
º          Further amendments to the law are necessary to facilitate healthy growth of Indian Corporate Sector under
liberalised and highly competitive environment.  Greater flexibility, transparency, disclosure, efficient enforcement,
tougher penalties, better investors’ protection are the felt needs of the time.
º          The requirements of liberalisation,  deregulation, simplification, changing economic scenario and international
corporate market make it necessary to amend the Company Law, lest our country would be lagging behind in terms of
growth, flexibility and international competitiveness in the globalised world. 
º          U.K., USA, Australia, Canada, EU etc. had already updated their Company Law. 
º          A Working Group was appointed by the Government on 5 August, 1996 which had  members  who were experts
in the fields of  law, economics and company affairs.  The Group  went into the entire gamut of the corporate laws and
submitted a comprehensive report in February 1997.  The said report was placed on the Table of both the Houses of
Parliament.  The comprehensive Companies Bill, 1997 is in essence the reflection of the consensus  in the report of the
Working Group. 
º          While drafting the Bill, the Department of Company Affairs took the help of the Reports  of  various 
Committees  which  went  into  the  concept  of  good   corporate governance, namely, the Cadbury Committee, the
Greenbury Committee, the Blue Ribbon Committee, the Organisation of Economic Cooperation  Development Code on
Corporate Governance (OECD) , besides the report of CII on Desirable Corporate Governance – A Code and Kumar
Mangalam Birla Committee on Corporate Governance.  The underlying themes of all these Reports are  transparency,
openness, disclosure, accountability etc.   The main principle that pervades corporate governance is the control of the
business by shareholders, reliable public reporting, avoidance of exclusive powers at the top, balanced board
composition, strong board of directors, strong audit process, assessment of risk and involvement of all  the shareholders
etc. 

64th report of committee on Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/64threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:35:37]
º          After the introduction of the comprehensive Companies Bill, 1997, certain provisions of the said Bill were
incorporated in the Companies Amendment Act, 1999 which came into force w.e.f. 1.4.1999, first through an ordinance
and thereafter the ordinance was replaced by the Act of Parliament. 
3
º          Following are the salient features of the Companies Amendment Act, 1999 :-
           •          To allow companies to buy-back their shares;
           •          Provide for nomination facility to investors;
           •          Setting up of Investor Education and Protection Fund.
•          To allow companies to issue sweat equity in lieu of intellectual property to employees and directors;
•          Permit inter-corporate investment without prior approval of Central Government;
•          Constitution of National Advisory Committee on Accounting Standards.
º          After having implemented some of the features of the 1997 Bill in the First Amendment Act of 1999, some other
important features of the said Bill  have been included in the Companies (Second Amendment) Bill, 1999. 
º          Early passage of the Companies (Second Amendment) Bill, 1999 is necessary for the following reasons :-
Provide Investor friendly environment and attract investment in Indian Capital Market.
It will prepare ground for Indian companies to excel in a globally competitive market.
Create wealth for the shareholder and the Nation.
Promote good corporate governance.
7.        The Secretary, Department of Company Affairs then made an audio-visual presentation on the salient features of
the Companies (Second Amendment) Bill, 1999.  The  following are the highlights from his presentation : -
To provide transparency and good corporate governance;
Investors Protection;
Stringent penalties;
Repeal of redundant provisions;
Investors Protection Measures
Dividend including Interim Dividend to be paid within 30 days.
Effective curb on changing registered office frequently.
Offer of securities to more than 50 persons in financial year to be treated as public offer.
Small shareholders right to be represented on the board.
Corporate Governance
Minimum paid-up capital Rs. 1 lac for private companies, Rs. 5 lacs for public limited companies to prevent misuse of
facility of limited liability companies.
Capital market related provisions to be administered by Securities & Exchange Board of India (SEBI).
Director’s report to include a Director’s Responsibility Statement.
4
Public listed companies with paid-up capital of Rs.5 crores to set up Audit Committee.
Companies with paid-up capital of Rs. 10 lakhs or more to obtain a Secretarial Compliance Certificate .
Introduction of Postal Ballot for certain important matters which are crucial to good corporate governance.
 Appointment of Auditors in the Government Companies directly by Comptroller and Auditor General of India and
fixation of their remuneration by the shareholders in the Annual General Meeting.
Directors to be disqualified to be appointed as Directors in other public companies in case of non-filing of Annual
Returns and Annual Accounts for a continuous period of 3 years and non-payment of deposits etc. on maturity.
A person can not be Director in more than 15 companies .
Security holder of a company not to be appointed as Auditor of that company.
Stringent Penalties
Certain offences relating to deposits made cognizable.
Fines and Penalties enhanced by 10 times.
Repeal of Redundant provisions
Managing Agents, Secretaries and Treasures.
Deemed public companies.
Public Trustee.
8.        Having regard to the special importance of the two Bills, the Committee decided to invite views/suggestions in
the form of memoranda from the individuals/organisations /institutions etc. interested in the subject matter of the Bills.
Accordingly, advertisements were published through DAVP in all the major national dailies and vernacular newspapers

all over the country. The Doordarshan’s national network had repeatedly telecast the contents of the press release in
prime time slots inviting suggestions from individuals/institutions/organisations on the provisions of the two Bills. 
9.        The Committee also invited suggestion/views of the major Chambers of Commerce and Industries, professional
bodies, such as, Confederation of Indian Industry (CII); Associated Chambers of Commerce and Industry of India
(ASSOCHAM); Punjab, Haryana and Delhi (PHD) Chamber of Commerce and Industry, Federation of Indian
Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI), Institute of  Company Secretaries of India (ICSI), Institute of Cost and
Works Accountants of India (ICWAI), Institute of  Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI), Securities & Exchange
Board of India (SEBI), Industrial Credit & Investment Corporation of India Limited (ICICI), Bombay Chamber of
Commerce & Industry (BCCI), Steel  Authority of India Limited (SAIL), the Council of EU Chamber of  Commerce in
India and the Associated Cement Companies Limited (ACC)  on the amendments sought to be effected in the
Companies Act through these Bill.
10.      In all 56 memoranda containing comments and suggestions on the provisions of these two Bills were received by
the Committee from various organisations, associations and individuals etc. (see list of organisations/individuals etc. at
Appendix – A).
5
11.0     The Committee heard the views of various Chambers of Commerce, professional bodies and other organisations
(vide list at Appendix ‘B’) in its sitting spread over four days i.e. on 1,2,13 & 14 June, 2000 as per schedule given
below :-
Date of  Meeting                            Names of  Organisations heard

Industries and ICSI

4.        14-6-2000                            FICCI
11.1     A summary of  the suggestions/views received from different organisations and the comments of the Department
of Company Affairs thereon have been placed at Appendix ‘C’.
11.2     In course of evidence of the aforesaid organisations, a large number of suggestions/amendments were placed
before the Committee for its consideration. However, the major thrust of the suggestions/amendments may be
categorised into following five areas:-
Change of Registered Office of a Company – The proposed Section 17A which requires permission from  the
Regional Director even for shifting the Registered Office from one place to another will cause difficulties to the
Companies.It should be clarified that the provision of this clause should apply only in the case of change of Registered
Office of a Company from the jurisdiction of  one ROC to another ROC in the same State.
Postal Ballot -  It was contended that this system would be expensive, time consuming and un-implementable.
Offences  with regard to small depositors proposed to be made cognisable – This provision was rather drastic and
needed deletion.  Only Managing Director, Whole Time Director and promoters should be held responsible.  Only such
offences as are committed knowingly, willfully or with fraudulent intention should be severely punished.
Audit Committee – It was contended that since the Audit Committee of the Board of Directors was a creation thereof,
it would not be proper  to make its recommendations binding on its creator i.e. the Board of Directors.
Representation of small shareholders on the Board of Directors -     The provision for appointment of Directors on
the Board of Directors to represent the small investors may jeopardise  the homogeneity and integrated character of the
Board of Directors.
12.      The Committee would like to place on record its appreciation of the Secretary, Department of Company Affairs
and his team of officers for rendering valuable assistance to it from time to time in the course of consideration of the
Bills. The Committee would also like to thank the officers of the Department of Legal Affairs and the Legislative
Department for the assistance provided to it during the consideration of the Bills. The Committee also wishes to express
its sincere thanks to all the organisations/ persons who either appeared before it and/ or sent their valuable
suggestions/views on the provisions of these two Bills.  A special word of thanks is due to ICAI who helped the
Secretariat in compiling summaries of suggestions received from different quarters on the Bills.
6
13.      The Committee considered various papers and memoranda placed before it, the views expressed by the witnesses
on the Bills and the Government’s comments thereon.
14.      At its sitting held on the  27 June, 2000 the Committee considered the Bill clause-by-clause.
The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its sitting held on  11 July, 2000.

16.      The observations of the Committee with regard to the principal changes proposed in the Bill are given below :-
CLAUSE 2
16.1     Clause 2(14A) provides for  the definition of  dividend viz. ‘(14A) “dividend” includes any interim dividend’.
SUGGESTIONS
Dividend amount should be transferred to a separate Bank account within 5 days from the date of Annual General
Meeting.  This amount  cannot be utilised for any other purpose.
It should be clarified whether interim dividend has to be declared in Annual General Meeting.
Payment of interim dividend should be in compliance of sections 205, 205A, 205D, 206, 206A and 207. No interim
dividend should  be paid in cash.  The dividend should be paid by cheque/dividend warrant.
Remittance of dividend even electronically is not possible unless stock exchange agree for notice of 15 days for book
closure etc.
Time limit of 90 days be prescribed for payment of interim dividend.
GOVERNMENT’S VIEWS
This suggestion may be accepted.
An explanation below 2(14A) may be added to clarify that Company’s Board of Directors may declare interim dividend
and provisions of section 205, 205A, 205C, 206, 206A and 207 shall apply to any interim dividend. The dividend should

19.0     The Committee notes that the nomenclature of the Companies Act  was framed almost a century ago.  In
the present day corporate parlance, corporate governance is being talked about.  In this context, the Committee
feels that the Government may deliberate on the need for changing the nomenclature of the Companies Act to
“Corporate Governance Act” because the whole purpose of the amendments sought to be made through the two
Bills  and those already enforced  by the Companies Amendment Act, 1999, is to ensure that there is 
transparency, efficiency, competitiveness  and effectiveness which are the hallmarks of good corporate

Clauses” appended to the Bill were  insufficient, incomplete and examples of  paraphrasing without being able to

help to the Members while considering the Bills either in Parliament or in Committees.  It was further pointed
out that “Notes on Clauses”  were  being prepared almost in a routine and ritualistic  manner.

and the Legislative Department to take note of the objections raised and take corrective steps in future.

and helpful to the Members.

g       The Committee notes that the nomenclature of the Companies Act  was framed almost a century ago.  In
the present day corporate parlance, corporate governance is being talked about.  In this context, the Committee
feels that the Government may deliberate on the need for changing the nomenclature of the

made through the two Bills  and those already enforced  by the Companies Amendment Act, 1999, is to ensure

corporate governance.  The Committee, thus, feels that it would be timely and appropriate if the essence of

appended to the Bill were  insufficient, incomplete and examples of  paraphrasing without being able to convey the
purport of the amendments and the rationale behind them.  Such deficient notes were of hardly any help to the Members
while considering the Bills either in Parliament or in Committees.  It was further pointed out that “Notes on Clauses” 
were  being prepared almost in a routine and ritualistic  manner.
After  some discussion,  the Committee  directed the representatives  of  theDepartment  of Company Affairs and the
Legislative Department to take note of the objections raised and take corrective steps in future.
19.2     The Committee hoped that in future the “Notes on Clauses”    appended to the Bills  would be meaningful and
helpful to the Members.

Clause 16-New Section 55A-Views of the Department of Company Affairs:
           Section  55A needs substantial  amendments to clarify the doubts expressed and issues raised by Securities &
Exchange  Board of India.  The power to administer  Company Law is conferred upon Department of Company Affairs
by allocation of business  rules.  Intention of 55A is not  to create a separate Companies Act exclusively  applicable  to
Public Listed Companies.  The function of Registering  Prospectus (Section 60), Statement in lieu of Prospectus (
Sec.70), Return of allotment (Sec. 75) will continue to be with the  Registrar of Companies.
           Powers to hear petitions  regarding issue of shares at a discount  (Sec.79). Redemption of irredeemable 
preference shares (Sec.80A), extension  of time to issue of shares/debentures  certificate (Sec.113) will  require to be
retained with the Company  Law Board as SEBI is not a quasi-judicial body.
           Powers to decide applications submitted to the Central Government.  Further issue of shares on conversion of
loan/debenture into equity (Sec.81 (3) & (4)), depreciation methods (Sec.205) and power to make Rule and prescribe
schedule will remain with Central Government.  Thus the above aspect need to be incorporated by suitable amendment
in Section 55A of the Companies (Second Amendment) Bill, 1999.

R E P O R T
           
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs, having been
authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf,  present  this Sixty-fifth Report of the Committee,
relating to the Companies Bill, 1997¨.      
2.         In pursuance of the Rules relating to Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees, the Chairman,
Rajya Sabha  referred** the Companies Bill, 1997,  as introduced in the Rajya Sabha on  14 August 1997 and pending
therein, to the Committee for examination  and report.
3.         The Department of Company Affairs was earlier part of the Ministry of Finance when   the Bill was introduced
in the Rajya Sabha, and as such was referred to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Finance
for examination and report on 2 September 1997.   Later on, the Department  of Company Affairs was  made  part of 
the Ministry of Law and Justice  (now known as Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs) and, therefore, the Bill
was referred to  this Committee on  3 July 1998.
4.         Meanwhile, the Secretary, Department of Company Affairs during the course of his presentation before the
Committee (1998-99) on 30 June, 1998 relating to the Demands for Grants of his Department, made the following
observations with regard to the Companies Bill, 1997  :-
“………..But in the meantime the Government has not yet made up its mind whether to continue  with this Bill
or not.  In all probability very soon they will take a decision  because they may  like  to make some changes in
the Bill.  But there is the question of procedure whether it can be  referred to a Committee when the Bill is
pending  in Parliament.  As per the Law Ministry’s advice,  it has to be withdrawn first before  it is  referred to
any other Committee.  So, at this  stage, I can only say that the Bill is under   review by the Government   and
very soon a decision  will be taken about the continuance of the Bill…..”
 
5.         The Companies Bill, 1997  having  been  referred  to   the  Committee  and  the       Secretary,
Department of Company Affairs having made the above observations, a reference   was  made to the
Department on 4 August 1998 to let the Committee know the thinking of the Government with regard to the  enactment
of the Bill in its present form, so as to enable the Committee to proceed further in the matter.
6.         The Department of Company Affairs vide
 their communication dated 5 November, 1998 conveyed that the
Cabinet had approved certain amendments in the Companies Act, 1956 and, accordingly, an Ordinance had been
promulgated on 31 October, 1998  amending the Principal Act.  That Department also conveyed the Cabinet’s decision
for taking appropriate  action to get the Companies   Bill, 1997,  pending in Parliament considered  and passed,
incorporating  the provisions in the Ordinance.   Accordingly, the Committee was requested for examination of the
Companies Bill, 1997 and for submission of the report at the earliest.
7.0       The Department of Company Affairs  vide
 their  Office Memorandum dated 8 February, 1999  brought the
following facts to the notice of the Committee:-
(i)                  Certain changes have been made in the Companies Act, 1956 through the Companies (Amendment)
Ordinance, 1998 promulgated  on 31 October 1998.  Some of the provisions brought through this
Ordinance such as buy-back of shares and inter-corporate investments etc. also find a place in the
Companies Bill, 1997.  Subsequently, the Companies (Amendment) Bill, 1998 was introduced in the Lok
Sabha on 22 December   to replace the Ordinance.  However, this Bill could not be passed as the Lok
Sabha was adjourned sine
 die on 23 December, 1998.
 

65th Report of Committee on Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/65threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:36:39]
(ii)                As explained above, since the Companies (Amendment) Bill, 1998 could not be passed during the
Winter Session (November/December, 1998), another Ordinance called the Companies (Amendment)
Ordinance, 1999 was promulgated on 7 January 1999.  This Ordinance was on similar lines as
Companies (Amendment) Bill 1998 and in the ensuing Budget Session this Bill will be taken up for
consideration and passing, with some amendments, by the Parliament so as to replace the Companies
(Amendment) Ordinance, 1999 issued on 7 January, 1999.
 
7.1       Since  Hon’ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha, had referred only the Companies Bill,1997, to the Committee for
examination and report and   the Companies (Amendment) Ordinance, 1998, promulgated on 31.10.1998, the
Companies (Amendment) Bill, 1998, introduced in Lok Sabha on 22.12.1998  and  the  Companies  (Amendment)
Ordinance, 1999, promulgated on 7.1.1999 were not under consideration of the Committee, it was not made clear  by the
Department as to what exactly it would like the Committee to consider in view of the fact that  it was seized of the
Companies Bill, 1997 only.
7.2       Accordingly the Department of Company Affairs  was requested vide
 Secretariat’s Office Memorandum dated
15 February, 1999 to let the Committee know in clear terms the purport of their communication dated 8 February, 1999.
7.3       In the meantime, the subject matter was briefly discussed in the meeting of the Committee held on 9 February,
1999 and was decided that since only the Companies Bill, 1997, had been referred to the Committee, it would consider
that piece of legislation only and so far as the Ordinance and the Bill replacing it were concerned, it was for the two
Houses to consider them.
7.4       The Department of Company Affairs then vide
 Office Memorandum dated 26 February, 1999, stated that the
purpose of the Department’s Office Memorandum dated 8 February, 1999, was just to keep the Committee informed
about the provisions of the Companies (Amendment) Ordinance, 1999, so that the same may be kept in mind at the time
the Companies Bills, 1997  was taken up for consideration.
8          Before the Committee could take up the Bill for consideration, its tenure came to an end consequent upon the
dissolution of  Twelfth Lok Sabha on 26 April, 1999.  The present Committee was  constituted w.e.f. 31 December,
1999.
9.         The Committee in its first meeting held on 18 January, 2000, reviewed the status of the Bills/subjects pending
consideration of the Committee and noted that  a new Bill, namely, the Companies (Second Amendment) Bill, 1999
introduced in the Lok Sabha on 23 December, 1999 and pending therein, had also been referred to it  for examination
and report.
10.       The Committee, in its meeting held on 7 February, 2000, decided that it might take up the Companies (Second
Amendment) Bill, 1999, for examination along with the Companies Bill, 1997, after the Budget Session, as it would
take considerable time to dispose them of.
11.       After the Budget Session was over, the Committee again  reviewed the position of the Bills pending before it, at
its meeting held on 17 May, 2000, and decided to give top priority to pending legislation and dispose them of in the
order of priority assigned by it. The Committee decided to take up the two Bills relating to the Company Law first
followed by other Bills, in the four rounds of sittings – 29, 30 & 31 May and 1 & 2 June,  in the first round; 12, 13 & 14
June in the second round; 26, 27, 28, 29 & 30 June in the third round;  and 10, 11, 12, 13 & 14 July, 2000 in the fourth
round. 
12.       The Companies Bill, 1997 seeks to remove existing lacunae in the Companies Act, 1956 and to streamline some
of the existing provisions for better working and administration of the Companies Act.  Certain incidental and
consequential changes are also sought to be made.  In view of  the extensive changes proposed to be  made in the
Companies Act, 1956, the Bill seeks to repeal and re-enact the said Act.
13.       The Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Bill states that -
“The Companies Act, 1956 has been in operation for the last forty year.  In the last four decades, the
economy has undergone considerable changes and the Companies Act, 1956 was amended as many as seventeen
times.
 
The objectives of liberalisation, deregulation, simplification of laws, rules, procedure and changing
economic, corporate and international corporate market require that the law on Companies –
 
            (i)         be moulded      in tune with the changing economic environment;
(ii)
                be responsive to the changing corporate practices;
(iii)               should incorporate appropriately the concepts developed in the international corporate market;

65th Report of Committee on Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/65threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:36:39]
(iv)              should protect the rights of investors, depositors, employees, creditors and other participants;
(v)                should restore corporate democracy and impose extensive obligations on the Board of Directors;
(vi)              should categorise the companies and provide for different degrees of regulations for the different
categories;
(vii)             should confer rights and impose duties, including obligations of disclosure, upon different categories of
companies;
(viii)           be restructured so as to remove or replace the inadequate and obsolete provisions;
(ix)              should incorporate a strong code of corporate governance.
 
A Working Group comprising of persons with knowledge of law, economics and company affairs was set
up in August, 1996 pursuant to the 1996 Budget speech to rework a new draft of the law on Companies and
make it available for public debate.
           
The Working Group had a series of meeting during which it interacted with, and received responses
from, Reserve Bank of India, Securities and Exchange Board of India, banks and financial institutions, merchant
bankers, capital market players, stock exchange officials, industry associations, professional bodies and others
who significantly contribute to the corporate environment.  The Group prepared a working draft of the
Companies Bill and submitted the same on 2.5.1997 to the Government which  was released for public debate. 
The suggestions and observations on the working draft were made known to Government through various
workshops and seminars organised by chambers of commerce, industry associations, professional institutes, etc. 
Memoranda and detailed suggestions/representations were received by the Government from various
organisations, Members of Parliament, professional bodies and other individual experts having extensive
knowledge and wide experience of corporate affairs.
 
The main objective of re-enacting the Companies Act is to facilitate a healthy growth of the Indian
corporate sector under a liberalised, fast changing and highly competitive environment.  While redrafting the
law, an endeavour has been made to adopt a balanced  approach that recognises an international trend, i.e.
flexibility and greater self regulation by companies subject to better disclosure, more efficient enforcement of
law, and prompt and deterrent punishments to those who violate the law.  The core object of the Companies Bill
is to provide effective protection to the different participants, leaving management free to direct its energies to
the pursuit of the company’s objectives”.
 
14.       The Bill has re-grouped the scattered provisions relating to specific subjects and deleted redundant provisions.
The salient features of the present Bill which seeks to repeal and re-enact the Companies Act, 1956 are as under -
(i)
                  Reducing the size of the present Companies Act, 1956, from 658 sections and fifteen Schedules to 458
sections and three Schedules;
(ii)        Providing for appropriate rules and guidelines to ensure flexibility and clarity;
                 (iii)       Providing three-fold classification of  companies, that is –
 
(a)                Private companies, which are proposed to be largely self-governing but prohibited from inviting
and accepting deposits from the public and not to be deemed as public companies;
(b)               Unlisted public companies, which will be subject to minimum Government regulations;
(c)                Listed public companies, which will be subject to greater regulation including stricter disclosure
norms;
 
(iv)              Permitting issue of shares with differential voting and dividend rights;
(v)                Enabling companies to mobilise funds through new forms of securities, such as hybrids, derivatives,
options, etc.
(vi)              Permitting companies to buy-back their own shares subject to certain rules and safeguards;
(vii)             Permitting issue of Indian Depository Receipts (IDRs) by foreign companies to enable them to tap the
Indian capital market for setting up enterprises in India;
(viii)           Permitting companies to make investments or loans to other bodies corporate without approval of the
Government but with the approval of the shareholders;
(ix)              Prescribing minimum paid up capital of one lakh rupees for private companies and five lakhs rupees for

public limited companies;
(x)                Giving option to companies for preparation of group accounts and conferring power upon the Central
Government to make mandatory the preparation of such group accounts from a future date to be notified;
(xi)              Limiting the age upto seventy-five years for all directors in public companies but those persons already
appointed as managing directors or whole time directors or directors may complete their current tenure;
(xii)             Simplifying depreciation rates of certain assets of a company;
(xiii)           Providing that a public company may have a maximum of fifteen directors;
(xiv)           Providing nomination facility to shareholders, debenture holders and deposit holders;
(xv)            Establishing the Investor Education and Protection Fund for the protection and education of investors;
(xvi)           Empowering the Central Government to appoint a Director General of Inspection and Investigation to
strengthen inspection and investigation of companies;
(xvii)         Empowering the Central Government to prepare panels of chartered accountants, advocates, company
secretaries or cost accountants eligible to be appointed as liquidators to facilitate expeditious winding up
of companies;
(xviii)        Providing for time limit within which various steps of winding up are to be completed;
(xix)           Constituting the Company Law Tribunal in place of the existing Company Law Board and vesting the
Tribunal with more functions and powers and providing it with wider jurisdiction;
(xx)            Providing for appointment of a Chief Accountants Officer in every listed company having a paid-up
capital of three crore rupees or more, who shall be responsible for timely preparation and finalisation of
the annual accounts of a company and be one of the signatories to the balance-sheet;
(xxi)           Permitting an auditor to conduct audit of twenty five companies irrespective of their size as against the
present limit of twenty companies and providing for stricter norms for audit and disclosures;
(xxii)         Empowering the Central Government to direct financial audit or cost audit or secretarial audit;
(xxiii)        Empowering the Central Government to appoint firms of professionals such as chartered accountants,
cost accountants, company secretaries and advocates as “Licensed Registrars” who would discharge
certain functions of the Registrar which may be entrusted by the Central Government. Licensed Registrar
will provide Registrar’s services in certain matters in addition to Registrars of Companies of the Central
Government;
(xxiv)
       Entrusting the administration and supervision (including powers to prosecute) of work relating to issue
of securities and other related matters in case of listed public companies to the Securities and Exchange
Board of India to avoid overlapping of functions.
(xxv)         Enhancing penalty and punishment for contravention of provisions so as to ensure better compliance of
law.

21.       Before the Committee commenced clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill, the Secretary, Department of
Company Affairs made a detailed statement for its consideration.  The relevant extracts therefrom are reproduced below
:-
“The Companies Bill, 1997 contains 458 clauses.  Apart from definitions, 34 clauses containing new concepts
were inserted in the said bill for the first time.  The other clauses of the Bill contains either minor amendments to
the sections of the Companies Act, 1956 or simply restructures these section according to the subject.
 
Out of these 34 clauses, the Companies Amendment Act, 1999  has already implemented concepts of Buy Back
of  shares (Section 77A), Nomination facility to investors (Section 109A & B), Investor Education and
Protection Fund (Section 205C), National Advisory Committee on Accounting Standards (Section 201A), Issue
of Sweat Equity Shares (Section 79A) and Infrastructure Default Finance Company defined as Public Financial
Institutions – Clause 4A.
 
With the approval of the Companies (Second Amendment) Bill, 1999 we are now left with only some more
important concepts inserted in the Companies Bill for the first time.  I would like to submit the position in regard
to such clauses, and group them into four distinct classes.
 
Firstly, concept which relates to definitions e.g. clause 2(1)’Abridged Prospectus’, clause 2(18) ‘Depository’,
clause 2(19) ‘Derivative’, clause 2(22) ‘Dividend, clause 2(24) ‘Employees Stock Option’. Clause 2(29)
‘’Hybrid, clause 2(30) ‘Information Memorandum’, clause 2(35) ‘Listed Public Companies’, clause 2(45)
‘option in securities’, clause 2(63) ‘Securities’, and clause 2(66) ‘share with differential rights’.  In addition
(clause 43) ‘Indian Depository Receipts’, (clause 51) ‘shelf prospectus’, (clause 52) ‘information memorandum’,
(clause 59) ‘initial offer of securities to be in dematerialised  form’, (clause 103) ‘debenture  trust deed’, (clause
104) ‘duties of debenture trustees’ (clause 105) ‘liability of the company to create security’.  All the provisions
relating to Capital Market were included in the Companies Bill, 1997.
 
The above clauses relate to the activity of the company for raising capital from the market after
introduction of the Companies Bill, 1997.  SEBI  has framed certain regulations on these subjects.
 
However, it is the view of the Department of Company Affairs that these should find a place in the
Companies Act which is a Mother Law.  This will also enable us to prescribe the modalities prevalent in the
modern capital world.   It is for consideration of the Hon’ble Members to kindly clear these provisions
containing basic concepts for inclusion in the Companies Act, 1956.
 
Secondly, the Company Bill, 1997 provide for certain measures to strengthen regulation of finance
function in companies,  Clause 172 proposes appointment of a qualified person as Chief Accounts Officer. 
Introduction of this concept is essential to prevent financial manipulation in companies.  I recommend it
endorsement by the Committee.
 
The concept of Consolidated Annual Balance-sheet is also globally prevalent and is essential for

transparency.  This was included in the Bill in Clause 168.  However, a review of the position in this regard with
the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India revealed that the Accounting Standards Board of ICAI is in the
process of preparing an accounting standard which is to be followed by the members of the Institute in
preparation of consolidated accounts and its audit.   Therefore, though this provision may also be approved, its
implementation may take another 2-3 months by which time accounting standards are expected to be in place.
 
Clause 402 had provided for power of Central Government to appoint Director General of Investigation
and Registration (DGIR) and Clause 404 to recognise statutorily the Regional Directors appointed by the
Government in the Act itself.  The creation of such a post would strengthen the inspection and audit function of
the Department.  However creation of a high level post requires discussions with Department of Administrative
Reforms, Department of Personnel and Ministry of Finance.  Therefore, the provision cannot be implemented
immediately.
 
The Companies Bill had also introduced a concept of Licence Registrars (Clause 406) it was provided in
the Bill under the impression that the private persons can reduce the burden of the Government officers
functioning as Registrars of Companies (ROCs).  However, a recent study indicates that computerizing and
modernising these offices, for which the Government has taken extensive steps will improve and streamline
working of ROC Offices.  This will enable the Department to provide service to public at large.  Therefore, it is
submitted that sovereign functions of the Government cannot be entrusted to private persons as Registrar of
Companies cannot be delegated.  This clause may, therefore, should not find place in the Companies Act.
 
Thirdly, Clauses 293, 306, 307, 308, 309, 311 of the Bill pertain to the entire gamut of winding
up/dissolution of companies.  In this connection it may be stated that Central Government has set up a High
Powered Committee in January, 2000 under the Chairmanship of Justice Shri Balkrishna Eradi, a Judge of the
Supreme Court of India.  This Committee would give its report on law relating to insolvency by 30 July, 2000, a
subject which is covered by the above clauses itself.  The detailed terms of reference are enclosed.  It is,
 
therefore, essential that in the matters pertaining to winding up which are contained in clauses 289-383 of the
Companies Bill, 1997, the views of the Justice Eradi will have to be considered at the highest level in the
Government.
 
Lastly, clauses relating to constitution of Benches of Company Law Tribunal, order of Tribunal – Clause
419 conferring powers of the High Court to Tribunal.  Clause 421 – power to punish for contempt of court by
Tribunal.  Clauses 422-Residuary Jurisdiction being conferred on Tribunal to hear all matters under the Act. 
Clause 423 are connected with Constitution of Company Law Tribunal.  The concept was last discussed by the
then Government in 1996 and it need a careful review by the present Government at the highest level as such the
Committee will like to take an appropriate view in this regard.
 
The arrangement of sections in the Companies Bill, 1997 have been basically different than what they are
in the Companies Act, 1956.  For this purpose and to facilitate comparison between the Companies Act, 1956,
Companies Bill, 1997, Companies Amendment Act, 1999 and the Companies (Second Amendment) Bill, 1999 a
comparative table has been circulated to the Hon’ble Members of the Committee.
 
The Hon’ble Committee may appropriately consider the Companies Bill in the light of the above facts”.

REPORT
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs having been
authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this Sixty-sixth Report on the Constitution (Eighty-
eighth Amendment) Bill, 1999*.
2.         In pursuance of the rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees the Chairman, Rajya
Sabha referred** the Constitution (Eighty-eighth Amendment) Bill, 1999 (Annexure-I), as introduced in the Rajya Sabha
on 23 December 1999 and pending therein, to the Committee for examination and report.
3.         The Bill seeks to  insert a proviso at the end of  Article 335 of the Constitution  with a view to enabling the State to
restore the relaxations of qualifying marks and standards of evaluation in the matters of reservation in  promotion for
Schedule Castes and Scheduled Tribes, which has been withdrawn w.e.f. 22 July, 1997.
4.0       The Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Bill explains that the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes had
been enjoying the facility of relaxation of qualifying marks and standards of evaluation in matters of reservation in
promotion. Such relaxations were withdrawn by the Government of India through Department of Personnel & Training
Office Memorandum dated 22 July 1997 (Annexure II) with a view to giving effect to the contentions of the Supreme
Court’s judgements in the case of  S. Vinod Kumar Vs. Union of India and Indra Sawhney and Others Vs. Union of
India.  The Supreme Court in both the judgements has held  that    relaxations    in matter of  reservations in promotion were
not permissible under  Article 16(4) in view of the command contained  in Article 335 of the Constitution.
4.1       It is further mentioned in the Statement of Objects and Reasons that Government has received representations from
several quarters including the Members of  Parliament to restore the relaxations existing prior to the issuance of Office
Memorandum dated 22 July 1997 for which the Bill has been introduced for restoration of such facilities to the Scheduled
Castes/Tribes.
5.0       Reservation in matters of direct appointment/promotion for Scheduled  Castes/Scheduled  Tribes  is provided 
through executive  instructions issued by the  Government  for which the Government derives its authority from Articles
16(4) & 16 (4A) of the Constitution.
5.1       Reservation to Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes  were  provided  in direct  recruitment   as well as promotion
w.e.f. 21 September, 1947  and 4 January, 1957, respectively, in accordance with the reservation policy of the Government
of India.
5.2       The percentage of reservation for Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes in direct recruitment  as well as  promotion is

5.3       Special dispensations in the   form of relaxation/concession in the standards of evaluation in initial appointment as
well as promotion have been provided to SCs/STs  to ensure reservation envisaged  under Article 16(4) and 16(4A) of the
Constitution.
5.4       In the Background Note on the Bill, it has been mentioned that relaxation in direct appointment  as well as promotion
were permissible in favour of the Scheduled Castes/Tribes  prior to the issuance of DOPT, OM dated 22 July 1997. 
Relaxation in matters of promotion included more number of chances to appear in qualifying promotional tests, extended
zone of consideration, relaxation in  maximum age limit wherever permissible,  qualifying marks and standard of evaluation.
Following are the main relaxations/concessions permissible   to SCs/STs:-
(i)                  Relaxation in upper age limit by 5 years in Direct Recruitment and also in promotions  where  prescribed
age is not exceeding 50 years.
(ii)                No fee to be paid by SCs/STs at recruitment stage.
(iii)               Relaxation of experience in direct recruitment.
(iv)              Relaxation in standards of suitability in Direct Recruitment.
(v)                When the promotion is by non-selection method, in the event of non-availability  in order  of seniority,
eligible SC/ST candidates could be picked up till the bottom of the Seniority List for filling up the reserved
vacancies.
(vi)              When the promotion is by Selection Method, the normal zone of consideration is extended up to five times
the number of vacancies proposed to be filled up by promotion in order to make up the short-fall of suitable
SCs/STs in the normal zone of consideration.
(vii)
             When recruitment is by promotion as well as Direct Recruitment and no SC/ST  candidate satisfying the
eligibility criteria is available, such a vacancy is temporarily  diverted from promotion method to Direct
Recruitment method in order to ensure that the reserved vacancy is filled up only by persons of the reserved
category.
(viii)
           In case of non-availability of  a SC or ST for a continuous period of 3 years, the vacancy is exchanged  with
the other category.  However, in case of promotion by Selection to Group `B’  posts and above  carry forward
is not allowed  but exchange is allowed in same year.
(ix)              Separate interview is held  for the SCs/STs in Direct  Recruitment.  SC/ST candidates called for interview by
the UPSC/SSC etc. are granted T.A.
(x)        Relaxation in qualifying marks in Limited Department Competitive Examination wherever held  for
promotion.
(xi)       Relaxation in qualifying examination for promotion wherever prescribed.  SC/ST candidates not upto the
general qualifying standard  could be considered for promotion provided they were not found unfit.
(xii)             Relaxation in standards of evaluation viz. SCs/STs not meeting the prescribed benchmark  could be
promoted provided they were not found unfit for  promotion.
 
6.0       The Office Memorandum under reference inter alia states that the Supreme Court in the case of S. Vinod Kumar Vs.
Union of India (JT 1996(8) S.C. 6431) has held that the provisions for lowering qualifying marks/lesser level of evaluation,
in the matter of promotion, provided for candidates belonging to the Scheduled Castes/Tribes under the Government’s
instruction is not permissible under Article 16(4) in view of the command contained in Article 335 of the Constitution.
6.1       The said OM  withdrew the relaxations/concessions enumerated  at Sr. Nos.(x), (xi) and (xii) of  para No. 5.4 supra
in pursuance of the  Supreme Court judgement in Vinod Kumar case which has reiterated the contentions of nine-judge
bench judgement in the case of Indra Sawhney  Vs. Union of  India,  popularly known as Mandal case.
7.0       The Indra Sawhney Vs. Union of India case basically relates to the issue  of making provision of reservation  to the 
Other Backward  Classes, wherein Article 16 (4)  was interpreted.  The Supreme Court  while interpreting Artilce 16(4) has
held that   reservation in promotion for the Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes is not sustainable  under Article 16(4)  in
view of provision laid down in Article 335.
7.1.0    Para 831 of the Supreme Court judgement in Indra Sawhney case reads as under :-
“We must also make it clear that it would not be impermissible for the State to extend concessions  and relaxations to
members of reserved categories in the matter of promotion without compromising the efficiency of the
administration.  The relaxation concerned in State of Kerala Vs. N.M. Thomas (1976) 2 SCC 310, and the
concessions namely carrying forward of vacancies and provisions for in-service coaching/training  in Akhil
Bharatiya Soshit karamchari Sangh V. Union of India. (1981) 1 SCC 246, are instances of such concessions and
relaxations.  However, it would not be permissible to   prescribe lower qualifying marks or a lesser level of
evaluation for the members of reserved categories since that would compromise the efficiency of administration.  We

66th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/66threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:36:40]
reiterate that while it may be permissible to prescribe a reasonably lesser qualifying marks or evaluation for the
OBCs, SCs and STs – consistent with the efficiency of administration and the nature of duties attaching to the office
concerned – in the matter of direct recruitment, such a course would not be permissible in the matter of promotions
for the reasons recorded hereinabove.”
 
7.1.1    Further,  has  para 829 of the Supreme Court judgement in Indra Sawhney’s case protection  has been given for
reservation in promotion for five years without permitting lower qualifying marks/lesser level of evaluations in the
examination for promotion.
7.1.2        In this context, the Supreme Court has also in the same case observed that:
“…We see no justification to multiply `the risk’, which would be the consequence of holding that reservation can be 
provided even in the matter of promotion.  While  it is certainly just to say that a handicap should be given to 
backward class of citizens at the stage  of initial appointment, it  would be a serious  and unacceptable inroad  into 
the  rule  of   equality of  opportunity   to say that such a    handicap   should   be
 provided  at every stage of promotion throughout their career.    That  would  mean creation of a permanent  separate
category apart from the mainstream – a vertical  division of the administrative  apparatus.  The members of reserved
categories need not have to compete  with others but only among themseleves.   There would  be no  will to work, compete
and excel  among  them.  Whether  they  work  or not, they tend to think, their  promotion is assured.  This in turn is bound
to generate a feeling of despondence  and “heart-burning” among open competition  members.   All this is bound  to affect
the efficiency of administration.  Putting the members of backward  classed on a fast-track would necessarily result in leap-
frogging and the deleterious  effects of “leap-frogging” need no illustration at our hands.  At  the initial stage of recruitment 
reservation can be made in favour of  backward  class  of  citizens  but once  they enter the service, efficiency  of
administration  demands that these members too compete  with others and earn promotion like  all others; no further
distinction can be made  thereafter with reference  to their “birth-mark”, as one of the learned Judges  of the Court has said
in another connection.  They are expected to operate  on equal footing with others.  Crutches cannot be provided throughout 
one’s career.  That would not be in the interest of efficiency  of administration nor in the larger  interest of the nation"”
 
7.2       Salient rulings/observations of the Supreme Court having bearing on various aspects of reservation policy in matter
of promotion as submitted by the Ministry are reproduced under:-
 
(i)
                  Nine-Judge Constitution  Bench Judgement dated 16.11.1992 in the case of Indra Sawhney Vs. Union of
India:-
 
(a)        In providing for the reservation of appointments or posts under Article  16(4), the State has to take
into consideration the claims of the members  of the backward    classes consistently  with the
maintenance  of the efficiency  of administration.
(b)
               It must not be forgotten that efficiency of administration is of such paramount importance that it
would be unwise and impermissible  to make any reservation at the cost of efficiency of
administration.  That undoubtedly  is the effect of Article 335.
(c)                It would not be permissible to prescribe lower qualifying marks or a lesser level of evaluation for the
members of reserved categories since that would compromise the efficiency of administration.
 
(ii)                Two-Judge Bench Judgement dated 1.10.96 of the Supreme Court in the case of  S. Vinod Kumar  Vs.
Union of India
 
(a)    The provision for lower qualifying marks or lesser standards of
evaluation, in matters of reservation in promotion is not permissible under Article  16(4) in view of
the command contained in Article 335 of the Constitution.
(b)   The protection for five years given to reservation in promotion by the judgement in Indra Sawhney case
did not apply  to such  concessions/relaxations.
 
(iii)               Five-judge Constitution bench judgement dated 16.9.1999 in the case of Ajit Singh and Ors  Versus the
State of Punjab  and others.
 
 
(a)        Article 335 takes care to make this an express Constitutional limitation upon the discretion vested in
the State while making provision for adequate  representation for the Scheduled Castes/Tribes.  Thus,
in the matter   of due  representation in service for Backward Classes and Scheduled Castes and

Tribes, maintenance of efficiency  of administration  is of paramount importance.  As pointed in Indra
Sawhney, the provisions of the Constitution must be interpreted in such a manner that a sense of
competition is cultivated among all service personnel, including the reserved categories.
 
8.0       The Government in order to overcome  the judgement of Supreme Court in Indra Sawhney case (1992)  had inserted
Article 16(4A)  making explicit  provisions of reservation for SCs/STs  in promotion   through  Constitution (Seventy-
seventh Amendment) Act, 1995. 
8.1       The said Article was again challenged in Vinod Kumar case (1996) which reiterated the judgement in Indra Sawhney
case  as result of which Para 829 of latter judgement became valid.  In short, both judgements of the Supreme Court lay
emphasis on the point that relaxations of  qualifying marks  and  standards  of  evaluation  in  matters  of  reservation  in
promotion are not permissible in view of the provisions laid down in Article 335 of the Constitution.
9.         In order to implement the above said judgement and also some other judgements, the Department of Personnel and
Training issued four Office Memoranda during 1997 (January 30, July 2, July 22, August 29), the impugned one being the
OM No.36012/23/96-Estt (Res) dated  22 July 1997 which withdrew the instructions in regard promotion for the SCs/STs
contained in a host of DOPT’s OM having Nos. i.e. (i) 8/12/69-Estt. (SCT) dated 23 December 1970; (ii) 36021/10/76-Estt.
(SCT) dated 21 January 1997 and (iii) para 6.3.2 of the DPC guidelines contained in OM No.22011/5/86-Estt. dated 10 April
1989, which prescribed lesser qualifying marks for the Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes in departmental
qualifying/competitive examination for promotion.  Fifth OM dated 13 August 1997 was issued in pursuance of Article
16(4A) of the Constitution to ensure that reservation in promotion for the Scheduled Castes/Tribes continues after 15
November, 1997.
10.       The Bill under consideration takes care of only one Office Memorandum dated 22.7.1997. In respect of another
Office Memorandum dated 29.8.1997, Constitution (Eighty-First Amendment) Act, 2000  has already come into  force. 
Office Memorandum  dated 2.7.1997 is still under examination.  As  regards the Office Memoranda  dated 30.1.1997 and
13.8.1997, it has been  decided to await the outcome of certain  Writ  Petitions which stand filed in the Supreme Court on
the content and constitutionality of Article 16 (4A) of the Constitution.
11.       The proceedings of the Lok Sabha were disrupted on 17 & 18 March, 1999 due to persistent demand from some of
the Members that the five OM issued by DOPT adversely affected the interests of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled
Tribes and should
be withdrawn.  Subsequently, an unscheduled debate took place on the reservation issue relating to these OM and the Prime
Minister made a statement in the Lok Sabha in which he stated as under :-
 
“….. In view of the various representations that have been received from several quarters and the debate in the
House, the Government has already  started  the process of    reviewing   of these memoranda. Two of  these
memoranda are currently
under  adjudication of the Supreme Court.  We would welcome the formation of a Committee of Members of 
Parliament who could go into the subject and assist the Government in this regard.  The Government is committed to
maintain the system of reservations that has been followed so far and is prepared to bring forward a legislation even
to amend the Constitution, if required to do so.”
12.       The Government  sought the legal opinion of Attorney-General on the subject matter of the office memorandum
dated 22 July 1997.  The opinion of Attorney-General as quoted in the Background Note  of the Ministry is produced as
under :-
(i)
                  the OM dated 22.7.1997 has correctly understood the judgement of the Supreme Court in Vinod  Kumar’s
case and implemented it.
 
(ii)
                the Supreme Court in Vinod Kumar’s case has taken the view that the relaxation in qualifying marks and
lesser standard of evaluation does affect the efficiency of the  administration.  There can be two opinions on
whether the understanding of the Supreme Court in Indra Sawhney’s case on the scope and effect of the
earlier 7-Judge Bench case in Thomas’ case is correct.  It is also arguable that this issue did not directly arise
for consideration in Indra Sawhney’s case.  It is equally arguable that the observations of the Supreme Court
in Indra Sawhney are obiter dicta.  Be that as it may, the Government is bound by the judgement in Vinod
Kumar’s case unless it is re-considered or over-ruled by a larger Bench.
(iii)               neither the judgement in Indra Sawhney’s case nor the judgement in Vinod Kumar’s case has been over-
ruled in a subsequent judgement and they constitute the correct law of the land and are binding under Article
141 of the Constitution.

SMALL VARIATION FROM OPINION OF THE
LEARNED ATTORNEY GENERAL OF INDIA
 
Since the relaxations withdrawn by OM dated 22.7.1997 also related to qualifying marks and standards of evaluation
otherwise than in a qualifying examination, it was considered that incorporation of a proviso on the lines exactly  as
suggested by the Learned Attorney General of India would not enable the Govt to restore the relaxations withdrawn by
OM dated 22.7.1997. Such restoration could be possible if the words "in a qualifying examination" appearing between the
words "standards of evaluation" and "in matters of promotion" in the suggestion of the Learned Attorney General of India
were not added in the amending Bill. While suggesting the proviso to Article 335 of the Constitution, the Learned Attorney
General of India had himself suggested that an appropriate amendment be drafted in consultation with the Legislative
Department.
 
The Legislative Department of the Ministry of Law accordingly drafted the Bill to amend Article 335 of the
Constitution by inserting the following proviso at the end of the said Article:-
 
"Provided that nothing in this article shall prevent in making of any   provision  in favour of the members of the
Scheduled Castes and the  Scheduled Tribes for relaxation in qualifying marks in any examination or lowering the
standards of evaluation, for reservation in matters of promotion to any class or classes of services or posts in
connection with the affairs of the Union or of a State."

•           Relaxation in standards of evaluation viz. SCs and STs not meeting the prescribed bench mark could be promoted
provided they were not found unfit for promotion.
 
Relaxations and concessions in Direct Recruitment and Promotions for SCs/STs which still continue after O.M.
dated 22-7-1997 are as under:-
 
(i)         Relaxation in upper age limit by 5 years in Direct Recruitment and also in promotions where prescribed age
is not exceeding 50 years.
(ii)
                No fee to be paid by SCs/STs at recruitment stage.
 
(iii)               Relaxation of experience in direct recruitment.

Query raised
 
*          Attorney General's opinion is a cautious opinion. He has acknowledged that Supreme Court will review this
matter again.
*          Will proviso to Article 335 (proposed) be read into the equality clause in the Chapter on Fundamental Rights?
*          Will the Vinod Kumar and Indra Sawhney judgments remain, even after the proposed Amendment?
 
Reply
 
Learned Attorney General of India has inter alia opined that if the intention is to get over the judgment in S. Vinod
Kumar's case, it can be done, if at all,  only by a constitutional amendment by the Parliament exercising its constituent power
and not by legislation. Brief opinion of the Learned Attorney General of India is as under:-
 
(i)
                 The Supreme Court in Vinod Kumar's case has taken the view that the relaxation in qualifying marks and
lesser standard of evaluation does affect the efficiency of the administration. There can be two opinions on
whether the understanding of the Supreme Court in lndra Sawhney's case on the scope and effect of the
earlier 7-Judge Bench case in Thomas' case is correct. It is also arguable that this issue did not directly arise
for consideration in Indra Sawhney's case. It is equally arguable that the observations of the Supreme Court in
Indra Sawhney are obiter dicta. Be that as it may, the Government is bound by the judgment in Vinod
Kumar's case unless it is re- considered or over-ruled by a larger Bench.
 
(ii)
                Neither the judgment in lndra Sawhney's case nor the judgment in Vinod Kumar's case has been over-
ruled in a subsequent judgment and they constitute the correct law of the land and are binding under Article
141 of the Constitution.
 
(iii)       If the intention is to get over the judgment in S. Vinod Kumar's case, it can be done, if at all, only by a
constitutional amendment by the Parliament exercising its constituent power and not by legislation. I must
point out that such an amendment would also be subject to judicial review   in view of the judgment in
Keshava Nanda Bharati's case' (1973) 4 SCC 225 for examining whether the Constitutional amendment is
violative of the basic structure of the Constitution. It is not, however, possible to predict with any
certainty the result of such judicial scrutiny.
 
(iv)       An amendment of the Constitution may be considered by way of a proviso to Article 335 rather than as a
sub-Article or proviso to Article 16. This could conceivably enable the Government  to contend that the Right
to Equality, which is a basic structure of the Constitution, is not, in any manner, being affected by the
amendment, and that the Article requiring maintenance of efficiency of the administration is being suitably

Judgments will remain operative or not after the proposed amendment. However, it may be mentioned that the purpose
behind the amendment is to enable the Government to restore the position that existed prior to 22.7.1997.

Reply
 
Where recruitment in central services in Mizoram is made on local or regional basis, there is no reservation for SCs.
Reservation for Scheduled Tribes is 45% and for OBCs it is 5%.
On the question of whether backward classes can be further divided into backward and more backward categories, Supreme
Court in Indra Sawhney case has observed as under:-
 
"We are of the opinion that there is no constitutional or legal bar to a State categorizing the backward classes as
backward and more backward. We are not saying that it ought to be done. We are concerned with the question if a
State makes such a categorization, whether it would be invalid? We think not. "

Judgment of the Supreme Court in the case of Vinod Kumar was on the SLP filed by the candidate (Vinod Kumar)

Reply
As per existing orders, carried forward reservation can be applied to a single post. However, Supreme Court in the
case of Post Graduate Institute of Medical Education and Research, Chandigarh Vs. Faculty Association, has held that
reservation cannot be provided in single post cadres. The question of issuing appropriate orders in implementation of this
judgment is under consideration.
Query raised
*          Reservation is justifiable at the initial stage of recruitment. However, after that to continue providing
reservation for SCs/STs in promotion also is not justifiable.
Reply
 
Supreme Court in lndra Sawhney case held that reservation in matter of promotion is not sustainable under Article
16(4) of the Constitution. Supreme Court also held that it would not be permissible to prescribe lower qualifying marks or a
lesser level of evaluation for the members of reserved categories since that would compromise the efficiency of
administration. Following observations of the Supreme Court in the Indra Sawhney case are relevant in this regard:-
 
“…We see no justification to multiply ‘the risk’, which would be the consequent of holding that reservation can be
provided even in the matter of promotion. While it is certainly just to say that a handicap should be given to
backward class of citizens at the stage of initial appointment, it would be a serious and    unacceptable inroad into the
rule of equality of opportunity to say that such a handicap should be provided at every stage of promotion throughout
their career.      That would mean creation of a permanent separate category  apart from the mainstream - a
vertical division of the administrative apparatus. The members of reserved categories need not have to compete
with others but only among themselves. There would be no will to work, compete and excel among them.
Whether they work or not, they tend to think, their promotion is assured. This in turn is bound to generate a
feeling of despondence and "heart-burning" among open competition members. All this is bound to affect the
efficiency of administration. Putting the members of backward classes on a fast-track would necessarily result in
leapfrogging and the deleterious effects of "leapfrogging" need no illustration at our hands. At the initial stage of
recruitment reservation can be     made in favor of backward class of citizens but once they enter the service ,
efficiency of administration demands that these members too compete with others and earn promotion like all
others; no further distinction can be made thereafter  with reference to their "birth-mark", as one of the learned
Judges of this Court has said in another connection. They are expected to operate on equal footing with others.
Crutches cannot be provided throughout one’s career.     That would not be in the interest of efficiency of
administration nor in the larger interest of the nation".
 
2.    However, Article 16(4A) was incorporated in the Constitution in mid 1995 with a view to enable the State to provide for
reservation in promotions.   In pursuance thereof, necessary orders were issued on 13.8.1997 to continue reservation in
promotion beyond 15.11.1997 when the five year period allowed by the Supreme Court for reservation in promotion to
remain operative would have come to an end.
