RECOMMENDATION (para no. 30) 
Situation in Jammu & Kashmir 
5. The Committee has been deeply anguished at the brutal killings of innocent 
people of Chatti Singhpura Village of Anantnag District of Jammu & Kashmir and is 
vel) much concerned at the rising number of attacks by the militants on security forces 
and their establishments. The Committee feels that there is an urgent need to have a 
comprehensive review of the strategy being used to fight the militants. The situation, 
grave as it is, calls for the adoption of a multi-pronged strategy. The strategy should not 
onl) focus on identifying potential 'soft targets' for militants but it should also ensure 
that our security forces and establishments do not fall prey to the militant s. The 
Committee urges upon the Government to spare no stone unturned to see that the back of 
the militancy is permanently broken, the nefarious designs of the hostile neighbouring 
country are defeated and normalcy in the beleaguered State is restored . 
ACTION TAKEN/PROPOSED TO BETAKEN 
5.1 Due to the Kargil incursions, Pak supported terrorist outfits were able to take 
advantage of the depleted security grid to push in armed foreign infiltrators in 
considerable number. This phase also witnessed introduction of suicide squads, 
intensificatiOn of attacks on security forces, upgradation of weaponry/hardware of the 
terrorists and efforts to garner local support as also to provide a Jehadi flavour to the 
ongoing terrorism in the State. The terrorists were keen on causing incidents that would 
attract instant media attention, their aim being to focus world attention on Kashmar. 
Massacre of Chitti Singhpura and focused attacks on security forces were part of the 
premeditated design . 
5.1.1 The Governme nt took a number of steps in the post Kargil phase which included, 
inter alia, strengthening of the counter terrorist grid, strengthening and modernisation of 
J&K Police, strengthening and expansion of Village Def~nce Committees , launching of 
pin pointed counter terrorist operations based upon action~ble intelligence, strengthening 
of security cover for areas inhabited by minorities including Sikhs, dividing the counter 
terrorist grid into integrated sectors for synergised operations and checking infiltration 
through improved border management. The aforementioned steps resulted in the killing 
of approximately 1520 terrorists from August, 99 to August 2000. 
5.1 2 As part of its resolve to bring back normalcy in the State of Jammu and Kashmir, 
the Government have embarked upon a three pronged strategy, which comprises: 
proactive tackling, with the help of security forces, the cross border terrorism that has 
been unleashed by Pakistan sponsored terrorist outfits; accelerating economic 
development as also redressing the genuine grievances of the people and initiating a 
dialogue, within the constitutional frame work, with alienated sections of the society, 
specially misguided youths. 
5.1.3 The strategy used to fight militants is dynamic in nature and is reviewed from 
time to time through the mechanism of Unified Head Quarters at the State level and also 
through the Operation Group meetings etc. at Central level. The security forces and State 
2 

Police have been alerted of the designs of the Pak sponsored militants to target the 
security forces and have been requested to take up appropriate preventive measures. To 
sharpen the anti-terrorist process in the State of J&K an inter ministerial group has been 
set up to review, revise and supplement the 1998 Action Plan in operation to tackle 
militancy in J&K. 
5.1.4 The Government is fully committed to eradicate terrorism and bring back 
normalcy in the State of Jammu & Kashmir. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE 
5.2 The Committee, having taken note of the reply of the Ministry, feels that 
economic development plays a crucial role in dissuading the misguided people 
from the path of violence and secession. It, therefore, recommends that adequate 
funds should be made available to the Government of Jammu & Kashmir for 
accelerating the pace of economic development. However, it should be ensured that 
the flow of funds must remain unhindered. 
RECOMMENDATION (para no. 31) 
5.3 This gruesome incident was followed by an attack on a BSF camp at Chandpur in 
Srinagar by a suicide squad of the militants. The attack on BSF camp is not an isolated 
incident rather just one of the series of such incidents. Evidently , there has been a 
calculated spurt in the attacks on security forces. This needs to be curbed . There is a 
need for upgrading security in and around the camps/company headquarters of security 
forces. Adequate steps should be taken to maintain foolproof security at all such places 
in order to see that security forces suffer lesser casualties while engaging the militants. 
(Para 31) 
ACTION TAKEN/PROPOSED TO BE TAKEN 
5.4 Kargi I incursion led to the breaking of the counter terrorist grid for a few months 
as security forces had to be deployed along the border resulting in gaps which were fully 
exploited by the terrorist organizations especially in Kupwara and Baramulla districts to 
push in battle hardened foreign terrorists with State of the art weapons and equipments. 
The emboldened the terrorists to embark upon bold action such as attack on security 
forces primarily to bring media attention as also to demoralize the security forces. The 
security forces and State Police have been alerted of the designs of Pak sponsored 
terrorists and they have been asked to take appropriate counter measures. During the 
period January to August, 2000 the security forces have killed 941 terrorists. 
5.4.1 After the attack on BSF Camps at Bandipore, instructions were issued to all the 
Central Para Military Forces to step up the security of their own establishments and to 
sensitize the field formations of the forces about the need to be in the state of total 
readiness to meet any such eventuality . 
5.4.2 The instructions for stepping up the security of the establishment of the forces 
have been reiterated and the forces have been advised to ensure that Senior Force 
Commanders, In-charge of operations should get each estabtishment physically checked 
and to ensure that the instructions have been implemented in letter and spirit. The forces 
have also been advised to introduce a system of certification by Senior Force 
3 

Commanders to the effect that they have personally checked the security system of the 
establishments. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE 
5.5 The initiatives taken to beef up the security in and around establishments of 
defence forces are noteworthy. Yet the Committee is constrained to observe that 
lessons are yet to be learnt from the past incidents. The recent bomb explosion in an 
abandoned car outside the Headquarters of 15 Corps in Srinagar in which 11 people 
were killed, can be a case in point. A car loaded with explosives is abandoned in a 
supposedly high security area and inexplicably fails to attract the attention of the 
security personnel manning the area. The situation warrants a thorough overhaul 
of the security apparatus as wide gaps in the security blanket continue to remain 
unplugged. 
RECOMMENDATION(para no. 32) 
5.6 The Committee is also of the opinion that the Government should take the people 
of the State along with it in its endeavour to fight the menace of militancy 
(Para 32) 
ACTION T AKENIPROPOSED TO BE TAKEN 
5.7 The Government have noted the recommendation of the Committee and the State 
Government have also been apprised of the same. 
5.7. 1 Besides involving the people in the Village Defence Committees, the three 
pronged strategy embarked upon by the Government provides, inter-alia, for accelerating 
economic development as also redressing the genuine grievances of the people and 
initiating a dialogue, within the Constitutional framework, with alienated sections of the 
society, specially misguided youths. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE 
5.8 The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry. 
RECOMMENDATION (para no. 33) 
5.9 The Committee having noted the information furnished by the Ministry in 
relation to VDCs recommends that the entire gamut of functioning of the VDCs, their 
utility and effectiveness need to be critically reviewed by the Ministry. 
ACTION T AKENIPROPOSED TO BE TAKEN 
5.10 The scheme of Village Defence Committees (VDCs) is being implemented by 
the State Government of Jammu & Kashmir. A VDCs consists of village volunteers and 
has been provided with a nucleus of 03 Specia l Police Officers (SPO), appointed by the 
State Police, in order to have a better command and control. The VDCs scheme is aimed 
at providing protection to the villages, encouraging people's involvement in fighting 
terrorism and strengthening the security grid. 
4 

5.1 0.1 The SPOs are anned with weapons (such as .303 Rifles, SLRs, Ashraf Karim 
Rifles along with required ammunition) and Wireless sets for better communication. 
5.1 0.2 The approved strength of VDCs in J&K at present is 2486 and that of SPOs 
attached with them is 7458. ln addition there is an approved strength of 10,542 other 
SPOs as well. Thus the total strength of SPOs is 18,000 and the GOI is reimbursing to 
the State Government the expenditure incurred in respect of SPOs attached to VDC @ 
Rs.20,000/- per SPO per annum, which includes cost of honorarium, 
weapons/equipments and training. 
5.10.3 Keeping in view the operational requirements, VDC members and SPOs have 
been imparted training, from time to time, through Army, BSF and JKP in handling of 
weapons, wireless sets, tactics and other defensive/operational measures. 
5.1 0.4 The VDCs/SPOs have played an important role in combating militancy in J&K. 
They have proved effective in far-flung and vulnerable hilly areas where population is 
scattered. The existence of VDCs has created an element of security amongst the masses. 
It has even resulted in preventing migration from various Districts.

Official Language 
29. The Committee feels that Government should take adequate measures so that 
constitutional obligations are met satisfactorily and tangible results are achieved in this 
regard. The Committee is of the view that the Resolution adopted by the Parliament has 
not been implemented in letter and spirit. The Committee, therefore, urges upon the 
Government to provide adequate budgetary support to various Hindi projects and 
programmes. 
ACTION T AKENIPROPOSED TO BE TAKEN 
29.1 The Government have been implementing the Official Language Policy for 
progressive use of Hindi in the Central Government Offices through persuasion, 
motivation and goodwill. According to the Resolution passed by both Houses of 
Parliament in December, 1967, the Department of Official Language have been preparing 
an intensive and comprehensive programme every year for the propagation and 
development of Hindi and for its progressive use for various official purposes of the 
Union. Accordingly, Annual Programme is prepared every year for transacting the 
official work of the Union in Hindi and all Ministries/Departments etc. are expected to 
achieve the targets fiXed in the programme. Besides this, the Department of Official 
Language have been providing training in Hindi, Hindi typing and Hindi stenography. 
The Administrative Heads of various Central Government Offices are expected to ensure 
that the provisions of the Official Languages Act, 1963, Official Language Rules and 
directions issued thereunder are properly complied with. 
41

programmes/schemes for progressive use of Hindi in Central Government Offices.

promoting the concept of linguistic federalism in the country. All Indian Languages 
should be promoted country-wide so that each one has a chance to learn the language of 
one's choice and interest . This idea can be translated into practice if the Government 
allocates more funds for the promotion of all Indian Languages throughout the count!').

production and training.

regional languages.

National Council for Promotion of Urdu and Sindhi has been set up. 
Rashtriya Sanskrit Sansthan propagates the learning of Sanskrit in the 
country.

the 9th Five Year Plan (1997-2002) is Rs.258.95 crore.

(No.l75) for appropriate action to the Ministry of Human Resource Development,

30. The Committee, however, feels that the budgetary provisions eannarked for the 
region are not commensurate v. ith the financial package announced by the Prime Minister 
and the recommendations of the H1gh Powered Commission. Therefore, the Committee 
is of the view that there is an urgent need to strengthen the Central Resource Pool meant 
for the reg1on at the RE stage. There is also need to strengthen the North-Eastern 
Council so that the initiatives taken for the soc1o-economic development of the region at 
the national level are taken to their logical end. 
ACTION TAKEN/PROPOSED TO BE TAKEN 
30. I All the Ministries and Departments in the Government of India, except those 
which were specifically exempted, have to spend 10 percent of their Budget in the North 
East. Considering that the population in the North East is only about 3.73 percent of the 
total Indian population, it is considered that this allocation is sufficient. 
30.1.1 The Agenda for socio-economic change announced by the Prime Minister at 
Shillong on January 22, 2000 concerns mainly the Central Ministries and these Ministries 
are making adequate provision for the same in their respective Annual Plans. In so far as 
the recommendations of the High Power Shukla Commission are concerned, that 
Commission had recommended an allocation of Rs.93619.0 I crores for infrastructure and 
Rs.9391 crores for basic minimum services as an additionality to the normal plan 
allocations. In view of budgetary constraints there is an urgent need to prioritise these 
recommendations so that it is possible to implement them in a time bound manner. The 
Planning Commission is currently engaged in this exercise. 
30.1.2 Insofar as the Non-Lapsable Central Pool of Resources is concerned, the funds 
for th1s are released from the unspent amount of the 'I 0 percent' allocated for the North 
East by various Ministries. As and when there is complete utilisation of the 10 percent 
allocation for the North East, there would be no Central Pool of Resources available. The 
accretions to the Central Resources Pool would, therefore, vary from year to year. 
30.1.3 The Government agree on the need to strengthen the North Eastern Council. The 
North Eastern Council (Amendment) Bill, 1998 has already been introduced in the Rajya 
Sabha It is hoped that this would be taken up for consideration during the next Session 
of Parliament.

30.2 The Committee while noting the reply of the Ministry wish to record that 
during its study visit to the North-Eastern region in October, 2000, a meeting at 
ltanagar with representatives of the North-Eastern Council bad to be abruptly 
because the NEC officials could not satisfactorily reply even to the initial queries of 
the Members. It appeared to the Committee that since the NEC representatives bad 
not come fully prepared for the meeting, no useful purpose would have served by 
carrying on wit the same. The Committee was of the strong view that a full-Hedged 
discu!.sion on the functioning of NEC needed to be belli. 
30.2.1 It bas since been decided to interact with the representatives ofl't"'EC as part 
of Committee 's scrutiny of tbe Demands for Grants (2001-2002) of the Ministry of 
Home Affairs. 
RECOMMENDATIONS (Para nos.178-182) 
General Observations 
Attitude of Ministries/Departments towards Parliamentary 
Standing Committees 
31. The prime objective of setting up of the Department-related Parliamentary 
Standing Committees was to facilitate detailed discussion on the Demands for Grants of 
the related Ministries/Departments in a free, frank and objective manner. To achieve that 
objective, the Committees have been closely interacting with the Secretaries and other 
senior officers of the related Ministries/Departments and have also been caUing for 
relevant papers and documents. The focus of the Committees has been to consider 
relevant issues in their right perspective with the aid of necessary inputs furnished by the 
Ministries/Departments and help the Ministries/Departments in arriving at appropriate 
decisions. Many a time it has been clarified that these Committees are not fault­
finding in nature; they are not courts of inquisition. On the contrary the aim of the 
Committees is to work in close cooperation with the executive in the discharge of its 
duties. 
31.1 However, it has been observed over the years that the related 
Ministries/Departments and their Secretaries and other senior officers are not frank and 
forthcoming with the Committees in sharing information/facts with them. Rather the 
tendency has been to be evasive and not to reply to specific points and queries. This 
makes the work of the Committee difficult. 
31.2 A special reference may be made about the quality of the Action Taken Replies 
furnished by the Ministry of Home Affairs on the recommendations/observations of the 
Committee as contained in its 54th Report ( 1999) on the Demands for Grants of the 
Ministry of Home Affairs. The Committee is constrained to observe that in response 
after response the Ministry bas been sketchy, evasive and has sought to bye-pass the main 
issues involved. In respect of certain matters particularly in relation to the grievances of 
the directly recruited Group 'A' Officers of CISF, the Ministry has repeatedly given 
factually incorrect and misleading information to the Committee. Here, it may be relevant 
44 

to point out that in the meeting of the Committee held on 31.3 .2000, the Home Secretary 
assured that be shall look into this matter and find out if there had been any misreporting 
or intentional withholding of information. The Home Secretary then informed the 
Committee that he shall report to it the outcome of his enquiries. It is astonishing that 
despite the specific and clear assurance of the Home Secretary on the floor of the 
Committee, the Ministry has chosen to send to it the same reply to which the Committee 
had taken serious exception. Then, in a bid to quickly retrace its steps, the Ministry of 
Home Affairs after two days, sent a revised reply and regretted to inconvenience caused. 
This speaks volumes of the fact that the Ministry of Home Affairs has been taking the 
Committee very lightly and paying scant regard to its observations/recommendations. 
31.3 The Committee thus places on record its strong sense of indignation over the 
indifferent attitude of the Ministry towards it. The matter will be placed before the 
Committee at its next meeting to consider the matter further in the light of reply from the 
Ministry ofHome Affairs. 
31.4 Nonetheless , the Committee once again wouJd like the Ministries/Departments to 
change their mindset and while dealing with the Parliamentary Committees, they should 
feel free and share all relevant information with it and offer their constructive cooperation 
in facilitating the Committees in fulfilling their charter of functions. 
ACTION TAKEN/PROPOSED TO BE TAKEN 
31.5 The Ministry of Home Affairs are fully alive to the importance of role and 
functions of the Hon'ble Committee, the valuable guidance and assistance provided by 
the Committee to the Ministry as also to the Ministry 's responsibiHties to the Committee. 
The Ministry have taken note of the displeasure of the Committee at factually incorrect 
replies submitted to the Committee on certain points/questions raised by the Hon'ble 
members in relation to the grievances of directly recruited Group ' A' officers of ClSF . 
The facts and circumstances leading to submission of factually incotrect information to 
the Committee have been explained in the Action Taken Notes on the recommendations 
contained in paragraphs 114 to 125. The Home Secretary has tendered unqualified 
apology to the Committee on behalf of the Ministry of Home Affairs for the lapse 
committed by officers of the Ministry and has assured the Committee that everything 
possible would be done to obviate such a mistake in future and to ensure that the 
recommendations of the Committee are dealt with, with utmost care and seriousness.

32. The Ministry in its detailed explanatory note on the Demands for Grants 2000-
200 I have explained the reasons for variation in the figure of BE and RE ( 1999-2000) 
and BE (2000-2001) in respect of each demand of the Ministry. In this regard the 
Committee notes that under Demand No.48 (Other Expenditure of MHA) the Ministry

detailed reasons in this regard. The Committee recommends that in future reasons for 
45 

variations between BE and RE of current year and BE figures of the coming year 
should be clearly spelt out under each demand. 
ACTION TAKEN/PROPOSED TO BE TAKEN 
(a) Under Relief and Rehabilitation of repatriates from Sri Lanka (Rs.S.Ol crore) 
32.1 The Chief Secretary, Government of Tamil Nadu had written to Home Secretary 
requesting for augmenting the budget provision meant for relief and rehabilitation of Sri 
Lankan repatriates/refugees at the RE stage in 1998-99 to a level of Rs.45 crore. The 
matter was considered in this Ministry and after due consideration of all the factors like 
the trend of past expenditure incurred in the past and the probable items of expenditure, it 
was decided to keep a budget provision of Rs.35 crore in the Budget Estimates for the 
year 1999-2000. 
32.1.1 The Government of Tamil Nadu were not able to prefer claims for expenditure to 
the extent of even this amount although they were reminded time and again in the matter. 
Keeping in view of the trend of expenditure, it was considered appropriate to bring down 
the requirement of funds to Rs.30 crore at theRE stage 1999-2000. 
(b) Under the Swatantrata Sainik Samman Pension Schemes based on the current 
trend of expenditure (Rs.3.23 crore) 
32.2 The actual expenditure durjng the last financial year i.e. 1998-99 was Rs.l77. 79 
crore. After making an additional provision ofRs.l2 crore for the payment of the second 
instalment of dearness reliefto freedom fighters w.e.f. 01.09.1999, the amount provided 
for in the Budget Estimates (1999-2000) was Rs.l89.45 crore. Keeping in view the 
expenditure during the first six months of the fmancial year (1999-2000) at an average of 
Rs.IS .25 crore per month, the amount provided for was scaled down marginally in the 
Revised Estimates 1999-2000 (i.e. from Rs.J89.45 crore provided in BE to Rs.J86.22 
crore) 
(c) Debt relief Scheme for borrowen in J&K due to less requirement (Rs.SS.OO 
crore): 
32.3 The variation in BE & RE for the year 1999-2000 was due to receipt of the less 
claims of borrowers as most of the borrowers have not been compensated. 
(d) Non-Payment to Chogyal (Rs.lO.OO crore) 
32.4 The issue of the settlement of the claims submitted by the Chogyal ofSikkim is a 
long standing issue following the merger of Sikkim with India in April, 1975. The then 
Chogyal of Sikk.im had submitted certain claims to the Government of India. The matter 
is under constderation ofthe Government of India since then. However, settlement is yet 
to be reached at between the Ex-Chogyal of Sikkim and the Government of India. This is 
due to the difficulty in assessing the exact value of the properties in respect of which 
compensations have been claimed by the Ex-Chogyal, at today's rate. Also, different 
Acts regarding property and land are required to be examined in detail. However, steps 
have been taken to resolve the issue and inter-ministerial Committees have been formed. 
Recently a meeting was held on the issues with the representatives of the Ministry of 
46 

Finance and the Department of Legal Affairs, etc. to suggest possible action towards 
settling the claims. Meetings have also been held with legal heirs of late ex-Chogyal and 
his lawyer. It is due to this that the amount of Rs.l 0 crore could not be utilised. 
(e) Less Subsidy in Helicopter (Rs.2.00 crore) 
32.5 The Helicopter Services could be operated only for 7 months during 1998-1999 
i.e. from 01.08.98 to 30.04.98 and Ol.l0.98 to 31.03.99. The services could not be 
operated during 01.05.98 to 30.09.98 due to early onset of monsoon in North Eastern 
Region and the prevailing bad weather conditions in that region. Further, there had been 
fewer demands for Heltcopter services by the Mmistries!Departments of the Government 
of India, as the services had been introduced recently and the officials were not familiar 
with the services. Therefore, the payment of hourly charges for the helicopter services 
has been considerably less, resulting in the excess savings. 
(f) Less requirement in Other Rehabilitation Programmes (Rs.J. 76 crore) 
32.6 In this connection it is stated that the money was provided in the budget of 
Ministry of Home Affairs for resettlement of refugees affected by ethnic violence in the 
State of Assam. Presently, 44,000 families (approx.) are staying in various camps ofthe 
Districts Kokrajhar, Bongaigaon Dhubri and Gossaigaon of Assam. 
32.6.1 A Central team comprising Joint Secretary (NE), Financial Adviser (Home) and 
other officials of the Ministry of Home Affairs visited Kokrajhar Camps, Assam on 
23rd/24111 October 1999 and askssed the situation on the ground . The Central team asked 
the State Government officials to chalk out an Action Plan to rehabilitate the refugees and 
wind up the carrl'ps within a time frame. 
32.6.2 Accordingly, the Government of Assam submitted their Action Plan in the month 
of November, 1999 to the Government of tndia to rehabilitate the refugees. The Action

the Government of Assam. In the said meeting, the aforesaid Action plan was approved 
in principle. However, it was felt that rehabilitation of refugee families could even be in 
manageable smaller batches supported by adequate security arrangements. The State 
Government were asked to submit their revised Action Plan along with a detailed 
Security Plan to shift the 15,000 refugee families to their erstwhile villages. It was noted 
that without Security Plan, shifting would not be effective. In the past, ~rsons who were 
rehabilitated were again attacked and lost everything and carne back to the refugee 
camps. 
32.6.3 Keeping in view the above facts, the above requirement was reduced to Rs.2.00 
crore. Rs.2.00 crore also could not be utilised because of delay in the submission of 
Action Plan by the Government of Assam to the Government of India resulting in 
savings. 
(g) Revision of the Plan outlay of the North Eastern Council (R.s.25.00 crore) : 
32.7 The Ministry of Finance in the mid year Pre-Budget review in September, 1999 
had reduced the NEC Plan Budget allocation from Rs.450.00 crore to Rs.425.00 crore.

financial year 1999-2000. Expenditure booked against the NECPian Budget during the

quite low in the schemes concerned with direct funding i.e. under Major Head "2552" 
where Rs.l5.03 crore was booked against BE figure ofRs.S6.52 crore.

32.8 The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry.

33. The Committee, therefore, recommends that candidates appearing in examination 
for recruitment as constables in CPMFs should be given an option to take the

ACTION T AKENIPROPOSED TO BE TAKEN 
33.1 The matter relating to recruitment of Constables in CPMFs was examined m 
consultation with the CPMFs and DOP&T. The recruitment to various posts in the 
Central Government is governed by the Official Language Resolution, 1968 adopted by 
both the Houses of Parliament. The said resolution provides that for selection against a 
post of Centra l Government being recruited through an agency other than the UPSC, 
compulsory knowledge of either Hindi or English is required. As such, the policy of the 
Government for holding the written test either in Hindi or English in respect of 
recruitment of Constables in CPMFs is in conformity with the Official Language 
Resolution, 1968 since the recruitment is being done by CPMFs themselves. 
33.1.1 ln view ofthe Official Language Resolution, 1968 adopted by both the Houses of 
Parliament, the recruitment of Constables in CPMFs cannot be held in regional 
languages. 
33 1.2 In view of the advice of DOP&T and impracticability of holding the 
examination in 18 languages, it is respectfully submitted that the recommendation 
of Parliamentary Standing Committee cannot be accepted at this juncture.

CITIZENS’ CHARTERS
 
Recommendation (para 10.4)
 
5.0       Committee feels that the initiative  taken by the Ministry to formulate  Citizens’ Charters on the pattern of the
UK Government is commendable one.  The Committee suggests that widest possible consultation should be undertaken
in formulating the Charters.  The Committee desires  that the Citizens’ Charters  so far formulated should be made
available to the public including representatives of people for information and review. The Committee strongly
recommends that all those States/UTs/Organisations who have not formulated the Citizens’ Charters be pursued to do so
at an early date.
 
 
Action Taken/Proposed to be taken
 
5.1       Ministries/Departments/Organisations and States/UTs have been addressed demi-officially vide d.o. letters on
25.5.2000 and 17.5.2000 emphasising the need for (a) consultation (b)  putting the Charter on Website and making it
available  to public including representatives of people, and (c) expediting formulation of Charters.
 
Observations/Recommendations  of the Committee
 
5.2.0    The Committee notes that the approach of Ministry of Personnel, Public  Grievances and Pensions for making
Citizens Charters a viable instrument has been confined merely to writing couple of d.o. letters to
Ministries/organizations for framing  their Citizens’ Charters and putting those on their respective websites for which no
time frame has been  indicated.  Further no clear cut instructions have been issued to the individual Ministry /Department
to give wide publicity to their respective websites, which could enable public to evaluate their Citizens’ Charters.
 
5.2.1    The Ministry has not clarified  how Citizens’ Charters framed so far  would be made available to public including
representatives  of the people for review.    The  Ministry is also silent  as to the  question of the mode of  receipt of
feedback from public and representatives  of the people  for their suitable  modifications by the concerned Ministry,  so
as to make  those citizen-friendly.
 
5.2.2    The Committee, therefore, desires  that Citizens Charters and websites  of the Ministries/Departments may be

 ADMINISTRATIVE COURTS
 
Recommendation (para 14.4)
 
9.0       The Committee suggests that the Lok Adalat in Delhi may be put on experimental  basis.  In  case it serves the
purpose, similar Court may be established in other parts of the country. The Committee also advocates the enactment of
an administrative procedure code whereby if any administrative officer fails in discharging his/her responsibility,  he/she
would be made punishable for dereliction of duty.
Action Taken/Proposed to be Taken
 
9.1.0    As already  stated in our reply to the Questionnaire on the Demands for Grants (2000-2001), Lok Adalat has
already  been set up in Delhi  under the Delhi Legal Services  Authorities Act, 1987  under  the aegis  of Ministry of
Law.  It has jurisdiction over all Central Ministries/Departments located in Delhi and falling within the jurisdiction  of
the  Delhi High Court.  It is seen that the Lok Adalat  Scheme  set up in Delhi  has been specifically  formulated  for
Ministries/Departments of the Government of India.  As   Lok Adalats are the concern  of Ministry of Law, the
recommendation of Committee to extend it to other parts of the country has been forwarded  to Ministry of Law vide a
d.o. letter dated 02.08.2000.
 
9.1.1    As regards enactment of an administrative procedure code, it may be mentioned that at present, recruitment  to
various Central Services  and posts is regulated  by separate  recruitment rules framed by the President in exercise   of
the powers  conferred  by the proviso  to Article 309.  No law has yet been enacted to regulate  the recruitment  and the
conditions  of service   of Central Government  employees  as contemplated   in Article 309,  excepting to a  limited
extent.  The question of enactment  of Act of Parliament under Article  309 was considered in 1950,  soon after the
Constitution  came into force.  After a protracted  discussion,  it was   decided in 1954 to continue  to regulate service 
conditions  by a “regimen of rules”, as it was found to be more convenient in practice.
 
9.1.2    The recommendation  of the Committee was examined in great detail and it was found not acceptable mainly for
following reasons:-
 
(i)
                  The number of posts and the  categories  under various Ministries  and Departments are too many 
having different conditions of service.  It would be an almost  impossible task  to codify all these different
rules  into a comprehensive legislation.
(ii)                The administrative machinery of the Government  has grown up so much in volume  and complexity.
(iii)               The existing  system also requires thorough scrutiny by the  various  agencies like   the Department of
Personnel, Ministry of Law, Ministry of Finance, C&AG, and  UPSC etc.   After the rules are framed,
these are also subject to scrutiny  by the Committee on Subordinate Legislation.
 
(iv)
              Even if a comprehensive Bill is drafted and passed into an Act of Parliament, in each and every
subsequent amendment, the matter will have to be processed in Parliament, which will burden both the

68th Report of Committee on Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/68threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:36:41]
Houses further.
(v)                The existing system of framing  rules has  got flexibility.  Rules are less formal and easier to operate  and
amend, compared to the Acts of Legislature, which involve a complicated process.
 
As regards the objective of the recommendation that if any administrative officer fails in discharging his/her
responsibility, he/she  would be made  punishable for dereliction of duty, it may be stated  that the existing  disciplinary
rules provide for imposition of any penalties (ranging  from ‘censure’ to ‘dismissal’)  for ‘good and sufficient  reasons’. 
Under the provisions of the Conduct  Rules, every  Government  Servant  is required to maintain  devotion to duty and
shall do nothing , which is unbecoming of a Government  Servant.  It has  been prescribed  in the Conduct Rules that a
Government  Servant who habitually fails to perform the task assigned to him  within  the time set for the purpose and
with the quality of performance  expected of  him shall be deemed to be lacking  in devotion  to duty.  Thus any case of
dereliction of duty can be dealt with under the existing rules itself.
 
Observations/Recommendations  of the Committee
 
9.2       Explanations offered for not enacting the administrative procedure code is noted.

Recommendation (para 17.12)

12.0     If the Ministry feels that in practice, it is not possible to adhere to six months schedule as provided in Rule 14(2),
has it ever considered revising this Rule for fixing more practical time period?
 
            Action Taken/Proposed to be taken
 
12.1.0  Rule 14(2) of Central Administrative Tribunal (Procedure) Rules, 1987 provides that every application shall be
heard and decided, as  far as  possible within six months from the date of its registration.  The cases in which both the
litigants and the respondents do not  seek  unnecessary adjournments,  such cases are generally decided within 6 months
from the date  of their  institution.  The Tribunal grants adjournments of the cases   in its judicial capacity taking into
account the circumstances of the case.  All the Benches of the Tribunal decided a total of 26081 cases within 6 months
during the last five years.
 
12.1.1  No proposal for revising this Rule has either been considered in the past or is under consideration at present.
 
Observations/Recommendations of the Committee

Administrative Tribunal.  Nothing is going to prevent the Ministry to consider revision of the Rule in question.  The

inviting nominations from State Governments/Cadre Authorities for Central deputation each year, nominations are
sought for filling the posts of Deputy Secretary level and above up to Joint Secretary/equivalent under the Central

the State Governments or Group ‘A’ Cadre authorities suo motu forward the names of officers for appointment at Under
Secretary level, they are considered for placement at that level.  Posts of Under Secretaries other than those held by CSS

details of such appointments, made between April 1993 and May 2000, are shown at ‘Annexure- X’.  The tables given
in the Annexure, however, include appointments at the level of Under Secretary, as Private Secretaries/OSDs to

st June, 2000, only 21 officers belonged to Services other than the CSS.  Further, if the post of

Recommendation (para 27.2)
 
23.0     Notwithstanding the fact that Ministry of Personnel in their answers have not provided the details of the case as

68th Report of Committee on Home Affairs

aforesaid, on merit as well, this Committee does not subscribe to the proposition of excluding nationalised sector
belonging to insurance and banking including Reserve Bank of India for the purpose of entitlement of counting of
service on movement to Government Departments and vice-versa.  The Committee urges upon the Government to give
effect to the recommendations made by it in this regard in its  Thirty-eighth  Report at the earliest.
                                                                                     
     
Action Taken/Proposed to be Taken
 
23.1.0  The Committee has, inter alia, observed that the various Committees of Parliament including Standing
Committee and  Committee  on Subordinate Legislation are the limbs of the Government and notwithstanding  the
judicial organ giving  an opinion, the legislature continues to exercise  legislative  power  to give shape to policy as it
feels reasonable and desirable.
 
23.1.2  The Government has once more gone through the Thirty-eighth Report of the Committee.  In the  Thirty-eighth
Report, while  considering the question of allowing counting of service in case of mobility between LIC, Banks etc. and
Government, the Committee assumed that the basic order of 29.8.84   had provided for such counting on mobility  but
the basic order was misinterpreted by the Government  and clarificatory order was issued on 30.5.95, based  on this
misinterpretation, which was  an act of impropriety and this action was not sustainable in law.  Some of the observations
of the Committee in the Report are:
 
(1)        Prior to 1995, a person moving from  Central Government  Departments to any of the central autonomous
organisations and vice-versa  was allowed the benefit of counting of past  service for pension purpose. 
However, since 1995 the Central  Government  employees on absorption in nationalised banks and
financial institutions like LIC and vice-versa are not entitled to counting of past service for pensionary
purposes.
 
(2)        Para 4 of the said OM provides definition of the term “Central Autonomous Body”.  It provides that it
includes a Central statutory body.  It does not provide for inclusion or exclusion of any specific body or
class of bodies.
 
(3)        The Committee feels that in the face of clear inclusionary provision in the definition and the hitherto
meaning prescribed and followed in relation to the term in matter of counting  of service and entitlement
of pro-rata pensionary benefit, there is no justification , both in law and in policy, for segregating
nationalised banks and insurance corporations which are all unambiguously statutory bodies.
 
(4)        The Committee is somewhat surprised that the rules vis-à-vis Central Government servants moving to
Central autonomous bodies and vice-versa  such as banks have been so interpreted as to cause immense
deprivation of pensionary benefits.
 
22.1.3  The CAT, Mumbai has considered at length the question of legal interpretation  of OM  dt.29.8.84  and
subsequent  clarification dt. 30.5.95 .  The following points were made by the Hon’ble CAT:-
 
(i)         The concept of an overriding consequence of the inclusionary  part in he definition of an autonomous
body, as given in para 4 of OM dt. 29.8.84, has been  negatived.  The CAT has clearly held that for counting of
past service in an autonomous body as per the extant rule i.e. OM dt. 29.8.84, the body  should be such institution
whose more than 50% expenditure is met with by Cess or Government grant.
 
(ii)        The CAT has clearly upheld the validity of the clarification provided vide OM dt.30.5.95, subsequent to
the definition of autonomous body indicated in OM dt. 29.8.84.
 
(iii)       The CAT has also gone into the question  of a body being considered as “the State”  and its
consequences, vide para 8 of the judgement.  The Hon’ble  CAT  has referred to the Supreme Court judgement in
this regard and held that the issue is not with regard to functions of the autonomous  body but the admissibility of
counting  the past service of working in the autonomous body when an employee joins  the Government service.

The CAT has held  that this benefit is governed  by specific  rules  and therefore the claim of an employee  has to
be gone into in terms of extant rules which specifically lay down the staff of a central autonomous  body are
entitled for counting past service if it is wholly or substantially financed from Cess or Central Government
grants.
 (iv)      The CAT has gone into  the  question of an institution  being considered as autonomous body for the
purpose of pro-rata pension and not being considered an autonomous body for the purpose of counting of
service.  The CAT has gone into rationale behind this  provision and upheld the legal validity of clarification
provided vide OM dt.30.5.95.
 
23.1.4  While a Parliamentary Committee unquestionably has the prerogative to decide on legislative action, as far as the
question of interpretation of  law is concerned, the verdict of  the judiciary is final.  Since, this issue has been decided by
the CAT, Mumbai and Mumbai High Court, the Government feels that the question of interpretation of existing order is
no longer open for discussion.
 
23.1.5  As regards desirability of extending the benefits of counting of past service  to cover cases of mobility between
LIC/Banks, etc. and Government and vice-versa,  the matter  does not  seem to have been considered by the
Parliamentary  Committee. However, in deference to wishes of the Committee,  the Government  has considered  the
desirability of extending  the provision of order dt 29.8.84 to LIC, Banks etc.  The Government feels that these
organisations are commercial institutions and they do not follow  the pattern  of  Central  Government rules including
CCS(P) Rules  for their employees.  The pension  structure  in these organisations is based   on a separate Pension Fund,
unlike  in the  Government.  These bodies  re-employ a large number of retired  employees from Defence/Civil
departments and counting  of their past  service would tremendously  increase the liability of their Pension  Fund. 
Besides,  in the  emerging  scenario of economic  liberalisation, the Banking and Insurance sectors are likely to open up 
in a rather  big way to private  equity participation.  In  such an eventuality  drastic  changes are likely in the institutional
structures affecting inter alia  the conditions of service in these organisations.  It would not be appropriate  to encourage 
mobility between these sectors and Government  and/or increase  financial liability in these sectors  at this juncture. 
These are intricate issues  that may have substantial impact on Government  finances and policy.  The Government is,
therefore, of the opinion that it would not be appropriate at this stage to initiate fresh action  to extend benefits of
counting past service in case of mobility between Government & LIC/Banks etc. and vice-versa.
 
Observations/Recommendations  of the Committee
 
23.2.0  It is understood that the Ministry of  Personnel, Public Grievances and  Pensions is the first respondent  in case
No. 591/98 (Manohar Burde vs. Union of India) in CAT Mumbai Bench. 
           
23.2.1  A perusal of the ATRs of the Ministry, does not reveal that the recommendations made by the two  Parliamentary
Committees (This Committee and  Committee on Petitions) were brought to the notice of the Tribunal by the Ministry. 
We in India have adversarial  system of adjudication taken from the English Legal System in contradistinction  to the
inquisitorial  legal system followed in the Continents.  In the adversarial  system, the judge is not  supposed  to search 
for the truth.  He has to decide the case based upon the material  produced before him.  In the instant case, out of all the
parties before the Tribunal, the Ministry of Personnel was surely in the know of the recommendations made by the two
Parliamentary Committees.  Therefore, it was incumbent upon the Ministry to bring the same to the notice of the
Tribunal along with other material facts.  Be that as it may, the Committee urges upon the Ministry to reconsider its
decision and intimate the outcome thereof.

given to those  cases, which are pending trial for over 8  years.  It has further been  informed  to the Committee that in
November 1997, the Cabinet  had decided  that the expenditure  to be incurred  on any court to be set up by a State
Government for exclusive  trial of CBI cases in future  would be reimbursed  by the Central Government.
 
24.1.2  The Central Government has reimbursed the expenditure incurred by some State Governments  in setting up
Special Courts.  Recently, the requirement of Special  Courts  for exclusive  trial of CBI cases under the PC Act, 1988 in
various States has been assessed and Secretary (P)  has written  to the concerned Chief Secretaries to set up the required
number of such  Courts.  Two Special Courts have been set up in Gujarat on 10.8.2000 and three in Maharashtra on
17.2.2000.
 
24.1.3  In so far as investigation of cases is concerned, the Committee has already been informed  that these are
constantly monitored by the senior supervisory  officers as per the  provisions  in the CBI Crime Manual, with special
attention being  given to disposal of cases pending investigation for over two years which are  regularly reviewed, during
the meeting  taken by Director, CBI with the concerned Joint Directors and DIGs.  The Committee  has been further 
informed   that  cases pending  investigation for over two years are now being centrally monitored at the CBI  Head
Office and all-out efforts are being made to reduce the pendency in the coming year.
 
24.1.4  The Central  Vigilance  Commission is also reviewing the cases being investigated by the  CBI under the
Prevention  of Corruption Act, 1988.  Apart from monthly  review of such important cases the CVC is also reviewing the
overall pendency  of cases   under  investigation  with  the CBI and is periodically calling for  reports in individual
cases.  Appropriate  directions are also issued by the CVC wherever necessary.
 
24.1.5  An Action Plan for disposal of cases pending investigation for over two years is being prepared by the CBI.
 
24.1.6  In the light of the observations of the  Committee, Secretary (P) has written to the CBI on 29.6.2000 to strengthen
its inner mechanism and to expedite  the preparation of  Action Plan for disposal  of cases pending investigation for over 
two years.
 
24.1.7  It may also be mentioned that the Supreme Court, in the Vineet Narain Case, had directed that a panel of
competent  lawyers of experience  and impeccable reputation should  be prepared  with the advice of the Attorney
General  and their services should be utilised as Prosecuting  Counsels  in cases of significance.  The Court had further
directed that in every prosecution which results in the discharge  or acquittal of the accused, responsibility should be
fixed  for dereliction of duty, if any, of the concerned  officer.  Action has  been taken in accordance with the aforesaid
directions of the Court.
 
Observations/Recommendations of the Committee
 
24.2     Action plan for disposal of cases pending for over two years which is under preparation by the CBI
alongwith comments of the Ministry may be communicated to the Committee for its consideration.
 
Recommendation (para 28.24)
 
24.3     The Committee is of the view that CBI prosecutors should be impressed upon to prepare a strong case and
lacunae,  if any, should be pointed out to the CBI before filing the chargesheet so that CBI can collect the required
evidence in this regard and the accused is not acquitted on the ground of insufficient evidence.

24.4     Instructions already exist in the CBI Crime Manual for thorough scrutiny of cases by prosecutors/Law Officers

ensure  that  sufficient  evidence  has been  collected before prosecution is initiated in a case.  The prosecutors  in the

24.5.0
    The Committee is not satisfied with the reply of the Ministry.
 
24.5.1  If the CBI Crime Manual contains detailed instructions for thorough scrutiny of cases by Prosecutors/Law

prosecution is initiated in a case as stated by the Ministry, then how come in quite a few significant and sensational
cases, the accused got acquitted on the grounds of insufficient evidence.
 
24.5.2  The Committee is, therefore, of the view that CBI Crime Manual needs to be thoroughly reviewed so that the

24.6     The Committee suggests that the officer held responsible for biased investigation must be   punished at     once

24.7.0  Instructions already exist in the CBI Crime Manual for critical examination of judgments resulting in acquittal of
accused  and fixing of responsibility  in this regard.  These instructions have been further reitereated vide Circular letter

APPOINTMENT OF NOTARIES
Recommendation (para 11.1)
 
5.0       The Committee does not find the pending position with regard to the applications for appointment of Notaries
satisfactory.  It reiterates its earlier  recommendation  and hopes that the Government would ensure  quick disposal of
applications for appointment of Notaries and feels that if a definite time frame is fixed for disposal of applications, it
will considerably reduce the pendency. The Committee further recommends that Government should ensure due
representation of Schedule Caste, Schedule Tribe and Other Backward Classes while appointing Notaries.

Action Taken/Proposed to be taken
5.1.0    Notaries are appointed under the Notaries Act, 1952  and the Notaries  Rules, 1956.   The Government of India
is empowered to appoint  Notaries for the whole or any part of India, whereas, a State Government is empowered to
appoint Notaries for the whole or any part of that State.  On an application made by eligible person,  by submitting a
memorial to the Competent Authority appointed  by the Government,  comments of the Bar Council, where the
applicant  is enrolled  are called for.  After considering various factors mentioned in the Notaries Rules, appropriate 
decision to appoint a person as Notary or otherwise  is taken by the Competent Authority.  Thus the procedure of
appointment of a Notary involves a number of statutory steps.  However, the requirement  of holding   of interviews has
been dispensed with since June, 1999 to quicken the process of appointment.
5.1.1    Of late,  a large number of applications are being received by the Government , which are being  processed on a
day to day basis, but the actual  appointments take some time due to the earlier  backlog  and the statutory procedure
explained  above.  As such, it may not  at present be  possible  to fix a time frame  for disposal of applications.
5.1.2    No data as to the number   of SC,ST and OBC candidates is available at present, as the basic  document  for
processing of the application, i.e.,  the ‘Memorial’ does not contain a column of the candidate’s caste and status.
5.1.3    The Notaries Rules, 1956 have been amended  and the eligibility criteria in respect of persons belonging  to the
Scheduled Castes/Tribes and Other Backward Classes and women have been  relaxed.   According to the amended 
provision, a person belonging to these classes would require  only seven years of legal practice instead of ten years as
required for general category candidates, for becoming eligible for appointment as a Notary.
Observations/Recommendations of the Committee
5.2.0    From the perusal of replies, it  appears  that the Ministry is taking considerably  long  time to complete the
process of appointment of Notaries as the persons interviewed  for the post  way back in June, 1999 were not appointed
till the submission of replies to the Committee i.e. 21 August 2000.  Further, the Ministry is not in a position to indicate
the time-frame  by which the pending applications for Notaries would be disposed.
5.2.1     The Committee expresses its displeasure over the casual approach of the Ministry to the pending applications
for Notaries and desires that the task should be completed within a given time-frame. If  required, a special cell may be
constituted for the purpose.
5.2.2      The Committee also points out that neither has the Ministry taken any action nor has it prepared any action plan
to assess  the requirement of Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes candidates for the post of
Notaries so as to give them their due  representations.  The reply that   data  in respect of  SC, ST & OBCs in Notaries
are not available, is a routine  approach and directs that the data may be compiled, which would ensure due
representation of SC,ST and OBCs candidates  in Notaries.
5.2.3    The Committee also desires that the feasibility of  introducing additional column for the category in the
‘Memorial’ prescribed for appointment of Notaries may be examined.

Recommendation (para 13.3)

Government to lay the  Annual Report and Audited Statement of Accounts of the NALSA before both the  Houses of
Parliament without any further delay.

States/Union Territories be persuaded to follow suit.  The Committee also recommends that all the States/Union
Territories be impressed upon to include legal aid as a subject in the training programme of judicial officers.
7.3.2    In view of the pendency of cases in High Courts and subordinate judiciary, the Committee reiterate that more

NATIONAL COMMISSION TO REVIEW THE WORKING OF THE CONSTITUTION
Recommendation (para 16)
 
9.0       The Committee is of the view that the Government should allay fears, if any, about the setting up of the
Commission.  Further the Committee is also of the opinion that the State Governments should have  been consulted in
the process and recommends that the public should be informed about the  subjects on which the Commission will work
so that the basic structure of the Constitution remains unchanged.
Action Taken/Proposed to be taken
 
9.1.0
    The National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution has been constituted by the Government
of India  to examine, in the light of the experience of past 50 years, as to how best the Constitution can respond the
changing needs of efficient, smooth  and effective system of goverance  and socio-economic development  of modern
India  within the framework of Parliamentary  Democracy and to recommend  changes, if any, that are required in the
provisions of the Constitution without interfering with its basic structure or features.  Its function is to review  the
working of the Constitution not to  rewrite the Constitution.  It emphasized  that its function is essentially advisory in
nature.
9.1.1    Broadly the Commission will examine the working of the present provisions in the constitution and the
applicable laws and practice  and consider how to better achieve  these objectives.  The Commission has identified the
following areas of immediate contemporary concern for its examination:-

(i)                  Strengthening the institutions of Parliamentary democracy and their accountability; the grave and
persisting menace of un-principled defection;
(ii)                Constitution and pace of socio-economic change and development, promoting, literacy, generating
employment, ensuring social security and removal of poverty;
(iii)               Union-State  relations: Working of Article 356, appointment and removal of Governor;
(iv)              Decentralization and devolution of powers strengthening of Panchayati Raj Institutions;
(v)                Fundamental rights; Enlargement of the Fundamental Right in Part III of the Constitution by specific
incorporation of the Freedom of the Media, Right to Compulsory Elementary Education, Right to Privacy
and Right  to Information;
(vi)              Effective enforcement of the Directive Principles of State Policy in Part IV  of the Constitution in order
to achieve  the goals enshrined   in the  Preamble and for good governance;
(vii)             Fundamental duties under  Part-IV – A  of the Constitution; and
(viii)           Fiscal and Monetary Policies, size of government expenditure,  Efficiency of Public audit mechanism.
 
9.1.2    The Commission proposes to prepare a consultation paper on each of these areas along with a questionnaire,
formulated in an appropriate format.  This shall be circulated to political parties, Constitutional and Statutory
Commissions such as, National Commission for  Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, National Commission for
other Backward Classes, National Commission for Minorities, National Human Rights  Commission, National
Commission for Women and other similar bodies;  Trade Unions; Representative Bodies of Trade and Industry; Bar

Internet for access to the general public and for eliciting its response and suggestions.
 
9.1.3    Thereafter, the recommendations of the Commission shall be put up to public debate.  After  considering the
various points and responses elicited and received the Commission would formulate its recommendations to the
Government of India.

ELECTORAL REFORMS
Recommendation (para 17.1)
 
10.0     The  Committee is of the view that Electoral  Reforms are overdue and  needs utmost attention of the
Government since it has a far   reaching impact on the political system of the country and as such it reiterate its earlier
recommendations made in its 56th Report that the  Government should consider the matter as early as possible.
Action Taken/Proposed to be taken
 
10.1.0  The Government  is committed to  bring necessary reforms in electoral laws  pertaining to elections to
Parliament and Legislatures of the States.  The President, in his Address to the Parliament, at the commencement of the
first session after constitution of the 13
th Lok Sabha, has also stressed the necessity of bringing   comprehensive 
reforms in the Electoral Laws of the country as a priority subject for the present Government.
10.1.1  The National Agenda for Governance of the previous Government had also mandated introduction of necessary
electoral reforms on the basis of recommendations of the Dinesh  Goswami  Committee  and, accordingly,  that
Government  took up on priority basis consideration of unimplemented  recommendations of the Dinesh Goswami
Committee.  In this connection, a meeting  was held with political parties on 22 nd May, 1998 to discuss  various

69th Report of Committee on Home Affairs

proposals  on electoral  reforms which mainly contained  unimplemented recommendations of the Dinesh Goswami
Committee.  Pursuant  to a decision taken in that  meeting,  a High Powered  Committee under the  Chairmanship of
Shri Indrajit Gupta  was constituted   to suggest concrete measures for providing State funding of elections  to
recognized political parties.  The Committee  was also to consider  the related proposals  pertaining to maintenance  of
accounts by political parties and audit thereof, ban on donations by companies to political parties, inclusion of
expenses   of political parties in the election expenses of candidates for the purposes of ceiling on election expenses and
empowering the Election Commission to fix ceiling on election expenses before every general election.  The
Committee, which submitted its report to the Government on 14 th  January, 1999 , has recommended, inter alia,  partial
State funding of elections, in kind only, to recognized political parties and candidates set up by them.  The various
recommendations of the Committee are being examined by the Government in consultation with the  Election
Commission and State Governments and may be discussed along with  other pending proposals on electoral  reforms
with political parties at an appropriate time.
10.1.2  Further, with a view to finding ways of expediting disposal of election petitions pending in courts, the Law
Commission which was requested by the Government  in November, 1995 to study  the problem of delay in disposal of
election petitions and to suggest   remedial  measures, took up, suo motu,  the subject of reform of electoral laws, in
addition, and made a number  of important  recommendations which are available in its 170 th report.  The
recommendations of the Law Commission are being examined by the Government  and may be discussed with political
parties  at an appropriate time.
10.1.3  Recently, the Government, keeping in view the fact that the members of the armed forces  at present have the
option to vote in  person or through the system of postal ballot at elections and that the minimum campaign period for
elections has been reduced from 20 days to 14 days  as also the logistic  constraints involved in dispatching postal
ballots to members of the armed forces through  their record offices and receiving these ballot papers back before
 counting process commences, on the recommendation of the Election Commission, decided  to provide  an additional
option to the members of the Armed Forces of the Union and of Forces to which the provisions of Army Act, 1950 have
been made applicable, whether with or without modifications, to vote through the system of proxy at elections.  A Bill,
namely, the Election Laws (Amendment) Bill, 1999 was accordingly introduced in the Lok Sabha on 9.12.99.  The Bill
has been  referred to the Department related Parliamentary Standing  Committee on Home Affairs for examination and
report.  The Committee met on the 31
st May and 14th June 2000 wherein it heard the oral presentation  of Secretaries of
different  concerned Departments including the  Legislative Department.  The Committee is again scheduled to meet on
10th July 2000 to undertake  clause-by-clause  consideration of the Bill.
10.1.4  The Government, as part of the National Population Policy strategy, has recently decided to extend the current
constitutional embargo on undertaking fresh delimitation of electoral constituencies up to the year 2026 as a
motivational measure  to enable state governments to fearlessly pursue the agenda for population   stabilization.  The 
embargo was laid through the Constitution  (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976  with a view to boost  family
planning norms  so that the States, which do not control their population, are not rewarded through  the delimitation
process. It was thought that by the year 2000, the progress of implementation of family  planning programmes would,
more or less, be uniform  throughout the country.  In this regard, the States in the South may be said to have achieved 
some comparative  success  in this direction vis-à-vis  the States in the North  and this situation  has prompted  the
former  to raise  the demand  for extending  the aforesaid  constitutional embargo.  The embargo would end after 
publication of figures of the first census to be held after the year 2000.  Recently, the Government convened a meeting
of leaders of political parties, on 13
th May, 2000, to discuss  the aforesaid  issue as well as some  other connected issues
viz. (i) delimitation of constituencies contained  within a  State, without altering the number of seats in legislatures 
presently allotted, so as to remove the imbalances caused due to uneven growth of population/electorate in different 
constituencies (ii) rotation of reserved constituencies  and (iii) entrusting the job of delimitation along with all
associated issues to the Election Commission of India on permanent  basis.  There was consensus in favour of 
extending the constitutional embargo on undertaking fresh delimitation of constituencies till 2026  AD.
10.1.5  In view of the political instability and repeated General Elections, however, no concrete action  could be possible
after the last batch of Electoral  Reforms in 1996  {The Representation of the People (Amendment) Act, 1996}, except
for some  piecemeal measures, like expanding   the category of employees to the enrolled for election duties {The
Representation of the People (Amendment) Act, 1998} and making of provision for postal ballot facility for migrant
voters {The Representation of the People (Amendment) Act, 1999}.  The  Government is, however, seriously engaged

in working out modalities for enacting a fresh batch of electoral reforms.  The proposals in this regard are, however, still
being examined.  Amendment in electoral laws is a serious and contentious   subject and the Government wishes to
examine the matters  in depth before coming out with concrete proposals.
Observations/Recommendations of the Committee
10.2     The Committee is of the view that the Government should come forward with comprehensive Electoral Reforms
at the earliest.      
OFFICIAL LANGUAGES WING
Recommendation (para 18.1)
 
11.0      The  Committee is of the considered view that   the Government should initiate   action to amend the Indian Legal
Service Rules, 1957 so as to include officers of the Official Languages Wing therein and remove discrimination  perpetrated 
against them.
Action Taken/Proposed to be taken
11.1.0  The Legislative Department does not propose, to accept the aforesaid recommendation of the Committee.  The
reasons for keeping separate recruitment rules for the Officers of the Hindi side of the Official Languages  Wing of the
Legislative Department and the Officers of the Indian Legal Service  are the separate duties and responsibilities of the
Officers of the Hindi side of the Official Languages Wing and the Indian Legal Service (ILS).  The duties and
responsibilities of the said officers are discussed below:-
 
11.1.1  According to the article 348(1)(b) of the Constitution, until Parliament by law otherwise provides, authoritative
texts of  all bills to be introduced  or amendments thereto to be moved in either House of Parliament, all Acts passed by
Parliament, all Ordinances promulgated by the President and all orders, rules, regulations and bye-laws issued under the
Constitution or under any law made by Parliament shall be in English.  The main duties of the Officers of the Indian 
Legal  Service  in the main Department in briefly are as follows:-
 
(i)         Scrutiny of Notes for the Cabinet in relation to all legislative proposals from drafting and constitutional
point of view.
(ii)
                Drafting of all Government Bills, Ordinances, President’s Act, Constitutional Orders, etc.
(iii)               Scrutiny of all statutory Rules,  Orders, Notifications, Schemes etc.
(iv)              Scrutiny of State Legislations in the concurrent field which requires the assent of the President  under
article 254 of the Constitution.
(v)                The work relating to Election Commission and Electoral Reforms
(vi)              Legislation with regard to subjects such as marriage, divorce; infants and minor; adoption, wills etc, and
certain other subject in List III of the  Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of India.
11.1.3  Since the introduction of the system of the Department related Parliamentary Standing Committees of the
Houses, an officer of the Indian Legal  Service  who is concerned with the drafting  of the Bill,  which has been referred
to the Committee, also attends the meetings of such Committees and renders  assistance to the said Committees and
Parliament till the Bill is passed by Parliament.
 
Duties and responsibilities of the Official Languages Wing
 
11.1.4   The Official Languages Wing of the Legislative Department, which includes officers both from the Hindi side and
regional languages, is primarily concerned with the over-all aspects of work relating to translation  in Hindi and other
languages.  The main duties of the Hindi side officers in the Official Languages Wing are as under:-
 
(i)                  The Bills to be introduced or amendments thereto to be moved in either House of Parliament drafted by
the Indian Legal Service Officers in the main Department are translated in Hindi by the officers of Hindi
Official Languages Wing as required under sub-section (2) of section 5 of Official Languages Act, 1963. 
All original drafting work and other work including scrutiny and preparation  of notes for the Cabinet as
well as dealing with matters mentioned above is being done by the Indian Legal Officers in the main

69th Report of Committee on Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/69threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:36:42]
Legislative  Department and where required, the same is translated by Hindi side officers in Hindi.
(ii)                The Official Languages Wing also processes proposals to secure authentication  by the President of the
translation of Central Acts in Hindi as well as regional languages before publication in the Official
Gazatte.  Approval for Hindi translation is required under section 5(1)(a)  of the Official Languages Act,
1963 and for regional languages under  section 2(a) of the Authoritative Texts (Central Laws) Act, 1973.
(iii)               The other duties of the said Wing are to prepare and publish standard legal terminology for use in all
Official Languages and formulate policy and programme to implement the Official Languages Act, 1963.
 
11.1.5  From the comparison of the duties and responsibilities, it is clear that they are quite  different.  The Indian Legal
Officers in the main Department are involved in legislative proposals from the very beginning.  They scrutinise the
legislative  proposals from the initial stage, attend the inter-ministerial  meetings for formulations of the legislative
proposals, examine the draft Notes for the Cabinet from drafting, legal and constitutional points of view.  After
approval  of the Cabinet, drafting is done in the main Legislative Department and Bills and amendments are finalized in
consultation with the  administrative Departments.  Similarly, the Ordinances  and Constitutional  Orders are finalized in
the Legislative Department.  After finalisation of Bills and amendments thereto, Ordinances, Constitutional Orders,
Regulations etc. are sent by the main Department to the Hindi side officers for translation thereto in Hindi.  Since  the
duties  of the Officers of the Hindi  side and the Officers of the Indian  Legal Service  are not the same, the recruitment 
rules also have been separately framed keeping in view of the requirements of the Officers proposed to  be appointed. 
For example  one of the essential qualifications required for appointment as Assistant  Legislative Counsel (Hindi
Branch) is “should have experience of translation into Hindi and Statutes Rules, Orders, Judgement of the Courts and 
Records, Leases and other documents of legal nature  in Central or State Government for not less than 7 years”. 
Another  essential qualification for the said post “is knowledge of Hindi at the higher secondary  or intermediate or any
other  higher  examination”, whearas there are no such requirements in the case of appointment as Assistant Legislative
Counsel of the Indian  Legal Service.  Similar provisions as mentioned above also exist in the case of the recruitment
rules of the regional language side.
 
11.1.6  It may also be reiterated that in the Official Languages Wing, besides the Officers of the Hind side, there is also
a separate cadre of  Officers  of the regional languages.  There is one officer each for each regional language included in
the Eighth Schedule to the Constitution.  As already mentioned the duties of the officers of the regional languages
primarily involves translation of the Central Acts and Ordinances into the regional Languages concerned.  These
Officers also have separate recruitment rules and are not part of the Indian  Legal Service, because of the same reasons
as already mentioned for officers of the Hindi side.
 
11.1.7  It would thus be seen that at present, duties and responsibilities of officers of the Indian  Legal Service are far
more  onerous and there is  hardly any comparison  with officers doing work in Hindi  and other languages.  In view  of
the aforesaid, it is considered not desirable to include the Officers of the Hindi and the regional languages side of the
Official Languages Wing in the Indian   Legal Service.  Further the recruitment rules framed for the Officers of the
Official Languages Wing are in consonance with the guidelines of the Government.
 
Observations/Recommendations of the Committee
 
11.2     The Committee notes the explanation offered  by Government.
 
Recommendation (para 18.3)
                       
11.3.0  The Committee is constrained  to note that there has been decreasing  trend in publishing the authoritative  texts
of Central Acts in Hindi and other regional languages.  The Committee also takes note of the fact that  the Hindi version
of the Acts are too  complex to be understood easily and feels that if simple Hindi words in common use is used, it will
be easy to understand.
Action Taken/Proposed to be taken
 
11.4     According  to the Report, the Committee has noted vide  para 18.3 that there has been decreasing  trend in
publishing the authoritative texts of Central Acts in Hindi  and other regional Languages.  But this is not true.  If we

JUDICIAL REFORMS
Recommendation (para 21.2)
14.0      The Committee would like to impress upon the Government to act seriously on  Judicial Reforms and take effective
steps in the matter of administration of justice since about 2.5 crores of cases are pending before the courts and the people is
being disillusioned in its disposal.
Action Taken/Proposed to be taken
14.1.0  Both the Government and Judiciary are concerned with the huge pendency of cases  in courts.  Judicial Reform
is a continuous process involving various Ministries/Departments.  Various steps  are being taken by the Government
for the speedy disposal of both  civil and criminal  cases.  These include  amendments of the Civil Procedure Code and
the Code of Criminal  Procedure.  The amendment of the Civil Procedure Code is  awaiting notification by the
Legislative  Department after the Code of Civil  Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999 was assented  to by the President. 
Various amendments by the Law Commission in its 154 th Report which inter alia  include mandatory trial of specified 
cases through the summary  procedure, compounding of offences etc.  These recommendations are under active
consideration of the Government in the Ministry of Home Affairs. 
14.1.1  The measures also include increase in the number of posts of Judges/Judicial Officers, appointment of Special
Judicial/Metropolitan Magistrates, establishment of Special Courts/tribunals, improvement in the standards of Legal
education, and adoption of alternative modes of dispute resolution, such as, arbitration and conciliation.  Lok Adalats
have been given a statutory base as supplementary forum for resolution of disputes.  Efforts are also  being made  for
increasing the use of information technology in courts for registration of cases, their allocation to judges, preparation of
case lists, maintenance of case history, preparation of notices, warrants and other processes, preparation of certified
copies, various reports and returns, accessing judicial pronouncements, databases, etc.  Computerised enquiry  and
facilitation centers  for helping litigants and advocates are also being set up in High Courts.  Such  centers are also
proposed to be set up in district courts.
Observations/Recommendations of the Committee
14.2     The Committee  expresses its serious concern over the pendency of cases. It directs the Government to furnish
facts and figures, of fresh appointments of judges/judicial officers, use  of information  technology in courts, Lok
Adalats conducted state-wise.
